items.m: to do something to relieve tension and start a conversation
items.os: From ships called icebreakers that crack frozen waterways so other boats can pass; used figuratively since the 1500s.
items.ex: A funny question can break the ice on the first day of school.

items.m: to reveal a secret
items.os: Often linked to ancient Greek voting with beans, but that story is unproven; the phrase is American, early 1900s.
items.ex: Don't spill the beans about the surprise party!

items.m: something very easy
items.os: American, 1930s; likely from cakewalk contests where cakes were prizes for an easy-looking strutting dance.
items.ex: That spelling quiz was a piece of cake.

items.m: to face something painful with courage
items.os: Said to come from soldiers biting a bullet during surgery before anesthesia; first recorded by Kipling in 1891.
items.ex: I bit the bullet and practiced my hardest word list.

items.m: feeling slightly ill
items.os: Nautical: seasick sailors were sent below deck, literally under the weather rail.
items.ex: Ahana stayed home because she felt under the weather.

items.p: let the cat out of the bag
items.m: to reveal a secret by mistake
items.os: Possibly from market fraud: sellers swapped a pig in a sack for a worthless cat; opening the bag exposed the trick.
items.ex: He let the cat out of the bag about the trophy.

items.m: to go to bed
items.os: From mattresses once stuffed with hay or straw; American, around 1900.
items.ex: Finals are tomorrow, time to hit the hay.

items.p: cost an arm and a leg
items.m: to be extremely expensive
items.os: American, mid-1900s; the popular portrait-painting explanation is a myth — it simply means costing something precious.
items.ex: That telescope costs an arm and a leg.

items.m: very rarely
items.os: A blue moon is the rare second full moon in one calendar month; the phrase dates to the 1500s meaning something absurdly rare.
items.ex: We eat dessert before dinner once in a blue moon.

items.p: the ball is in your court
items.m: it is your turn to act or decide
items.os: From tennis: once the ball crosses the net, only the other player can hit it.
items.ex: I've apologized; now the ball is in her court.

items.m: to work late into the night
items.os: From studying by oil lamps before electricity; recorded in English since 1635.
items.ex: She burned the midnight oil before the regional bee.

items.m: what you do matters more than what you say
items.os: Proverb form appears in English by 1721, with the idea traced to ancient sources.
items.ex: He never brags — actions speak louder than words.

items.m: pursuing a mistaken idea or the wrong person
items.os: From raccoon hunting with dogs: the raccoon escapes through branches while the dog barks at the tree it climbed first.
items.ex: If you think I ate the cookies, you're barking up the wrong tree.

items.m: the final small problem that makes everything unbearable
items.os: Short for 'the straw that broke the camel's back' — one tiny addition to a huge load causes collapse.
items.ex: Losing my notes was the last straw that day.

items.m: to destroy a relationship or path so you cannot go back
items.os: From armies burning bridges behind them so retreat was impossible — traced to Roman generals.
items.ex: Don't burn your bridges when you leave a team.

items.m: to give up
items.os: From boxing: a fighter's corner throws a towel into the ring to stop the match.
items.ex: She refused to throw in the towel after round one.

items.m: sudden loss of courage before a big event
items.os: American college slang from the 1890s; possibly from soldiers whose frozen feet kept them from battle.
items.ex: He got cold feet right before the oral round.

items.m: to do something the cheap or lazy way
items.os: From drivers or runners rounding a corner too tightly to save time.
items.ex: Never cut corners when studying etymology.

items.p: hit the nail on the head
items.m: to be exactly right
items.os: From carpentry: a clean hammer strike drives the nail perfectly; used in English since the 1500s.
items.ex: Her guess about the Greek root hit the nail on the head.

items.m: something that seems bad but turns out good
items.os: From an 18th-century English hymn by James Hervey describing hardships as hidden blessings.
items.ex: Missing that bus was a blessing in disguise.

items.m: to make a bad situation even worse
items.os: From Aesop-style fable retold by Roman writer Phaedrus: a bald man swats a fly, misses, and hits his own head.
items.ex: It rained, and to add insult to injury, we lost the keys.

items.m: to avoid saying something directly
items.os: From medieval bird hunting: beaters struck around a bush to flush birds out rather than hitting it directly.
items.ex: Stop beating around the bush and tell me my score.

items.m: to stop working for now
items.os: From 19th-century labor slang 'call it half a day' — leaving before the shift ended.
items.ex: We mastered forty words; let's call it a day.

items.m: an obvious problem everyone avoids mentioning
items.os: Popularized in the 20th century from the image of ignoring something as huge as an elephant; echoed in a Russian fable by Krylov.
items.ex: Nobody mentioned the broken trophy — the elephant in the room.

items.p: kill two birds with one stone
items.m: to achieve two things with one action
items.os: English by the 1600s; the image is from slinging stones at birds.
items.ex: Studying roots kills two birds with one stone: spelling and vocabulary.

items.m: very common and of little value
items.os: American, 1800s, when a dime literally bought a dozen eggs or oranges.
items.ex: Easy words are a dime a dozen at nationals.

items.m: to make more effort than required
items.os: From the Sermon on the Mount: 'whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain.'
items.ex: Champions go the extra mile on origin languages.

items.m: in trouble
items.os: English since the 1500s; the image is of being scalded.
items.ex: He's in hot water for skipping practice.

items.m: extremely happy
items.os: Popularized in 1950s America; one story credits weather-bureau cloud classifications where nine was the towering cumulonimbus.
items.ex: She was on cloud nine after spelling 'psammophile.'

items.m: raining very heavily
items.os: English, 1600s; origin unknown — the story about animals falling off thatched roofs is a myth.
items.ex: We can't practice outside; it's raining cats and dogs.

items.m: a small visible part of a much larger problem
items.os: About seven-eighths of an iceberg is underwater — popular after the Titanic disaster of 1912.
items.ex: These ten misspellings are just the tip of the iceberg.

items.m: never; impossible
items.os: A sarcastic 'adynaton' — an impossibility — used in Scotland and England since the 1600s.
items.ex: He'll clean his room when pigs fly.

eq.p: quand les poules auront des dents

eq.lit: when the crayfish whistles on the mountain

items.m: a dangerous person pretending to be harmless
items.os: From Aesop's fable and the Gospel of Matthew.
items.ex: Beware of flattery from a wolf in sheep's clothing.

items.m: fake sadness
items.os: From the ancient legend that crocodiles weep while eating their prey; spread by medieval travel tales.
items.ex: His apology was pure crocodile tears.

items.m: a clear sign that disaster is coming
items.os: From the Book of Daniel: mysterious writing appears at Belshazzar's feast predicting Babylon's fall.
items.ex: Falling scores were the writing on the wall.

items.m: pretending to despise what you cannot have
items.os: From Aesop's fox, who calls the grapes he cannot reach sour.
items.ex: Saying trophies don't matter sounds like sour grapes.

items.m: the hottest weeks of summer
items.os: From Roman astronomy: the Dog Star Sirius rises with the sun in late July, blamed for the heat.
items.ex: The finals fall in the dog days of summer.

items.m: to make peace after a quarrel
items.os: From a Native American (Iroquois) peace ceremony of literally burying weapons when wars ended.
items.ex: The rivals buried the hatchet after the bee.

items.m: to rely on past success instead of trying to improve
items.os: Ancient Greeks crowned victors with laurel wreaths; resting on them meant coasting on old glory.
items.ex: Last year's trophy means nothing if you rest on your laurels.

items.m: a source of many unforeseen troubles
items.os: Greek myth: Pandora opens a forbidden jar, releasing all evils into the world, leaving only hope inside.
items.ex: Changing the rules opened a Pandora's box of complaints.

items.m: a single fatal weakness
items.os: Greek myth: Thetis dipped baby Achilles in the River Styx, holding his heel, which stayed vulnerable.
items.ex: Silent letters are my Achilles' heel.

items.m: the ability to make everything succeed
items.os: Greek myth: King Midas's wish turned everything he touched to gold — including his food.
items.ex: Her study plans have the Midas touch.

items.m: a trick that sneaks an enemy inside
items.os: From the wooden horse the Greeks used to smuggle soldiers into Troy.
items.ex: The free app was a Trojan horse full of ads.

items.m: a job needing enormous strength or effort
items.os: From the Twelve Labors of Heracles (Hercules) in Greek myth.
items.ex: Memorizing 128,000 words is a herculean task.

items.m: to pass a point of no return
items.os: In 49 BC Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon river with his army, illegally, making civil war certain.
items.ex: Registering for nationals crossed the Rubicon — no backing out.

items.m: a constant looming danger
items.os: Roman story: courtier Damocles feasts under a sword hung by a single horsehair to learn how kings live.
items.ex: The tiebreaker rule hung over the round like the sword of Damocles.

items.m: a win that costs more than it gains
items.os: King Pyrrhus of Epirus beat Rome in 279 BC but lost so many soldiers he said another such victory would ruin him.
items.ex: Winning the argument but losing the friend was a Pyrrhic victory.

items.m: an impossibly tangled problem solved by bold action
items.os: Alexander the Great, unable to untie the legendary knot of Gordium, sliced it with his sword.
items.ex: She cut the Gordian knot by studying patterns, not lists.

items.m: trapped between two dangers
items.os: From the Odyssey: sailors had to pass between a six-headed monster and a whirlpool.
items.ex: Choosing between two hard word lists felt like Scylla and Charybdis.

items.p: carthago delenda est spirit — salt the earth
items.m: to destroy so completely nothing can recover
items.os: Legend says Rome sowed salt into Carthage's fields in 146 BC so nothing would grow — the salting itself is a later myth.
items.ex: The review crushed the proposal and salted the earth.

items.m: to give a stern warning or scolding
items.os: Britain's Riot Act of 1714 was literally read aloud to crowds ordering them to disperse or face arrest.
items.ex: Coach read us the riot act about skipping drills.

items.m: to take credit for another's idea
items.os: Playwright John Dennis invented a thunder machine in 1709; a rival theater copied it, and he cried they had stolen his thunder.
items.ex: He stole her thunder by announcing the results first.

items.m: to deliberately ignore something
items.os: Admiral Nelson allegedly raised his telescope to his blind eye at Copenhagen in 1801 to miss a retreat signal.
items.ex: The referee turned a blind eye to the delay.

items.m: to reveal your real character
items.os: From naval warfare: ships sailed under false flags and hoisted their true colors before attacking.
items.ex: Pressure makes players show their true colors.

items.m: an unpredictable person who may cause damage
items.os: A cannon that broke loose on a warship's deck rolled with the waves, crushing everything.
items.ex: He's talented but a loose cannon in team rounds.

items.m: in general; on the whole
items.os: Sailing term: 'by' means into the wind, 'large' means with the wind — a ship handling both sails well overall.
items.ex: By and large, French-origin words keep silent endings.

items.m: everything; the full amount
items.os: American; despite dozens of theories (machine-gun belts, cement trucks, fabric), the true origin remains unknown.
items.ex: She prepared flashcards, audio, quizzes — the whole nine yards.

items.m: to celebrate wildly
items.os: Often traced to the Marquis of Waterford's drunken 1837 spree literally painting an English town red — plausible but unproven.
items.ex: After the trophy, the team painted the town red.

items.m: completely crazy
items.os: Hat makers inhaled mercury fumes while curing felt, which caused tremors and confusion — a real occupational disease.
items.ex: The professor's schemes were mad as a hatter.

items.m: someone overwhelmed and unable to cope
items.os: Grim WWI origin: rumored soldiers who lost all four limbs carried in baskets; now used only figuratively.
items.ex: Before results, I'm a total basket case.

items.m: a time limit (now standard English, once an idiom)
items.os: From Civil War prison camps: a literal line prisoners were shot for crossing.
items.ex: The registration deadline is Friday.

items.m: almost successful, but not quite
items.os: Carnival games once gave cigars as prizes; near-misses earned this call from the operator.
items.ex: 'Belligerant?' Close, but no cigar — it's belligerent.

items.m: to annoy someone deliberately
items.os: Racing lore says calming goats were stabled with racehorses, and rivals stole them to upset the horse — colorful but unverified.
items.ex: The slow clapping really got his goat.

items.m: to make every possible effort
items.os: From pipe organs: pulling every stop knob lets air through all pipes at maximum volume.
items.ex: In the final month we pull out all the stops.

items.m: to accept unpleasant consequences
items.os: American, 1830s; possibly from performers facing the orchestra pit, or soldiers drummed out of the army.
items.ex: He skipped practice and had to face the music.

items.m: to join something because it is popular
items.os: From 1800s American politics: candidates rode literal band wagons through town and supporters climbed aboard.
items.ex: Everyone jumped on the etymology-study bandwagon after she won.

items.p: throw your hat in the ring
items.m: to announce you are competing
items.os: From boxing: challengers literally tossed their hats into the ring to volunteer to fight.
items.ex: She threw her hat in the ring for the vocabulary bee too.

items.m: an unexpected competitor who wins
items.os: From horse racing via Disraeli's 1831 novel: an unknown horse that surges to victory.
items.ex: The quiet newcomer was the dark horse of the bee.

items.m: undecided until the very last moment
items.os: Racetracks stretched a wire over the finish line to judge close races.
items.ex: The spell-off went down to the wire.

items.m: applying to everyone or everything
items.os: From horse-race betting boards: a bet covering win, place, and show.
items.ex: Scores improved across the board.

items.m: good luck (said to performers)
items.os: Theater superstition avoids wishing 'good luck'; among proposed origins, bowing so much you bend a leg — none proven.
items.ex: Break a leg at the finals tonight!

items.m: excellent; the very best
items.os: 1920s American flapper slang from a fad of nonsense animal phrases (cat's pajamas, snake's hips).
items.ex: This new study app is the bee's knees.

items.m: very hardworking (idiomatic simile)
items.os: One of English's oldest similes — Chaucer used it in the 1300s.
items.ex: She's busy as a bee before nationals.

items.m: why are you not speaking?
items.os: Origin unknown; the stories about naval whips or ancient punishments are inventions.
items.ex: Suddenly shy? Cat got your tongue?

items.m: a cherished person
items.os: Old English 'æppel' meant both apple and pupil — the eye's most protected part; appears in the Bible and Shakespeare.
items.ex: His granddaughter is the apple of his eye.

items.m: a thoroughly good, honest person
items.os: From the Sermon on the Mount, when salt was precious.
items.ex: Her coach is the salt of the earth.

items.m: thirteen
items.os: Medieval English bakers added a 13th loaf to avoid harsh penalties for selling underweight bread.
items.ex: She spelled a baker's dozen of champion words.

items.m: to earn a living or win
items.os: Possibly from the Dunmow Flitch: since 1104, English couples proving marital devotion won a side of bacon.
items.ex: She brought home the bacon — first place!

items.m: to flatter someone for favor
items.os: Possibly from the ancient Indian custom of throwing butterballs at statues of gods to seek favor.
items.ex: Don't butter up the judges; just spell.

items.m: summarized very briefly
items.os: Pliny the Elder claimed the entire Iliad was once copied small enough to fit in a nutshell.
items.ex: In a nutshell: study roots, not lists.

items.m: a place of privileged separation from real life
items.os: From French critic Sainte-Beuve's 'tour d'ivoire' (1837), describing a poet aloof from the world.
items.ex: Professors in ivory towers forget how kids learn.

items.m: someone who argues the opposing side to test an idea
items.os: From the Vatican's 'advocatus diaboli,' appointed to argue against candidates for sainthood.
items.ex: Let me play devil's advocate: why not study fewer words?

items.p: crossing the t's and dotting the i's
items.m: being meticulous about details
items.os: From penmanship: unfinished letters made documents ambiguous or invalid.
items.ex: Contracts need every t crossed and i dotted.

items.m: behave carefully and politely
items.os: Competing tales — pints and quarts on tavern tabs, or printers confusing mirrored letters; none confirmed.
items.ex: Mind your p's and q's at the ceremony.

items.m: harmed by your own trick
items.os: From Hamlet: a petard was a small bomb, and a careless engineer could be blown up by his own device.
items.ex: The prankster was hoist with his own petard.

items.m: a hopeless pursuit
items.os: Coined in Romeo and Juliet, originally a horse race following a lead rider in goose-flight formation.
items.ex: Looking for that rulebook was a wild goose chase.

items.m: jealousy
items.os: Shakespeare coined it in Othello, where Iago warns of jealousy that 'doth mock the meat it feeds on.'
items.ex: Ignore the green-eyed monster when rivals win.

items.m: a no-win situation with contradictory rules
items.os: From Joseph Heller's 1961 novel: pilots could skip missions only if insane, but asking proved sanity.
items.ex: You need experience to compete, but competing gives experience — a catch-22.

items.m: authorities are monitoring everything
items.os: From George Orwell's 1984 and its all-seeing Party leader.
items.ex: Cameras everywhere — Big Brother is watching.

items.m: a person unfairly blamed for others' faults
items.os: From Leviticus: a goat symbolically loaded with the people's sins and sent into the wilderness.
items.ex: Don't make the newest teammate the scapegoat.

items.m: a hidden weakness in an admired person
items.os: From Daniel's dream: a golden statue with clay feet crumbles when struck.
items.ex: Even champions have feet of clay.

items.m: a stranger who helps someone in need
items.os: From the parable in Luke of a Samaritan who helps a robbed traveler when others pass by.
items.ex: A good Samaritan returned my flashcards.

items.m: the last possible moment
items.os: From the parable of vineyard workers hired at the eleventh hour yet paid a full day.
items.ex: She mastered the list at the eleventh hour.

items.p: not my circus, not my monkeys
items.m: not my problem
items.os: A beloved Polish shrug of non-responsibility that went globally viral in translation.
items.ex: They're arguing again? Not my circus, not my monkeys.
items.lit: nie mój cyrk, nie moje małpy

items.p: to have tomatoes on your eyes
items.m: to be oblivious to what is around you
items.os: German idiom for failing to see the obvious, likely from red, tired eyes.
items.ex: You missed the sign? You have tomatoes on your eyes!

items.m: to stand someone up
items.os: French 'poser un lapin' — leaving someone waiting; 19th-century slang originally meaning skipping payment.
items.ex: He gave me a rabbit; I waited an hour at the library.

items.m: it's over; nothing can be changed
items.os: French: once carrots are cooked, they cannot be raw again.
items.ex: The results are posted — the carrots are cooked.

items.m: to be trapped in a risky venture you cannot quit
items.os: From the Chinese proverb: he who rides a tiger is afraid to dismount.
items.ex: Once the startup grew, he was riding the tiger.
items.lit: 骑虎难下 (qí hǔ nán xià)

items.p: to draw legs on a snake
items.m: to ruin something by overdoing it
items.os: From a Chinese tale: contestants raced to draw a snake; the finisher added legs and lost.
items.ex: The essay was perfect until he added three more endings — drawing legs on a snake.
items.lit: 画蛇添足 (huà shé tiān zú)

items.m: even experts make mistakes
items.os: A Japanese proverb of comfort after failure.
items.ex: The champ misspelled an easy word — even monkeys fall from trees.
items.lit: 猿も木から落ちる (saru mo ki kara ochiru)

items.m: substance over style
items.os: Japanese hanami saying: choosing dango snacks over admiring cherry blossoms.
items.ex: Skip the fancy binder; content first — dumplings over flowers.

items.p: to put a spoke in someone's wheel
items.m: to sabotage someone's plan
items.os: From carts: jamming a stick between spokes stops the wheel; common across European languages.
items.ex: The rule change put a spoke in our wheel.

items.p: to slide in on a shrimp sandwich
items.m: to get success without effort
items.os: Swedish jab at people born into advantage, gliding smoothly on luxury.
items.ex: He slid in on a shrimp sandwich while we studied for years.

items.p: there's no cow on the ice
items.m: there's no need to panic
items.os: Swedish: as long as the cow hasn't wandered onto thin ice, all is calm.
items.ex: Relax, the deadline is next month — no cow on the ice.
items.lit: det är ingen ko på isen

items.p: to hang noodles on someone's ears
items.m: to fool someone with lies
items.os: Russian idiom of unknown origin — possibly wordplay on 'lapshit,' old slang for chatter.
items.ex: Don't hang noodles on my ears; I know you skipped practice.

items.p: to make an elephant out of a fly
items.m: to wildly exaggerate a small problem
items.os: Russian/German version of making mountains out of molehills, traced to the ancient Greek satirist Lucian.
items.ex: It was one typo; don't make an elephant out of a fly.
items.lit: делать из мухи слона / aus einer Mücke einen Elefanten machen

eq.p: make a mountain out of a molehill

items.m: to be popular with many connections
items.os: Japanese: a 'wide face' (kao ga hiroi) is known everywhere.
items.ex: Ask Dev — he has a wide face in the bee circuit.

items.p: in the mouth of the wolf
items.m: good luck!
items.os: Italian performers' blessing ('in bocca al lupo'); the reply is 'crepi il lupo' — may the wolf die.
items.ex: Finals tomorrow? In the mouth of the wolf!

items.p: to have your nose up in the clouds
items.m: to be arrogant or dreamy
items.os: Hindi 'नाक आसमान पर होना' — the nose raised to the sky signals pride.
items.ex: Since winning, his nose has been up in the clouds.

items.p: to rub chili on a wound
items.m: to make someone's pain worse
items.os: Hindi 'जले पर नमक/मिर्च छिड़कना' — sprinkling salt or chili on a burn.
items.ex: Reminding her of the missed word rubbed chili on the wound.

items.p: the camel finally came under the mountain
items.m: an arrogant person finally met their match
items.os: Urdu/Hindi proverb: only beside a mountain does a camel see its true size.
items.ex: The unbeaten champ lost round one — the camel came under the mountain.
items.lit: ऊँट पहाड़ के नीचे आ गया

items.p: to feed a mango to a monkey
items.m: to waste something precious on one who can't value it
items.os: South Asian saying: 'bandar kya jaane adrak (ya aam) ka swaad' — what does a monkey know of ginger or mangoes.
items.ex: Explaining etymology to him is feeding a mango to a monkey.
items.lit: बंदर क्या जाने अदरक का स्वाद

items.p: to become garlic in every stew
items.m: to be nosy; involved in everything
items.os: Spanish/Arabic-world idiom for someone who appears in every affair like garlic in every dish.
items.ex: She's garlic in every stew — every club, every committee.

items.p: to have a heart of chicken
items.m: to be cowardly
items.os: Common across Persian and South Asian languages for timidity.
items.ex: Don't have a heart of chicken; raise your hand.

items.p: a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush
items.m: what you already have is more valuable than what you might get
items.os: From medieval falconry: the hunting bird on your fist was worth more than two unseen in the bushes.
items.ex: Keep the prize you won — a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.

items.m: tell me what you are thinking
items.os: English by the 1500s, when a penny was real money — Sir Thomas More used an early version.
items.ex: You've been quiet all ride — a penny for your thoughts?

items.p: a picture is worth a thousand words
items.m: an image explains something better than lots of words
items.os: Popularized by American advertising in the 1920s; often falsely credited as an ancient Chinese proverb.
items.ex: The diagram proved it — a picture is worth a thousand words.

items.p: a stitch in time saves nine
items.m: fixing a small problem early prevents a big one
items.os: From sewing: mend a small tear now or sew nine stitches later; recorded in 1732.
items.ex: Review missed words daily — a stitch in time saves nine.

items.p: a taste of your own medicine
items.m: the same bad treatment you give others
items.os: From Aesop's fable of a swindler forced to take his own fake cure.
items.ex: The prankster got a taste of his own medicine.

items.m: time drags when you anxiously wait
items.os: Attributed to Benjamin Franklin's writings — anxiety stretches time.
items.ex: Stop refreshing the results page; a watched pot never boils.

items.m: listening with full attention
items.os: English since the 1700s: your whole self becomes ears.
items.ex: Tell me about the new word list — I'm all ears.

items.m: clumsy with your hands
items.os: If every finger were a thumb, you could grip nothing; recorded since the 1500s.
items.ex: I'm all thumbs with origami cranes.

items.m: a hidden personal motive
items.os: From a story by Charles Miner (1810): a stranger flatters a boy into sharpening his axe, then leaves without thanks.
items.ex: He praises the judges, but he has an axe to grind.

items.m: unable to sit still
items.os: American, 1930s: imagine literal ants — instant fidgeting.
items.ex: She had ants in her pants waiting for her round.

items.m: starting over from the beginning
items.os: Likely from board games like Snakes and Ladders; the radio-football story is unproven.
items.ex: The file corrupted, so it's back to square one.

items.m: a failed plan must be redesigned
items.os: From a 1941 New Yorker cartoon: an engineer walks away from a crashed plane saying it.
items.ex: The schedule flopped — back to the drawing board.

items.m: one bad person who spoils the group
items.os: From the proverb that one rotten apple spoils the barrel — rot literally spreads.
items.ex: Don't let one bad apple ruin team practice.

items.m: a rough estimate
items.os: American baseball: anywhere inside the stadium counts as 'in the ballpark.'
items.ex: Give me a ballpark figure for the trip cost.

items.m: fancy extra features
items.os: From fairground organs and early machines decked with literal bells and whistles.
items.ex: I need a simple timer, not bells and whistles.

items.m: to try extremely hard to help
items.os: From acrobatics — the backbend is the effortful pose; American 1920s.
items.ex: The librarian bent over backwards to find the etymology book.

items.m: assuming someone is right when unproven
items.os: From law: if guilt is doubtful, the verdict favors the accused.
items.ex: She was late but give her the benefit of the doubt.

items.m: doing it late beats not doing it
items.os: Ancient — appears in Livy's history of Rome and later Chaucer.
items.ex: He joined in June — better late than never.

items.p: between a rock and a hard place
items.m: facing two bad choices
items.os: American, early 1900s, from miners choosing between dangerous work and unemployment in Arizona.
items.ex: Homework or practice tonight — I'm between a rock and a hard place.

items.p: big fish in a small pond
items.m: important only within a small group
items.os: American 1800s: the same fish looks huge in a pond, tiny in a lake.
items.ex: Regional champ, but nationals makes you a small fish — enjoy being a big fish in a small pond while it lasts.

items.p: bite off more than you can chew
items.m: to take on too much
items.os: American 1800s, from chewing tobacco plugs offered in overambitious bites.
items.ex: Five clubs this term? You bit off more than you can chew.

items.m: to stop yourself from saying something
items.os: Literally pressing the tongue between teeth to stay silent; Shakespeare used it.
items.ex: I wanted to correct him but bit my tongue.

items.m: the odd or disgraceful member of a family
items.os: Black wool couldn't be dyed and was worth less; shepherds disliked black lambs.
items.ex: Every family has a black sheep — ours became a drummer.

items.m: to release pent-up energy or anger
items.os: From steam engines venting pressure to avoid explosion.
items.ex: He runs laps to blow off steam after tests.

items.m: a total surprise
items.os: A thunderbolt from a clear blue sky — the image is ancient; Carlyle popularized the English phrase.
items.ex: Her withdrawal was a bolt from the blue.

items.m: the subject everyone argues about
items.os: Two dogs fighting over one bone; English since the 1500s.
items.ex: Screen time is the bone of contention at home.

items.m: a complaint to discuss
items.os: A dog picks a bone clean slowly — like working through a grievance; 1500s.
items.ex: I have a bone to pick about the schedule.

items.m: born into wealth
items.os: Godparents traditionally gifted silver spoons; rich babies had them from birth.
items.ex: He was born with a silver spoon but works hard anyway.

items.m: talented people leaving a place
items.os: Coined by the Royal Society in the 1960s for British scientists moving to America.
items.ex: The lab suffered brain drain after funding cuts.

items.m: your main source of income
items.os: Bread with butter was the basic daily food — your livelihood covers at least that.
items.ex: Tutoring is her bread and butter.

items.m: to cost more than you can afford
items.os: From gambling: winning more than the casino table holds.
items.ex: One trophy case won't break the bank.

items.p: bury your head in the sand
items.m: to ignore an obvious problem
items.os: From the myth that ostriches hide their heads when scared — they actually don't.
items.ex: Ignoring the deadline is burying your head in the sand.

items.p: by the skin of your teeth
items.m: just barely
items.os: From the Book of Job: 'I am escaped with the skin of my teeth' — teeth have no skin, so by nothing at all.
items.ex: She advanced by the skin of her teeth.

items.m: to speak plainly and directly
items.os: From ancient Greek via Erasmus, who translated Plutarch's 'call a fig a fig, a trough a trough.'
items.ex: Let's call a spade a spade: we're behind schedule.

items.m: to be in charge
items.os: From billiards, where players announce which shot they'll play; possibly also marksmanship.
items.ex: On word selection, the head judge calls the shots.

items.m: a problem that creates many more problems
items.os: American fishing bait: open the can and the worms escape everywhere.
items.ex: Reopening the score dispute is a can of worms.

items.m: caught in the act of wrongdoing
items.os: Scottish law: caught with blood literally on your hands after poaching or murder.
items.ex: He was caught red-handed peeking at the list.

items.m: to lose courage and withdraw
items.os: American slang: chickens are folklore's cowards.
items.ex: Don't chicken out of the oral round.

items.m: a fresh start with past mistakes erased
items.os: Shops and pubs chalked debts on slates; wiping it cleared the record.
items.ex: New season, clean slate.

items.m: a small, replaceable part of a big organization
items.os: Industrial-age image: one gear tooth among thousands.
items.ex: He felt like a cog in the machine at the mega-firm.

items.m: a lazy person who watches TV all day
items.os: Coined in 1976 California as a joke on 'boob tuber' — a potato is a tuber.
items.ex: Weekends turn him into a couch potato.

items.p: count your chickens before they hatch
items.m: to assume success too early
items.os: From Aesop's milkmaid who plans her riches, then spills the milk.
items.ex: Don't celebrate yet — don't count your chickens before they hatch.

items.m: to be upset about what cannot be undone
items.os: English proverb since the 1600s; spilled milk cannot return to the jug.
items.ex: The round is over — no use crying over spilled milk.

items.m: to raise false alarms until nobody believes you
items.os: Aesop's shepherd boy jokes about a wolf until a real one comes.
items.ex: If you cry wolf about emergencies, help stops coming.

items.m: asking too many questions can get you in trouble
items.os: Originally 'care killed the cat' (worry); curiosity replaced it in the 1800s — and the lesser-known reply is 'satisfaction brought it back.'
items.ex: Stop snooping — curiosity killed the cat.

items.m: to meet the required standard
items.os: American 1900s; 'mustard' was slang for the genuine article — the keen thing.
items.ex: Half-hearted practice won't cut the mustard at nationals.

items.m: skip the boring part; get to the point
items.os: From silent-film editing: cut from dull dialogue to the chase scene.
items.ex: Cut to the chase — did we qualify?

items.m: an exact look-alike
items.os: American horse racing: a 'ringer' was a substitute horse raced under a false name; 'dead' means exact.
items.ex: She's a dead ringer for her mother.

items.m: small overlooked things cause failure
items.os: A twist on the older 'God is in the details'; popular in the 20th century.
items.ex: Check every accent mark — the devil is in the details.

items.m: ruthlessly competitive
items.os: Inverts the Latin proverb 'dog does not eat dog' — modern life got harsher than the Romans imagined.
items.ex: Streaming is a dog-eat-dog business.

items.p: don't judge a book by its cover
items.m: don't judge by appearance
items.os: Mid-1800s English; libraries of plain-bound treasures made the point daily.
items.ex: The quiet kid won it all — never judge a book by its cover.

items.p: don't look a gift horse in the mouth
items.m: don't criticize a free gift
items.os: You check a horse's age by its teeth; inspecting a gifted horse insults the giver — St. Jerome used it in 400 AD.
items.ex: Free coaching? Don't look a gift horse in the mouth.

items.p: don't put all your eggs in one basket
items.m: don't risk everything on one plan
items.os: Old proverb across Europe: drop that basket and lose everything; popularized in English by Cervantes translations.
items.ex: Apply to several bees — don't put all your eggs in one basket.

items.m: practical and unpretentious
items.os: Aviation-age contrast with having your head in the clouds.
items.ex: For a champion, she's remarkably down to earth.

items.m: to fail to remember
items.os: From lotteries since Elizabethan times: tickets without prizes were literally blanks.
items.ex: I drew a blank on the second definition.

items.m: to set a firm limit
items.os: Possibly from early tennis courts or land surveys — a literal boundary line.
items.ex: I'll help daily, but I draw the line at doing it for you.

items.m: to negotiate toughly
items.os: From market haggling; 'hard' bargains squeezed every penny since the 1500s.
items.ex: She drives a hard bargain on chores-for-screen-time.

items.m: to fail at your responsibility
items.os: American sports — a fumbled catch loses the play.
items.ex: I dropped the ball on registration; it closed yesterday.

items.m: the one who starts first wins
items.os: English proverb recorded in 1636 — first bird at dawn eats.
items.ex: Sign-ups open at 8: the early bird catches the worm.

items.m: simple to propose, hard to do
items.os: Ancient sentiment; the exact English phrase appears by the 1400s.
items.ex: 'Just relax on stage' — easier said than done.

items.m: to admit a humiliating mistake
items.os: From 'umble pie,' a dish of deer innards served to servants; the pun stuck.
items.ex: After mocking the study plan, he ate humble pie.

items.m: embarrassed by your own blunder
items.os: American mid-1900s; possibly from sloppy eating or theater audiences throwing eggs.
items.ex: The pundit's wrong prediction left egg on his face.

items.p: every cloud has a silver lining
items.m: something good hides in every bad situation
items.os: From Milton's Comus (1634): a dark cloud turns its 'silver lining' to the moon.
items.ex: Missing the trip meant extra prep — every cloud has a silver lining.

items.m: a friend only in good times
items.os: Sailing-era image: some companions vanish when storms come.
items.ex: He disappeared after the loss — a fair-weather friend.

items.m: an achievement to be proud of
items.os: From the custom of adding a feather to your hat for each deed — recorded across Europe and in hunting tradition.
items.ex: The vocabulary trophy is another feather in her cap.

items.m: rare
items.os: Originally of scattered settlements and oases on long journeys; Thomas Campbell's 1799 poem fixed it.
items.ex: Perfect rounds are few and far between.

items.m: to use the opponent's own methods
items.os: From real firefighting: controlled burns stop wildfires; settlers used the tactic and the phrase.
items.ex: They advertise big, so we fight fire with fire.

items.m: someone uncomfortable outside their element
items.os: Chaucer used it in the 1300s — the flopping fish is instantly understood.
items.ex: At the dance class, the coder was a fish out of water.

items.m: a brief success that fizzles
items.os: From flintlock muskets: gunpowder in the pan sometimes flared without firing the shot.
items.ex: One good round doesn't make a champion — don't be a flash in the pan.

items.m: an unseen observer
items.os: 20th-century image: the fly sees everything and no one notices it.
items.ex: I'd love to be a fly on the wall in the judges' room.

items.m: something worth thinking about
items.os: The mind 'digests' ideas — the metaphor is ancient, the phrase 1800s English.
items.ex: Her etymology method is food for thought.

items.m: something attractive but worthless
items.os: Pyrite glitters like gold and fooled prospectors — the mineral's real nickname.
items.ex: Shortcut apps are fool's gold; roots are the real treasure.

items.m: a first small step toward a goal
items.os: From door-to-door salesmen literally blocking the door with a foot.
items.ex: The junior bee got her foot in the door of competitive spelling.

items.m: directly from the original source
items.os: You verify a horse's age from its teeth, not the seller's claims.
items.ex: The rule change is real — I heard it from the horse's mouth.

items.m: lively and energetic
items.os: From feeding horses beans — a well-fed horse was frisky.
items.ex: After breakfast she's full of beans.

items.m: to focus on the essential facts
items.os: American; theories include fabric measured against brass tacks on shop counters — unproven.
items.ex: Enough chit-chat; let's get down to brass tacks.

items.m: to become uncontrollable
items.os: From horse driving: lose the reins from your hands and the team bolts.
items.ex: The joke war got out of hand.

items.m: to start something
items.os: From ball games or 1840 US campaign 'victory balls' rolled between towns.
items.ex: Let's get the ball rolling with introductions.

items.m: to hear a rumor of something secret
items.os: From hunting: animals literally smell hunters on the wind.
items.ex: Mom got wind of the surprise party.

items.m: to over-decorate something already beautiful
items.os: A misquote of Shakespeare's King John — 'to gild refined gold, to paint the lily.'
items.ex: The essay is perfect; more adjectives would gild the lily.

items.m: to quit a habit abruptly
items.os: American 1920s; likely from 'talking cold turkey' (blunt truth) applied to abrupt withdrawal.
items.ex: He quit video games cold turkey before finals.

items.m: to take a risky position to help or claim something
items.os: Climbing far along a branch that may break; American 1890s.
items.ex: I'll go out on a limb and predict she wins.

items.m: to do something completely
items.os: American/English 1800s; possibly from buying the entire pig instead of cuts.
items.ex: They went the whole hog: banners, cake, and a band.

items.m: to try desperate, useless solutions
items.os: From the proverb of a drowning man clutching floating straws — Thomas More used the image.
items.ex: Guessing random letters is grasping at straws.

items.m: to endure something unpleasant cheerfully
items.os: English 1700s stoicism — smile through the pain.
items.ex: The bus has no AC; grin and bear it.

items.p: to let a frog out of your mouth
items.m: to blurt out something rude or foolish
items.os: Finnish saying: a frog leaping from your mouth is a blunder you can't catch back.
items.ex: I let a frog out of my mouth at dinner and apologized fast.

items.m: to be fiercely ambitious
items.os: French: 'avoir les dents longues' — teeth long enough to bite into anything in your way.
items.ex: The new intern has long teeth; she wants the director's chair.

items.m: to endure insults without replying
items.os: French 'avaler des couleuvres' — you're fed something unpleasant and must gulp it down.
items.ex: In that meeting he swallowed grass snakes for an hour.

items.m: to get nowhere; make no progress
items.os: French 'pédaler dans la choucroute' — cycling through sticky cabbage, from Tour de France slang.
items.ex: This proof has me pedaling in the sauerkraut.

items.m: to feel full of energy
items.os: French 'avoir la pêche' — round, sweet, bursting with juice; likely from boxing slang for punch.
items.ex: After a good sleep I've got the peach!

items.m: to tell tall tales or lies
items.os: French 'raconter des salades' — a lie mixes many ingredients until it sounds tasty.
items.ex: Don't tell salads about why the homework's late.

items.m: to faint
items.os: French 'tomber dans les pommes' — possibly from 'être dans les pommes cuites' (worn out), origin debated.
items.ex: It was so hot she nearly fell in the apples.

items.p: to have a hair in your hand
items.m: to be extremely lazy
items.os: French 'avoir un poil dans la main' — a hair grows undisturbed in a palm that never works.
items.ex: He has a hair in his hand when it's chore time.
items.lit: avoir un poil dans la main

items.p: the mustard rises to my nose
items.m: I am losing my temper
items.os: French 'la moutarde me monte au nez' — strong mustard literally burns up the nose.
items.ex: Third interruption and the mustard rose to her nose.
items.lit: la moutarde me monte au nez

items.p: to break sugar on someone's back
items.m: to gossip about someone behind their back
items.os: French 'casser du sucre sur le dos de quelqu'un' — sweet-sounding words that crumble someone's reputation.
items.ex: They broke sugar on the coach's back all bus ride.
items.lit: casser du sucre sur le dos

items.m: to do pointless, useless work
items.os: French 'peigner la girafe' — grooming a giraffe is long, absurd labor with no result.
items.ex: Reformatting the formatted list is combing the giraffe.

items.p: to have other cats to whip
items.m: to have more important things to do
items.os: French 'avoir d'autres chats à fouetter' — the cruel image is centuries old; today purely figurative.
items.ex: Skip the gossip; I have other cats to whip.

items.m: to scorn what feeds you
items.os: French 'cracher dans la soupe' — ruining the very dish you eat from.
items.ex: He mocks the bee that made him famous — spitting in the soup.

eq.p: bite the hand that feeds you

items.p: to make a whole cheese of it
items.m: to make a huge fuss over something small
items.os: French 'en faire tout un fromage' — from milk (nothing) you inflate a whole cheese.
items.ex: It's one typo; don't make a whole cheese of it.

items.m: to be naive and easily used
items.os: French 'être une bonne poire' — a ripe pear practically falls into the taker's hand.
items.ex: He lends everything and gets nothing back — a good pear.

items.p: to put rabbit ears on someone
items.m: to cheat on or fool a partner (put horns on)
items.os: Spanish 'poner los cuernos' — the horns of mockery; kid-safe版 use: to trick someone.
items.ex: In the comedy, the fool gets rabbit ears put on him twice.

items.m: to be delightfully crazy
items.os: Spanish 'estar como una cabra' — goats leap where no sane animal goes.
items.ex: She's like a goat — she practices spelling while unicycling.

items.m: to reject or turn someone down
items.os: Spanish 'dar calabazas' — in old exams and courtship, pumpkins meant a flat no.
items.ex: He asked to copy my notes and I gave him pumpkins.

items.p: to throw the house out the window
items.m: to spare no expense
items.os: Spanish 'tirar la casa por la ventana' — from lottery winners in old Madrid tossing furniture to buy all new.
items.ex: For the finals party they threw the house out the window.
items.lit: tirar la casa por la ventana

items.m: to have a nasty temper
items.os: Spanish 'tener mala leche' — from the old belief that a nurse's milk shaped a baby's character.
items.ex: Careful with the referee; he has bad milk today.

items.p: to speak without hairs on the tongue
items.m: to speak bluntly and honestly
items.os: Spanish 'no tener pelos en la lengua' — nothing muffles the words.
items.ex: She speaks without hairs on her tongue about scores.
items.lit: no tener pelos en la lengua

items.p: to look for three feet on the cat
items.m: to look for problems that don't exist
items.os: Spanish 'buscarle tres pies al gato' — originally five feet; overanalyzing until you invent trouble.
items.ex: The rule is clear; stop looking for three feet on the cat.

items.p: to be more lost than an octopus in a garage
items.m: to be completely lost or confused
items.os: Modern Spanish humor: nothing is further from home than an octopus among cars.
items.ex: In the chemistry unit I'm more lost than an octopus in a garage.
items.lit: más perdido que un pulpo en un garaje

items.p: to send someone to fry asparagus
items.m: to tell someone to get lost
items.os: Spanish 'vete a freír espárragos' — a 19th-century polite stand-in for ruder dismissals.
items.ex: He kept teasing until she sent him to fry asparagus.

items.p: to have a flea behind the ear
items.m: to be suspicious that something is wrong
items.os: German/Dutch/French: 'einen Floh im Ohr' / 'la puce à l'oreille' — an itch of doubt you can't ignore.
items.ex: The too-good deal put a flea behind my ear.

items.m: to wish someone luck
items.os: German 'die Daumen drücken' — Germans squeeze thumbs instead of crossing fingers, a custom traced to Roman arenas.
items.ex: Finals at nine — we're pressing our thumbs for you!

items.m: an exclamation of astonishment
items.os: German 'mein lieber Herr Gesangverein' — invoking the venerable local choir club as mock formality.
items.ex: My dear Mr. Singing Club, that word has six silent letters!

items.p: to live like a maggot in bacon
items.m: to live in luxury
items.os: German 'leben wie die Made im Speck' — for a maggot, a side of bacon is paradise.
items.ex: At grandma's house we live like maggots in bacon.
items.lit: leben wie die Made im Speck

items.m: to have unexpected luck
items.os: German 'Schwein haben' — likely from medieval contests where the consolation prize was a piglet.
items.ex: The word I'd just studied came up — I had pig!

items.p: everything has an end only the sausage has two
items.m: everything must finish eventually
items.os: German proverb 'alles hat ein Ende, nur die Wurst hat zwei' — butcher-shop wisdom turned pop song.
items.ex: Summer break is over; everything has an end, only the sausage has two.
items.lit: alles hat ein Ende, nur die Wurst hat zwei

items.m: to sulk dramatically
items.os: German 'die beleidigte Leberwurst spielen' — old medicine blamed the liver for moods; the sausage made it funny.
items.ex: He lost one round and played the offended liverwurst all day.

items.m: to try to do two incompatible things at once
items.os: German/Yiddish 'auf zwei Hochzeiten tanzen' — you cannot celebrate in two halls at once.
items.ex: Two team finals same day? You can't dance at two weddings.

items.p: to tie a bear to someone
items.m: to fool someone with a tall tale
items.os: German 'jemandem einen Bären aufbinden' — origin uncertain; perhaps from 'Bär' punning on an old word for burden.
items.ex: He tied a bear to me about a 500-word list overnight.

items.m: to butt in with your opinion
items.os: German 'seinen Senf dazugeben' — innkeepers once added mustard to every dish, wanted or not.
items.ex: Uncle must add his mustard to every family plan.

items.m: to be past the worst; recovering
items.os: German 'über den Berg sein' — the hardest part of any journey is the climb.
items.ex: Fever's gone — she's over the mountain.

items.m: to be empty-headed
items.os: Polish 'mieć siano w głowie' — hay where the brain should be, scarecrow-style.
items.ex: Cramming without sleep leaves you stuffed with hay.

items.m: to make a chaotic mess
items.os: Polish: bigos is hunter's stew of everything in the pantry — delicious food, terrible filing system.
items.ex: Renaming files mid-project made bigos of the folder.

items.m: very rarely; almost never
items.os: Polish 'raz na ruski rok' — a folk unit of time meaning longer than anyone waits.
items.ex: He cleans his desk once in a Russian year.

items.p: to promise pears on a willow
items.m: to make impossible promises
items.os: Polish 'obiecywać gruszki na wierzbie' — willows never bear pears.
items.ex: Politicians promise pears on the willow every spring.

items.m: to daydream idly
items.os: Polish 'myśleć o niebieskich migdałach' — blue almonds exist only in dreams.
items.ex: Quit thinking of blue almonds and finish your list.

items.p: to have flies up your nose
items.m: to be irritated for no clear reason
items.os: Polish 'mieć muchy w nosie' — invisible flies, visible mood.
items.ex: She's had flies up her nose since breakfast.

items.m: to be completely tone-deaf
items.os: Russian 'медведь/слон на ухо наступил' — after that footstep, no melody survives.
items.ex: I sing like an elephant stepped on my ear.

items.p: to hang all the dogs on someone
items.m: to pile all the blame on one person
items.os: Russian 'вешать всех собак' — 'dog' was an old word for burdock burrs stuck onto someone.
items.ex: When the project failed they hung all the dogs on the intern.

items.m: neither one thing nor another; mediocre
items.os: Russian/European 'ни рыба ни мясо' — from fasting rules dividing all food into fish days and meat days.
items.ex: The essay is neither fish nor meat — pick a side.

items.p: to lead someone by the nose
items.m: to deceive and control someone
items.os: Russian/English shared image: bulls and bears were literally led by nose rings.
items.ex: The scammer led them by the nose for months.

items.m: to idle; do nothing useful
items.os: Russian 'бить баклуши' — baklushi were wooden blanks for spoons; splitting them was the easiest job in the shop.
items.ex: Stop beating the thumbs and start your flashcards.

items.m: never (politely)
items.os: Russian 'после дождичка в четверг' — Thursday was thunder-god Perun's day; his rain never obeyed schedules.
items.ex: He'll return the book after rain on Thursday.

items.m: to threaten someone with a harsh lesson
items.os: Russian 'показать, где раки зимуют' — serfs were once sent to catch crayfish from icy winter rivers.
items.ex: Mess with her word list and she'll show you where crayfish winter.

items.p: without a tsar in the head
items.m: reckless; without common sense
items.os: Russian 'без царя в голове' — the head's ruler is missing, so chaos reigns.
items.ex: He rode the shopping cart downhill — no tsar in his head.

items.p: the first pancake is always lumpy
items.m: first attempts usually fail
items.os: Russian 'первый блин комом' — the first blin off the pan sticks and folds; wisdom for every beginner.
items.ex: Her first mock round scored poorly — the first pancake is always lumpy.

items.p: to be born in a shirt
items.m: to be born lucky
items.os: Russian 'родиться в рубашке' — babies born in the caul were folklore's luckiest.
items.ex: Missed the storm by minutes — born in a shirt!

items.m: to be embarrassed by failure
items.os: Russian 'сесть в галошу' — likely from circus clowns plopping into a giant rubber boot.
items.ex: He bragged, misspelled 'rhythm,' and sat in a galosh.

items.p: a spoonful of tar in a barrel of honey
items.m: one flaw that spoils everything good
items.os: Russian 'ложка дёгтя в бочке мёда' — the proverb every quality inspector lives by.
items.ex: One rude reply was a spoonful of tar in the barrel of honey.

items.p: the monkey in its mother's eye is a gazelle
items.m: everyone's own child seems perfect
items.os: Arabic proverb 'القرد في عين أمه غزال' — love redraws the picture.
items.ex: She thinks his scribbles are art — the monkey is a gazelle in its mother's eye.

items.p: the dogs bark and the caravan moves on
items.m: ignore critics; keep going
items.os: Arabic/Turkish proverb: caravans never stopped for barking village dogs.
items.ex: Ignore the trolls — the dogs bark and the caravan moves on.

items.p: he who digs a pit falls into it
items.m: schemers are caught by their own schemes
items.os: From Proverbs and Ecclesiastes; shared across Arabic, Hebrew, and European tradition.
items.ex: His trick question got him disqualified — he who digs a pit falls into it.

items.m: two matching people found each other
items.os: Arabic/Hebrew: every pot, however odd, has a lid that fits.
items.ex: Those two argue in rhymes — the pot found its lid.

items.p: a day of honey, a day of onion
items.m: life alternates good and bad days
items.os: Arabic 'يوم عسل يوم بصل' — the rhyme makes the wisdom stick.
items.ex: Won Monday, lost Tuesday — a day of honey, a day of onion.

items.m: practice works on everyone
items.os: Arabic 'التكرار يعلّم الحمار' — a rhyming classroom proverb across the Arab world.
items.ex: Drill the list daily; repetition teaches even a donkey.

items.p: the camel cannot see its own hump
items.m: people are blind to their own faults
items.os: Arabic/Persian proverb — the camel mocks others' backs.
items.ex: He calls others careless — the camel cannot see its own hump.

items.m: he succeeded and no longer needs anyone
items.os: Persian 'خرش از پل گذشت' — once the nervous donkey is across, the owner forgets who helped push.
items.ex: After the promotion he stopped calling — his donkey crossed the bridge.

items.m: my darling (term of deep affection)
items.os: Persian 'jigar' — in Persian, Urdu, and Hindi the liver, not the heart, is the seat of love.
items.ex: Well done, my liver! Grandma beamed.

items.p: water doesn't move under his skin
items.m: completely unflappable
items.os: Persian 'آب از آب تکان نمی‌خورد' — stillness so deep even his water is calm.
items.ex: Buzzer pressure everywhere, and water doesn't move under her skin.

items.p: one flower does not bring spring
items.m: one good sign isn't proof things changed
items.os: Persian/Turkish 'با یک گل بهار نمی‌شود' — spring needs a meadow.

items.ex: The mnemonic-rap idea? Pure outside-the-box thinking.

items.m: to betray someone for your own benefit
items.os: Late-20th-century political slang, origin murky; brutal image, instantly understood.
items.ex: He blamed the intern — threw her under the bus.

items.m: to get married
items.os: From handfasting: couples' hands literally tied together in old wedding rites across Europe.
items.ex: Coach ties the knot in June, so camp starts July.

items.p: tip of the iceberg reference — tip of the tongue
items.m: a word you know but can't retrieve
items.os: Psychology adopted the folk phrase; William James described the state in 1890.
items.ex: The champion word was on the tip of my tongue all day.

items.m: to start behaving better
items.os: The 'leaf' is a book page — turning to a blank one; 1500s English.
items.ex: New term, new leaf: no more skipped drills.

items.m: to reverse a situation against your opponent
items.os: From backgammon ('tables'): rotating the board swaps fortunes.
items.ex: Down five points, she turned the tables in the oral round.

items.m: undecided; uncertain
items.os: English 1700s: unresolved matters float like things tossed skyward.
items.ex: The venue is still up in the air.

items.m: to act with extreme caution around someone
items.os: 19th-century image — earlier 'walking on eggs'; one wrong step, everything cracks.
items.ex: After the loss we walked on eggshells at dinner.

items.m: past troubles no longer worth worrying about
items.os: The river flows on; the quarrel flowed with it. English 1900s.
items.ex: Our old rivalry is water under the bridge.

items.p: wear your heart on your sleeve
items.m: to show emotions openly
items.os: From Othello — Iago scorns it — and possibly knights wearing ladies' tokens on armor sleeves.
items.ex: She wears her heart on her sleeve after every round.

items.m: inexperienced
items.os: From newborn farm animals, last dry behind the ears.
items.ex: Talented but wet behind the ears — give him a season.

items.m: a person who spoils fun
items.os: A literal wet blanket smothers fire — and enthusiasm; 1700s English.
items.ex: Don't be a wet blanket; join the karaoke.

items.m: a costly, useless possession
items.os: Siamese kings allegedly gifted sacred white elephants to ruin rivals with upkeep costs — the tale is likely legend.
items.ex: The unused smartboard is a white elephant.

items.m: an unpredictable factor or entrant
items.os: From card games where a designated card takes any value; sports adopted the entry meaning.
items.ex: The wildcard speller shocked everyone.

items.m: to win effortlessly
items.os: Horse racing: a jockey so far ahead he drops his hands and stops whipping.
items.ex: She won the written round hands down.

items.m: information spread person to person
items.os: Ancient and literal; marketing's oldest channel.
items.ex: The app grew purely by word of mouth.

items.m: deserving your pay; competent
items.os: Roman soldiers' 'salarium' was salt money — salary's own etymology.
items.ex: Any coach worth her salt teaches roots first.

items.p: you can't have your cake and eat it too
items.m: you can't enjoy both of two exclusive things
items.os: English proverb since 1538; logically it's 'eat your cake and still have it.'
items.ex: Sleep in or make the early prep — you can't have your cake and eat it too.

items.m: paying someone back with exactly the same treatment they gave you
items.os: English, 1500s, from the older 'tip for tap' — a blow returned for a blow.
items.ex: She hid my pencil because I hid hers — pure tit for tat.

items.m: everyone is entitled to their own tastes and choices
items.os: From the Latin motto 'suum cuique' — to each his own — quoted by the Roman orator Cicero.
items.ex: Dad likes olives on pizza and I don't — to each their own.

items.m: to obey the rules exactly
items.os: From runners and sailors standing with toes touching a chalked line before a race or muster, early 1800s; it is 'toe,' not 'tow.'
items.ex: The new coach expects everyone to toe the line at practice.

items.m: said as a joke while pretending to be serious
items.os: From the old habit of pressing your tongue into your cheek to show you were not serious; English, 1700s.
items.ex: Her tongue-in-cheek claim that homework is her favorite hobby made us laugh.

items.p: too many cooks spoil the broth
items.m: too many people managing one task ruin it
items.os: An English kitchen proverb recorded since the 1570s: each cook adds another pinch of salt until the soup is ruined.
items.ex: When all four of us grabbed the poster project at once, Mom said too many cooks spoil the broth.

items.m: very uncertain or risky for a while
items.os: Possibly from ships touching the seabed and slipping free, or coach wheels grazing in a near-crash; neither story is proven.
items.ex: It was touch and go whether we'd finish the science fair board before bedtime.

items.m: a strong, determined person who is hard to discourage
items.os: American slang from the 1920s, when 'cookie' was an affectionate word for a person.
items.ex: Grandma broke her wrist and still baked our birthday cake — she's a tough cookie.

items.p: two heads are better than one
items.m: two people solve a problem better than one alone
items.os: Recorded in John Heywood's famous English proverb collection of 1546.
items.ex: We cracked the riddle together because two heads are better than one.

items.m: in plain sight, right in front of you
items.os: English, 1500s: what sits closest to your face is often exactly what you fail to notice.
items.ex: My glasses were under my nose the whole time — on the kitchen table.

items.m: for a very long time
items.os: From farm life in 1500s Britain, where cows amble back from pasture at their own unhurried pace.
items.ex: You can beg until the cows come home, but bedtime is still nine o'clock.

items.m: very angry and protesting loudly
items.os: From the 1500s, when it literally meant taking up weapons in revolt; Shakespeare used it in his history plays.
items.ex: The whole class was up in arms when recess got cancelled.

items.m: to ruin a plan or comfortable arrangement
items.os: Street sellers' carts piled high with apples tipped spectacularly; English by 1788, and Roman comedy had 'you've upset the cart' centuries earlier.
items.ex: Moving the spelling bee to Monday upset the applecart for everyone's study plans.

items.m: to show disapproval by leaving
items.os: American, 1900s: instead of casting a ballot, you simply walk away.
items.ex: When the chess club got boring, kids voted with their feet and joined robotics.

items.m: including every flaw, hiding nothing
items.os: Oliver Cromwell supposedly told his portrait painter to include 'roughnesses, pimples, warts' — a great tale, but it was first written down a century later.
items.ex: Mom loves my messy handwriting journal, warts and all.

items.m: to refuse any further responsibility for something
items.os: From the Bible: the Roman governor Pontius Pilate washed his hands before the crowd to reject blame.
items.ex: After the third broken vase, Dad washed his hands of our indoor soccer games.

items.m: to survive a difficult time
items.os: From sailing: a ship weathers a storm by holding steady until the winds pass; figurative since the 1600s.
items.ex: Our team lost three games but weathered the storm and made the finals.

items.p: when in rome do as the romans do
items.m: follow local customs wherever you are
items.os: From advice Saint Ambrose gave Saint Augustine around 387 AD: in Rome, fast on Saturday as the Romans do.
items.ex: At my cousin's house we eat dinner at five — when in Rome, do as the Romans do.

items.m: the entire collection, everything included
items.os: American, 1800s; 'caboodle' grew from 'boodle,' from the Dutch 'boedel,' meaning all one's possessions.
items.ex: She packed her flashcards, dictionary, and lucky pencil — the whole kit and caboodle — for the bee.

items.m: to forget past mistakes and start fresh
items.os: Shopkeepers and innkeepers chalked customers' debts on slates and wiped them away once paid, 1800s.
items.ex: After their quarrel, the sisters agreed to wipe the slate clean.

items.p: work your fingers to the bone
items.m: to work extremely hard for a long time
items.os: English, 1800s, a grim image of hands worn down by endless labor.
items.ex: Mom worked her fingers to the bone sewing all the costumes for the school play.

items.m: to aim all your attention at one exact target
items.os: American, from World War II riflemen adjusting their sights to 'zero' for a perfect aim.
items.ex: She zeroed in on the tricky silent letters before the spelling bee.

items.m: to tease someone by fooling them playfully
items.os: British, 1800s; the stories about street thieves tripping victims or hangmen tugging legs are myths — its real origin is unknown.
items.ex: Dad said the school was giving out free puppies, but he was just pulling my leg.

items.m: someone or something you are delighted to see
items.os: First recorded by Jonathan Swift in 1738: a welcome sight so good it could soothe aching eyes.
items.ex: After a week at camp, my own bed was a sight for sore eyes.

items.m: constantly arguing or fighting fiercely
items.os: From the image of fighting dogs lunging straight for the throat; English, 1700s.
items.ex: The twins were at each other's throats over who got the window seat.

items.m: long-lasting anger or dislike between people
items.os: From the old belief that feelings lived in the blood, so lasting hatred literally soured it; English, 1700s.
items.ex: There's been bad blood between the two soccer teams since last year's final.

items.m: only the most basic, essential parts
items.os: From a skeleton stripped of everything but what holds it up; figurative in English by the 1900s.
items.ex: Our book report was just the bare bones, so the teacher asked for more detail.

items.m: done secretly, without a person knowing
items.os: Medieval English: what happens behind you is what you cannot see or defend against.
items.ex: It's unkind to whisper about a classmate behind her back.

items.p: bite the hand that feeds you
items.m: to harm someone who helps you
items.os: An ancient image of an ungrateful dog; the statesman Edmund Burke made the phrase famous in the 1790s.
items.ex: Complaining about Grandpa's pancakes while eating a third helping is biting the hand that feeds you.

items.m: to make someone deeply sad
items.os: English since the Middle Ages — Chaucer wrote of hearts breaking from sorrow in the 1300s.
items.ex: It broke her heart to miss the class trip because of chickenpox.

items.m: a fluttery, nervous feeling before something big
items.os: American, early 1900s, describing nervous flutters as tiny wings beating inside you.
items.ex: She had butterflies in her stomach walking up to the spelling bee microphone.

items.m: spread by people telling each other, not in writing
items.os: English, 1500s, from the days when most news traveled by spoken retelling.
items.ex: News of the bake sale spread by word of mouth before the flyers even went up.

items.m: to attract someone's attention
items.os: English, 1800s; a glance snags on something striking as if hooked.
items.ex: The glittery science fair poster caught the judge's eye right away.

items.m: deliberate unfriendliness toward someone
items.os: Often traced to serving unwelcome guests cold mutton shoulder, but that story is a myth; Walter Scott coined it in 1816 for a chilly, turned-away shoulder.
items.ex: After I forgot her birthday, my best friend gave me the cold shoulder all morning.

items.m: to be very expensive
items.os: English, early 1700s, when 'pretty' meant considerable — a handsome sum of coins.
items.ex: Dad said the new trombone cost a pretty penny, so I'd better practice.

items.m: to cry very hard for a long time
items.os: English, 1700s, a playful exaggeration — weeping so hard your eyes might wash away.
items.ex: She cried her eyes out when the family goldfish died.

items.m: hard physical effort, especially scrubbing or polishing
items.os: An English joke from the 1600s: the best furniture polish is sold nowhere — it is your own hard rubbing.
items.ex: The muddy bike needed a bucket of water and plenty of elbow grease.

items.m: punishment that exactly matches the harm done
items.os: From the Bible's book of Exodus and, even earlier, Babylon's Code of Hammurabi — almost 4,000 years old.
items.ex: Scribbling on his notebook because he scribbled on yours is just eye for an eye.

items.m: accepting something exactly as it first appears
items.os: From coins and banknotes, whose 'face' shows their printed worth — real or not; 1800s.
items.ex: Don't take the rumor at face value; ask the teacher what really happened.

items.m: to grow confident in a new situation
items.os: English, like a newborn foal learning to stand steadily; recorded since the 1800s.
items.ex: It took a week at the new school, but she soon found her feet.

items.m: hoping hard for good luck
items.os: Likely from making a cross shape with the fingers to ask for luck or protection, though how the gesture began is unproven.
items.ex: Fingers crossed the snow is deep enough for a school closing tomorrow!

items.m: your own family; also a real, living human
items.os: Ancient phrase found in Old English and the Bible, naming kin by the body they share.
items.ex: Of course I'll help my brother study — he's my own flesh and blood.

items.m: stop criticizing or nagging me
items.os: American, 1900s, picturing a critic as a weight riding on your back.
items.ex: "Get off my back — I already finished my math homework," he groaned.

items.m: to confess a worry that has been bothering you
items.os: English, early 1900s; the chest, home of the heart, is where guilt feels like it presses.
items.ex: He finally got it off his chest that he'd lost the library book.

items.m: to be willing to give up a lot for something
items.os: English, 1800s: for most people the right arm is the strong one, so offering it is the ultimate price.
items.ex: I'd give my right arm for front-row seats at the championship spelling bee.

items.m: to fail completely, especially a business or plan
items.os: From dead fish, which float to the surface belly up; American, 1900s.
items.ex: Our lemonade stand went belly up after it rained all weekend.

items.m: a natural talent for growing plants
items.os: Early 1900s: a gardener so gifted their thumb might as well be plant-green; Britons say 'green fingers.'
items.ex: Grandma's green thumb turned our tiny balcony into a tomato jungle.

items.m: please show some kindness or mercy
items.os: American, early 1900s, an appeal to the heart as the seat of pity.
items.ex: Have a heart, Mom — one more chapter before lights out?

items.m: to be completely busy
items.os: English since the 1400s: hands so loaded they cannot take on one thing more.
items.ex: With triplets and a puppy, our neighbors truly have their hands full.

items.m: an advantage from beginning ahead of others
items.os: From racing, where a runner or horse begins a head's length in front; 1800s.
items.ex: Studying her word list in June gave her a head start on the fall spelling bee.

items.m: suddenly very frightened or anxious
items.os: An ancient image — Homer's Iliad has a pounding heart leaping toward the mouth; English usage since the 1500s.
items.ex: My heart was in my mouth as the teacher read out the test scores.

items.m: an honest, private talk about feelings
items.os: English, 1800s: two hearts speaking directly, nothing held back.
items.ex: After the bad report card, Dad and I had a heart-to-heart about homework.

items.m: involved in something too difficult for you
items.os: From swimming in water deeper than you are tall; figurative in English since the 1600s.
items.ex: He signed up for the eighth-grade math club and quickly felt in over his head.

items.m: a restless longing to travel or move on
items.os: English, 1900s: feet that itch to be walking somewhere new.
items.ex: By the last week of summer, Mom gets itchy feet and plans a road trip.

items.m: two people who are always together
items.os: American, mid-1900s, inspired by conjoined twins such as the famous brothers Chang and Eng Bunker.
items.ex: My cousin and her best friend are joined at the hip all summer long.

items.m: to react to someone with sudden, sharp anger
items.os: American, 1800s, picturing a scolding so fast it dives straight at the speaker's words.
items.ex: I only asked one question and my sister jumped down my throat.

items.m: to watch carefully
items.os: English since the 1400s, when a single steady eye already stood for watchfulness.
items.ex: Keep an eye on the cookies so they don't burn while I set the table.

items.m: to stop something dangerous from coming closer
items.os: From medieval hunting: a cornered stag turns to face the baying hounds and holds them off; 'bay' is the hounds' bark.
items.ex: A big breakfast keeps my rumbling stomach at bay until lunch.

items.m: to help someone
items.os: English, 1500s: offering your hand — your working tool — to another person's task.
items.ex: Everyone lent a hand carrying chairs for the school concert.

items.m: to stop being careful or alert
items.os: From boxing and fencing: dropping your guarding arm leaves you open to a hit.
items.ex: She let her guard down on an easy word and misspelled it in round two.

items.m: so delicious it makes you smack your lips
items.os: From the happy popping sound lips make over tasty food; English, 1800s.
items.ex: Grandpa's lip-smacking mango lassi disappears in about a minute.

items.m: to make someone furious
items.os: From the ancient belief that anger literally heats the blood; English since the 1600s.
items.ex: Seeing someone tease the new kid made her blood boil.

items.p: make your hair stand on end
items.m: to terrify someone
items.os: Shakespeare's Hamlet promises a tale to make 'each particular hair to stand on end' — and goosebumps really do lift hairs.
items.ex: The ghost story at the sleepover made my hair stand on end.

items.m: the neighborhood or area where someone lives
items.os: American frontier speech, 1800s, when a 'neck' was a narrow strip of settled forest.
items.ex: What brings your family to our neck of the woods this weekend?

items.m: working hard and steadily without stopping
items.os: Recorded since the 1530s; probably from tool-sharpeners bent low over the spinning grindstone, though millers claim it too.
items.ex: She kept her nose to the grindstone all week and aced the vocabulary quiz.

items.p: off the top of my head
items.m: said instantly, without checking or thinking hard
items.os: American, mid-1900s: an answer skimmed straight from the surface of the mind.
items.ex: Off the top of my head, I'd say our class read forty books this year.

items.m: a very experienced person
items.os: From the 1700s, when sailors and workers were called 'hands'; an old hand had done the job for years.
items.ex: After three spelling bees, she's an old hand at staying calm on stage.

items.p: on the tip of my tongue
items.m: almost remembered but not quite
items.os: English since the 1700s; the word feels physically ready to jump off the tongue.
items.ex: The capital of Australia was on the tip of my tongue all through the quiz.

items.m: very old, ill, or near the end
items.os: English, 1600s, picturing someone already half-buried — usually said with a wink rather than a tear.
items.ex: Grandpa jokes he has one foot in the grave, then beats us all at badminton.

items.m: an annoying person or thing
items.os: American, early 1900s, a polite substitute for a ruder anatomical version.
items.ex: Untangling the holiday lights every year is a real pain in the neck.

items.m: to support something in words but not in actions
items.os: English, 1600s, echoing the Bible's complaint about people honoring 'with their lips' while their hearts stay far away.
items.ex: He pays lip service to sharing chores but never actually washes a dish.

items.p: play it close to the chest
items.m: to keep your plans and thoughts secret
items.os: From card games: cautious players hold their cards against the chest so no one can peek.
items.ex: She played it close to the chest about her science fair project until judging day.

items.m: to blame someone
items.os: From the age-old accusing gesture — one finger aimed straight at the suspect.
items.ex: Instead of pointing the finger, let's just clean up the spilled paint together.

items.m: to make a silly or grumpy expression
items.os: English, 1800s, as if the face were putty you could tug into shapes; Americans usually 'make' a face.
items.ex: He pulled a face when Mum served broccoli again.

items.m: to identify exactly what is wrong or different
items.os: English, 1800s: pinning an elusive answer down under a fingertip.
items.ex: Something about the puzzle felt off, but I couldn't put my finger on it.

items.m: to cause mild shock or disapproval
items.os: From the face itself — eyebrows lift on their own at surprising behavior; figurative since the early 1900s.
items.ex: Wearing pajamas to the awards assembly raised a few eyebrows.

items.m: to spend time among important or famous people
items.os: English, 1800s, from crowded gatherings where shoulders literally brush.
items.ex: At the national bee she rubbed shoulders with last year's champion.

items.m: to become suddenly furious
items.os: American, around 1900, evoking a bull charging the matador's red cape — though real bulls are colorblind to red and charge the motion.
items.ex: She saw red when her little brother scribbled all over her book report.

items.m: to speak or act quickly without thinking first
items.os: From Wild West gunslingers who fired the instant the gun left the holster, without aiming.
items.ex: He shoots from the hip in class discussions, then wishes he'd raised his hand slower.

items.m: a person who listens kindly to your troubles
items.os: From the natural gesture of weeping against a comforter's shoulder; 1900s.
items.ex: After the lost championship, Coach was a shoulder to cry on for the whole team.

items.m: to start something with real enthusiasm
items.os: From biting eagerly into food — a task chewy enough to be satisfying; 1900s.
items.ex: She sank her teeth into the volcano project the day it was assigned.

items.m: dangerously thin
items.os: English since the 1400s: a body so wasted that only skin and skeleton remain.
items.ex: The stray kitten was skin and bones until Grandma started feeding it.

items.m: to make a rude, teasing face at someone
items.os: An ancient mocking gesture found in cultures worldwide; described in English by the 1800s.
items.ex: The toddler stuck her tongue out at the mirror and giggled.

items.m: a love of sugary foods
items.os: Surprisingly old — English speakers have had a 'sweet tooth' since the 1300s.
items.ex: Dad's sweet tooth means the cookie jar never stays full for long.

items.m: to be deeply affected by advice or criticism
items.os: English since the 1300s: letting words sink into the heart, the old seat of feeling.
items.ex: She took the judge's pronunciation tip to heart and practiced every night.

items.m: a sign of approval
items.os: Often traced to Roman crowds sparing gladiators, but that story is a myth — the real Roman signals are unknown; the modern gesture spread through a famous 1872 painting and World War II pilots.
items.ex: Mom gave me a thumbs up through the window as the bus pulled away.

items.m: too shy or nervous to speak
items.os: From a real condition in which a band of skin restricts the tongue; figurative in English since the 1500s.
items.ex: He got tongue-tied when the principal asked him to explain his winning project.

items.m: to attract admiring attention
items.os: From people literally swiveling to look as something striking passes; 1800s.
