items.ex: Her hand-painted bicycle turned heads all along the parade route.

items.m: to reject something as not good enough
items.os: From the sniffing, nose-lifted face of disdain; English, 1700s.
items.ex: She turned her nose up at the school lunch and traded for my sandwich.

items.m: to pressure someone into doing something
items.os: American, 1900s, softening a real wrestling hold into playful persuasion.
items.ex: I didn't want dessert, but my sister twisted my arm — one scoop, then.

items.m: very clumsy, especially at dancing
items.os: English, early 1900s: with two left feet, every dance step lands wrong.
items.ex: Dad has two left feet, but he still leads the family dance party.

items.m: completely controlled by someone
items.os: English, 1700s; perhaps from a falconer pinning the bird's leash under the thumb, though the origin is unproven.
items.ex: The bossy team captain kept every player under her thumb.

items.m: so nervous, scared, or thrilled you can barely stand
items.os: From the real wobble that strong emotion sends to the legs; English, 1800s.
items.ex: Walking on stage for the final round made her weak at the knees.

items.m: to hold several jobs or roles at once
items.os: From the days when a hat marked a profession — a chef's toque, a fire helmet, a sea captain's cap; American, 1900s.
items.ex: Our teacher wears many hats: coach, choir director, and spelling bee judge.

items.m: with a warm, eager welcome
items.os: From the embrace-ready posture of welcome; English since the 1600s.
items.ex: The class welcomed the exchange student with open arms.

items.m: to work extremely hard
items.os: British, 1900s, a cheerful exaggeration — effort so fierce even your socks fly off.
items.ex: She worked her socks off memorizing two hundred words before the regional bee.

items.m: to work as hard as you possibly can
items.os: From heavy lifting that bends and strains the spine; English, 1800s.
items.ex: The volunteers broke their backs setting up the school carnival in one afternoon.

items.m: to pause and rest until your breathing calms
items.os: English since the 1400s, when 'catch' meant to recover something escaping — here, your own breath.
items.ex: We stopped at the top of the hill to catch our breath before the bike ride home.

items.m: to avoid embarrassment and keep your dignity
items.os: Formed in English around 1900 as the opposite of 'lose face,' which traders had translated from Chinese.
items.ex: Admitting the mistake with a joke helped him save face in front of the class.

items.m: to be embarrassed and lose others' respect
items.os: Translated into English in the 1800s by traders in China from the Chinese 'diū liǎn,' to lose face.
items.ex: He worried he'd lose face if he asked for help, but nobody laughed.

items.p: in the blink of an eye
items.m: extremely fast, almost instantly
items.os: Echoes the Bible's 'in the twinkling of an eye'; a real blink takes about a third of a second.
items.ex: Summer vacation was over in the blink of an eye.

items.m: to look at someone with special interest or warning
items.os: American slang, early 1900s, from the days when one loaded look said everything.
items.ex: Mom gave me the eye when I reached for a third cupcake.

items.m: watching and listening with complete attention
items.os: English, joining two older phrases — 'all ears' for keen listening, recorded by the 1700s, and 'all eyes' for keen watching.
items.ex: The kids were all eyes and ears when the firefighter visited class.

items.p: by the sweat of your brow
items.m: through your own hard work
items.os: From the Bible's book of Genesis, where Adam must earn his bread 'in the sweat of thy face.'
items.ex: Grandpa built the treehouse by the sweat of his brow, one plank at a time.

items.m: to get your first experience doing something
items.os: From babies cutting their first teeth on teething rings; figurative in English since the 1700s.
items.ex: She cut her teeth on classroom bees before winning the district championship.

items.m: to try something new for the first time, gently
items.os: From wading into water one cautious step at a time instead of diving.
items.ex: Join the chess club for a week just to get your feet wet.

items.m: to face something unpleasant with determination
items.os: From clenching the jaw against pain or effort; English, 1700s.
items.ex: He gritted his teeth and finished the last lap of the fitness test.

items.m: to notice every tiny detail
items.os: Eagles can spot a rabbit from more than a mile up; English writers borrowed their sharp sight by the 1500s.
items.ex: Our teacher has an eagle eye for missing commas.

items.p: in one ear and out the other
items.m: heard but instantly forgotten or ignored
items.os: An ancient complaint — Chaucer used it in the 1300s for words that never stop inside the head.
items.ex: The reminder to bring gym shoes went in one ear and out the other.

items.m: to barely manage to survive troubles or debts
items.os: From a tiring swimmer straining not to go under; figurative in English since the 1700s.
items.ex: With three tests in one week, she could barely keep her head above water.

items.m: to start working seriously
items.os: From the game of marbles, where players must press their knuckles to the ground before shooting; 1700s.
items.ex: Time to knuckle down — the book report is due Friday.

items.m: almost worn out or about to fail
items.os: English, 1500s, picturing a walker or workhorse about to collapse.
items.ex: My sneakers are on their last legs after a whole summer of soccer.

items.m: to nudge feet secretly and playfully under a table
items.os: American, 1900s, from mischievous under-the-table games at dinner; also used for sneaky cooperation.
items.ex: The twins played footsie under the dinner table until Mom noticed the giggling.

items.m: to use all your strength and effort
items.os: From rowing and heavy lifting, where real power comes from the back; 1800s.
items.ex: "Put your back into it!" Dad called as we shoveled the driveway.

items.p: stand on your own two feet
items.m: to be independent and support yourself
items.os: English, 1800s: balanced on your own footing, no longer leaning on anyone.
items.ex: Packing her own school bag every night taught her to stand on her own two feet.

items.m: staying calm and brave without showing distress
items.os: Famously British but first recorded in America in 1815 — a trembling upper lip betrays fear, so keep it stiff.
items.ex: She kept a stiff upper lip when her word was misspelled, and cheered for the winner.

items.m: to accept trouble bravely without complaining
items.os: From boxing: absorbing a punch square on the chin and staying upright; early 1900s.
items.ex: He took the losing score on the chin and shook hands with the other team.

items.m: to talk confident nonsense about things you don't understand
items.os: American slang, 1880s; why the hat, nobody knows — perhaps empty words pulled from an empty hat.
items.ex: Anyone claiming homework is banned next year is talking through his hat.

items.m: seeing without a telescope, microscope, or other aid
items.os: From 1600s science writing, when new lenses made unaided eyes seem 'naked.'
items.ex: You can see Jupiter with the naked eye on a clear night.

items.m: to answer an insult with patience instead of revenge
items.os: From Jesus's Sermon on the Mount in the Bible: struck on one cheek, offer the other.
items.ex: When the rival team jeered, our captain turned the other cheek and kept playing.

items.m: a public show of support for someone
items.os: From parliaments, where a formal vote decides whether the government keeps its job.
items.ex: Being picked to lead the group project felt like a vote of confidence from the teacher.

items.m: to win by the smallest possible margin
items.os: From horse racing, where a photo finish can be decided by the length of a nose.
items.ex: She won the classroom geography quiz by a nose — one point ahead.

items.m: to show helpless worry instead of taking action
items.os: A grief gesture recorded since medieval times — twisting the hands as if squeezing out sorrow.
items.ex: Instead of wringing our hands over the rained-out picnic, we built a blanket fort.

items.p: have your cake and eat it too
items.m: wanting to enjoy two good things that cannot both happen
items.os: First recorded in a 1538 letter to Thomas Cromwell: 'a man cannot have his cake and eat his cake.'
items.ex: You can't watch the movie and finish your homework — you can't have your cake and eat it too.

items.m: stuck in a difficult situation
items.os: American, early 1900s; from 'jam' meaning to squeeze or crush — being caught in a tight press, not the fruit spread.
items.ex: I was in a jam when I left my project poster on the bus.

items.m: worried, flustered, and agitated
items.os: English, 1800s: fretting until you feel as heated and stirred up as a bubbling pot of stew.
items.ex: Mom was in a stew when we couldn't find the car keys before the bee.

items.p: know which side your bread is buttered
items.m: know exactly who or what benefits you most
items.os: From John Heywood's 1546 collection of English proverbs — you take good care of the buttered side.
items.ex: He's extra helpful to the coach who picks the team — he knows which side his bread is buttered.

items.p: like taking candy from a baby
items.m: extremely easy, because the other side cannot put up a fight
items.os: American, early 1900s: a baby can't stop you — though it will certainly cry about it.
items.ex: Beating my little brother at checkers is like taking candy from a baby.

items.p: milk it for all it's worth
items.m: squeeze every possible advantage or sympathy from a situation
items.os: From milking a cow dry — pulling out every last drop.
items.ex: With one tiny scrape on his knee, my brother milked it for all it was worth.

items.m: not something you enjoy or care for
items.os: British, where 'my cup of tea' meant anything pleasing since the 1800s; the polite negative form took over in the 1920s.
items.ex: Scary movies are just not my cup of tea.

items.m: a crazy or silly idea
items.os: From 1800s slang 'nut' for head: anyone 'off their nut' was nutty, and the wildness spread to their ideas.
items.ex: Building a roller coaster in the backyard is a nutty idea, Dad.

items.m: not paying attention; unaware of what's happening
items.os: American office slang, 1950s: someone whose mind has left the desk even though they haven't.
items.ex: I was out to lunch in class and missed the homework page number.

items.m: crowded very tightly together
items.os: From tins of sardines, sold since the 1800s with the little fish squeezed in without a gap to spare.
items.ex: The school bus on field-trip day was packed like a sardine can.

items.m: an excellent bargain or arrangement
items.os: American, late 1800s, when 'peach' was slang for anything as sweet and perfect as ripe fruit.
items.ex: Two books for the price of one is a peach of a deal.

items.m: the carefree, inexperienced time of your youth
items.os: Coined by Shakespeare in Antony and Cleopatra (1606): 'my salad days, when I was green in judgment.'
items.ex: Grandpa calls his summers at the lake his salad days.

items.m: the assistant or less important person
items.os: From American burlesque theater, early 1900s, where the star comic was the 'top banana' and his sidekick came second.
items.ex: In the class play I'm the second banana, feeding lines to the lead.

items.m: something too minor to matter
items.os: American, 1800s: potatoes too small to be worth digging up.
items.ex: A one-point quiz is small potatoes next to the final exam.

items.m: a clever, capable person
items.os: American slang, 1920s, when 'cookie' became an affectionate word for a person.
items.ex: Grandma says my sister is one smart cookie for winning the bee.

items.m: modified to be more powerful or flashy than normal
items.os: American, 1930s; possibly from 'soup,' slang for a drug injected to make racehorses run faster, later applied to hot-rod engines.
items.ex: My cousin souped up his go-kart until it was the fastest on the block.

items.m: make something more exciting or interesting
items.os: From the kitchen, where a pinch of spice rescues a bland dish; the figurative use is centuries old.
items.ex: Our teacher spiced things up with a spelling relay race.

items.m: a full, satisfying, nourishing meal
items.os: The story about square wooden plates in the Royal Navy is a myth; the phrase is American, 1800s, from 'square' meaning honest and solid, as in 'fair and square.'
items.ex: After the tournament, Mom made sure I got a square meal.

items.m: make something unpleasant seem nicer than it really is
items.os: From 1800s pharmacists, who coated bitter pills in sugar so patients could swallow them.
items.ex: The coach didn't sugar-coat it: we need to practice more.

items.p: that's the way the cookie crumbles
items.m: that's just how things turned out; accept the bad luck
items.os: American, 1950s: once a cookie crumbles, nobody can put it back together.
items.ex: We lost the raffle — oh well, that's the way the cookie crumbles.

items.m: the most admired and celebrated person around
items.os: From the 1700s custom of raising toasts to honor a celebrity — 'toast' itself came from spiced toast floated in wine.
items.ex: After the spelling-bee win, she was the toast of the town.

items.m: the boss or most important person
items.os: American burlesque slang, early 1900s: the lead comedian in the show was the top banana, his sidekick the second banana.
items.ex: When the teacher stepped out, the hall monitor acted like the top banana.

items.m: a very difficult problem, or a person hard to persuade
items.os: Short for 'a hard nut to crack,' used since the 1700s — Benjamin Franklin applied it to enemy fortresses.
items.ex: That last math puzzle was a tough nut, but we cracked it together.

items.m: think hard; use your brain
items.os: 'Noodle' has been slang for the head since the 1700s, long before it meant pasta to most English speakers.
items.ex: Use your noodle before you guess the spelling.

items.m: weaken something by removing its strength or bluntness
items.os: From taverns that quietly diluted drinks with water to stretch their profits.
items.ex: The teacher didn't water down the test just because it was Friday.

items.m: give a small taste that makes you eager for more
items.os: 'Whet' means to sharpen a blade on a whetstone — a first taste sharpens your hunger; figurative since the 1600s.
items.ex: The first chapter whetted my appetite for the whole series.

items.m: your food shapes your health and character
items.os: From French food writer Brillat-Savarin, 1826: 'Tell me what you eat and I shall tell you what you are.'
items.ex: Dad quotes 'you are what you eat' whenever I reach for a third cookie.

eq.p: dis-moi ce que tu manges, je te dirai ce que tu es
eq.lit: tell me what you eat and I will tell you what you are

items.p: bread always falls butter side down
items.m: when things go wrong, they go wrong the most annoying way
items.os: Victorian comic pessimism: an 1884 magazine poem moaned that dropped toast always lands on the buttered side.
items.ex: I dropped my toast on bee morning — bread always falls butter side down.

items.m: share a meal with someone in friendship
items.os: From the Bible, where tearing and sharing loaves — 'breaking bread' — sealed fellowship, as at the Last Supper.
items.ex: Our team broke bread with the rival school after the match.

items.m: someone who keeps dropping things
items.os: As if your fingers were slippery with butter; Charles Dickens used it in 1836 for a clumsy cricket fielder.
items.ex: I dropped the relay baton twice — total butterfingers.

items.m: an ear swollen and lumpy from repeated blows
items.os: Boxing and wrestling slang, early 1900s: a battered ear puffs up until it looks like a cauliflower floret.
items.ex: The wrestling coach makes everyone wear headgear so nobody gets cauliflower ear.

items.m: two people or things that are completely different
items.os: British, since the 1300s: chalk and cheese can look alike — pale crumbly lumps — but could not be more different.
items.ex: My twin cousins are chalk and cheese: one loves math, the other art.

items.m: cook a huge amount with great energy
items.os: American, 1900s: 'up a storm' tacked onto a verb means doing it with wild, weather-sized energy.
items.ex: Grandma cooked up a storm for the family reunion.

items.p: full of the milk of human kindness
items.m: naturally gentle, caring, and compassionate
items.os: From Shakespeare's Macbeth (1606): Lady Macbeth complains her husband is 'too full o' the milk of human kindness' to seize the crown.
items.ex: Our librarian, full of the milk of human kindness, never scolds anyone for late books.

items.p: go together like peas and carrots
items.m: match perfectly; be constant companions
items.os: American Southern saying made world-famous by Forrest Gump (1994): 'Me and Jenny goes together like peas and carrots.'
items.ex: My best friend and I go together like peas and carrots.

items.m: everything tastes wonderful when you are truly hungry
items.os: Traced to the Roman writer Cicero, who called hunger the finest seasoning for any dish.
items.ex: After the long hike, plain sandwiches vanished fast — hunger is the best sauce.

items.m: a pleasant promise that never actually arrives
items.os: From Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass (1871): the White Queen offers 'jam to-morrow and jam yesterday — but never jam to-day.'
items.ex: Extra recess 'next term' sounds like jam tomorrow to us.

items.p: life is a bowl of cherries
items.m: life is delightful and easy — now usually said ironically
items.os: Title of a 1931 American song by Ray Henderson and Lew Brown, sung just as the Depression made the line feel ironic.
items.ex: No homework, sunshine, and mango ice cream — life is a bowl of cherries today.

items.m: the most basic and important parts of something
items.os: American, 1900s: the plain, filling heart of a dinner plate stood for the plain, essential heart of any job.
items.ex: Root words are the meat and potatoes of spelling practice.

items.p: one bad apple spoils the barrel
items.m: one bad person can ruin the whole group
items.os: Medieval storage wisdom, cited since Chaucer's day — rot really does spread from one apple through the barrel.
items.ex: The coach benched the teaser, saying one bad apple spoils the barrel.

items.m: drunk, or dazed with wide blank eyes
items.os: American slang, early 1900s; perhaps from eyes as round and glassy as pies, though no one has proven the image.
items.ex: After the sleepover we stumbled to breakfast pie-eyed with tiredness.

items.m: a combination of things guaranteed to go wrong
items.os: A 20th-century kitchen metaphor: mix the wrong ingredients and the dish is doomed before the oven.
items.ex: Packing your bag five minutes before the bus is a recipe for disaster.

items.m: what is fair for one person is fair for another
items.os: Short for the 1600s proverb 'what is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander' — the gander being the male goose.
items.ex: If I have to show my homework, so does my brother — sauce for the goose.

items.m: be left alone to suffer the results of your own actions
items.os: Borrowed from the French 'cuire dans son jus'; by the 1800s English used the image of meat simmering in its own liquid.
items.ex: Mom let him stew in his own juice after he skipped practice and lost his spot.

items.m: add something extra to make an offer more tempting
items.os: From American poker slang 'sweeten the pot' — tossing extra chips onto the pile, 1900s.
items.ex: Dad sweetened the deal: finish homework early and we get ice cream.

items.p: the land of milk and honey
items.m: a place of plenty, ease, and comfort
items.os: From the Bible: God promises the Israelites Canaan, 'a land flowing with milk and honey.'
items.ex: To the hungry campers, the snack bar looked like the land of milk and honey.

items.p: variety is the spice of life
items.m: trying different things is what keeps life interesting
items.os: From William Cowper's 1785 poem The Task: 'Variety's the very spice of life, that gives it all its flavour.'
items.ex: Mom mixes swim, chess, and art camp — variety is the spice of life.

items.m: make income and spending records match exactly
items.os: From double-entry bookkeeping, perfected in Renaissance Italy, where every ledger must balance to the last penny.
items.ex: The bake-sale treasurer balanced the books down to the last quarter.

items.m: value received for the money spent
items.os: American Pentagon slang, 1950s: defense plans promising 'a bigger bang for a buck' — more firepower per dollar.
items.ex: The giant crayon box gives you the most bang for your buck.

items.m: risk everything you own on a single chance
items.os: American: a farmer wagering the family land has staked absolutely everything.
items.ex: Don't bet the farm on one guess — check the dictionary first.

items.m: so valuable that no money could buy it
items.os: An ancient praise formula: the Bible says wisdom's price is 'above rubies' — beyond anything money measures.
items.ex: Grandma says her old photo albums are beyond price.

items.m: unlimited freedom or money to do whatever is needed
items.os: A signed check with the amount left blank lets the holder fill in any sum; famously, Germany's 1914 'blank cheque' promise to Austria.
items.ex: The librarian gave our club a blank check to decorate the reading corner.

items.m: naive and easily fooled
items.os: American, 1800s: only a day-old baby would know so little; the 1946 Broadway comedy Born Yesterday spread it further.
items.ex: I know that trick — I wasn't born yesterday!

items.m: the final result or the point that matters most
items.os: From the last line of a financial statement, where profit or loss finally shows; figurative since the mid-1900s.
items.ex: The bottom line: practice ten words a night and you'll be ready.

items.m: end up with neither a profit nor a loss
items.os: Gambling and trading term, 1800s: the accounts 'break' exactly even.
items.ex: Our lemonade stand broke even after we paid Mom back for lemons.

items.m: punish or stop something with full force
items.os: American, 1900s; perhaps from a judge's gavel or a revolver's hammer snapping down — the exact image is unproven.
items.ex: The referee brought down the hammer on pushing during the game.

items.m: quit while you're ahead; also a joking way to say die
items.os: From poker: when you leave the table, you trade your chips back for cash.
items.ex: After winning twice at the fair booth, I cashed in my chips and went home happy.

items.m: a joking way of saying something is a real bargain
items.os: British market-stall humor, 1800s–1900s; probably a deliberate muddle of 'cheap at twice the price,' though its logic is still argued about.
items.ex: Fifty cents for that huge poster? Cheap at half the price, Dad laughed.

items.m: the person who does every job, grand and humble alike
items.os: American, early 1800s: in a one-cook kitchen the same person makes the dinner and scrubs the bottles.
items.ex: For the class party our teacher was chief cook and bottle washer.

items.m: rise step by step to higher jobs in a company
items.os: A 20th-century business image: each promotion is one rung up a ladder.
items.ex: Aunt Priya climbed the corporate ladder from intern to manager in five years.

items.m: gain control of the entire supply of something
items.os: American, 1800s: traders who bought up all the wheat drove prices into a 'corner' no rival could escape.
items.ex: My sister cornered the market on glitter pens before the poster contest.

items.m: abandon a failing plan before it costs you even more
items.os: From trading advice: sell a sinking stock early rather than ride it to the bottom.
items.ex: Our volcano model kept collapsing, so we cut our losses and made a poster instead.

items.m: charging an outrageously unfair price
items.os: The tale that it comes from Britain's window tax 'stealing daylight' is a myth; it simply means theft so bold it happens in broad daylight.
items.ex: Five dollars for a tiny juice box? That's daylight robbery, Mom said.

items.m: extremely inexpensive
items.os: English, 1800s: nothing is more common or costless than dirt; it replaced the older 'dog cheap.'
items.ex: The library sale sold paperbacks dirt cheap, three for a dollar.

items.m: a sure bet; almost certainly true
items.os: American betting talk, 1800s: you're so confident you'll stake real dollars against mere donuts.
items.ex: Dollars to donuts our teacher gives a pop quiz on Friday.

items.m: an early effort or sacrifice that secures better things later
items.os: From real estate, 1900s: a down payment is the first slice of money that locks in the whole purchase.
items.ex: Dad calls my library card a down payment on the future.

items.m: either far too much or nothing at all
items.os: From farming life, where harvests swung between overflowing tables and empty ones; English paired 'feast' with 'fast' by the 1600s.
items.ex: Bee practice is feast or famine: fifty words one night, none the next.

items.m: extremely wealthy
items.os: From 'filthy lucre,' William Tyndale's 1526 Bible phrase for shameful money — wealth so big it looked dirty.
items.ex: Winning the lottery wouldn't make us filthy rich, Dad says, but he'd still dance.

items.m: having no money at all
items.os: American, 1800s: 'broke' came from 'broken' merchants and banks, and 'flat' squashes it completely.
items.ex: After the book fair I was flat broke but happy.

items.m: pay the whole cost
items.os: From 'footing up' a bill — adding the total at the foot, or bottom, of the page — and then paying it; 1800s.
items.ex: Grandpa footed the bill for the whole team's pizza.

items.m: for very little money
items.os: Street ballads once sold for pennies; Shakespeare was already writing 'sold for a song' in the 1600s.
items.ex: Mom found my desk at a yard sale for a song.

items.m: stop chatting and start the real work
items.os: American meeting-room talk, 1800s: once the pleasantries end, the business begins.
items.ex: After roll call, our study group got down to business.

items.p: give someone a run for their money
items.m: compete so well that the favorite must struggle to win
items.os: From horse racing, 1800s: bettors wanted their horse at least to give them 'a run for their money.'
items.ex: The new speller gave last year's champion a run for her money.

items.m: split the bill so each person pays their own share
items.os: American, 1800s, from 'Dutch treat' — one of many old jibes at Dutch thriftiness left over from Anglo-Dutch rivalry.
items.ex: My sister and I went Dutch on a giant pretzel at the fair.

items.m: a source of steady wealth that must not be destroyed
items.os: From Aesop's fable: a greedy farmer kills the goose that lays golden eggs and loses everything.
items.ex: The bake sale is our club's golden goose, so we guard the recipes.

items.m: a huge payout promised to a boss who loses their job
items.os: American business term from the 1980s takeover wars: executives floated safely away from mergers on rich exit deals.
items.ex: The news said the CEO left with a golden parachute bigger than our school's budget.

items.m: so poor that money is spent on food the moment it arrives
items.os: From famine times, 1500s: food went straight from hand to mouth, with nothing left over to store.
items.ex: In the story, the family lived hand to mouth until the harvest came in.

items.m: money gained through real work and effort
items.os: A plain English pairing, centuries old: wages earned the hard way deserve respect.
items.ex: Dad spent his hard-earned money on my dictionary, so I use it every day.

items.m: have plenty of money available to spend
items.os: American, 1900s: the image of pockets so deep the money never runs out.
items.ex: Our rival school has deep pockets and brand-new uniforms every season.

items.m: an outrageously high price
items.os: From real highwaymen of the 1600s–1700s who held up travelers on English roads; later aimed at anyone overcharging.
items.ex: Ten dollars for popcorn is highway robbery, Grandpa grumbled.

items.m: strike sudden success or something valuable
items.os: From American gold miners, 1800s: 'pay dirt' was soil holding enough gold to pay for the digging.
items.ex: Searching Grandma's attic, we hit pay dirt: a box of her old spelling medals.

items.m: earning more than you spend
items.os: From ledgers where bookkeepers wrote profits in black ink and losses in red.
items.ex: After selling fifty cupcakes, the class fund was back in the black.

items.m: suddenly rich or in a winning position
items.os: From horse racing: a horse finishing 'in the money' earns a payout for its backers.
items.ex: If my raffle ticket wins, we're in the money!

items.m: record all the money coming in and going out
items.os: From merchants' account books; careful traders have 'kept books' since the Middle Ages.
items.ex: Mom keeps the books for our family's lemonade stand.

items.p: laughing all the way to the bank
items.m: making lots of money despite others' mockery
items.os: Popularized by the flashy pianist Liberace in the 1950s, who told sneering critics he 'cried all the way to the bank' — meaning the opposite.
items.ex: Everyone teased her sticker shop until she was laughing all the way to the bank.

items.m: spend more money than you earn
items.os: 'Means' has meant income since the 1600s, and moralists have warned against outspending it ever since.
items.ex: Dad says a giant TV on credit would be living beyond our means.

items.m: a lender who charges brutally unfair interest
items.os: American, late 1800s: predatory lenders circling desperate borrowers like sharks.
items.ex: In the movie, the hero owes money to a loan shark and hides from him.

items.m: lose all your money
items.os: American, Depression-era 1930s: a ruined gambler is wiped out down to the shirt on his back.
items.ex: Uncle Ravi joked he'd lose his shirt betting against my spelling streak.

items.m: earn money quickly, often by cutting corners
items.os: 'Buck' has meant a dollar since frontier days — possibly from deerskins traded as currency — and the 'fast buck' chase is 1900s American slang.
items.ex: The comic-book villain schemes to make a fast buck selling fake tickets.

items.m: earn a huge profit very quickly
items.os: American hunting-and-gambling slang, 1800s: one lucky strike brings home the whole prize.
items.ex: Our class made a killing selling friendship bracelets at the fair.

items.p: money burns a hole in your pocket
items.m: you feel desperate to spend money the moment you have it
items.os: Nearly five centuries old: Thomas More wrote in the 1530s of money that 'burned out the bottom of his purse.'
items.ex: My allowance burns a hole in my pocket every Saturday.

items.m: money is limited and must be earned, not wasted
items.os: A parents' proverb from the 1800s: unlike apples, coins cannot be picked from a branch.
items.ex: When I begged for new sneakers, Dad sighed, 'Money doesn't grow on trees.'

items.m: wealth buys influence and attention
items.os: The idea is ancient — Greek writers joked about it — but the blunt American form 'money talks' spread in the late 1800s.
items.ex: The team with rich sponsors got the best practice field; money talks.

items.m: drain someone with many small charges; also, small-time
items.os: From America's five-and-ten-cent stores, 1900s: tiny coins and tiny amounts — until they add up.
items.ex: The game app nickel-and-dimes players with tiny fees for hats and pets.

items.m: provided free by the business
items.os: From 1800s American saloons, where the 'house' — the establishment itself — stood customers a free round.
items.ex: The baker gave us cookies on the house for winning the bee.

items.m: the opposite way of looking at the same situation
items.os: Every coin has two faces; by the mid-1900s English had flipped the older 'other side of the medal' into coins.
items.ex: Winning is fun, but the other side of the coin is extra practice.

items.m: face the cost or consequences of your choices
items.os: From the 1600s proverb 'he who pays the piper calls the tune'; the Pied Piper of Hamelin — a town that refused to pay — darkened the meaning.
items.ex: I skipped studying all week, and on Friday's quiz I paid the piper.

items.m: pay the highest possible price
items.os: American, 1900s: bidding at the very top of the price range in dollars.
items.ex: Collectors pay top dollar for that rare trading card.

items.m: a person extremely careful or stingy with money
items.os: 'Pinchpenny' goes back to the 1400s — a miser squeezing every coin before letting it go.
items.ex: Grandpa the penny pincher reuses birthday wrapping paper every year.

items.m: pay the bill for everyone
items.os: American, 1900s: 'tab' is short for tabulation, the running bill kept at a diner.
items.ex: Aunt Meera picked up the tab for our celebration dinner.

items.m: spend as little money as possible
items.os: The same squeeze as the 1400s 'pinchpenny' — gripping each coin tight; the verb form spread in 1900s America.
items.ex: We pinched pennies all month to afford the museum trip.

items.m: a large amount of money
items.os: English, 1700s: 'pretty' once meant considerable, so a pretty penny was a hefty sum.
items.ex: That telescope cost a pretty penny, so handle it gently.

items.m: add your opinion to a discussion
items.os: American, late 1800s; perhaps from the two-cent stamp on a mailed letter of opinion, or a tiny poker stake — no one has proven which.
items.ex: Everyone put in their two cents about where the class trip should go.

items.m: earn money rapidly and in large amounts
items.os: From casino croupiers, who pull piles of chips across the table with a little rake.
items.ex: The school carnival raked in the money for new library books.

items.m: fix one debt by creating another
items.os: English since the 1300s; the story that it began with St. Peter's church funds repairing St. Paul's Cathedral is a myth — the phrase is older than that event.
items.ex: Borrowing Monday's lunch money to repay Friday's is robbing Peter to pay Paul.

items.m: the first money used to start a project
items.os: A farming metaphor, 1900s: like seed corn, this money is planted so a business can grow.
items.ex: Grandma gave us seed money for our comic-book stand.

items.m: value yourself or your abilities less than you should
items.os: From the stock market, where 'selling short' bets that something is worth less than its price.
items.ex: Don't sell yourself short — you spelled every practice word right.

items.m: pay money, usually reluctantly
items.os: English, 1800s: coins pried out of a purse like peas popped from their shells.
items.ex: Dad shelled out for front-row seats at the science show.

items.m: a plan run on very little money
items.os: American, late 1800s; perhaps from street peddlers whose entire stock was a tray of shoelaces — the true origin is unproven.
items.ex: We built the class parade float on a shoestring budget of ten dollars.

items.p: burn the candle at both ends
items.m: to exhaust yourself by staying up late and getting up early
items.os: From the French brûler la chandelle par les deux bouts, 1600s: candles were costly, and lighting both ends wasted one twice as fast.
items.ex: Mom says studying past midnight and waking at five is burning the candle at both ends.

items.m: time off spent doing the same thing you do at work
items.os: British, 1890s: London omnibus drivers were said to spend days off riding their own buses to check the horses were treated well, though that tale is unproven.
items.ex: Our teacher's beach trip turned into a busman's holiday when she graded essays under her umbrella.

items.m: by any means possible, fair or unfair
items.os: English, 1300s; one old story says villagers could take only the firewood they could reach with a reaper's hook or shepherd's crook, but that is unproven.
items.ex: Priya vowed to reach the spelling-bee finals by hook or by crook.

items.m: to rise step by step to higher positions
items.os: English, 1800s; success pictured as a ladder, each promotion one rung higher.
items.ex: Dad started as a shelf-stocker and climbed the ladder to store manager.

items.m: to prepare for every possibility
items.os: American, 1900s; from baseball, where fielders must guard all four bases at once.
items.ex: I covered all the bases by packing extra pencils, a snack, and my word lists.

items.m: to be less strict or demanding with someone
items.os: Likely from sailors easing — slackening — a taut rope; the figurative sense is American, mid-1900s.
items.ex: Cut your little brother some slack; it's his first spelling bee.

items.m: to prepare carefully by learning the facts first
items.os: American, mid-1900s; schoolwork done at home, stretched to cover any careful preparation.
items.ex: Before buying my bike, Dad did his homework and compared ten models.

items.p: dot the i's and cross the t's
items.m: to finish something with careful attention to every detail
items.os: From penmanship, 1800s: careless writers left i's undotted and t's uncrossed, so teachers demanded both.
items.ex: Check your entry form and dot the i's and cross the t's before mailing it.

items.m: to prove yourself and deserve your position
items.os: Military, 1800s: soldiers earn the cloth chevrons — stripes — sewn onto a sergeant's sleeve with each promotion.
items.ex: She earned her stripes by winning the classroom bee before trying regionals.

items.m: to stop delaying and start working seriously
items.os: English, 1800s; from 'get down to it,' settling firmly onto a task like sitting down to a desk.
items.ex: Recess is over — time to get down to work on our science posters.

items.m: to be fired or thrown out
items.os: English, 1880s; from the picture of being literally kicked out the door.
items.ex: The lazy mascot got the boot after sleeping through three games.

items.m: to be dismissed from a job
items.os: American, early 1900s; supposedly from firing notices printed on pink paper, yet searches of company archives have never turned up a single one.
items.ex: In our board game, Dad's banker character got the pink slip.

items.m: to organize yourself and start doing things properly
items.os: American, 1960s show business: performers had to polish an 'act' before it was fit for the stage.
items.ex: Get your act together tonight — backpack packed, word list reviewed, alarm set.

items.p: go back to the drawing board
items.m: to start over after a plan fails
items.os: From a 1941 New Yorker cartoon by Peter Arno: as a plane crashes, the engineer strolls off saying 'Well, back to the old drawing board.'
items.ex: Our volcano model fizzled, so it's back to the drawing board.

items.m: to keep going until something is completely finished
items.os: From boxing, early 1900s: a fighter who goes the distance lasts every scheduled round without being knocked out.
items.ex: Twenty rounds of words, and Maya went the distance.

items.m: being planned or built right now
items.os: American, 1900s; from a factory's works, where products take shape before anyone sees them.
items.ex: A school garden is in the works for spring.

items.m: to memorize something perfectly
items.os: From the ancient Greek belief that the heart, not the brain, housed memory — French still says apprendre par cœur.
items.ex: She learned all fifty state capitals by heart.

items.m: to learn from your own painful mistakes
items.os: American, early 1900s; possibly from craps, where 'the hard way' is the riskiest roll to win.
items.ex: I learned the hard way that skipping practice shows on stage.

items.m: to change your behavior after a bad experience
items.os: From the schoolroom, where a lesson was a passage drilled until it stuck; figurative since the 1500s.
items.ex: After losing his library book twice, Sam finally learned his lesson.

items.m: to reach the required standard
items.os: American, early 1900s; likely from railroading, where a locomotive that made the grade climbed the slope without stalling.
items.ex: Practice every night and your spelling will make the grade.

items.m: traditional, in the style of an earlier time
items.os: English, 1700s: 'a gentleman of the old school' was one trained in an earlier generation's ways.
items.ex: Grandpa is old school — he drills me with paper flashcards, not apps.

items.m: to succeed outstandingly, far beyond just passing
items.os: From universities, where degrees above a plain pass are awarded 'with honors' — in Latin, cum laude.
items.ex: She didn't just survive the tryout; she passed with honors.

items.m: to stay up all night studying or working
items.os: American college slang, mid-1900s, from cramming for exams until sunrise.
items.ex: Coach says champions sleep — never pull an all-nighter before the bee.

items.m: to do your fair share of the work
items.os: From rowing, early 1900s: each crew member must pull the oar hard enough to move their own body weight.
items.ex: Everyone pulls their weight on chore day, even the twins.

items.p: put your nose to the grindstone
items.m: to work hard and steadily without stopping
items.os: English, 1500s; probably from knife-grinders who bent so low over the spinning grindstone their faces nearly touched it.
items.ex: With the bee two weeks away, it's time to put my nose to the grindstone.

items.m: learning from tough real-life experience instead of classrooms
items.os: American, 1800s; a joking 'university' whose only lessons are life's knocks and setbacks.
items.ex: Grandma never finished school, but she graduated from the school of hard knocks.

items.m: to teach someone the basics of a task
items.os: Nautical, 1800s: new sailors had to learn which of a ship's many ropes hauled which sail.
items.ex: The fifth-graders showed the new kid the ropes at lunch.

items.m: to learn something quickly in a short, intensive burst
items.os: American, mid-1900s; 'crash' meaning done at sudden, urgent speed, as in a wartime crash program.
items.ex: Mom took a crash course in Greek roots to quiz me properly.

items.m: to punish someone so they won't repeat a mistake
items.os: From the schoolroom, 1600s: a lesson was drilled until it stuck, so any correcting experience became a 'lesson.'
items.ex: The stomachache after three desserts taught him a lesson.

items.m: the teacher's favorite student
items.os: American school slang, early 1900s; the favored child was 'petted' — an old word for pampered.
items.ex: Erasing the board every day earned Mia the teacher's pet label.

items.m: reading, writing, and arithmetic — the basics of schooling
items.os: English, early 1800s; often credited to a toast by London alderman Sir William Curtis — 'reading, riting and rithmetic' — though the attribution is shaky.
items.ex: Our principal says spelling sharpens the first of the three R's.

items.m: good enough; meeting the required standard
items.os: From bare-knuckle boxing, 1800s: a fighter had to toe a line scratched in the ground to prove he could go on.
items.ex: My handwriting wasn't up to scratch, so I recopied the essay.

items.m: to hurry to finish before time runs out
items.os: From racing, early 1900s: in time trials, riders compete against the clock instead of each other.
items.ex: We worked against the clock to finish the diorama before bedtime.

items.m: to work perfectly and effortlessly
items.os: English, early 1900s; from dreams, where everything happens smoothly without effort.
items.ex: Dad's trick for remembering 'necessary' works like a dream.

items.m: to rise gradually through effort from a low position
items.os: English, 1800s; success as a climb, each job a rung nearer the top.
items.ex: She worked her way up from classroom bee to the national stage.

items.m: to get a top score on a test
items.os: American student slang, mid-1900s: the ace, the highest card in the deck, turned into a verb for a perfect score.
items.ex: Study your roots tonight and you'll ace the test tomorrow.

items.m: to imitate someone's idea or plan instead of creating your own
items.os: Modern American slang from the classroom joke 'Can I copy your homework? Sure, just change it a little,' which spread online in the 2010s.
items.ex: The rival robotics team copied our homework, right down to the wheel design.

items.m: jobs get done faster when everyone helps
items.os: English proverb recorded since the 1300s, in the medieval tale of Sir Bevis of Hampton.
items.ex: Many hands make light work, so the whole family folded laundry together.

items.m: the more you practice, the better you become
items.os: English proverb from the 1500s, first recorded as 'use makes mastery.'
items.ex: Practice makes perfect, so we run twenty spelling words every night.

items.m: a small gift meant to please someone in charge
items.os: American, 1800s: frontier families often paid poorly salaried teachers in food, and a shiny apple became the classic offering.
items.ex: Bringing cookies to the coach felt like an apple for the teacher.

items.m: a narrow escape from danger or failure
items.os: American, late 1800s; likely from sports officials' calls in contests too close to judge.
items.ex: Spelling 'rhythm' right on my last breath was a close call.

items.m: something bad that very nearly happened
items.os: From World War II, when a bomb that barely missed its target was logged as a near miss.
items.ex: Forgetting my permission slip until the bus door opened was a near miss.

items.m: despite every difficulty, when success seemed impossible
items.os: From betting, 1800s: the odds are the numbers bookmakers stack against an unlikely winner.
items.ex: Against all odds, our smallest speller beat three eighth-graders.

items.m: surprising early success by someone brand new
items.os: From 1800s card tables, where newcomers seemed to win their first games uncannily often.
items.ex: She called my first-round win beginner's luck, so I won the second too.

items.m: it is wiser to be careful than to take risks
items.os: Popularized by Samuel Lover's 1837 Irish novel Rory O'More, first as 'better sure than sorry.'
items.ex: Pack the umbrella — better safe than sorry.

items.m: naturally fortunate your whole life
items.os: From astrology: for centuries people believed the stars overhead at your birth fixed your fate.
items.ex: Winning the raffle twice, Leo must be born under a lucky star.

items.m: to end a magical or trance-like influence
items.os: From fairy tales, where a witch's spell holds until one act — often a kiss or a spoken word — shatters it.
items.ex: The recess bell broke the spell of our silent reading hour.

items.m: to narrowly escape dying
items.os: English, 1800s; from the old image of Death as a figure you might trick out of his prize.
items.ex: In the movie, the explorer cheats death three times before breakfast.

items.m: to take reckless, life-risking chances
items.os: British, mid-1900s: motor-racing reporters wrote of drivers 'dicing' wheel-to-wheel, gambling their lives like a throw of dice.
items.ex: Riding without a helmet is dicing with death, Dad warns.

items.m: to barely avoid disaster
items.os: American, 1900s; from the battlefield image of a bullet that just misses.
items.ex: I dodged a bullet — the pop quiz covered the one chapter I'd read.

items.m: going through a stretch of misfortune and hardship
items.os: English, 1800s gamblers' talk: being 'down' meant losing money at the tables.
items.ex: Our team was down on its luck until the new goalie arrived.

items.m: good luck comes your way
items.os: From Fortuna, the Roman goddess of luck, whose smile or frown was believed to decide human fate.
items.ex: Fortune smiled on me: my final word was one I'd practiced that morning.

items.m: to keep surviving trouble that should have finished you
items.os: From the old belief that cats, agile enough to survive great falls, live nine times; an English proverb by the 1500s.
items.ex: Our class hamster has nine lives — he's escaped his cage four times.

items.m: to have sudden, enormous good luck
items.os: American, 1900s; from winning a lottery jackpot on a single lucky ticket.
items.ex: Getting the last two tickets to the game felt like hitting the lottery.

items.m: exactly what was needed
items.os: English, early 1900s, from the days when a doctor's prescription — rest, sea air, a tonic — was treated as a command.
items.ex: A quiet Saturday was just what the doctor ordered after exam week.

items.m: something that seems friendly but brings ruin
items.os: An allusion to the Bible, where Judas betrays Jesus with a kiss; the phrase spread in 1940s America.
items.ex: Bragging before the bee is the kiss of death, our coach says.

items.m: a superstitious tap on wood to keep good luck from turning
items.os: The tale that pagans knocked on trees to summon protective spirits is a myth; it more likely comes from tiggy-touchwood, a Victorian children's chasing game where touching wood made you safe.
items.ex: No spelling slip-ups yet this season — knock on wood.

items.m: luck imagined as a woman who helps or abandons you
items.os: A modern echo of Fortuna, Rome's luck goddess; American gamblers of the 1900s begged Lady Luck for winning rolls.
items.ex: Lady Luck was with us — every green light on the way to school.

items.m: a final performance or effort before stopping
items.os: From Edwin O'Connor's 1956 novel The Last Hurrah, about an aging mayor's final campaign.
items.ex: The eighth-graders' talent-show act was their last hurrah before graduation.

items.m: a rare, almost impossible success captured for a moment
items.os: American; it evokes Benjamin Franklin's 1752 kite experiment drawing lightning's charge into a jar, but the idiom spread through 1940s baseball talk.
items.ex: Our whole class acing the same test was lightning in a bottle.

items.m: a result decided purely by chance
items.os: From card games, where your hand depends on the cards you draw, not on skill.
items.ex: Getting the easy word list was just the luck of the draw.

items.m: extraordinary good fortune
items.os: American, 1800s: when Irish miners kept striking gold and silver out West, envious rivals sniffed that it was luck, not skill.
items.ex: Finding five dollars and winning the raffle? That's the luck of the Irish.

items.m: a sudden piece of good fortune
items.os: American, 1800s; probably from billiards, where a good opening break scatters the balls your way.
items.ex: Her lucky break came when the champion misspelled an easy word.

items.m: a run of repeated good luck
items.os: From gambling, 1800s: a streak is an unbroken line, like one stroke of paint, of win after win.
items.ex: My lucky streak at checkers ended when Grandma stopped letting me win.

items.m: fresh energy or a fresh chance after a bad period
items.os: English, 1800s, from property law: renewing a lease lets a tenant stay on, as if life's contract were extended.
items.ex: New sneakers gave Grandpa's morning walks a new lease of life.

items.m: no; it is not going to happen
items.os: American, 1920s: players in illegal street craps games hid the dice from police, and judges threw out cases with no dice as evidence.
items.ex: I begged for ice cream before dinner, but Mom said no dice.

items.m: to risk losing what you have by demanding more
items.os: American gamblers' warning, early 1900s: keep betting after a winning streak and luck will turn.
items.ex: You got an extra cookie already — don't push your luck.

items.m: a single sudden piece of good fortune
items.os: English, 1800s; a 'stroke' was a sudden blow, like a stroke of lightning out of nowhere.
items.ex: By a stroke of luck, the library's last copy was still on the shelf.

items.m: to accept a risk and hope for the best
items.os: English, 1500s; 'chance' comes from a Latin word for how the dice fall.
items.ex: I forgot to study the bonus words, so I'll just take my chances.

items.m: outrageously good luck
items.os: British, 1800s, from the grumble that the wicked escape every scrape — the devil looks after his own.
items.ex: He guessed every answer right — the luck of the devil.

items.m: a topic too dangerous for anyone to touch
items.os: American politics, 1980s: a Speaker's aide called Social Security 'the third rail of politics — touch it and you die,' after the electrified rail that powers subway trains.
items.ex: Asking to skip the science fair is the third rail with Dad.

items.m: to take a foolish risk that invites bad luck
items.os: From the Greek and Roman Fates, three goddesses who spun each life's thread — provoking them was asking for trouble.
items.ex: Don't tempt fate by bragging before the winners are announced.

items.m: to attempt something and see if fortune favors you
items.os: English, 1700s, from fairground games and lotteries inviting passers-by to try their luck.
items.ex: At the school fair, I tried my luck at the ring toss.

items.m: a sudden change in luck, good or bad
items.os: From the medieval Wheel of Fortune: the goddess Fortuna spun a great wheel that lifted people up or dashed them down.
items.ex: A lucky turn of fortune put the easiest word last on my list.

items.m: when your time to die or lose finally comes
items.os: Soldiers' slang from around World War I: when a man's service number 'came up,' his luck was over.
items.ex: In dodgeball, when your number is up, you're out — no arguing.

items.m: to enjoy and use every moment you have
items.os: Modern English, 1900s; from the picture of filling life like a cup to the brim.
items.ex: Grandma lives life to the fullest — salsa class Mondays, kayaking Saturdays.

items.m: bolder, louder, and more impressive than ordinary people
items.os: English, 1900s; from statues and portraits made bigger than their subjects to look heroic.
items.ex: Our principal's larger-than-life laugh fills the whole gym.

items.m: an exciting, risky, high-speed way of living
items.os: American, 1970s, from highway fast lanes; the Eagles' 1976 song 'Life in the Fast Lane' fixed it in the language.
items.ex: Three clubs, two teams, and piano — my sister loves life in the fast lane.

items.p: life is not a bed of roses
items.m: life includes hardship, not only comfort
items.os: From Christopher Marlowe's 1599 poem promising his love 'beds of roses' — an image of perfect ease later turned on its head.
items.ex: Losing in round one taught me life is not a bed of roses.

items.m: something extremely serious and urgent
items.os: English, 1600s, from sickbeds and trials where the outcome literally decided whether someone lived.
items.ex: Finding my lucky pencil before the bee felt like a matter of life and death.

items.m: so sick you seem close to dying
items.os: English, 1500s; it pictures Death as a doorkeeper whose threshold the gravely ill stand upon.
items.ex: I had a cold, not the flu, but I moaned like I was at death's door.

items.m: completely, unmistakably dead or finished
items.os: English, 1300s, beloved by Shakespeare and Dickens; carpenters 'deadened' a doornail by bending its point flat so it could never be reused — though that explanation is uncertain.
items.ex: My tablet battery was dead as a doornail by the third quiz app.

items.m: so deeply asleep that nothing wakes you
items.os: English, 1800s; earlier a religious phrase for monks who had renounced worldly life.
items.ex: After the sleepover, my brother was dead to the world until noon.

items.m: to die, or to finally stop working
items.os: From the King James Bible (1611), where the dying 'give up the ghost' — release the spirit.
items.ex: Our old printer gave up the ghost right before the project deadline.

items.m: a work shift through the middle of the night
items.os: The story that it comes from men guarding graves against accidental burials is a myth; American, 1880s, named for the ghostly quiet of working past midnight.
items.ex: Mom works the graveyard shift at the hospital, so we whisper all morning.

items.m: I will never allow that to happen
items.os: English, 1800s; the ultimate refusal — you would have to defeat me first.
items.ex: 'Skip your homework for video games? Over my dead body,' said Dad.

items.m: a race or contest ending in an exact tie
items.os: From 1700s horse racing: a 'heat' was one round, and a tied heat was 'dead' — void, so it was run again.
items.ex: The spelling bee ended in a dead heat, so both champions got trophies.

items.m: stunningly beautiful
items.os: American, 1980s; beauty so striking it could stop onlookers cold, spread by fashion magazines.
items.ex: Mom looked drop-dead gorgeous in her old prom photos.

items.m: a group whose inner quarrels will destroy it
items.os: From the Bible, Mark 3:25 — 'a house divided against itself cannot stand' — made famous by Abraham Lincoln's 1858 speech.
items.ex: Arguing over team names left our project group a house divided.

items.p: a place for everything and everything in its place
items.m: keep things organized; every item has its proper spot
items.os: A Victorian tidiness motto of the 1800s, preached in household guides and often credited, without proof, to Benjamin Franklin.
items.ex: Mom's craft closet proves a place for everything and everything in its place.

items.m: somewhere to live
items.os: English, 1500s; shelter reduced to its barest essential — a roof.
items.ex: Dad says be thankful for dinner and a roof over your head.

items.m: to delight an audience into wild applause
items.os: Theater slang, 1700s: the 'house' is the audience, and applause could roar loud enough to collapse the building.
items.ex: Her tap-dance finale brought the house down at the talent show.

items.m: to destroy everything, including what you value, over one problem
items.os: From the old English proverb 'burn not your house to fright the mouse away' — total destruction for a small pest.
items.ex: Quitting the whole team over one bad game is burning the house down.

items.m: care for your own family before helping outsiders
items.os: English proverb echoing the Bible's call to care for one's own household; in this form by the 1600s, in Sir Thomas Browne.
items.ex: Charity begins at home, so I helped my little sister study first.

items.m: to sweep away bad practices or replace a whole group
items.os: American, early 1900s; from spring cleaning, when a home is scrubbed top to bottom, applied to scandal-hit teams and offices.
items.ex: The new coach cleaned house, changing every drill and warm-up.

items.m: affecting you personally, sometimes uncomfortably so
items.os: English, 1800s; a remark that lands near where you actually live — your private life.
items.ex: The story about a nervous speller hit close to home for me.

items.m: past wrongdoings return to cause you trouble
items.os: From the motto of Robert Southey's 1810 poem The Curse of Kehama: curses, like chickens, come home to roost.
items.ex: Skipping practice all month came home to roost at tryouts.

items.p: eat someone out of house and home
items.m: to eat so much you strain a household's supplies
items.os: From Shakespeare's Henry IV, Part 2 (1600), where Mistress Quickly complains Falstaff has 'eaten me out of house and home.'
items.ex: My teenage cousins visited for a week and ate us out of house and home.

items.p: get on like a house on fire
items.m: to become fast friends immediately
items.os: English, early 1800s: wooden, thatch-roofed houses burned ferociously fast — like an instant friendship catching.
items.ex: The two new students got on like a house on fire by lunchtime.

items.p: people who live in glass houses shouldn't throw stones
items.m: don't criticize others for faults you have yourself
items.os: Traced to Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde (1385) and polished into this form by George Herbert in 1651.
items.ex: You missed three words too — glass houses, remember?

items.m: to rise extremely high, or to explode with anger
items.os: American, 1900s; prices or tempers shooting up so fast they burst through the ceiling and keep going.
items.ex: When the bake sale made triple last year's money, our cheers went through the roof.

items.m: home and family life, warm and dear
items.os: An old English pairing: the hearth — the fireplace — was the warm center where families cooked and gathered.
items.ex: The holidays pull everyone back to hearth and home.

items.m: to strike you as personally and painfully true
items.os: English, 1600s; from fencing, where a thrust that 'hits home' reaches the body itself.
items.ex: The coach's speech about teamwork really hit home after our loss.

items.m: a place as comfortable as your own home
items.os: English, 1800s, from travelers' praise for inns that felt homelike.
items.ex: Grandma's kitchen is my home away from home.

items.p: home is where the heart is
items.m: your true home is wherever the people you love are
items.os: Often credited to the Roman writer Pliny the Elder, though no one has found it in his works; common in English by the 1800s.
items.ex: Our new apartment felt strange until Mom said home is where the heart is.

items.m: blunt, uncomfortable facts about yourself
items.os: British, 1700s: truths told at home, where family members spare no feelings.
items.ex: My sister told me some home truths about my messy binder.

items.m: someone or something everyone knows
items.os: English, 1800s; a name so familiar it is spoken in every household.
items.ex: Winning nationals made the young speller a household name in town.

items.m: to manage a home's cooking, cleaning, and daily running
items.os: English, 1400s, from the days when running a household was itself a full occupation.
items.ex: While Mom traveled, Dad and I kept house together.

items.m: relax and act as comfortably as in your own house
items.os: English, 1800s hospitality formula, granting a guest a family member's freedoms.
items.ex: Make yourself at home while I grab the flashcards.

items.m: ordinary; not especially good
items.os: Late 1800s, from soldiers and travelers whose letters home reported only the remarkable; popularized in World War I.
items.ex: The cafeteria's new pizza is nothing to write home about.

items.m: among the people at home while others are away at work or war
items.os: From World War I, when civilians' effort at home was declared a second battle front.
items.ex: With Dad at the tournament, all was calm on the home front.

items.m: to fix your own affairs before criticizing others
items.os: From the Bible, Isaiah 38: 'Set thine house in order,' a prophet's warning to a dying king.
items.ex: Clean your own desk first — put your house in order before judging mine.

items.m: to celebrate or cheer very loudly
items.os: American, 1800s; noise so mighty it could lift the roof clean off.
items.ex: The gym raised the roof when our team scored at the buzzer.

items.m: completely safe and dependable
items.os: British, mid-1800s: after risky railway shares crashed, Victorians called bricks and mortar the surest investment of all.
items.ex: Your secret is safe as houses with me.

items.p: the lights are on but nobody's home
items.m: someone looks alert but isn't really thinking
items.os: American, late 1900s; a joking picture of a lit-up house standing empty.
items.ex: I asked my brother the same question three times — lights on, nobody home.

items.m: to welcome everyone in freely
items.os: English, 1800s; from flinging a grand house's doors wide on feast days.
items.ex: The school threw open the doors for family science night.

items.m: for a very long time, maybe forever
items.os: English, 1500s: cows amble back from pasture at their own unhurried pace, sometimes not until dawn.
items.ex: You can beg till the cows come home; bedtime is still nine.

items.m: almost everything imaginable, far more than needed
items.os: Early 1900s; in the World Wars soldiers joked that bombardments hurled everything at them but the kitchen sink — the one thing plumbed down too tight to throw.
items.ex: My sister packed everything but the kitchen sink for one night at camp.

items.m: in trouble with someone because of what you did
items.os: American, 1920s; often traced to Peter Pan (1904), where Mr. Darling punishes himself by living in the dog's kennel, though the link is unproven.
items.ex: I'm in the doghouse for tracking mud across Mom's clean floor.

items.m: to share information or feelings openly and honestly
items.os: From meetings and card games, where papers or cards laid on the table are visible to everyone; nothing stays hidden.
items.ex: At the family meeting, Dad asked everyone to lay it on the table and share what was bothering them.

items.m: no longer available as an option
items.os: From negotiations, where offers sit on the table while under discussion and are removed when withdrawn; American, 1900s.
items.ex: After the broken lamp, video games before homework were off the table.

items.m: offered and open for discussion or consideration
items.os: From diplomacy and business: a proposal placed on the meeting table is there for everyone to examine.
items.ex: A trip to the science museum is on the table if we finish our chores.

items.p: put all your cards on the table
items.m: to reveal your plans and intentions honestly
items.os: From card games: a player who shows every card in their hand is hiding nothing; recorded in English since the 1500s.
items.ex: I put all my cards on the table and admitted I hadn't studied my word list.

items.m: to hide a problem instead of dealing with it
items.os: From lazy housecleaning: dirt swept under a rug looks gone but is still there; American, early 1900s.
items.ex: Don't sweep the bad test grade under the rug — tell Mom and make a study plan.

items.p: wake up and smell the coffee
items.m: to finally notice the reality of a situation
items.os: American, mid-1900s; advice columnist Ann Landers used it so often that readers made it her signature line.
items.ex: Wake up and smell the coffee — the spelling bee is Friday and you haven't practiced.

items.p: wash your dirty linen in public
items.m: to discuss private family problems where strangers can hear
items.os: From a French proverb Napoleon famously quoted: dirty laundry should be washed at home, within the family; in English since the 1800s.
items.ex: Grandma says arguing at the school picnic is washing your dirty linen in public.

items.m: a new leader arrives full of energy and makes big changes
items.os: An English proverb recorded in John Heywood's famous 1546 collection: a fresh broom, its bristles unworn, sweeps best.
items.ex: Our new principal banned gum on day one — a new broom sweeps clean.

items.p: too many irons in the fire
items.m: trying to handle too many projects at once
items.os: From blacksmiths who heat several iron pieces in the forge at once; with too many, some burn before they can be hammered.
items.ex: With soccer, piano, and the spelling bee, Maya has too many irons in the fire.

items.m: no longer keeping a personal secret hidden
items.os: American, 1900s; grew from the older 'skeleton in the closet,' a secret shut away where visitors cannot see it.
items.ex: My brother finally came out of the closet as the one who ate the last cookies.

items.m: in private, hidden from public view
items.os: From meetings where the doors are literally shut so outsiders cannot listen; English, 1800s.
items.ex: The judges chose the championship words behind closed doors.

items.m: a rule that anyone is welcome to come in and talk
items.os: Named for America's 1899 Open Door policy, which asked that all nations be free to trade with China; later applied to welcoming bosses and teachers.
items.ex: Our teacher has an open-door policy, so you can ask questions any time.

items.m: to refuse to consider something or make it impossible
items.os: From the plain image of closing a door in a visitor's face so they cannot enter; English, 1800s.
items.ex: Missing tryouts shut the door on joining the team this year.

items.p: when one door closes another opens
items.m: when one chance is lost, a new one appears
items.os: Recorded in Cervantes' Don Quixote (1605) as 'where one door is shut, another is opened.'
items.ex: She missed the bee finals, but when one door closes another opens — the writing club invited her the same week.

items.m: to show up somewhere you are not welcome
items.os: Your body blocking the light in a doorway casts a shadow inside; used since the 1700s, usually as 'never darken my door again.'
items.ex: After the food fight, the twins were told never to darken the cafeteria's door again.

items.m: visiting every house in an area, one by one
items.os: From salesmen and canvassers of the 1800s who knocked at each house along a street in turn.
items.ex: Our class went door to door selling cookies for the field-trip fund.

items.m: very close by, or suddenly yours to deal with
items.os: From the step outside a front door: whatever is left there — a gift or a problem — greets you the moment you open it.
items.ex: With the state finals at our doorstep, the whole team practiced every night.

items.m: the one thing that matters most for succeeding
items.os: 'Key' has meant 'the thing that unlocks' since medieval times, when treasure chests and castle gates opened to a single key.
items.ex: Coach says practicing a little every day is the key to success.

items.m: to argue or clash stubbornly with someone
items.os: From stags and bulls whose antlers or horns tangle together when they fight head to head; American, 1800s.
items.ex: My sister and I lock horns over whose turn it is to load the dishwasher.

items.m: kept safely locked away
items.os: Recorded in English since the 1300s, when valuables were kept in heavy wooden chests with iron locks.
items.ex: Mom keeps the birthday presents under lock and key until the party.

items.m: a short time when something is possible
items.os: Popularized by space-program talk of 'launch windows' — the brief moments when a rocket can lift off and still reach its target; 1960s.
items.ex: Sign-ups close Friday, so the window of opportunity to enter the bee is small.

items.m: looking at goods in store windows without buying anything
items.os: From strolling past the big glass shop displays of early-1900s department stores, admiring without spending.
items.ex: We went window shopping at the mall but only bought a pretzel.

items.m: a task that is pointless or certain to fail
items.os: English, 1700s; echoes the old workshop prank of sending a new apprentice to fetch striped paint or a left-handed hammer.
items.ex: Looking for my brother's 'invisible pet' turned out to be a fool's errand.

items.m: someone who ignores the rules and does as they please
items.os: From the Bible, Romans 2:14, which describes people who 'are a law unto themselves.'
items.ex: You can't be a law unto yourself at school — everyone follows the same rules.

items.p: a legend in your own lifetime
items.m: famous for great deeds while still alive
items.os: First written of nurse Florence Nightingale in Lytton Strachey's 1918 book Eminent Victorians: 'she was a legend in her lifetime.'
items.ex: Winning the national bee three times made her a legend in her own lifetime.

items.m: something done only to achieve something else
items.os: From philosophy: thinkers like Immanuel Kant warned against treating people as mere means to an end rather than ends in themselves.
items.ex: For Leo, flashcards are just a means to an end: the championship trophy.

items.m: something unpleasant that must be accepted to get results
items.os: An ancient idea; Thomas Paine's 1776 pamphlet Common Sense called government 'a necessary evil.'
items.ex: Dad calls early alarm clocks a necessary evil on school days.

items.p: a shadow of your former self
items.m: much weaker or less impressive than you once were
items.os: Shadows are thin, gray copies of solid things; English writers have used the image for faded people since the 1500s.
items.ex: After the flu, our goalie was a shadow of his former self at practice.

items.m: something that shows what the current era is like
items.os: From the Bible, Matthew 16:3, where Jesus asks whether people can read 'the signs of the times.'
items.ex: Kids studying spelling words on phones instead of index cards is a sign of the times.

items.m: honest and open, with nothing hidden
items.os: From card players keeping their hands above the table — the 'board' — where no one can swap cards secretly; English, 1600s.
items.ex: The judges kept the scoring completely above board, showing every point.

items.m: to make an argument or bad situation even worse
items.os: The Roman historian Livy used the image of pouring fuel on flames two thousand years ago.
items.ex: Teasing your sister when she's already mad just adds fuel to the fire.

items.p: all that glitters is not gold
items.m: attractive things are not always valuable
items.os: Made famous by Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice (1596): 'All that glisters is not gold.'
items.ex: The shiny claw-machine trophy broke in a day — all that glitters is not gold.

items.m: a good ending makes the earlier troubles worth it
items.os: An old English proverb that Shakespeare turned into the title of his comedy around 1605.
items.ex: We got lost on the field trip but found the museum anyway — all's well that ends well.

items.m: a proposal so tempting or so threatening that refusing is impossible
items.os: Made famous by the 1972 film The Godfather: 'I'm going to make him an offer he can't refuse.'
items.ex: Extra dessert for washing the dishes? That's an offer I can't refuse.

items.m: by chance; as things happened to turn out
items.os: Shakespeare used it in The Merry Wives of Windsor (1602).
items.ex: As luck would have it, the final word was one I'd practiced that very morning.

items.m: at a point where you must make an important choice
items.os: Travelers at a crossroads must pick one road; in old folklore, crossroads were magical places where fateful choices were made.
items.ex: At a crossroads between band and chess club, Mia finally chose band.

items.m: accepting something as it appears, without checking deeper
items.os: From coins and banknotes, whose 'face value' is the number stamped on the front — whatever the metal or paper is really worth.
items.ex: Don't take the rumor about canceled recess at face value — ask a teacher.

items.m: returning to the simplest, most important ideas
items.os: American, 1970s: a 'back to basics' movement pushed schools to refocus on reading, writing, and arithmetic.
items.ex: After three misspelled words, Coach took us back to basics with short-vowel drills.

items.m: holding your breath in worry or excitement
items.os: 'Bated' is a shortened 'abated,' meaning held back; Shakespeare coined the phrase in The Merchant of Venice (1596).
items.ex: The audience waited with bated breath — that's b-a-t-e-d, not fishing bait — as she spelled the final word.

items.m: the most important thing of all
items.os: Coined by Shakespeare in Macbeth (1606), where Macbeth wishes one blow could be 'the be-all and the end-all.'
items.ex: One quiz isn't the be-all and end-all of your report card.

items.m: to assume the very thing you are trying to prove
items.os: A 1500s English translation of the Latin logic term petitio principii; today many people use it loosely to mean 'raise the question.'
items.ex: Saying 'I'm right because I'm never wrong' just begs the question.

items.m: people who need help must accept whatever is offered
items.os: Recorded in John Heywood's 1546 collection of English proverbs.
items.ex: I wanted the blue cupcake, but beggars can't be choosers when you arrive last.

items.m: happening privately, out of public view
items.os: From the theater: stagehands work behind the painted scenery, where the audience cannot see them; English, 1700s.
items.ex: Parent volunteers work behind the scenes to run the spelling bee.

items.m: eagerly and with great enthusiasm
items.os: American, early 1900s; origin uncertain — perhaps from the jingling brass bells that decorated horses' harnesses on festive wagon rides.
items.ex: 'Will you come to my recital?' 'I'll be there with bells on!'

items.m: to stretch the rules slightly without fully breaking them
items.os: From the image of bending a stick just short of snapping it; English, 1900s.
items.ex: The teacher bent the rules and gave us five extra minutes on the quiz.

items.m: not related to the main topic
items.os: 'Point' has meant the heart of an argument since medieval times; a remark beside it lands off target.
items.ex: Whether the homework was fun is beside the point — it was due today.

items.m: even the most careful plans can go wrong
items.os: From Robert Burns's 1785 poem To a Mouse, written after his plough wrecked a mouse's nest: 'the best-laid schemes o' mice an' men gang aft agley' (often go astray).
items.ex: Our best-laid plans for a picnic ended when the thunderstorm rolled in.

items.m: completely unacceptable behavior
items.os: A 'pale' was a boundary fence of wooden stakes; the popular story tying the phrase to the English Pale around Dublin is a myth — the figurative use appeared later, in the 1700s.
items.ex: Peeking at another speller's word list is beyond the pale.

items.m: to wait patiently for the right moment
items.os: 'Bide' is an Old English word for 'wait' that survives almost nowhere else in modern speech.
items.ex: Bide your time in the early rounds and save your energy for the hard words.

items.m: the overall situation rather than the small details
items.os: American, early 1900s, when 'the big picture' meant the main feature film showing at a movie theater.
items.ex: One lost game doesn't matter in the big picture of a whole season.

items.m: the very end, no matter how hard it gets
items.os: Sailors call the last stretch of anchor rope, fastened to deck posts named 'bitts,' the bitter end — though the Bible's 'her end is bitter' may have shaped the phrase too.
items.ex: She stayed at the bee until the bitter end, cheering her friend in the final round.

items.m: to be the first to do something, showing others the way
items.os: American pioneers 'blazed' trails by slicing pale marks into tree bark so followers could find the path; 1700s.
items.ex: My aunt blazed a trail as the first person in our family to finish college.

items.m: an ugly thing that spoils a beautiful place
items.os: From ink blots that ruin a clean page, transferred to eyesores that ruin a view; British, 1900s.
items.ex: Grandpa calls the new parking garage a blot on the landscape of his old neighborhood.

items.m: to report wrongdoing to people who can stop it
items.os: From referees whistling to stop a game and old-time police blowing whistles to halt a crime; American, 1930s in the informer sense.
items.ex: Ana blew the whistle when she saw older kids copying homework answers.

items.m: to do something in a completely new way
items.os: From casting: the mold that shapes a statue is smashed afterward so no identical copy can ever be made.
items.ex: Her science project broke the mold — a volcano that erupted glitter.

items.m: an urgent question everyone wants answered
items.os: From the 1800s, echoing the French 'question brûlante' — an issue too hot to touch yet impossible to ignore.
items.ex: The burning question at dinner was who ate the last slice of pizza.

items.m: improving or growing very quickly
items.os: A doubled phrase — a leap and a bound are both jumps — beloved of English writers since the 1700s.
items.ex: His spelling improved by leaps and bounds once he practiced ten words a night.

items.m: for the same reason; in the same way
