items.os: 'Token' meant a piece of evidence in medieval English, so the phrase originally meant 'by the same proof' (1400s).
items.ex: I should sleep early before the bee; by the same token, so should my study buddy.

items.m: to win or come out on top
items.os: From battle reports: the side that 'carried the day' still held the field when the fighting ended.
items.ex: Careful practice with root words carried the day at the regional bee.

items.m: to be the first to blame someone, despite your own faults
items.os: From the Bible, John 8:7: 'He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone.'
items.ex: Before you cast the first stone about messy desks, look at your own.

items.m: using any method you can manage, however messy
items.os: From an old English wrestling style, popular at Lancashire fairs, in which almost any hold was legal.
items.ex: With the printer broken, homework was catch as catch can — we wrote everything by hand.

items.m: failing because you could not choose between two options
items.os: From a joke recorded since medieval times: someone trying to sit on two stools at once lands on the floor between them.
items.ex: Trying to join both the play and the team, Sam was caught between two stools and missed both tryouts.

items.m: to suddenly change your opinion or attitude
items.os: From music: a performer switching to a different melody when the mood — or the audience — changes; English, 1500s.
items.ex: My brother changed his tune about broccoli when Dad added cheese.

items.m: small consolation that does not really help
items.os: English, 1300s; Shakespeare liked it enough to use it in several plays — comfort served cold warms nobody.
items.ex: Being told 'it was a hard word' was cold comfort after I lost in round two.

items.m: to become less shy and more friendly
items.os: From turtles and snails, which hide inside their shells until they feel safe enough to poke out.
items.ex: Drama club helped my quiet cousin come out of her shell.

items.m: to reach a crisis point that demands action
items.os: A doctor's image from the 1500s: a boil swells until it forms a 'head' and finally bursts.
items.ex: The argument over the class hamster's name came to a head at Friday's meeting.

items.m: to accept a difficult situation
items.os: 'Terms' are the conditions of a peace agreement; enemies who come to terms stop fighting; English, 1700s.
items.ex: Jae came to terms with losing the bee and started studying for next year.

items.m: ideas or interests that people share
items.os: Perhaps from the village 'common,' land all the farmers shared for grazing — though it may simply picture two people standing on the same patch of earth.
items.ex: Pizza was the common ground when the twins couldn't agree on a birthday menu.

items.m: what most people believe, which may not actually be true
items.os: Coined in its modern sense by economist John Kenneth Galbraith in his 1958 book The Affluent Society.
items.ex: Conventional wisdom says cramming works, but a little practice each day beats it.

items.m: a fast, intensive lesson in something new
items.os: American, mid-1900s: wartime 'crash' programs trained pilots and nurses at top speed.
items.ex: Grandma gave me a crash course in bread baking the night before the fair.

items.m: the very best of all
items.os: French for 'the cream of the cream': the richest cream rises to the very top of fresh milk; borrowed into English in the 1800s.
items.ex: The national finalists are the crème de la crème of young spellers.

items.p: cross that bridge when you come to it
items.m: deal with a problem only when it actually happens
items.os: An old traveler's proverb; Henry Wadsworth Longfellow quoted it in 1851: 'Don't cross the bridge till you come to it.'
items.ex: Worry about the semifinals later — we'll cross that bridge when we come to it.

items.m: to demand something impossible to get
items.os: From babies who reach and wail for the moon in the sky; Dickens used it in Bleak House (1853).
items.ex: Asking to skip school for a whole month is crying for the moon.

items.m: to skip the details and give the main point
items.os: A storyteller's apology recorded in English since the 1800s, trimming a rambling tale down to its point.
items.ex: To cut a long story short, the dog really did eat my homework.

items.m: a sad or difficult period of time
items.os: Winter's short, lightless days have stood for hard times since Old English; Churchill spoke of 'dark days' in World War II.
items.ex: Grandpa remembers the dark days when the town's factory closed.

items.m: a street or situation with no way forward
items.os: From streets that stop at a wall; printed on maps and street signs since the 1880s.
items.ex: Guessing the spelling without knowing the root was a dead end.

items.m: someone with great qualities hidden under an unpolished surface
items.os: Uncut diamonds look like dull pebbles until a jeweler polishes them; English, 1600s.
items.ex: The shy new student turned out to be a diamond in the rough at math.

items.m: a decision is final and cannot be changed
items.os: Julius Caesar reportedly said 'alea iacta est' — the die is cast — as he crossed the Rubicon river in 49 BC, starting a civil war.
items.ex: Once I handed in my entry form, the die was cast — I was competing.

items.m: a completely different situation or matter
items.os: 'Kettle of fish' comes from 1700s Scottish riverside picnics where fresh salmon boiled in huge kettles — though how it came to mean a situation is uncertain.
items.ex: Spelling words aloud on stage is a different kettle of fish from writing them at home.

items.m: demanding total effort because failure is not an option
items.os: From battle poetry: Robert Burns in 1793 and Tennyson's Charge of the Light Brigade — 'theirs but to do and die.'
items.ex: It was do or die in the final round: spell 'rhythm' or go home.

items.m: two bad things hitting at the same time
items.os: American, 1940s; Al Capp's comic strip Li'l Abner popularized the 'whammy,' a jinxing magical stare.
items.ex: A pop quiz and a fire drill in one morning — what a double whammy.

items.m: having no money, no home, and little hope
items.os: From boxing: a fighter who is knocked down and counted out cannot get up to continue; American, 1800s.
items.ex: The shelter helps neighbors who are down and out get back on their feet.

items.p: draw a line in the sand
items.m: to set a firm limit that must not be crossed
items.os: Old stories tell of a Roman envoy who drew a circle in the sand around a king and demanded an answer before he stepped out — but the modern phrase is American, 1900s.
items.ex: Mom drew a line in the sand: no screens until homework is done.

items.m: wearing clothes that make you look confident and professional
items.os: From John T. Molloy's 1975 bestseller Dress for Success, which coached job-seekers on what to wear.
items.ex: Marcus arrived at the bee dressed for success in his lucky bow tie.

items.m: some people remember everything, especially wrongs done to them
items.os: Elephants really do recall distant water holes and old companions for decades; the saying grew from a Greek proverb about camels and settled on elephants by the early 1900s.
items.ex: Grandma remembered my one fib from kindergarten — an elephant never forgets.

items.m: an unofficial rule treated as seriously as a real one
items.os: A joking addition to the Bible's Ten Commandments, recorded since the 1800s; the most famous version is 'thou shalt not get caught.'
items.ex: In our house the eleventh commandment is 'thou shalt not wake Dad before coffee.'

items.m: the point where something finally stops
items.os: From railroads: the last station, where the track ends and every passenger must get off; American, 1800s.
items.ex: Missing 'onomatopoeia' was the end of the line for me at the regional bee.

items.m: everyone gets a moment of luck or success eventually
items.os: An ancient proverb the scholar Erasmus traced to the Greeks; Shakespeare used it in Hamlet: 'The cat will mew, and dog will have his day.'
items.ex: Last year's first-round loser won the whole bee — every dog has its day.

items.m: everyone must look after themselves; no one will help you
items.os: A sailor's cry when a ship is sinking and order breaks down; Chaucer used a version in the 1300s.
items.ex: When the bell rang for bake-sale leftovers, it was every man for himself.

items.m: every possible method, fair or sneaky
items.os: The 'book' is an imaginary rulebook of schemes and shortcuts; American, 1900s.
items.ex: My little brother tried every trick in the book to stay up past bedtime.

items.m: to be overlooked or missed by a system
items.os: Small things drop through the gaps between floorboards and vanish; American, 1900s.
items.ex: The permission slip fell between the cracks, so Dad signed it a day late.

items.m: to be given up or abandoned before the finish
items.os: From the Bible's parable of the sower (Luke 8:5): seeds that fell by the wayside were trampled and eaten by birds.
items.ex: Piano practice fell by the wayside during spelling-bee season.

items.m: to fail to happen after being planned
items.os: English, 1800s: a plan that falls through drops away beneath you like ground giving way underfoot.
items.ex: Our zoo trip fell through when the bus broke down.

items.m: very different from something
items.os: From the old Scottish saying 'it's a far cry to Lochow' — a place farther away than a shout can carry.
items.ex: The quiet library is a far cry from our noisy cafeteria.

items.m: to look at something with great pleasure
items.os: Shakespeare used it in his sonnets (1590s): eyes can 'feast' on beauty the way mouths feast on food.
items.ex: Feast your eyes on my science-fair volcano!

items.m: a state of extreme excitement
items.os: From the peak of a fever, when a patient's temperature — and wildness — runs highest; English, 1800s.
items.ex: Excitement hit fever pitch when the final two spellers stood up.

items.m: an extra person who is not needed
items.os: A wagon needs only four wheels, so a fifth just adds weight; English by the 1600s, from an older French joke about carriages.
items.ex: With four seats at the game table, I felt like a fifth wheel.

items.m: to keep working bravely for what is right
items.os: From the Bible, 1 Timothy 6:12 — 'Fight the good fight of faith' — later the title of a famous hymn.
items.ex: The librarian fights the good fight to keep story hour running every week.

items.m: to be exactly what is needed
items.os: From American theater posters called 'bills': a star act big enough to fill the whole poster needed no supporting acts; 1800s.
items.ex: We needed a fast reader for the relay, and Priya filled the bill.

items.m: a very small difference between two things
items.os: From drawing: one thin pencil stroke is all that separates the two sides; English, 1900s.
items.ex: There's a fine line between helping with homework and doing it for someone.

items.m: people are helped in the order they arrive
items.os: Chaucer used a version around 1386: whoever comes first to the mill grinds their grain first.
items.ex: Front-row seats at the bee are first come, first served.

items.m: in irregular bursts, stopping and starting
items.os: 'Fit' meant a sudden burst of activity in the 1500s; the pair 'by fits and starts' appeared by the 1600s.
items.ex: My essay grew in fits and starts between snack breaks.

items.m: to do the same as someone else
items.os: From card games: players must play a card of the same suit that was led if they can.
items.ex: When Ava started using flashcards, half the class followed suit.

items.m: a result everyone already knows before it happens
items.os: Coined by Shakespeare in Othello (1604).
items.ex: After she aced every practice round, her victory felt like a foregone conclusion.

items.m: knowing about danger early lets you prepare for it
items.os: From the Latin military maxim 'praemonitus, praemunitus'; in English since the 1500s.
items.ex: The coach shared last year's word list — forewarned is forearmed.

items.m: dishonest or violent wrongdoing
items.os: From unfair play in sports; Shakespeare gave it its dark, criminal twist in Hamlet: 'I doubt some foul play.'
items.ex: When the class hamster's cage stood open, we suspected foul play.

items.m: complete freedom to act as you wish
items.os: From horseback riding: loosening the reins lets the horse choose its own pace — which is why it's spelled 'rein,' not 'reign.'
items.ex: Our teacher gave us free rein to pick any book for the report.

items.m: a new person checking work to catch missed mistakes
items.os: An editors' saying: a reader who has never seen the page spots errors the writer's tired eyes slide past.
items.ex: Ask Mom for a fresh pair of eyes before you turn in your essay.

items.m: back to where something began
items.os: From Shakespeare's King Lear — 'The wheel is come full circle' — fortune's wheel turning back to its starting point.
items.ex: She came full circle: once a nervous speller, now the bee's announcer.

items.m: to learn how to do something after some practice
items.os: American, 1800s; origin uncertain — perhaps from learning the 'hang,' or balance, of a tool like an axe or scythe.
items.ex: Long division was confusing until I got the hang of it.

items.m: compromise, with each side yielding something
items.os: From 1700s English horse racing, where a 'give and take plate' was a race that balanced big and small horses with different weights.
items.ex: Sharing a bedroom takes give and take from both sisters.

items.m: to do the opposite of what most people are doing
items.os: Swimmers and ships struggle when the tide flows the other way; the image is as old as sailing itself.
items.ex: Riya went against the tide and chose the poetry unit when everyone picked comics.

items.m: to be lost, abandoned, or wasted
items.os: Nautical: the 'board' is a ship's side, and masts shot down in battle went by the board into the sea.
items.ex: When the new baby arrived, our quiet mornings went by the board.

items.m: to keep fighting your hardest even when you will probably lose
items.os: From baseball: a batter who strikes out swinging at least went down trying; American, 1900s.
items.ex: Even on the hardest word list, she goes down swinging.

items.m: to keep growing more and more successful
items.os: From Psalm 84 — pilgrims 'go from strength to strength' on the road to Jerusalem.
items.ex: Since joining the study club, her spelling has gone from strength to strength.

items.m: to stop working properly; to spin out of control
items.os: American, early 1900s: haywire, the springy wire that bales hay, tangles wildly and was used for sloppy quick fixes.
items.ex: The projector went haywire right before our class presentation.

items.m: to start behaving wildly or drift far from the plan
items.os: From railways — a train that leaves its rails causes chaos; figurative since the 1800s.
items.ex: Our science project went off the rails when we lost the instructions.

items.m: to try extremely hard, doing whatever it takes
items.os: 'Lengths' once meant the distances a person would travel for a goal; English since the 1600s.
items.ex: Mom went to great lengths to find that out-of-print word book.

items.m: to do something with huge energy and enthusiasm
items.os: American, 1800s: for farm families, a trip to town was the big, thrilling event of the week.
items.ex: The twins went to town decorating their book-report posters.

items.m: to tackle an unpleasant problem boldly and at once
items.os: From garden lore in a 1700s rhyme: stroke a nettle and it stings, but grasp it firmly and it stays soft.
items.ex: She grasped the nettle and told the teacher she'd lost the permission slip.

items.p: the grass is always greener on the other side
items.m: other people's lives always look better than your own
items.os: The Roman poet Ovid wrote that the harvest is richer in another man's field; the grassy English version is American, early 1900s.
items.ex: He wished he were in the other class, but the grass is always greener.

items.m: a situation where the rules are unclear
items.os: From the shades between black (forbidden) and white (allowed); common in English since the mid-1900s.
items.ex: Whether calculators count as homework help is a gray area in our house.

items.m: a playful remark when two people have the same idea
items.os: English, 1600s, originally 'great wits jump' — 'jump' meant agree; teasers later added 'and fools seldom differ.'
items.ex: We both picked 'onomatopoeia' to study — great minds think alike!

items.m: any experience or material you can put to good use
items.os: Grist is grain brought for grinding — a miller profits from every sackful; proverbial since the 1500s.
items.ex: Every tricky word she misses becomes grist for the mill at practice.

items.m: to pass control or leadership to someone else
items.os: From driving horses: whoever holds the reins steers the team.
items.ex: The club president handed over the reins to a fifth grader.

items.m: a sensible middle point between two extremes
items.os: English, 1700s, echoing the Greek 'golden mean' — Aristotle's virtue that sits between too much and too little.
items.ex: We found a happy medium: one hour of practice, then the park.

items.m: to enjoy yourself hugely, especially at a rare opportunity
items.os: Originally an army 'field day' of outdoor drills, 1700s; schools later borrowed it for a day of games.
items.ex: The class had a field day when the teacher misspelled a word.

items.p: have an ace in the hole
items.m: to keep a hidden advantage ready for when you need it
items.os: From stud poker, where the facedown card is 'in the hole'; American, 1880s.
items.ex: Her ace in the hole is knowing all the Greek root words.

items.m: to enjoy two opposite advantages at once
items.os: English, 1800s; usually heard as 'you can't have it both ways' — cousin to having your cake and eating it too.
items.ex: You can't skip practice and win the bee — you can't have it both ways.

items.m: a place or moment of perfect happiness
items.os: From centuries of religious writing dreaming of paradise arriving in this world; English since the 1500s.
items.ex: A rainy Saturday with library books is heaven on earth for her.

items.m: a secret plan hiding behind someone's stated reasons
items.os: 'Agenda' is Latin for 'things to be done'; the suspicious phrase spread through 20th-century politics.
items.ex: His offer to help with chores had a hidden agenda: extra screen time.

items.m: acting as if you are more important than everyone else
items.os: In the 1400s a genuine title of honor for kings and princes; centuries of mocking use flipped it.
items.ex: Winning one round is no reason to get all high and mighty.

items.m: mistakes look obvious after they have already happened
items.os: From eye charts, where 20/20 means perfect vision; American, mid-1900s.
items.ex: Hindsight is twenty-twenty — of course I should have asked for the language of origin.

items.m: unpredictable — sometimes good, sometimes not
items.os: English, 1500s, from shooting practice: some shots hit the mark, others fly wide.
items.ex: My spelling of French loanwords is still hit or miss.

items.m: to be sound and stand up to questioning
items.os: A sound jug holds water without leaking, as a sound excuse holds up without gaps; English, 1600s.
items.ex: His excuse about the missing homework didn't hold water.

items.m: to keep hoping when there is almost no chance left
items.os: From the Bible: Paul says Abraham 'against hope believed in hope' (Romans 4:18).
items.ex: She hoped against hope that her name would be called for the finals.

items.m: if every other plan comes to nothing
items.os: English, in use since the 1600s to introduce the last resort.
items.ex: If all else fails, sound the word out syllable by syllable.

items.p: if it ain't broke, don't fix it
items.m: leave alone what already works well
items.os: American folk advice made nationally famous in 1977 by Bert Lance, President Carter's budget director.
items.ex: Dad kept his old study method — if it ain't broke, don't fix it.

items.m: instantly and without hesitation
items.os: American, 20th century: a heartbeat is the quickest tick the body keeps.
items.ex: I'd trade my dessert for that book in a heartbeat.

items.p: in a league of your own
items.m: so good that nobody else even compares
items.os: From sports leagues that group teams by level; a team above them all has no rivals.
items.ex: At memorizing Latin roots, Priya is in a league of her own.

items.m: openly, where everyone can see — usually of something shocking
items.os: English since the 1500s, pairing bold wrongdoing with full, undeniable sunlight.
items.ex: Someone took my lunch right off the table in broad daylight!

items.m: about to get an unpleasant surprise about the truth
items.os: From being shaken roughly out of sleep instead of waking gently; English, 1800s.
items.ex: Skip the study guide and you're in for a rude awakening on Friday's test.

items.m: at its busiest, liveliest stage
items.os: English, 1600s: 'swing' meant the free, steady motion of something at full power, like a pendulum.
items.ex: By seven o'clock the school fair was in full swing.

items.m: having the title but not the reality
items.os: Said for centuries of kings who wore the crown while others held the real power.
items.ex: He's team captain in name only; his sister makes every decision.

items.m: very clearly and forcefully
items.os: American, 1800s: a double negative that leaves zero room for doubt.
items.ex: Mom said in no uncertain terms that homework comes before video games.

items.m: undecided, with success and failure equally possible
items.os: From weighing scales that hover before tipping; in the Bible, Daniel tells a king he was 'weighed in the balances.'
items.ex: With two spellers left, the championship hung in the balance.

items.m: kept from knowing what is going on
items.os: Darkness has stood for ignorance since ancient philosophy; English speakers have been 'kept in the dark' since the 1600s.
items.ex: We kept Dad in the dark about his surprise birthday cake.

items.m: when everything is weighed up; ultimately
items.os: Borrowed in the 1800s from the French 'en dernière analyse', a favorite phrase of philosophers.
items.ex: In the final analysis, steady practice matters more than luck.

items.m: having inside information others lack
items.os: English, 1800s; 'the know' was slang for the circle that shares a secret.
items.ex: Kids in the know line up early for the good library beanbags.

items.m: included among the people kept informed
items.os: American office and military slang, mid-1900s, likely from communication circuits that 'loop' messages to everyone connected.
items.ex: Keep Grandma in the loop about the bee schedule — she wants to come.

items.m: still forming; on the way to becoming something
items.os: English since the 1400s: 'making' as manufacture — a loaf still in the oven, a champion still in training.
items.ex: With all that practicing, she's a champion in the making.

items.m: right after something, and as a result of it
items.os: A ship's wake is the churned trail it leaves behind; events have followed 'in the wake' since the 1800s.
items.ex: In the wake of the snowstorm, the spelling bee moved to Monday.

items.m: doing what you love and do best
items.os: From the ancient four elements — earth, air, fire, water; every creature was believed to thrive in its own.
items.ex: On stage with a microphone, my sister is in her element.

items.m: to raise a price suddenly and sharply
items.os: From the jack, the tool that cranks cars and houses upward; American, early 1900s.
items.ex: The fair jacked up the price of popcorn on opening day.

items.m: to help someone remember something
items.os: 'Jog' has meant to nudge or shake since the 1500s — a little push to wake a sleepy memory.
items.ex: Maybe this photo of the field trip will jog your memory.

items.m: no decision or answer has been reached yet
items.os: From courtrooms: while jurors deliberate away from the room, there is no verdict; figurative since the 1800s.
items.ex: The jury is still out on whether flashcards beat word lists.

items.m: coming very soon
items.os: From street directions — a short walk away; Depression-era leaders promised 'prosperity is just around the corner.'
items.ex: Summer vacation is just around the corner.

items.m: to delay choosing so you can still pick later
items.os: From 'option', a paid-for right to choose later in law and business; everyday English by the mid-1900s.
items.ex: She's keeping her options open between chess club and choir.

items.m: to hide troubles by acting as if everything is fine
items.os: English, 1700s: polite society judged a family by the front it showed the street.
items.ex: He kept up appearances at practice even after a rough report card.

items.m: to buy things just because the neighbors have them
items.os: From 'Keeping Up with the Joneses,' a 1913 American comic strip about a family straining to match richer neighbors.
items.ex: We don't need a bigger TV just to keep up with the Joneses.

items.m: extreme gentleness and care in handling someone
items.os: Gloves of kidskin — soft young-goat leather — were too fine for rough work; 'handled with kid gloves' since the 1800s.
items.ex: After his tough loss, the coach treated him with kid gloves.

items.m: to greedily destroy the thing that keeps rewarding you
items.os: Aesop's fable: a farmer cuts open the goose that lays golden eggs to grab them all at once, and gets nothing.
items.ex: Charging friends for homework help might kill the golden goose.

items.m: to know exactly how someone feels about you or your position
items.os: From standing your ground: you cannot defend a spot you have not located; English, 1800s.
items.ex: After the tryout list went up, at least I know where I stand.

items.m: final in order but just as important
items.os: English, 1500s; already a stock phrase when Shakespeare echoed it in King Lear.
items.ex: Last but not least, please welcome our youngest speller!

items.m: survival of the strongest, with no rules or mercy
items.os: Coined by Rudyard Kipling in The Jungle Book (1894) — though his jungle law actually taught the wolves teamwork.
items.ex: Saturday-morning cartoons before chores? In this house it's the law of the jungle.

items.m: to show the right way by doing it yourself first
items.os: Leadership advice as old as armies: commanders who share the march earn more trust than those who only give orders.
items.ex: The captain leads by example, practicing her word list before anyone else.

items.m: with very fast, impressive progress
items.os: A doubled jump — leap and bound both mean spring forward; English writers have paired them since the 1700s.
items.ex: Her vocabulary is growing by leaps and bounds this year.

items.m: to abandon someone right when they need help
items.os: From lourche, a 1500s French board game: a player 'in the lurch' was hopelessly far behind.
items.ex: My project partner moved schools and left me in the lurch.

items.m: don't tamper with something that is already fine
items.os: English proverb, 1700s, originally 'let well alone.'
items.ex: Your essay is great — leave well enough alone and go to bed.

items.m: the less harmful of two bad choices
items.os: From Greek philosophy — Aristotle advised choosing the lesser evil; English by Chaucer's day, the 1300s.
items.ex: Missing recess was the lesser of two evils compared to redoing the whole project.

items.m: forgive past quarrels and move on
items.os: 'Bygones' are simply things gone by; the full saying was already proverbial in 1600s Scotland.
items.ex: The sisters let bygones be bygones and shared the last cupcake.

items.m: to let events unfold without interfering
items.os: Old medical wisdom: when no remedy helps, doctors let the body — nature — do the healing; English since the 1500s.
items.ex: We stopped fussing over the classroom caterpillar and let nature take its course.

items.m: to push a slow person into acting fast
items.os: American, mid-1900s: the joke image of flames under the seat of the world's laziest mule.
items.ex: The deadline lit a fire under both of us to finish the poster.

items.m: mistakes teach us as life goes on
items.os: English proverb since the 1500s: 'one may live and learn.'
items.ex: I packed the wrong word list — oh well, live and learn.

items.m: accept others as they are and expect the same back
items.os: Recorded in the 1600s as a proverb of Dutch traders before English adopted it.
items.ex: Our lunch table's rule is live and let live — no teasing anyone's snacks.

items.p: the long arm of the law
items.m: the police's power to reach wrongdoers anywhere
items.os: From the ancient warning that kings have long arms — Ovid wrote it — updated for the police in the 1800s.
items.ex: In our board game, no robber escapes the long arm of the law.

items.m: skipping the details and getting to the point
items.os: Clipped from 'to make a long story short,' common by the 1800s — Thoreau used it in a letter.
items.ex: Long story short, the dog buried my spelling notebook.

items.m: to focus on the good parts of a bad situation
items.os: English, 1700s–1800s: light as hope — every situation has a sunlit side and a shadowed one.
items.ex: Look on the bright side: you'll know that word for next year's bee.

items.m: to make the standard easier to meet
items.os: From the high jump: drop the crossbar and anyone can clear it — the opposite of raising the bar.
items.ex: The coach refused to lower the bar just because the list was hard.

items.m: to become known and respected for what you do
items.os: An ancient wish — the Tower of Babel's builders wanted to 'make us a name' (Genesis).
items.ex: She made a name for herself as the fastest fact-checker in class.

items.m: to manage with whatever you have
items.os: English, 1800s; Britain's WWII slogan 'Make Do and Mend' urged families to patch old clothes instead of buying new.
items.ex: We forgot the flashcards, so we made do with sticky notes.

items.m: bringing either total success or total failure
items.os: From the older 'make or mar,' used since the 1400s; 'break' won out in 1800s English.
items.ex: The last word of the round can make or break a speller.

items.m: to finish something quickly and easily
items.os: English, 1500s: the 'work' is the task itself, dispatched before it can drag on.
items.ex: My brother made short work of the leftover birthday cake.

items.m: a person who speaks little but means what he says
items.os: Ancient praise: the Bible advises 'let thy words be few,' and Sparta made short speech legendary.
items.ex: Grandpa is a man of few words, but his 'well done' means everything.

items.m: a very long time ago
items.os: Months were once counted by full moons; 1800s English storybooks spread the phrase, often imitating Native American speech.
items.ex: Many moons ago, Dad won his own school spelling bee.

items.m: remember what I say — it will prove true
items.os: First printed in Coverdale's English Bible of 1535: 'heare, and marke my wordes.'
items.ex: Mark my words, that quiet new student will reach the finals.

items.m: something expected that happens automatically
items.os: From law: requests granted 'of course' needed no special permission; everyday English by the 1700s.
items.ex: Checking her backpack the night before school is a matter of course now.

items.m: to compromise, with each side giving up part
items.os: Two travelers who each walk half the distance meet in the middle; proverbial since the 1600s.
items.ex: Mom met me halfway: twenty words tonight, twenty tomorrow.

items.m: the one piece needed to complete a chain or explanation
items.os: From Victorian science's hunt for a fossil creature between apes and humans — a gap in the 'chain of being.'
items.ex: The dictionary's etymology was the missing link for spelling that word.

items.m: a brief time of fame or glory
items.os: Cousin of 'a place in the sun,' the sunny spot the French thinker Pascal described everyone fighting over in the 1600s.
items.ex: Winning the class bee gave him his moment in the sun.

items.m: the bigger the group, the more fun
items.os: Medieval English proverb — the 1300s poem Pearl already has 'the mo the myryer.'
items.ex: Bring your cousins to game night — the more the merrier!

items.m: the biggest, most extreme example of its kind
items.os: From Saddam Hussein's 1991 Gulf War boast, translating Arabic 'umm al-ma'arik' — in Arabic the 'mother' of something is its greatest.
items.ex: Cleaning the garage turned into the mother of all chores.

items.m: to try everything imaginable to make something happen
items.os: English, 1700s: the boast of shifting the two biggest things there are.
items.ex: Dad moved heaven and earth to get to my recital on time.

items.m: to refuse to say anything about a topic
items.os: 'Mum' imitates lips pressed shut — mmm; English since the 1300s, as in 'mum's the word.'
items.ex: She kept mum on the subject of what's inside the birthday box.

items.m: the real point or most important part of an activity
items.os: American, mid-1900s, from sports and showbiz talk; a 1968 TV series fixed it in everyday speech.
items.ex: In spelling bees, careful listening is the name of the game.

items.p: necessity is the mother of invention
items.m: problems push people to invent solutions
items.os: The idea appears in Plato's Republic; the English wording was proverbial by the 1600s.
items.ex: No whiteboard? Necessity is the mother of invention — we used the window and dry-erase markers.

items.m: obviously; as everyone surely knows
items.os: English since the 1500s — a polite wink before saying it anyway.
items.ex: Needless to say, the class hamster is the most popular classmate.

items.m: beside the point; not important to the matter
items.os: English, 1500s; Shakespeare drops it into Othello.
items.ex: Whose turn it was is neither here nor there — the vase is broken.

items.m: never give up, whatever happens
items.os: English, early 1800s; Dickens gave the cry to Grip, the talking raven of Barnaby Rudge.
items.ex: Down to her last lifeline word, she whispered 'never say die.'

items.m: new members who bring fresh energy and ideas
items.os: From the old belief that blood carries a family's vigor — fresh blood renews the whole group; English, 1800s.
items.ex: The debate team needs new blood, so they invited third graders to try out.

items.m: open dislike between two people
items.os: English, 1600s — it once meant the very opposite, love fully returned, before the unfriendly sense won out.
items.ex: There's no love lost between our school's chess team and their rivals.

items.m: improvement demands hard, sometimes uncomfortable effort
items.os: Ben Franklin printed 'no gains without pains' in the 1700s; 1980s workout videos made today's rhyme famous.
items.ex: Drilling fifty words a night is tough, but no pain, no gain.

items.m: the best moment to act is right now
items.os: English proverb recorded since 1562.
items.ex: No time like the present — let's start the book report today.

items.m: absolutely certain; there is only one way to see it
items.os: American, early 1800s: there is just one road to the conclusion.
items.ex: No two ways about it, that was the best science fair project.

items.m: still not knowing, even after it happened
items.os: English, 1500s: slip something past someone and they end up 'never the wiser.'
items.ex: We fixed the torn page, and the librarian was none the wiser.

items.m: too experienced to be tricked
items.os: American, 1800s: only a day-old baby believes everything; the 1950 Broadway hit Born Yesterday kept it famous.
items.ex: Nice try hiding the broccoli, but I wasn't born yesterday.

items.p: not for all the tea in China
items.m: not for any reward, however enormous
items.os: Australian English, 1890s, when China grew most of the world's tea — so all of it meant unimaginable riches.
items.ex: I wouldn't trade my lucky pencil, not for all the tea in China.

items.m: not nearly as good as someone or something else
items.os: Apprentices once held candles so masters could work after dark; anyone unfit even for that couldn't 'hold a candle'; 1600s.
items.ex: Store-bought cookies can't hold a candle to Grandma's.

items.m: to carry on smoothly without pausing or being thrown off
items.os: From music: a good drummer never drops the rhythm; American, 1900s.
items.ex: The fire alarm interrupted her word, and she spelled on without missing a beat.

items.m: not something I am good at
items.os: From card games: your 'strong suit' — hearts or spades — is where your hand wins tricks; 1800s.
items.ex: Fractions are not my strong suit, but spelling is.

items.m: to lose control and react wildly
items.os: From the deep end of a swimming pool, where a rash jump puts you in over your head; early 1900s.
items.ex: Don't go off the deep end over one missed word.

items.m: a traditional belief that is not actually true
items.os: 'Wife' once simply meant woman; Tyndale's 1526 English Bible already warns against 'old wives' fables.'
items.ex: That carrots give you night vision is mostly an old wives' tale.

items.m: enjoying one success after another
items.os: From dice games: a shooter on a hot streak keeps rolling; American, mid-1900s.
items.ex: Ten correct words in a row — she's on a roll!

items.m: friendly with each other
items.os: From 'terms,' the conditions of an agreement — friends keep theirs good; English since the 1600s.
items.ex: Even after the tournament, the two rival schools stayed on good terms.

items.m: in a safe, well-supported position
items.os: A builder's and sailor's relief — firm earth instead of sand or sea; echoes the parable of the house built on rock.
items.ex: Review the root words first so you're on solid ground for the quiz.

items.m: at the very edge of something about to happen
items.os: 'Brink' is an old word for a cliff's edge; English speakers have teetered there figuratively since the 1600s.
items.ex: With one word left, she was on the brink of the championship.

items.m: using the newest and most advanced methods
items.os: The cutting edge is the sharpened part of a blade that slices first; figurative since the mid-1900s.
items.ex: Our science teacher keeps the lab on the cutting edge with new robot kits.

items.m: visible ahead; likely to happen soon
items.os: Sailors watch the horizon — Greek for 'boundary' — where ships and storms first appear.
items.ex: Report cards are on the horizon, so the whole house is studying.

items.m: recovering after an illness or setback
items.os: 'Mend' as in repairing torn clothes; the sick have been 'on the mend' in English since the 1600s.
items.ex: After a week of soup and rest, my brother is on the mend.

items.m: exactly right or accurate
items.os: American, 1900s; probably from betting or marksmen's talk, but no origin is proven.
items.ex: Her guess about the word's Latin origin was right on the money.

items.m: exactly right; precisely on target
items.os: Often traced to early radio, where a finger on the nose signaled a show running exactly on time — plausible but unproven.
items.ex: The bake sale raised one hundred dollars on the nose.

items.m: in deep trouble and close to failing
items.os: From ships driven onto coastal rocks and wrecked; figurative since the 1800s.
items.ex: Our volcano project was on the rocks until Aunt Mia found more baking soda.

items.m: alert and ready to react
items.os: From boxing and dance: weight on your toes lets you spring instantly.
items.ex: Surprise quizzes keep the whole class on their toes.

items.m: finally and for the last time
items.os: English since the 1400s, short for 'once for all time.'
items.ex: Let's settle once and for all who gets the top bunk.

items.m: so remarkable it deserves to be written down
items.os: American, early 1900s, from the record books that log the greatest feats.
items.ex: Spelling the champion word blindfolded at practice — that was one for the books.

items.m: a playful way to say you heard a secret without naming who told you
items.os: Possibly from the Bible's Ecclesiastes, which warns that 'a bird of the air' may carry your words; common in English by the 1500s.
items.ex: A little bird told me you've been practicing your spelling words at recess.

items.m: a burden or past mistake that keeps weighing you down
items.os: From Coleridge's 1798 poem The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, in which a sailor must wear the albatross he shot.
items.ex: The unfinished science project hung like an albatross around her neck all vacation.

items.m: measured in a straight line, ignoring roads and turns
items.os: English, 1700s: crows were believed to fly straight to their destination, so the crow's path meant the shortest route.
items.ex: Our school is only a mile away as the crow flies, but the bus winds for three.

items.m: to pester someone with repeated questions or demands
items.os: From badger-baiting, an old English sport in which dogs relentlessly pestered a badger; the verb stuck by the 1700s.
items.ex: My little brother badgered Mom for ice cream until she finally said yes.

items.m: an idea you cannot stop thinking or talking about
items.os: From the 1500s image of bees buzzing inside one's head; Scottish writers had pinned the bee inside a bonnet by the 1700s.
items.ex: Ever since the science fair, Ria has had a bee in her bonnet about building a robot.

items.m: a silly or scatterbrained person
items.os: American slang from the 1920s, when a bird's tiny brain was assumed to mean tiny intelligence.
items.ex: I felt like a bird brain when I forgot my own locker combination.

items.m: a period when stock prices keep rising
items.os: Named in 1700s London finance as the opposite of the bear market; one guess says bulls toss their horns upward, but that is unproven.
items.ex: Dad said his savings grew because of the bull market, so we celebrated with pizza.

items.m: a period when stock prices keep falling
items.os: From an old proverb about selling the bearskin before catching the bear: 1700s London 'bearskin jobbers' sold shares they didn't yet own, betting prices would drop.
items.ex: Grandpa explained that a bear market is why the news kept showing red arrows.

items.m: a very small amount of money
items.os: American, 1800s: small coins seemed as trifling as the grain scattered for chickens.
items.ex: Ten cents a chore is chicken feed, so I asked Dad for a real allowance.

items.m: something or someone truly wonderful
items.os: American flapper slang of the 1920s, born in the same playful fad that produced the bee's knees.
items.ex: Grandma says my spelling-bee trophy is the cat's pajamas.

items.m: a puzzle where you cannot tell which of two things caused the other
items.os: Ancient thinkers, including Plutarch around 100 CE, seriously debated whether the chicken or the egg came first.
items.ex: Needing experience to get experience is a chicken and egg problem, my sister groans.

items.m: to suddenly refuse to speak
items.os: American, early 1900s, from the way a clam snaps its shell shut tight.
items.ex: The new student clammed up when the teacher asked him to introduce himself.

items.m: a far-fetched story that is hard to believe
items.os: Often traced to tall tales swapped at the Cock and the Bull, two coaching inns in Stony Stratford, England — but that story is a myth; the phrase more likely comes from old fables of talking animals.
items.ex: He gave Mom a cock and bull story about aliens eating his homework.

items.m: someone who imitates what another person does
items.os: New England, 1890s; writer Sarah Orne Jewett was among the first to put it in print.
items.ex: My little sister is such a copycat that she ordered exactly what I ordered.

items.m: a complete mess
items.os: British, 1930s: a botched job looked like scraps fit only for the dog's bowl.
items.ex: My first try at the poster was a dog's breakfast, so I started over.

items.m: the hard, boring part of a job
items.os: English, 1800s, when donkeys hauled the heaviest loads no one else wanted to carry.
items.ex: I did the donkey work of cutting out fifty paper stars for the class play.

items.m: to leave quickly and quietly, often to avoid something
items.os: American, 1800s, from ducking your head low to slip away unseen.
items.ex: He tried to duck out of dish duty by hiding in his room.

items.m: a person who is very enthusiastic and hardworking
items.os: American military slang from World War II for recruits keen to impress, borrowing the beaver's famous busyness.
items.ex: The eager beaver in our class finished the worksheet before the teacher even sat down.

items.m: to eat noisily, messily, or far too much
items.os: An old farmyard comparison: pigs gobble noisily from the trough, snout and all.
items.ex: Mom told me not to eat like a pig at Grandma's birthday dinner.

items.m: to hunt out hidden information
items.os: From the 1500s practice of sending ferrets down burrows to flush out rabbits.
items.ex: The librarian helped me ferret out the one book on medieval castles.

items.m: to try to get information by hinting rather than asking directly
items.os: An angling metaphor used in English since the 1500s: you dangle bait and wait for a bite.
items.ex: My cousin fished for information about her surprise party all week.

items.m: to escape or leave suddenly
items.os: American slang, early 1900s: chickens escaping the henhouse — it first meant breaking out of jail.
items.ex: The moment the last bell rang, we flew the coop for summer vacation.

items.m: to become wildly excited or angry
items.os: American teen slang of the 1950s, comparing wild excitement to a frenzied ape.
items.ex: The crowd went ape when our team won the district spelling bee.

items.m: to behave with wild, unrestrained excitement
items.os: American, early 1900s, from hogs stampeding and squealing at feeding time.
items.ex: The class went hog wild when the teacher announced a pizza party.

items.m: a person or thing used to test something new
items.os: Guinea pigs were common laboratory animals in the 1800s, so by the early 1900s any test subject took their name.
items.ex: I was the guinea pig for Dad's brand-new pancake recipe.

items.p: have a whale of a time
items.m: to enjoy yourself enormously
items.os: American college slang, early 1900s, when 'a whale of' anything meant the biggest and best.
items.ex: We had a whale of a time at the school carnival.

items.m: to become extremely upset or anxious
items.os: English, early 1900s; one old explanation ties it to folk beliefs about cats and expectant mothers, but the true origin is unclear.
items.ex: Mom nearly had kittens when I came home covered in mud.

items.m: a party for women only, often before a wedding
items.os: From the 1800s habit of calling a gathering of women a flock of hens; now it usually means the bride's pre-wedding party in Britain.
items.ex: Aunt Priya's hen party was so loud we could hear the singing next door.

items.m: an arrogant, superior attitude
items.os: In the Middle Ages the powerful literally rode the tallest horses in processions; John Wyclif mentioned 'high horse' around 1380.
items.ex: Get off your high horse and admit you spelled it wrong too.

items.m: to play in a rough, silly way
items.os: From 'horseplay', English for rough frolicking since the 1580s.
items.ex: The coach told us to stop horsing around near the pool.

items.m: a completely different matter
items.os: Shakespeare wrote 'a horse of that colour' in Twelfth Night (1601); Americans later flipped it to a different color.
items.ex: Spelling 'cat' is easy, but 'chiaroscurist' is a horse of a different color.

items.m: in a dangerous place surrounded by hostile people
items.os: From the Bible story of Daniel, thrown into a den of lions and found unharmed the next morning.
items.ex: Walking into the rival school's gym for the final felt like entering the lion's den.

items.m: an unfair, fake court that has already decided you are guilty
items.os: American, 1850s Gold Rush — not Australian; perhaps because such courts 'jumped' over proper legal steps, though no one is sure.
items.ex: The clubhouse trial felt like a kangaroo court because they never let me explain.

items.p: let the dog see the rabbit
items.m: step aside and let someone get on with the job
items.os: From British greyhound racing, where the dog cannot chase until it can see the lure.
items.ex: 'Move over and let the dog see the rabbit,' said Grandpa, taking the jammed printer.

items.m: frozen with surprise or fear
items.os: American, 20th century: deer caught in a car's headlights at night often freeze instead of fleeing.
items.ex: When the announcer called my name, I stood like a deer in headlights.

items.m: someone who prefers to work or live alone
items.os: From wolves that leave the pack to hunt alone; applied to people in early 1900s America.
items.ex: Sam is a lone wolf who studies his word lists by himself in the library.

items.m: to go straight toward something quickly
items.os: American, 1800s, from the belief that a nectar-laden bee flies dead straight back to its hive.
items.ex: After the final bell, we made a beeline for the ice-cream truck.

items.m: people copy what they watch others do, without thinking
items.os: An American saying from the early 1900s, often said to echo older folk tales about imitating monkeys.
items.ex: The toddler copies everything my brother does — monkey see, monkey do.

items.m: a person who stays up late at night
items.os: Owls hunt after dark, and English has called late-nighters night owls since the 1500s; Shakespeare used the image.
items.ex: Dad is a night owl, so he quizzes me on spelling words after dinner.

items.m: no longer young
items.os: Chickens hatched in spring sold at the best prices, so by the 1700s anyone past their freshest years was 'no spring chicken' — a tidy story, though not fully proven.
items.ex: Grandma jokes she's no spring chicken but still beats us at badminton.

items.m: someone or something with only one skill
items.os: From small traveling circuses whose pony could perform just a single trick; American, early 1900s.
items.ex: He's no one-trick pony — he wins at spelling, chess, and soccer.

items.m: crowded very tightly together
items.os: From sardines pressed in neat rows into tins; English, 1800s.
items.ex: We were packed like sardines on the field-trip bus.

items.m: an enemy or threat that looks fierce but is actually weak
items.os: A Chinese expression, made world-famous in 1946 when Mao Zedong used it to dismiss powerful-seeming foes.
items.ex: The quiz looked terrifying, but it was a paper tiger — I knew every word.

items.m: to eat a huge amount greedily
items.os: American slang from the 1970s, borrowed straight from the pig's table manners.
items.ex: We pigged out on popcorn during family movie night.

items.m: to pretend to be asleep or dead
items.os: American, 1800s: opossums flop over and play dead so convincingly that predators lose interest.
items.ex: When Dad called bedtime, my brother played possum on the couch.

items.m: a young, short-lived crush
items.os: English, 1800s, likening a first crush to a puppy's eager, bouncy devotion; 'calf-love' came earlier.
items.ex: Mom says my sister's fifth-grade crush is just puppy love.

items.m: an exhausting, competitive routine that never seems to end
items.os: American, 1930s; it first named a wild dance and a training chase, then settled on the picture of rats endlessly circling a maze.
items.ex: Dad says summer break is his escape from the rat race.

items.m: a driver who selfishly takes up too much road
items.os: Coined in the 1890s, when cyclists and early motorists accused each other of hogging the whole road.
items.ex: Dad muttered 'road hog' when a truck blocked both lanes near school.

items.m: a person who is easily frightened
items.os: American schoolyard slang, early 1900s; Dorothy Parker was among the first to put it in print, in 1933.
items.ex: Don't be a scaredy-cat — the haunted house is just paper decorations.

items.m: to seem suspicious or dishonest
items.os: English, 1800s: fish spoils fast, and its smell betrays it no matter what the seller claims.
items.ex: His excuse about the missing cookies smelled fishy to Mom.

items.m: a person who flits happily from friend to friend
items.os: English, 1800s, comparing a lively guest to a butterfly flitting from flower to flower.
items.ex: Nina is the class social butterfly, chatting with every table at lunch.

items.m: a person who secretly informs on others
items.os: From 1800s American hunters who tied a decoy pigeon to a stool or perch to lure other birds; the 'stool' part is still debated.
items.ex: Nobody wanted to be the stool pigeon who told the teacher about the paper airplanes.

items.m: to wander about grandly doing nothing useful
items.os: British slang from World War II, when tanks cruising aimlessly were said to be swanning about.
items.ex: Instead of packing her schoolbag, my sister swanned around in her new dress.

items.m: to protect and guide someone less experienced
items.os: From a hen sheltering her chicks under her wing, an image as old as the Bible.
items.ex: The fifth-grade champion took the newest speller under her wing.

items.m: to talk honestly and get down to business
items.os: American, 1800s; the famous tale of a settler cheating a Wampanoag hunter out of the turkey is a myth — the real origin is unknown.
items.ex: 'Let's talk turkey,' said Coach: practice is every day or we forfeit.

items.m: a gentle way to explain to children how babies are made
items.os: Often credited to Cole Porter's 1928 song 'Let's Do It', but poets paired courting birds and bees earlier; the coiner is unknown.
items.ex: Dad turned red when my little brother asked about the birds and the bees.

items.m: the person in charge or the winner
items.os: Often traced to sawpit workers, but that story is a myth; it comes from 1800s dogfights, where the winning dog ended up on top.
items.ex: After winning regionals, Maya was top dog at spelling club.

items.m: someone awkward at first who grows into something wonderful
items.os: From Hans Christian Andersen's 1843 tale of a mocked 'duckling' that grows up to be a swan.
items.ex: Our squeaky school band was an ugly duckling that won awards by spring.

items.m: to watch very closely, missing nothing
items.os: From the hawk's famously sharp eyes, which can spot a mouse from far overhead; English by the 1800s.
items.ex: The proctor watched us like a hawk during the spelling test.

items.m: to escape a duty in a sneaky way
items.os: Weasels were said to suck eggs empty while leaving the shell looking whole — an image Shakespeare used; Americans made it a verb around 1900.
items.ex: He tried to weasel out of raking leaves by claiming extra homework.

items.m: to eat something extremely fast
items.os: English, 1800s, from the wolf's reputation for gulping its food without chewing.
items.ex: I wolfed down breakfast so I wouldn't miss the bus.

items.p: you can't teach an old dog new tricks
items.m: people set in their ways struggle to learn new habits
items.os: First recorded in a 1534 English farming book — originally advice about actual old sheepdogs.
items.ex: Grandpa says you can't teach an old dog new tricks, yet he just learned to video-call.

items.m: a bag for taking restaurant leftovers home
items.os: American, 1940s: wartime thrift let diners carry scraps home 'for the dog', though the treats usually fed people.
items.ex: We brought Dad's birthday-dinner leftovers home in a doggy bag.

items.m: a restaurant discount for customers who eat early
items.os: American, mid-1900s, riding on the proverb that the early bird catches the worm.
items.ex: Grandpa loves the diner's early bird special before our evening study sessions.

items.m: for a very long time
items.os: British, early 1900s: a pun stretching 'donkey's ears' — famously long — into donkey's years.
items.ex: We haven't visited the science museum for donkey's years.

items.m: fallen into a much worse condition
items.os: English, 1500s; food not fit for people was thrown to the dogs, so anything ruined had 'gone to the dogs' — the usual, if unproven, explanation.
items.ex: Grandpa grumbles that his favorite team has gone to the dogs.

items.p: like a bear with a sore head
items.m: in a very grumpy, irritable mood
items.os: British, 1800s, from the fearsome temper of a wounded bear.
items.ex: Dad is like a bear with a sore head before his morning coffee.

items.p: like a cat on a hot tin roof
items.m: extremely nervous and unable to keep still
items.os: An American twist on the older British 'cat on hot bricks'; Tennessee Williams's 1955 play made it famous.
items.ex: Waiting for the spelling-bee results, I was like a cat on a hot tin roof.

items.m: rushing around in a panicked, disorganized way
items.os: A farmyard fact: a chicken can dash about briefly after losing its head, so the picture stuck for frantic scrambling.
items.ex: I ran around like a headless chicken looking for my permission slip.

items.p: like shooting fish in a barrel
items.m: extremely easy to do
items.os: American, early 1900s; probably from market fish packed tight in barrels, though no one really shot them — the origin is unproven.
items.ex: For the returning champion, the first-round words were like shooting fish in a barrel.

items.m: furiously angry
items.os: American farm talk from the 1800s — a hen dunked in water flaps and squawks in outrage.
items.ex: Mom was mad as a wet hen when the dog tracked mud across the clean floor.

items.p: put the fox in charge of the henhouse
items.m: to give a job to someone certain to abuse it
items.os: An old farmyard warning found across many languages — Latin speakers already joked about setting a wolf to guard sheep.
items.ex: Letting my candy-loving brother guard the Halloween haul is putting the fox in charge of the henhouse.

items.m: a rare, unpredictable event with huge consequences
items.os: Europeans used 'black swan' for something impossible — until real ones were found in Australia in 1697; writer Nassim Taleb revived the term for finance in 2007.
items.ex: The surprise school closure was a black swan event that upended the bee calendar.

items.p: the canary in the coal mine
items.m: an early warning of danger
items.os: British miners carried caged canaries underground; if the bird wobbled, poisonous gas was near — a practice that lasted until 1986.
items.ex: My falling quiz scores were the canary in the coal mine for my skipped homework.

items.p: the goose that laid the golden egg
items.m: a precious source of ongoing benefit, often destroyed by greed
items.os: From Aesop's fable of the farmer who kills his golden-egg-laying goose expecting a treasure inside — and finds none.
items.ex: The bake-sale brownie recipe is our club's goose that laid the golden egg.

items.p: there are plenty of fish in the sea
items.m: there are many other chances or people left to choose from
items.os: An English proverb since the 1500s: 'there are as good fish in the sea as ever came out of it.'
items.ex: When I lost the raffle, Mom smiled and said there are plenty of fish in the sea.

items.p: when the cat's away the mice will play
items.m: people misbehave when the person in charge is gone
items.os: In English by the 1600s, with even older French and Latin versions of mice celebrating an absent cat.
items.ex: The substitute stepped out, and — when the cat's away, the mice will play — paper planes flew.

items.p: wild horses couldn't drag me away
items.m: nothing could make me leave or miss it
items.os: Perhaps an echo of old tales in which prisoners were dragged by teams of horses; a much gentler figure of speech since the 1800s.
items.ex: Wild horses couldn't drag me away from the championship round.

items.p: you can lead a horse to water but you can't make it drink
items.m: you can give someone an opportunity, but not force them to take it
items.os: One of the oldest recorded English proverbs, written down around 1175 in a book of sermons.
items.ex: I printed the study list, but you can lead a horse to water — my brother won't open it.

items.m: many responsibilities to handle at once
items.os: English, early 1900s, picturing duties heaped up like food on a dinner plate.
items.ex: Between rehearsals and word lists, Ana has a lot on her plate this month.

items.m: a small thing that starts a big quarrel
items.os: In Greek myth, Eris tossed a golden apple marked 'for the fairest' among the goddesses, sparking the quarrel that led to the Trojan War.
items.ex: The last cupcake became the apple of discord at the birthday party.

items.m: two things too different to compare fairly
items.os: English speakers have compared mismatched fruit for centuries — John Ray's 1670 proverb collection used 'apples and oysters'.
items.ex: Comparing soccer and spelling is apples and oranges — I love them both.

items.p: as easy as taking candy from a baby
items.m: extremely easy to do
items.os: American, early 1900s: a baby cannot stop you — though anyone who tries learns a baby can certainly cry.
items.ex: He bragged that the bonus round was as easy as taking candy from a baby.

items.m: the most important person in a group
items.os: Probably from Urdu and Persian 'chiz', meaning 'thing' — Britons in India brought home 'the real chiz', which English ears turned into cheese.
items.ex: The principal is the big cheese who decides when the bee starts.

items.m: something essential that feeds your spirit
items.os: From the Bible, where Jesus says 'I am the bread of life' in the Gospel of John.
items.ex: At choir practice, Grandma calls her old hymn book the bread of life.

items.p: butter wouldn't melt in his mouth
items.m: he looks sweetly innocent but probably is not
items.os: English since the 1530s: someone acting so cool and prim that even butter would stay solid on their tongue.
items.ex: My brother sat there as if butter wouldn't melt in his mouth, hiding the empty cookie jar.

items.m: a mix of rewards and punishments used to persuade someone
items.os: From 1800s cartoons of riders urging a donkey onward with a dangled carrot and a ready stick.
items.ex: Mom uses carrot and stick: dessert for finished homework, no tablet for whining.

items.m: a wide, silly, often fake smile
items.os: Probably from photographers asking subjects to 'say cheese', the word that stretches mouths into a smile; 1900s.
items.ex: He flashed a cheesy grin for the class photo.

items.m: a final small touch that makes something even better
items.os: From the American ice-cream sundae, crowned with a single cherry since the early 1900s.
items.ex: Winning the bee was great; the photo in the paper was the cherry on top.

items.m: to think about something slowly and carefully
items.os: From cattle chewing their cud for hours; English, 1800s.
items.ex: Dad said he'd chew it over before answering my request for a later bedtime.

items.m: great; wonderful
items.os: American student slang of the 1970s and 80s, possibly playing on older bean expressions; a TV catchphrase helped spread it.
items.ex: 'Cool beans!' said Leo when practice moved to the big gym.

items.m: the best people or ideas eventually stand out
items.os: From fresh unhomogenized milk, where the cream really does float up to the top of the pail.
items.ex: Coach says to keep practicing — cream rises to the top.

items.m: the kind of thing you like and enjoy
items.os: British, early 1900s, when tea was such a daily comfort that anything pleasing became 'my cup of tea'.
items.ex: Scary movies aren't my cup of tea; I'd rather do a word puzzle.

items.m: something extremely easy
items.os: American slang first spotted in a 1902 T.A. Dorgan cartoon; why duck soup meant 'easy' was never explained.
items.ex: Fixing the wobbly desk was duck soup for the janitor.

items.m: a teasing way to say someone should feel envious
items.os: Ancient Greeks spoke of 'eating one's heart' with grief; the modern jealous taunt grew up in 1900s America, perhaps via a Yiddish phrase.
items.ex: Eat your heart out, big sister — I finally beat your puzzle record.

items.m: to admit that what you said was wrong
items.os: English since the 1500s — legend says some offenders were made to swallow real documents, though the phrase likely just pictures taking words back.
items.ex: You said I'd never spell 'onomatopoeia' — get ready to eat your words.

items.m: to urge someone to do something, often something foolish
items.os: Nothing to do with eggs: from the Old Norse verb 'eggja', to urge — a cousin of the word 'edge'.
items.ex: His friends egged him on to try the super-spicy salsa.

items.m: involved in many different activities at once
items.os: Shakespeare grumbled in Henry VIII that one meddler had his finger in every man's pie.
items.ex: Our class rep has a finger in every pie — yearbook, recycling club, and the bee.

items.m: the sleepy, sluggish feeling after eating a big meal
items.os: American slang from the late 1900s, dressing post-feast drowsiness in hospital language.
items.ex: After Thanksgiving dinner, the whole family slid into a food coma.

items.m: something wanted more because it is not allowed
items.os: From Eden's forbidden tree in Genesis — the Bible never says apple; that detail came later.
items.ex: The teacher's locked prize cabinet made those stickers forbidden fruit.

items.m: to become wildly excited or crazy
items.os: American campus slang of the 1960s, likely riffing on 'go ape' and monkeys' love of bananas.
items.ex: The gym went bananas when our mascot did a backflip.

items.m: to become crazy, furious, or wildly excited
items.os: From 1800s slang 'nut' for head — to go off your nut was to lose your mind.
items.ex: Mom will go nuts if we track sand through the hallway.

items.m: not properly thought through
items.os: English, 1600s: like bread pulled from the oven too soon — doughy in the middle.
items.ex: Building a treehouse in one afternoon was a half-baked idea.

items.m: bad luck — often said without much sympathy
items.os: British, 1800s; perhaps from being served cheese too hard to enjoy, though no one recorded why.
items.ex: 'Hard cheese,' said my cousin when rain cancelled the picnic.

items.m: a desperate last-chance attempt with little hope of success
items.os: From American football: quarterback Roger Staubach said he closed his eyes and said a Hail Mary prayer before his desperate game-winning pass in 1975.
items.ex: Cramming the whole word list in the car was a hail mary before the bee.

items.m: three wins or successes in a row by one person
items.os: From cricket, 1858: bowler H. H. Stephenson took three wickets with three balls, and fans passed a hat to buy him a prize hat.
items.ex: Winning her third spelling bee in a row completed the hat trick.

items.m: to have a special advantage over competitors
items.os: From 1800s horse racing: the horse on the innermost lane of an oval track runs the shortest distance.
items.ex: Having read the book twice gave Maya the inside track in the trivia contest.

items.m: a powerful, important person in a field
items.os: American, late 1800s, from baseball and boxing, where the heavy hitters delivered the hardest swings and punches.
items.ex: Grandma is the heavy hitter of our family trivia team.

items.m: to succeed impressively at something
items.os: From baseball, where a home run sails clear over the outfield fence — America's favorite picture of total success.
items.ex: Her volcano project hit a home run with the science fair judges.

items.m: to do something unfair or hurtful
items.os: From boxing: the Queensberry rules of 1867 banned punches below the belt as dangerous and unfair.
items.ex: Teasing your brother about his reading struggles is hitting below the belt.

items.m: to control a situation completely
items.os: From card games: the player dealt all the strong cards decides how every trick will go.
items.ex: In the negotiations over screen time, Dad holds all the cards.

items.m: the final part of a task or journey
items.os: From 1800s American horse racing: the home stretch is the last straight run of track before the finish line.
items.ex: One chapter left — we're in the home stretch of the book report.

items.m: likely to happen; seemingly destined
items.os: From fortune-tellers of the 1700s and 1800s, who claimed a person's future could be read in a spread of cards.
items.ex: With storm clouds like these, a canceled picnic was always in the cards.

items.m: supporting and ready to help you
items.os: From boxing, where a fighter's trainer waits in their corner of the ring, coaching and encouraging between rounds.
items.ex: Whatever the report card says, Mom is in your corner.

items.m: to keep an activity going without a pause
items.os: In the 1840 US presidential campaign, supporters rolled a ten-foot 'victory ball' from town to town chanting 'keep the ball rolling.'
items.ex: Each cousin added a verse to keep the ball rolling on the birthday song.

items.p: keep your eye on the ball
items.m: to stay focused on what matters most
items.os: The first rule of every bat-and-ball sport: a batter who glances away for an instant misses the ball.
items.ex: Ignore the giggles from the audience and keep your eye on the ball — one letter at a time.

items.m: to begin an event or activity
items.os: From football and soccer, where every game officially begins with a kick of the ball.
items.ex: The school fair kicks off with a pancake breakfast.

items.p: knock it out of the park
items.m: to do something extremely well
items.os: From baseball: a ball hit clear out of the ballpark is the grandest hit possible.
items.ex: Priya knocked it out of the park with her history presentation.

items.m: an attempt with only a small chance of success
items.os: From early guns and cannon, which rarely hit distant targets; by the 1860s a 'long shot' was a risky racetrack bet.
items.ex: Winning regionals on her first try is a long shot, but she's studying anyway.

items.m: an unfair or cruel act or remark
items.os: American, early 1900s, from boxing, where a punch below the belt breaks the rules.
items.ex: Bringing up her lost library book in the middle of the game was a low blow.

items.m: to qualify or be chosen for the next stage
items.os: From golf tournaments, where only players with the best halfway scores 'make the cut' and keep playing.
items.ex: Twenty spellers tried out for the team, and Aanya made the cut.

items.m: to make a noticeable difference
items.os: From measuring dials like speedometers and gauges: only a real change makes the needle visibly swing.
items.ex: Ten extra minutes of reading each night really moved the needle on her fluency.

items.p: not playing with a full deck
items.m: acting foolish or not thinking clearly
items.os: American, mid-1900s: a card game is hopeless with cards missing; the tale that it comes from dodging a card tax by buying 51-card decks is a myth.
items.ex: The dog buried Dad's phone again — that pup is not playing with a full deck.

items.m: mistaken or completely wrong
items.os: From baseball: a runner caught off base is in danger of being tagged out.
items.ex: Your guess about the surprise party is way off base.

items.m: accurate; exactly right or on schedule
items.os: From archery and gunnery, where a shot that lands on the target is a success.
items.ex: Her definition of 'onomatopoeia' was right on target.

items.m: alert, quick, and doing things well
items.os: From ball games, where sharp players keep their eye on the ball; the story crediting railroad watchmaker Webb C. Ball is a myth.
items.ex: You packed the permission slip a day early — nice to see you on the ball.

items.m: recovering from a loss or disappointment
items.os: From ball games of the 1800s, where a ball caught on the rebound is snatched as it bounces back.
items.ex: After losing the chess final, Leo was on the rebound by dinnertime, planning next year's strategy.

items.m: close to defeat or failure
items.os: From boxing: a fighter trapped against the ring's ropes is nearly beaten.
items.ex: Our quiz team was on the ropes until the final science question.

items.m: completely unexpected and strange
items.os: American baseball slang, 1900s; why left field is the odd one is unclear — the story about an asylum behind a Chicago outfield is a myth.
items.ex: Her question about penguins came out of left field in the middle of math.

items.m: too good or advanced for you
items.os: From sports leagues, which rank teams by skill so beginners never face champions.
items.ex: The eighth-grade word list felt out of her league — until she studied.

items.m: to struggle against strong opposition
items.os: From canoeing: paddling against a river's current is slow, exhausting work; figurative in American English since the 1800s.
items.ex: Convincing the class to read during recess felt like paddling upstream.

items.m: a contest so close the winner is decided by a tiny margin
items.os: From 1930s horse racing, when finish-line cameras began deciding races too close for human eyes.
items.ex: The bee ended in a photo finish, settled by one silent letter.

items.m: to cooperate or agree to take part
items.os: 'Play ball!' is the American umpire's traditional shout that starts a baseball game.
items.ex: The little kids will play ball with the cleanup plan as long as they get first turn at the games.

items.m: to act tough and compete without mercy
items.os: American, 1970s: baseball's hard ball is the serious professional game, softball the gentler one.
items.ex: Mom played hardball: no dessert until every spelling word was perfect.

items.m: to try many options before committing to one
items.os: From horse-race betting, where 'playing the field' meant backing every horse except the favorite.
items.ex: Sam played the field — chess, choir, then robotics — before picking a club.

items.m: to handle a situation cleverly for the best result
items.os: From card games, played in English parlors since the 1600s, where victory hangs on when you play each card.
items.ex: Play your cards right with early chores and we might make the museum by noon.

items.m: a blank expression that hides your true feelings
items.os: From American poker of the 1800s, where players smother every flicker of feeling so opponents can't read their cards.
items.ex: Rhea kept a perfect poker face when she drew an easy final word.

items.m: to perform better than expected for your size or level
items.os: From boxing, where fighters are matched in weight classes so no one meets a far bigger opponent.
items.ex: Our tiny school punches above its weight at the state bee every year.

items.m: to increase the risks or rewards involved
items.os: From betting: the stakes are the money on the table, and raising them makes every move riskier.
items.ex: The teacher raised the stakes — the winning team skips Friday's homework.

items.m: immediately; without any delay
items.os: American, 1880s, from baseball, where the ball rockets away the instant it leaves the bat.
items.ex: Right off the bat, Grandpa guessed the answer to my riddle.

items.m: to take a chance on an uncertain outcome
items.os: From dice games, where everything rests on one unpredictable tumble.
items.ex: Skipping the review sheet the night before a test is really rolling the dice.

items.m: to clear away problems so someone else can succeed
items.os: From American football, where blockers run ahead of the ball carrier, sweeping defenders out of the path.
items.ex: Dad ran interference with the chatty neighbors so Mia could finish studying.

items.m: to harm yourself by your own action
items.os: From soccer, where an own goal is the misery of knocking the ball into your own team's net.
items.ex: Bragging about the test before failing it was a classic own goal.

items.m: to get even for a past wrong
items.os: A 'score' was once a tally of debts notched on a stick or slate; settling it meant paying off every notch.
items.ex: The rematch let our chess club settle the score with the rival school.

items.m: to reveal your secret plans or intentions
items.os: From card games: showing your hand lets everyone see exactly what cards you hold.
items.ex: Asking to borrow the big cake pan showed Mom's hand about the surprise party.

items.m: kept out of the action or ignored
items.os: From sports, where injured players sit on the sidelines and watch the game go on without them.
items.ex: A sprained wrist sidelined Jo from the handwriting contest.

items.m: a guaranteed success; something certain
items.os: Basketball's showiest shot, stuffing the ball straight down through the hoop; announcer Chick Hearn popularized the name in the 1970s.
items.ex: After three weeks of practice, her book report felt like a slam dunk.

items.m: to take responsibility and act when needed
items.os: From baseball, where the batter must step up to home plate and face the next pitch.
items.ex: When the club needed a treasurer, Priya stepped up to the plate.

items.m: a tricky, awkward situation
items.os: From cricket: rain turns the wicket's turf sticky, making the ball bounce unpredictably and batting treacherous.
items.ex: Two birthday parties on the same afternoon — what a sticky wicket.

items.p: take a shot in the dark
items.m: to make a wild guess
items.os: From firing a gun blindly at night, when you cannot see the target at all.
items.ex: Unsure of the state capital, he took a shot in the dark and said Helena.

items.m: to accept something unpleasant to help your group
items.os: American sports slang: a baseball batter may let a pitch hit him, taking the bruise so his team gains a base.
items.ex: Ella took one for the team and played the boring narrator so the class play could go on.

items.m: polite behavior has ended; real conflict begins
items.os: Probably from boxing — bare fists hit harder than padded gloves — though some trace it to gentlemen removing soft kid gloves.
items.ex: After the tied quiz score, the gloves were off between the two teams.

items.m: to surprise someone with something unexpected
items.os: From baseball's curveball, a pitch that swerves at the last moment and fools the batter.
items.ex: The judges threw a curveball by asking for each word's language of origin.

items.m: to give up on something
items.os: From card games: a player who quits tosses their cards face-down into the middle of the table.
items.ex: Halfway through the thousand-piece puzzle, Uncle Raj threw in his hand.

items.m: facing an opponent directly as an equal
items.os: From boxing, where two fighters stand toe to toe and trade punches without backing away.
items.ex: Maya went toe to toe with last year's champion in the final round.

items.m: to make brief contact to share news
items.os: From baseball, where a runner must touch each base to score; American offices adopted it by the mid-1900s.
items.ex: Ms. Rivera touches base with parents every Friday by email.

items.m: a hidden advantage saved for the right moment
items.os: From 1500s card games: a trump — short for 'triumph' — beats any card of another suit.
items.ex: Her trump card at the bake sale was Grandma's secret brownie recipe.

items.m: to improve your performance
items.os: From sports coaching: to compete with stronger players, you must raise the level of your play.
items.ex: New rivals joined the bee this year, so Zoe upped her game with daily drills.

items.m: a public celebration of a success
items.os: From track and motor racing, where the winner circles the course one more time to soak up the cheers.
