items.ex: After acing the recital, Leo took a victory lap around the kitchen.

items.m: to win by a very large margin
items.os: American, late 1800s: newspapers compared crushing election victories to a landslide burying the whole hillside.
items.ex: The pizza-party option won the class vote by a landslide.

items.m: to defeat someone totally and easily
items.os: British slang from the late 1800s, picturing a winner mopping the floor with the loser like a rag.
items.ex: Big sister wiped the floor with us at charades again.

items.m: a long angry argument, especially in public
items.os: English, 1700s: a battle fought entirely with insults and arguments instead of weapons.
items.ex: The two debate teams kept up a war of words all week.

items.p: all quiet on the western front
items.m: nothing new is happening; a calm period
items.os: The title of Erich Maria Remarque's 1929 novel, echoing World War I army reports that called days of trench warfare 'quiet.'
items.ex: 'All quiet on the western front,' Dad whispered, peeking in at the napping twins.

items.m: carrying every possible weapon or resource
items.os: The hilt is a sword's handle: a blade driven 'to the hilt' goes all the way in, so armed to the hilt means completely.
items.ex: Nina arrived at the bee armed to the hilt: flashcards, dictionary, and three sharpened pencils.

items.m: absent without permission
items.os: A US military acronym for 'absent without leave,' stamped on records of missing soldiers; by World War II it was spoken as a word.
items.ex: The stapler has gone AWOL from the teacher's desk again.

items.m: a contest of cleverness between rivals
items.os: English, 1500s: a duel fought with quick thinking and sharp words instead of swords.
items.ex: The chess final turned into a battle of wits between the twins.

items.m: to leave quickly to avoid trouble
items.os: Armies once signaled retreat by drumbeat — drummers literally 'beat' the retreat as soldiers fell back.
items.ex: Smelling burnt cookies, the kids beat a hasty retreat from the kitchen.

items.m: to fail, break, or be defeated
items.os: Ancient battle poetry: English translations of Homer's Iliad have fallen warriors 'bite the dust,' and American Westerns made it slang.
items.ex: My old backpack finally bit the dust on the last day of school.

items.m: to stop supporting your own group publicly
items.os: From army drill, where soldiers march in tight rows called ranks; stepping out breaks the formation.
items.ex: Ben broke ranks with his buddies and voted for the museum trip.

items.m: to use your strongest resources or people
items.os: From warfare: when small arms fail, armies roll out their heaviest artillery.
items.ex: For the final round, Coach brought out the big guns: last year's championship words.

items.m: an urgent appeal for people to act
items.os: The military summons ordering soldiers to grab their weapons and assemble for battle.
items.ex: The flooded book fair was a call to arms for the whole PTA.

items.m: harmed by a conflict between others
items.os: From battle, where crossfire is shooting from two directions and anyone caught between is in danger.
items.ex: When the twins argued over the remote, the cat got caught in the crossfire.

items.m: to unite and protect your own group
items.os: From infantry drill: attacked soldiers stepped tightly together, shoulder to shoulder, sealing every gap in the line.
items.ex: When outsiders teased the new kid, our class closed ranks around him.

items.m: to respond to trouble with energy and determination
items.os: From boxing: at the bell, a fighter leaves the corner ready to attack.
items.ex: After a low quiz score, Ana came out fighting with a color-coded study plan.

items.m: to announce a determined campaign against something
items.os: From the formal declarations nations issue before fighting; borrowed for peaceful crusades like America's 1964 'war on poverty.'
items.ex: Mom has declared war on the sock pile under my bed.

items.m: to refuse stubbornly to change or move
items.os: From stubborn mules and horses that brace their hooves and lean back rather than be led forward.
items.ex: Priya dug in her heels about keeping her lucky pencil for every test.

items.m: to strike the first blow in a contest
items.os: From dueling and boxing, where the first fighter to wound the other 'draws first blood.'
items.ex: Our team drew first blood with a perfect score in round one.

items.m: to reveal shocking, unexpected news
items.os: From World War I, when falling artillery shells brought sudden devastation; newspapers soon used it for stunning announcements.
items.ex: Grandpa dropped a bombshell at dinner: we're moving to Seattle in June.

items.m: to accept all the blame and resign
items.os: In the Bible, King Saul falls on his own sword after losing his final battle, and defeated Roman generals did the same; today it only means taking the blame.
items.ex: After the group project flopped, the team captain fell on his sword and took the blame.

items.m: to keep trying at something that cannot succeed
items.os: A soldier's image: some battles are lost no matter how bravely the troops fight on.
items.ex: Keeping glitter off the floor during craft hour is fighting a losing battle.

items.m: to fight or resist with every ounce of effort
items.os: English, 1500s, from the ancient Latin picture of fighting with teeth and fingernails when no weapon is left.
items.ex: Ravi fought tooth and nail for the last spot on the mathlete team.

items.m: the first protection against a problem
items.os: From battlefield defenses: the front trench or wall must hold before attackers can reach anything else.
items.ex: Washing your hands is the first line of defense against classroom colds.

items.m: accidental harm caused by your own side
items.os: A military term — 'friendly' forces are your own — for shots that hit comrades by mistake; common by the Vietnam War era.
items.ex: Dad's joke about my haircut was friendly fire — he'd meant to tease my brother.

items.m: people whose jobs face danger or the public directly
items.os: From the front line, the trench nearest the enemy in World War I; the 2020 pandemic made it everyday praise for nurses and grocery clerks.
items.ex: Our class made thank-you cards for the front line workers at the hospital.

items.m: to make progress or become more accepted
items.os: From warfare: an advancing army gains the ground it captures, yard by hard-won yard.
items.ex: Her reading is gaining ground — up two levels in one year.

items.m: to keep trying until the very end
items.os: The soldier's ideal of never surrendering: even facing certain defeat, you resist to the last.
items.ex: Down to his last card in the tournament, Milo went down fighting.

items.m: to succeed quickly and energetically
items.os: From 1700s sailors, who called a roaring gale 'blowing great guns' because the wind boomed like cannon fire.
items.ex: The lemonade stand is going great guns — three pitchers sold before lunch.

items.m: to be determined to beat or bring down someone
items.os: American, 1800s: in frontier towns, a man 'gunning for' a rival was literally hunting him with a pistol.
items.ex: Every speller in the county is gunning for the returning champion.

items.m: a big part of finishing something difficult
items.os: From the 1700s proverb 'the first blow is half the battle' — a strong start decides much of the fight.
items.ex: Just opening the math book is half the battle.

items.m: to keep things running while others are away
items.os: Linked to an 1864 Civil War signal — 'Hold the fort! I am coming' — though General Sherman's actual message was different; an 1870 hymn spread the popular wording.
items.ex: Mom held the fort at the bake-sale table while we hunted for extra napkins.

items.m: to wait before attacking or criticizing
items.os: The battlefield order that keeps soldiers from shooting until exactly the right moment.
items.ex: Hold your fire until your sister finishes explaining what happened to the cake.

items.m: in a position to be blamed or attacked
items.os: From the firing line, the front row of soldiers standing closest to the enemy's guns.
items.ex: As team captain, Rosa was in the firing line when the project ran late.

items.m: doing the hard, unglamorous work firsthand
items.os: From World War I, when soldiers lived and fought for months in muddy trenches dug across the front.
items.ex: Ms. Lee has spent twenty years in the trenches of third-grade teaching.

items.m: to get fully ready for action
items.os: A World War II rifle command — originally 'load and lock' — that actor John Wayne flipped into fame in a 1949 war film.
items.ex: Backpacks zipped and lunches packed — lock and load for the field trip.

items.m: a long, exhausting effort toward a distant goal
items.os: From China's Long March of 1934-35, when Mao's Red Army trekked some 6,000 miles over mountains to escape encirclement.
items.ex: Learning cursive felt like a long march, one loopy letter at a time.

items.m: to fall behind or lose an advantage
items.os: From battle: an army pushed backward loses the ground it once held.
items.ex: Skipping practice all week made Dev lose ground to the other spellers.

items.m: to rise up and defend a cause
items.os: From revolutionary Paris, where citizens in 1830 and 1848 piled paving stones and furniture into street barricades.
items.ex: When the library budget was cut, parents manned the barricades at the town meeting.

items.m: to wait without making real progress
items.os: From marching drill: soldiers ordered to 'mark time' stamp their feet in place without moving forward.
items.ex: We marked time with word searches until the assembly began.

items.m: to suffer a final, crushing defeat
items.os: From the Battle of Waterloo in Belgium, 1815, where Napoleon was defeated once and for all.
items.ex: The defending champion met her Waterloo on the word 'chiaroscuro.'

items.m: a dangerous or unclaimed in-between area
items.os: Named in the 1300s for unowned ground outside London's walls; World War I made it the deadly strip between enemy trenches.
items.ex: The hallway between the two rival classrooms became no man's land during the prank war.

items.m: very angry and looking for a confrontation
items.os: From 1700s American frontier English: the warpath was the trail a war party traveled to battle.
items.ex: Somebody tracked mud across the new carpet, and Mom is on the warpath.

items.m: to begin attacking or criticizing
items.os: The commander's order that unleashes every gun at once; used for launching criticism since the 1800s.
items.ex: The moment the debate began, both sides opened fire with statistics.

items.m: a final sharp remark made while leaving
items.os: Possibly from the 'Parthian shot' — ancient Persian horsemen fired arrows backward while galloping away — though the link is debated.
items.ex: Her parting shot as she left the game: 'Practice spelling W-I-N.'

items.m: to spend energy only on fights worth winning
items.os: Old military wisdom — no army can fight everywhere at once — turned into modern advice for parents and teachers.
items.ex: Dad picks his battles: messy rooms slide, but homework never does.

items.m: to use your higher position to force obedience
items.os: From the military, where an officer of higher rank can simply order a lower one.
items.ex: The big kids pulled rank and claimed the good swings.

items.m: to finally make a decision and act
items.os: From firearms: squeezing the trigger is the one tiny motion that cannot be taken back.
items.ex: After weeks of debating, we pulled the trigger on adopting the shelter puppy.

items.m: to gather and inspire your group to act
items.os: From battle, where commanders rally scattered soldiers — 'rally' comes from French rallier, to join together again.
items.ex: Before the relay, Coach rallied the troops with a silly cheer.

items.m: to endure attacks or criticism from all sides
items.os: From a 1600s army punishment, the Swedish 'gatlopp': a soldier ran between two rows of men swinging at him; no relation to the glove called a gauntlet.
items.ex: Every science fair idea must run the gauntlet of the judges' questions.

items.m: stunned and dazed by a shocking experience
items.os: Coined in 1915 for World War I soldiers left trembling by endless artillery shelling — an early name for battle trauma.
items.ex: We walked out of the surprise math test looking shell-shocked.

items.m: something that quickly restores energy or confidence
items.os: American, early 1900s: from an injection of medicine that revives a patient almost instantly.
items.ex: Winning the class quiz was a shot in the arm for Theo's confidence.

items.m: to keep going despite difficulty or discouragement
items.os: British, 1900s: from soldiers who must keep marching whatever the weather or their weariness.
items.ex: Her voice was scratchy, but Lena soldiered on through the whole recital.

items.m: to refuse to retreat from your position or belief
items.os: From battle orders of the 1600s: soldiers told to stand their ground hold their spot against any charge.
items.ex: Kim stood her ground about the answer, and the key proved her right.

items.m: to hold firm to your beliefs despite pressure
items.os: From the naval order 'stand to your guns,' keeping crews at their cannons even as battle raged around them.
items.ex: Everyone doubted his book-club pick, but Amir stuck to his guns.

items.m: to impress or conquer suddenly and completely
items.os: From storming a fortress: attackers pour over the walls in one furious rush instead of a slow siege.
items.ex: The kindergartners' kazoo band took the talent show by storm.

items.m: to hide quickly from danger
items.os: The battlefield shout to duck behind anything solid when fire rains down.
items.ex: The picnic ended with everyone taking cover from a sudden hailstorm.

items.m: to receive strong criticism
items.os: World War II bomber crews flew through 'flak' — German shorthand for anti-aircraft cannon — and brought the word home as slang for criticism.
items.ex: Sam took flak from his cousins for rooting against their team.

items.m: to act with ruthless determination
items.os: From armies so fierce they refused to capture enemies; softened now to describe all-out effort.
items.ex: Grandma takes no prisoners at the Scrabble board.

items.m: the most powerful or important people
items.os: A navy's biggest guns decided battles, so by the 1800s 'big guns' meant the people with real power.
items.ex: For the spring concert, the school brought in the big guns: the high school orchestra.

items.m: to fight imaginary enemies or hopeless causes
items.os: From Cervantes' 1605 novel Don Quixote, whose hero charges windmills with his lance, certain they are giants; 'tilt' means to joust.
items.ex: Arguing with the vending machine is tilting at windmills, Dad.

items.m: money saved up for a big campaign or fight
items.os: Medieval commanders hauled real chests of coins to pay their soldiers on campaign; American politics revived the term around 1900.
items.ex: The club's cookie-sale war chest will buy new dictionaries.

items.p: win the battle but lose the war
items.m: to gain a small victory that costs the bigger goal
items.os: Echoes King Pyrrhus, 279 BC, whose 'victories' over Rome wrecked his own army — winning fights while losing everything.
items.ex: He won the battle over bedtime but lost the war when Mom canceled the sleepover.

items.m: an impatient young person pushing for change
items.os: From the Young Turks, the young officers who forced reforms on the Ottoman sultan in 1908.
items.ex: The young Turks of the student council want recess moved before lunch.

items.m: the exact moment something important begins
items.os: World War I staff officers counted down to 'zero hour,' the planned minute an attack would begin.
items.ex: Zero hour for the science-fair setup is 8 a.m. sharp.

items.m: wasting effort on something already settled or hopeless
items.os: British, 1800s; politician John Bright mocked a colleague's doomed cause in Parliament as flogging a dead horse.
items.ex: Asking for a later bedtime again is flogging a dead horse.

items.m: one small flaw that spoils something good
items.os: From the Bible's Ecclesiastes: dead flies make the perfumer's precious ointment stink.
items.ex: The picnic was perfect except one fly in the ointment: we forgot the lemonade.

items.m: to lose your temper suddenly
items.os: American, 1840s; from loose axe heads that flew off mid-swing, wild and out of control.
items.ex: Dad tries not to fly off the handle when we spill juice in the car.

items.m: worthless or not worth taking seriously
items.os: American army slang of the 1940s, politely trimmed from a ruder joke about birds pecking at horse droppings.
items.ex: Marco says homework on weekends is for the birds.

items.m: brave people are the most likely to succeed
items.os: From the Latin motto 'audentes fortuna iuvat' in Virgil's Aeneid, shouted as a battle cry.
items.ex: Fortune favors the bold, so raise your hand even if you're not sure.

items.m: rising from poverty to wealth
items.os: American, 1800s; Horatio Alger's hugely popular novels about poor boys working their way up made the plot famous.
items.ex: The spelling champ went from rags to riches: last place one year, the trophy the next.

items.m: from the very beginning, using nothing ready-made
items.os: From the scratch line drawn in the dirt as the starting point of old footraces.
items.ex: We baked the birthday cake from scratch, flour and all.

items.m: moving forward with all possible speed and energy
items.os: From steamships of the 1800s, whose engine rooms fed the boilers full power on the captain's order.
items.ex: With the science fair one week away, it's full steam ahead on our volcano.

items.m: to really enjoy something
items.os: American, early 1900s; Cole Porter's 1934 hit song 'I Get a Kick Out of You' fixed it in everyday talk.
items.ex: Grandma gets a kick out of hearing me spell 'onomatopoeia.'

items.m: to escape without any punishment or cost
items.os: 'Scot' was a medieval English tax, so scot-free meant paying nothing; the stories about Scotland or Dred Scott are myths.
items.ex: The cat knocked over the vase and got off scot-free because we blamed the dog.

items.m: to be fired from a job
items.os: Probably from the days when workers kept their tools in a sack and were handed it when dismissed — a story told in French since the 1600s but never proven.
items.ex: In our class store game, the napping shopkeeper got the sack.

items.p: get your ducks in a row
items.m: to get everything organized before starting
items.os: American, mid-1900s; perhaps from ducklings paddling in a neat line behind their mother, though bowling pins called ducks are another suspect.
items.ex: Mom had us get our ducks in a row the night before the bee: pencils, water, word list.

items.p: give the benefit of the doubt
items.m: to believe someone is innocent or honest when you are unsure
items.os: From the courtroom rule of the 1700s that jurors who are not fully certain must vote not guilty.
items.ex: I couldn't find my eraser, but I gave my desk mate the benefit of the doubt.

items.m: to be opposite to what feels natural or usual
items.os: From carpentry: planing wood against its grain tears the surface; Shakespeare used the image in Coriolanus.
items.ex: It goes against the grain for Priya to leave a puzzle unfinished.

items.m: to fail suddenly and spectacularly
items.os: From World War I dogfights, when a hit plane fell from the sky burning.
items.ex: Our plan to surprise Mom went down in flames when the balloons popped early.

items.m: to risk everything on one big effort
items.os: Hawaiian Pidgin gambling slang for betting it all; the Japanese-American 442nd Regiment made it their World War II motto.
items.ex: Down to the final round, she went for broke and asked for the hardest word.

items.m: to go badly wrong
items.os: British slang, often traced to Royal Air Force pilots whose sloppy practice loops bulged like pears — a fun story, but unproven.
items.ex: The bake sale went pear-shaped when the oven quit an hour before school.

items.m: to fall into a much worse condition
items.os: English, 1500s; likely from food not fit for people being thrown to the dogs, though the exact start is unproven.
items.ex: Grandpa jokes the playground has gone to the dogs since they removed the tire swing.

items.m: a large payment given to someone leaving a job
items.os: Coined in 1950s Britain by a newspaper City editor for the fat farewell payments handed to departing executives.
items.ex: The retiring principal got a golden handshake and a very long round of applause.

items.m: an easy job or situation that pays very well
items.os: American slang, 1920s; said to come from railroad crews calling an easy, well-paid run a gravy train, though proof is thin.
items.ex: Being line leader is no gravy train; you have to hold every single door.

items.m: to make things run smoothly, often with favors or money
items.os: From wagon days, when greasing the axles kept the wheels turning without squeaks or sticking.
items.ex: A thank-you note to the librarian greased the wheels for our book-club room.

items.m: a little more of what hurt you, taken as a cure
items.os: From the medieval belief that laying hairs of the dog that bit you on the wound would heal it.
items.ex: Sore from practice, Dad joked that a light jog was the hair of the dog.

items.m: quickly and in large amounts, especially money
items.os: From sailors hauling rope hand over hand, then hand over fist, as fast as they could pull.
items.ex: The lemonade stand made money hand over fist during the heat wave.

items.m: to be in a very fragile, risky situation
items.os: From the Greek tale of Damocles, who feasted beneath a sword hung by a single horsehair.
items.ex: Our team's win hung by a thread until the other finalist missed.

items.m: to be undecided, with success or failure equally possible
items.os: From weighing scales: an unsettled fate sits in the pans, ready to tip either way — the Bible's Daniel was 'weighed in the balance.'
items.ex: The class party hangs in the balance until our reading-minutes chart is tallied.

items.m: a problem or person that is difficult to figure out
items.os: English, 1700s; Benjamin Franklin used it for fortresses too tough to capture.
items.ex: The bonus word was a hard nut to crack, even for the champ.

items.m: rushing causes mistakes that cost more time
items.os: An old rhyme recorded in John Heywood's 1546 book of English proverbs.
items.ex: I glued the wrong flap first — haste makes waste.

items.m: to have a complaint to argue out with someone
items.os: English, 1500s; from a dog settling in over a bone, working at it stubbornly for hours.
items.ex: Mia has a bone to pick with her brother about the missing markers.

items.m: to have more important things to deal with
items.os: English, 1600s; John Evelyn's memoirs carry an early version of the kitchen image.
items.ex: Coach ignored our jersey debate; she had bigger fish to fry before the tournament.

items.m: daydreaming instead of paying attention
items.os: English, 1600s: a head floating so high in the sky it cannot see the ground.
items.ex: Leo missed his turn to spell because his head was in the clouds.

items.m: completely, especially completely in love
items.os: Began in the 1300s as 'heels over head,' meaning upside down; the words flipped by the 1700s.
items.ex: Grandpa is still head over heels for Grandma after fifty years.

items.m: a truly kind and generous nature
items.os: From Shakespeare's Henry V, where a soldier calls the king 'a bawcock... a heart of gold.'
items.ex: The crossing guard who remembers every kid's name has a heart of gold.

items.m: a cold nature with no pity
items.os: Ancient image; the Bible's Ezekiel promises to swap a heart of stone for a heart of flesh.
items.ex: You'd need a heart of stone to say no to the puppy's eyes at dinner.

items.m: to protect yourself by backing more than one option
items.os: English, 1600s: to hedge a bet was to fence it in with smaller bets on the other side.
items.ex: Sam hedged his bets by studying both word lists in case the bee used either.

items.m: to reach the lowest possible point
items.os: American, 1800s mining talk: dig past the ore and you strike solid rock with nothing below.
items.ex: My motivation hit rock bottom until Mom turned flash cards into a game.

items.m: to leave or begin a journey
items.os: American, early 1900s, from hooves and wheels literally striking the road at the start of a trip.
items.ex: Pack the snacks — we hit the road for Grandma's at seven.

items.m: to go to bed
items.os: American, around 1900, when a mattress was often a sack stuffed with hay.
items.ex: Big test tomorrow, so I'm hitting the sack early.

items.m: believing something completely, without any doubt
items.os: American, 1800s: a fish so greedy it swallows not just the baited hook but the line and lead weight too.
items.ex: Dad fell for our fake birthday plans hook, line and sinker.

items.m: in control of what happens
items.os: From carriages and early cars: whoever holds the reins or the wheel decides where everyone goes.
items.ex: With the highest score, Ava is in the driver's seat going into the final round.

items.m: already being worked on and coming soon
items.os: From oil pipelines, early 1900s: oil already in the pipe is on its way even though you cannot see it.
items.ex: The librarian says more graphic novels are in the pipeline for spring.

items.m: losing money or in debt
items.os: From account books, where bookkeepers wrote losses in red ink and profits in black.
items.ex: Our bake-sale budget was in the red until Saturday's cookie rush.

items.m: to abandon a group or job, often for another
items.os: From sailors slipping ashore in port and deserting their ship.
items.ex: Half the chess club jumped ship when the robotics team got new kits.

items.m: to start before the proper time
items.os: From track races of the early 1900s: a runner who leaps off before the starting pistol fires.
items.ex: Don't jump the gun — wait until the judge finishes saying the word.

items.m: to stay brave and hide your feelings in hard times
items.os: American, early 1800s, though now famously attached to the British; a trembling upper lip is the first giveaway of tears.
items.ex: Ben kept a stiff upper lip after misspelling, then practiced twice as hard.

items.m: to avoid becoming close or friendly with someone
items.os: English, 1500s, first as 'at arm's end': close enough to see, too far to touch.
items.ex: Mom keeps the class hamster at arm's length because of her allergies.

items.p: keep the wolf from the door
items.m: to earn just enough to avoid hunger or poverty
items.os: English, 1500s; the wolf has stood for gnawing hunger since ancient fables.
items.ex: Grandpa says his first paper route barely kept the wolf from the door.

items.p: keep your ear to the ground
items.m: to stay alert for early news or changes
items.os: American, 1800s; from the frontier tale of scouts listening to the ground for far-off hoofbeats — vivid, but likely folklore.
items.ex: Keep your ear to the ground for the soccer tryout dates.

items.m: to stay out of trouble
items.os: American, late 1800s, adapted from the older British warning to keep your hands clean.
items.ex: The coach's only rule over break: keep your nose clean and stretch daily.

items.m: to stay calm and save your resources until truly needed
items.os: Attributed to Oliver Cromwell — 'trust in God and keep your powder dry' — but the quote first surfaces in an 1834 poem, so the story is a myth.
items.ex: Don't argue every little call, Dad says — keep your powder dry for what matters.

items.m: to exaggerate praise, flattery, or drama
items.os: From spreading paint or plaster too heavily; Shakespeare made the same joke as 'laid on with a trowel.'
items.ex: Jaya laid it on thick about Mom's haircut right before asking for a sleepover.

items.m: fair conditions where no one starts with an advantage
items.os: American business talk of the 1970s: on a sloped field, one team always runs uphill.
items.ex: Giving younger spellers easier words keeps a level playing field.

items.m: repeating the same thing over and over
items.os: From scratched vinyl records, whose needle sticks and replays the same line endlessly.
items.ex: I sound like a broken record: shoes off at the door!

items.m: support given in words but not in actions
items.os: English, 1600s, from prayers recited with the lips while the heart stays elsewhere.
items.ex: Paying lip service to tidying up won't actually clean the toy shelf.

items.m: to live or operate on very little money
items.os: American, late 1800s; perhaps from street peddlers whose whole stock was a few shoelaces, though no one is sure.
items.ex: The drama club lives on a shoestring, so we paint our own sets.

items.m: absolutely everything, the whole of something
items.os: The three parts of a musket — lock, stock, and barrel — make up the entire gun; Walter Scott used it in the early 1800s.
items.ex: We moved Grandma's sewing room lock, stock and barrel to the new house.

items.m: getting old
items.os: Horses' gums recede with age, so long teeth mark an old horse — buyers always checked the mouth first.
items.ex: Our minivan is long in the tooth, but it still makes the school run.

items.m: the easiest tasks or targets to start with
items.os: From orchards — fruit you can pick without a ladder; it became business slang in the late 1900s.
items.ex: Start your review with the low-hanging fruit: the words you almost know.

items.m: to cause a stir or challenge how things are done
items.os: American, mid-1900s: one swimmer's splashing rocks the calm water for everybody.
items.ex: The new student made waves by suggesting homework-free Fridays.

items.m: a hidden plan behind seemingly crazy behavior
items.os: From Hamlet: 'Though this be madness, yet there is method in't.'
items.ex: Dad's messy desk has a method to the madness; he finds any paper in seconds.

items.m: more interesting or complicated than it first appears
items.os: English, recorded since the 1700s: worth hiding beyond what plain sight can catch.
items.ex: There's more than meets the eye to the quiet kid who won the chess trophy.

items.m: to change the rules or target unfairly partway through
items.os: British, mid-1900s, from football: imagine the goal sliding away just as you shoot.
items.ex: First it was ten books, now it's fifteen — stop moving the goalposts!

items.m: news that is delightful to hear
items.os: English; writers since the 1500s have compared welcome words to sweet music.
items.ex: 'Snow day' was music to my ears.

items.m: a contest or story so tense you can hardly watch
items.os: American, mid-1900s, from nervously biting your nails through a close game.
items.ex: The bee came down to two spellers — a real nail-biter.

items.m: exactly even in a close race
items.os: From horse racing, 1800s: two horses so level their necks stay side by side.
items.ex: Maya and Josh were neck and neck until the final word.

items.m: money saved up for the future
items.os: English, 1600s: farmers left an egg in the nest to coax the hen to keep laying.
items.ex: My allowance nest egg is finally big enough for the telescope.

items.m: a fresh chance to enjoy living, with renewed energy
items.os: From property law of the 1800s: a renewed lease gives a tenant — or a life — a fresh run.
items.ex: New glasses gave Grandpa a new lease on life at his woodworking bench.

items.p: not the sharpest tool in the shed
items.m: not very smart
items.os: American, late 1900s, one of a family of joking 'not the sharpest' put-downs measured in garden tools.
items.ex: Our goldfish, bless him, is not the sharpest tool in the shed.

items.m: spoken without preparation
items.os: American, 1930s; said to come from speakers jotting last-second notes on their shirt cuffs, though proof is thin.
items.ex: Asked about her win, Zoe gave a sweet off-the-cuff thank-you speech.

items.m: freed from blame or an unwanted duty
items.os: From fishing: a fish that wriggles off the hook swims away free.
items.ex: Rain canceled practice, so I'm off the hook for cleaning the equipment.

items.m: a person you loved in the past
items.os: English; 'flame' has meant a sweetheart since the 1600s, from love pictured as fire.
items.ex: At the reunion, Grandma laughed with an old flame from her school dances.

items.p: on a wing and a prayer
items.m: barely managing, relying on luck and hope
items.os: From a 1943 song about a damaged World War II bomber limping home 'on a wing and a prayer.'
items.ex: We finished the poster on a wing and a prayer, gluing as the bell rang.

items.m: set aside to deal with later
items.os: From American stove tops, mid-1900s: pots on the rear burner simmer while the front gets the attention.
items.ex: The treehouse plan is on the back burner until report cards come out.

items.m: to start something that creates many new problems
items.os: American, 1950s, from anglers' bait cans: open one and the worms squirm everywhere.
items.ex: Asking who broke the stapler opened a can of worms in class.

items.m: to be independent and manage your own affairs
items.os: American, early 1800s; an 1854 magazine song with the refrain 'paddle your own canoe' made it a motto.
items.ex: Grandpa's graduation advice was simple: paddle your own canoe.

items.m: just what you would expect, often mildly disappointing
items.os: From golf, early 1900s: par is the score an ordinarily good round should take.
items.ex: Losing one mitten by January is par for the course in our family.

items.m: careful with small amounts of money but wasteful with big ones
items.os: English, 1600s; Robert Burton used it when pennies and pounds were everyday coins.
items.ex: Skipping the two-dollar bike lock and losing the bike was penny wise, pound foolish.

items.m: a lovely promise that will never really happen
items.os: From Joe Hill's 1911 protest song, which mocked preachers' promises of 'pie in the sky when you die.'
items.ex: A pool in our backyard is pie in the sky, but we keep asking.

items.m: to argue the opposite side just to test an idea
items.os: From the Catholic Church's advocatus diaboli, the official assigned to argue against making someone a saint.
items.ex: Dad played devil's advocate at dinner, defending broccoli against us all.

items.m: to stop something for good by cutting off its support
items.os: English, 1800s: it first meant yanking the plug of an old-style toilet; the electrical picture came later.
items.ex: The principal pulled the plug on the fog machine after one hazy assembly.

items.p: put your foot in your mouth
items.m: to say something embarrassing or tactless by accident
items.os: American, 1800s, grown from the older English 'put your foot in it' — stepping straight into a mess.
items.ex: I put my foot in my mouth asking about the party I wasn't supposed to know about.

items.m: to sit in the front passenger seat
items.os: Stagecoach guards really sat beside the driver holding a shotgun, but the phrase itself comes from 1900s Western movies, not the Old West.
items.ex: I called riding shotgun before my sister even had her shoes on.

items.m: perfectly fine or healthy
items.os: British, late 1800s; nobody knows why rain is 'right' — the alliteration probably did the work.
items.ex: After a nap and some soup, Theo was right as rain for the recital.

items.m: to adapt calmly when things go wrong
items.os: From boxing: leaning away as a punch lands softens the blow.
items.ex: Our picnic moved indoors twice, but we rolled with the punches.

items.m: to mix socially with people, especially important ones
items.os: American version of Britain's 'rub shoulders,' from crowded rooms where sleeves literally brush.
items.ex: At the state bee, we rubbed elbows with last year's champion.

items.m: to annoy someone without meaning to
items.os: Probably from stroking a cat against the lie of its fur; the tale about servants mis-rubbing oak floors is a myth.
items.ex: The new kid's bragging rubbed the whole team the wrong way.

items.p: separate the wheat from the chaff
items.m: to sort the valuable from the worthless
items.os: From the Bible's threshing floor, where winnowing tossed grain so the wind carried the husks away.
items.ex: Tryouts separate the wheat from the chaff before the mathletes pick a team.

items.m: fixed and impossible to change
items.os: From laws carved into stone tablets, like the commandments Moses carried down the mountain.
items.ex: The seating chart isn't set in stone; Ms. Rivera shuffles it monthly.

items.m: improve your behavior or leave
items.os: American military slang from World War II: meet the standard or be shipped to a rougher posting.
items.ex: After the third missed practice, the coach's message was shape up or ship out.

items.p: ships that pass in the night
items.m: people who meet briefly and then go their separate ways
items.os: From Longfellow's 1874 poem: 'Ships that pass in the night, and speak each other in passing.'
items.ex: My camp bunkmate and I were ships that pass in the night — one week, then different schools.

items.m: to chat casually about nothing important
items.os: American slang, 1910s: idle talk pictured as firing shots at nothing but the wind.
items.ex: Dad and the neighbor shot the breeze over the fence while we drew chalk cities.

items.m: a guess made with almost no information
items.os: From firing blindly at a target you cannot see; figurative by the 1890s.
items.ex: I hadn't studied that word, so my spelling was a shot in the dark.

items.m: one simple solution that fixes everything instantly
items.os: From folklore in which only a silver bullet can bring down a werewolf.
items.ex: Flash cards help, but there's no silver bullet for learning five hundred words.

items.m: born into wealth and comfort
items.os: From 'born with a silver spoon in his mouth': christening gifts of real silver spoons marked well-off families.
items.ex: The book's hero had no silver spoon — she built her robot from junkyard parts.

items.m: to avoid choosing a side
items.os: American politics, 1800s: a fence-sitter perches between two fields, committed to neither.
items.ex: Quit sitting on the fence — pizza party or movie day?

items.m: an easy, defenseless target
items.os: From hunting: a duck bobbing on the water is far easier to hit than one in flight; popularized around World War II.
items.ex: Without an umbrella, I was a sitting duck for the sprinklers.

items.m: to take a foolish risk
items.os: American, 1800s; Emerson quoted the skaters' proverb that over thin ice, your only safety is speed.
items.ex: Turning in homework late twice in one week is skating on thin ice.

items.m: to wait until the next day before deciding
items.os: English, 1500s; a Tudor state paper records the king wishing to 'sleep and dream upon the matter.'
items.ex: Mom didn't say no to the sleepover; she said she'd sleep on it.

items.m: clever tricks that hide the truth
items.os: From stage magicians' illusions built with smoke and hidden mirrors; writer Jimmy Breslin pinned the phrase on politics in 1975.
items.ex: The 'mystery prize' was smoke and mirrors — just extra recess, which honestly we loved.

items.m: a hidden enemy pretending to be a friend
items.os: From the Roman poet Virgil's warning: 'a snake lurks in the grass.'
items.ex: In the board game, my sweet little cousin turned out to be the snake in the grass.

items.m: completely clean and tidy
items.os: From 1500s 'spick and span new' — as fresh as a new nail (spick) and a just-cut wood chip (span).
items.ex: Our room has to be spick and span before screen time.

items.m: a betrayal by someone you trusted
items.os: An image as old as Julius Caesar, attacked by his friends; fixed as an English phrase by the early 1900s.
items.ex: Sharing my secret hideout spot with the whole class felt like a stab in the back.

items.m: quiet people often have deep thoughts and strong feelings
items.os: From a Latin proverb that the deepest rivers flow with the least sound; in English since the 1400s.
items.ex: Rosa barely talks in class, but her poems prove still waters run deep.

items.m: directly from the most reliable source
items.os: From racetracks, early 1900s: the surest tip would come from the horse itself — whose teeth also reveal its true age.
items.ex: The field trip is Friday — straight from the horse's mouth, our principal.

items.p: strike while the iron is hot
items.m: act quickly while the chance is there
items.os: From the blacksmith's forge, where iron bends only while glowing hot; English since Chaucer's time, the 1300s.
items.ex: Dad was in a great mood, so I struck while the iron was hot and asked about the puppy.

items.m: a final performance or last piece of work
items.os: From the ancient Greek legend that a swan sings one glorious song just before dying — untrue of real swans, but the story stuck.
items.ex: The retiring music teacher's spring concert was her swan song.

items.m: to be the most surprising or extreme of all
items.os: American, 1800s: cakewalk contests awarded a real cake to the fanciest strutting pair.
items.ex: Of all your excuses, blaming the goldfish takes the cake.

items.m: to finally commit to something big and scary
items.os: English, 1800s, from the shivery leap into cold water.
items.ex: Nina took the plunge and signed up for the district bee.

items.m: to feel offended
items.os: From Latin umbra, 'shade': an insult falls across you like a shadow; English since the 1600s.
items.ex: The cat took umbrage when we laughed at her tumble, and stalked off.

items.p: the apple doesn't fall far from the tree
items.m: children usually turn out like their parents
items.os: An old European proverb — German has 'the apple falls not far from the trunk' — that entered English in the 1800s.
items.ex: She fixes computers just like her mom — the apple doesn't fall far from the tree.

items.p: the bigger they are, the harder they fall
items.m: the powerful fail more dramatically than the small
items.os: Made famous around 1900 by boxer Bob Fitzsimmons, reportedly said before facing a much heavier opponent.
items.ex: Facing the returning champ, Coach whispered, 'The bigger they are, the harder they fall.'

items.p: the early bird gets the worm
items.m: whoever acts first gets the reward
items.os: Recorded in William Camden's 1636 collection of English proverbs as 'the early bird catcheth the worm.'
items.ex: I claim the comfy beanbag at library time — the early bird gets the worm.

items.p: the proof is in the pudding
items.m: you can only judge something by trying it
items.os: A squashed version of the 1600s proverb 'the proof of the pudding is in the eating' — proof meant test.
items.ex: The study plan looks great, but the proof is in the pudding: Friday's quiz.

items.p: the straw that broke the camel's back
items.m: the last small problem that finally causes collapse
items.os: English, 1800s; an older version blamed 'the last feather that breaks the horse's back.'
items.ex: The spilled glitter was the straw that broke the camel's back; craft time ended early.

items.p: there's no such thing as a free lunch
items.m: everything costs something, even gifts
items.os: From 1800s American saloons whose 'free lunch' came only with drinks you paid for; economists later made it a slogan.
items.ex: The 'free' game needed twenty dollars of gems — no such thing as a free lunch.

items.m: extremely close friends who share every secret
items.os: English, early 1800s, when 'thick' meant intimate — echoing a French saying about thieves at a fair.
items.ex: My cousin and I are thick as thieves every summer at the lake.

items.m: an extra person who isn't really needed
items.os: American twist on 'fifth wheel' — a wagon needs only four, so a spare just hangs there useless.
items.ex: When my sister brings her best friend, I ride along as the third wheel.

items.m: to stop worrying and take a bold risk
items.os: English, 1800s, from the older image of scattering something to the winds, gone for good.
items.ex: On the last word, he threw caution to the wind and spelled it fast.

items.p: throw the baby out with the bathwater
items.m: to discard something valuable while getting rid of the bad
items.os: From a German proverb first printed in 1512; the tale of family baths so murky a baby could vanish is a myth.
items.ex: Don't quit piano over one hard song — that's throwing the baby out with the bathwater.

items.m: to spend less and live more carefully
items.os: English, early 1900s: hunger loosens a belt's fit, so hard times mean cinching it tighter.
items.ex: We're tightening our belts before vacation, so it's library movies this month.

items.m: time passes surprisingly quickly
items.os: From the Latin 'tempus fugit' — time flees — in Virgil's poetry.
items.ex: Time flies at Grandma's — suddenly it's dinner and we never left the pillow fort.

items.m: so close to remembering a word you can almost say it
items.os: English, 1700s: the word feels perched on the tongue's very tip, ready to jump.
items.ex: Her name was on the tip of my tongue all through roll call.

items.m: your smartest, fanciest clothes
items.os: English, 1700s: a 'bib' covered a gentleman's shirt front and a 'tucker' was the lace at a lady's neckline.
items.ex: Dad put on his best bib and tucker for the school awards night.

items.m: bare skin; wearing no clothes at all
items.os: English joke from the 1700s: the only 'suit' you wore on the day you were born is your own skin.
items.ex: The toddler escaped bath time and ran down the hall in his birthday suit.

items.m: to start working hard and seriously
items.os: Perhaps from knights buckling on armor before a fight; 'buckle to' appears by the 1500s, and Americans said 'buckle down' by the 1860s.
items.ex: With the spelling bee a week away, Priya buckled down and drilled her word lists.

items.m: so full there is no room for anything more
items.os: From clothes packed so tight that their stitched seams threaten to split.
items.ex: The gym was bursting at the seams for the district spelling bee.

items.m: to stop talking and keep a secret
items.os: American slang, 1800s, picturing a chatty mouth fastened shut like a coat button.
items.ex: Ben buttoned his lip about the surprise party for Grandma.

items.m: asking for help humbly, like a beggar
items.os: From the old custom of removing your cap and holding it out when begging a favor from someone important.
items.ex: After losing his bus money, Sam went cap in hand to his big sister.

items.m: full of secrecy, spying, and mystery
items.os: From 1600s Spanish 'cloak-and-sword' plays about disguised heroes; English writers made it 'cloak and dagger' in the 1800s.
items.ex: The twins planned Mom's gift with cloak-and-dagger secrecy, passing notes under the table.

items.m: completely invented; utterly false
items.os: 'Whole cloth' meant fabric woven full-size, not pieced from scraps; Americans in the 1800s flipped it to mean a story spun from nothing, perhaps mocking cheating tailors.
items.ex: His excuse about a homework-eating parrot was cut from whole cloth.

items.m: wearing extremely stylish, show-stopping clothes
items.os: English, early 1800s, using 'kill' as slang for making a knockout impression.
items.ex: Aunt Rosa arrived at graduation dressed to kill in a bright red suit.

items.m: to take over someone's role and do it as well
items.os: English, 1700s, picturing a successor stepping straight into the shoes the last person left behind.
items.ex: When the team captain moved away, Zoe worked hard to fill her shoes.

items.m: in excellent spirits or splendid condition
items.os: From birds, whose glossy new feathers after molting are a sign of health; English since the 1500s.
items.ex: Grandpa was in fine feather at breakfast, telling jokes over his pancakes.

items.m: to fit perfectly
items.os: English, 1700s, when gloves were sewn to match a customer's hand exactly; novelist Tobias Smollett used it in 1771.
items.ex: The rented spelling-bee blazer fit Marcus like a glove.

items.p: fly by the seat of your pants
items.m: to act on instinct, without plans or instructions
items.os: From 1930s aviation: pilots without instruments felt the plane's motion through their seats; newspapers said it of Douglas Corrigan's 1938 flight.
items.ex: Nobody explained the science-fair rules, so we flew by the seat of our pants.

items.m: to get cross or annoyed
items.os: British slang, 1800s, cousin to 'keep your shirt on' — an angry man was ready to pull off his shirt and fight.
items.ex: Don't get shirty with me for pausing your game — it's homework time.

items.m: working closely together, often in secret
items.os: English, 1600s, first as 'hand and glove' — as close as a hand inside its own glove.
items.ex: The two class reps worked hand in glove to plan the bake sale.

items.m: to treat someone very gently and tactfully
items.os: Kid gloves, sewn from soft young-goat leather, were too delicate for any rough work; English, 1800s.
items.ex: After Mia's rough day at school, Dad handled her with kid gloves at dinner.

items.m: get ready for something fast or surprising
items.os: American, early 1900s, when open cars and carnival rides could whip a hat clean off your head.
items.ex: Hang on to your hat — I got first place in the spelling bee!

items.m: to stall and mumble instead of answering plainly
items.os: English since the 1400s: 'hem' and 'haw' spell out the throat-clearing sounds of a speaker stalling for time.
items.ex: Asked who broke the vase, Theo hemmed and hawed until Mom raised an eyebrow.

items.m: angry, flustered, or embarrassed
items.os: English, late 1800s: an angry man's neck flushes red and sweaty inside a stiff buttoned collar.
items.ex: Dad got hot under the collar when the printer jammed on my report — again.

items.m: if a criticism applies to you, accept it
items.os: American twist on the 1700s British saying 'if the cap fits, wear it,' which pointed at a fool's cap.
items.ex: 'Are you calling me messy?' Jake asked, and his sister shrugged: 'If the shoe fits.'

items.p: put yourself in someone else's shoes
items.m: imagine how another person feels in their situation
items.os: English, 1700s, from the picture of literally standing in another person's shoes and living their part.
items.ex: Before laughing at the new student's mistake, put yourself in his shoes.

items.m: keep it secret
items.os: English, 1800s: what sits under your hat stays next to your own head only. The story about archers hiding spare bowstrings in their caps is a myth.
items.ex: I'm getting Mom a scarf for her birthday — keep it under your hat.

items.m: stay calm; don't lose your temper
items.os: American, 1800s: men peeled off their good shirts before a fistfight, so keeping yours on meant staying peaceful.
items.ex: Keep your shirt on — the pizza will be here in five minutes.

items.m: to amaze or impress you completely
items.os: American, mid-1800s: first a boast about beating someone so hard his socks flew off, later softened into pure amazement.
items.ex: Wait till you hear Ana's poem — it'll knock your socks off.

items.m: to be secretly amused at someone
items.os: From the 1500s, when wide hanging sleeves could hide a smirking mouth.
items.ex: Rex pretended to sympathize, but he was laughing up his sleeve at the prank.

items.m: so familiar it is boring or outdated
items.os: English, early 1900s: hat fashions changed so quickly that last season's hat stood for anything stale.
items.ex: Long division is old hat to the fifth graders now.

items.m: make a real effort to improve
items.os: British, early 1900s: the image of a scruffy schoolboy yanking up his fallen socks to smarten up for inspection.
items.ex: Coach told the relay team to pull up their socks before the county meet.

items.m: stop talking; be quiet
items.os: British, early 1900s. The tale that people muffled gramophone horns by stuffing socks inside is popular but unproven.
items.ex: 'Put a sock in it, you two,' Dad sighed from the front seat, 'or no radio.'

items.m: to gain success from someone else's achievements
items.os: American politics, 1800s: a popular candidate's long coattails 'carried' weaker candidates into office with him.
items.ex: Don't ride on your lab partner's coattails — do your half of the project.

items.m: get ready to work hard
items.os: From workers shoving their sleeves out of the way before heavy or messy labor; English, 1800s.
items.ex: The whole family rolled up their sleeves to clean the garage on Saturday.

items.p: the shoe is on the other foot
items.m: the situation is reversed; positions have swapped
items.os: English, 1800s, from the earlier 'the boot is on the other leg' — just as shoes newly cut for left and right feet felt wrong when swapped.
items.ex: Lily always quizzed her brother; now that she's in the bee, the shoe is on the other foot.

items.m: to avoid a difficult subject instead of facing it
items.os: From 'skirt' meaning a garment's outer edge, hence the border of anything: you walk around the problem, never through it.
items.ex: When Mom asked about his math grade, Aiden skirted the issue by praising dinner.

items.m: to admire and respect someone's achievement
items.os: From the old custom of doffing your hat as a mark of respect; English, 1800s.
items.ex: I take my hat off to anyone who can spell 'onomatopoeia' under pressure.

items.m: something everyone praises though they secretly see it is fake
items.os: From Hans Christian Andersen's 1837 tale: an emperor parades in invisible 'clothes' until a child shouts that he is wearing nothing.
items.ex: Everyone claimed the glitchy new app was amazing, but Dad called it the emperor's new clothes.

items.m: acting more important than you really are
items.os: English, mid-1800s: a puffed-up sense of self pictured as feet swelling out of your own boots; Americans say 'too big for your britches.'
items.ex: Winning one quiz doesn't mean you can get too big for your boots.

items.m: to be the one in charge at home
items.os: From the centuries when only men wore trousers, so the phrase asked who really ruled the household.
items.ex: Our cat clearly wears the trousers in this house — we all obey her meow.

items.m: relating to office work rather than manual labor
items.os: American, early 1900s: office clerks wore white shirt collars that stayed clean all day; writer Upton Sinclair helped make the label stick.
items.ex: Mom's white-collar job means a desk, a computer, and far too many meetings.

items.m: relating to manual or factory work
items.os: American, 1920s: laborers wore tough blue denim and chambray shirts that hid the day's dirt, unlike clerks' white collars.
items.ex: Grandpa is proud of his blue-collar years building bridges.

items.m: stop talking and keep quiet
items.os: American, 1920s–30s, arriving soon after the zipper itself was named in 1923.
items.ex: Zip your lip during the test, or the teacher will move your seat.

items.m: a very long time
items.os: English, by the 1830s: thirty Sundays — once slow, hushed days when games were forbidden — would feel endless.
items.ex: It'll take a month of Sundays to sort all these old family photos.

items.m: a scramble to finish before a deadline
items.os: English, 1800s, casting time itself as the rival you must outrun.
items.ex: Finishing the diorama before bedtime became a race against time.

items.m: rushing to finish before time runs out
items.os: From races like cycling time trials, run against the clock instead of side-by-side rivals.
items.ex: We worked against the clock to hang decorations before the guests arrived.

items.m: having ideas too modern for your era
items.os: English, 1800s: visionaries were said to belong to a later age than the one they were born in.
items.ex: Great-Grandma coded computers in the 1960s — she was ahead of her time.

items.m: be patient; it will happen at the right moment
items.os: An English counsel of patience recorded since the 1500s.
items.ex: 'When can I open presents?' 'All in good time — after cake.'

items.m: all day and all night without stopping
items.os: From a clock's hands sweeping the whole dial; the 1954 hit 'Rock Around the Clock' sealed its fame.
items.ex: The animal shelter volunteers cared for the rescued puppies around the clock.

items.m: at the very last possible moment
items.os: From Jesus's parable in Matthew 20: workers hired at the eleventh hour still receive a full day's pay.
items.ex: Dev finished his book report at the eleventh hour, printing it as the bus arrived.

items.m: to finish just before time runs out
items.os: American, from timed games and races; the 1950s TV game show 'Beat the Clock' made it a household phrase.
items.ex: Rosa beat the clock, bubbling in her last answer as the timer buzzed.

items.m: old-fashioned; unaware of modern ways
items.os: English, 1800s, picturing time as a march that some people fail to keep up with.
items.ex: Dad still burns CDs for the car — he's a little behind the times.

items.m: the top, most successful level of anything
items.os: American vaudeville slang, early 1900s: 'big time' theaters booked stars for two shows a day, while 'small time' acts slogged through five.
items.ex: Making the national spelling bee means you've hit the big time.

items.m: to declare something over
items.os: From referees and British pub landlords shouting 'Time!' to end play or last orders.
items.ex: Mom called time on video games until everyone's homework was done.

items.m: seize the day; make the most of today
items.os: From the Roman poet Horace's Odes, 23 BC: pluck the day like ripe fruit, trusting tomorrow as little as possible.
items.ex: 'Carpe diem,' said Ms. Alvarez, 'sign up for the talent show today.'

items.m: every single day, without variation
items.os: English, 1800s, doubling 'day' to stress unbroken routine.
items.ex: Day in, day out, Milo practices piano scales before school.

items.m: a playful age scale where one human year counts as seven for dogs
items.os: American, 1900s, from the rough rule that dogs age about seven times faster than people — vets say the real math is fuzzier.
items.ex: Our beagle is nine, which Grandpa says makes her sixty-three in dog years.

items.m: an extremely long time
items.os: British, early 1900s, a joking twist on 'donkey's ears,' which are famously long.
items.ex: We haven't visited the science museum in donkey's years.

items.m: continuing until the latest possible moment
items.os: From clock-timed exams and contests, where every remaining minute gets used.
items.ex: Priya reviewed her spelling flashcards down to the last minute backstage.

items.m: the faint stubble on a man's face by late afternoon
items.os: Coined in late-1930s American ads for Gem razor blades, warning that a morning shave fades by five o'clock.
items.ex: By dinner Dad's five o'clock shadow makes his goodnight kiss scratchy.

items.m: for now, until things change
items.os: English, 1500s: 'being' here is an old noun for existence, so it means 'for the time now existing.'
items.ex: For the time being, the twins have to share a bedroom.

items.m: from the very beginning
items.os: American, 1900s, counting a venture's life from its first calendar day.
items.ex: Coach said hustle matters from day one of practice.

items.p: have the time of your life
items.m: to enjoy yourself tremendously
items.os: English, late 1800s; the 1987 hit '(I've Had) The Time of My Life' keeps it singing.
items.ex: Maya had the time of her life at the class camping trip.

items.m: deep sadness, especially when doing something you wish you didn't have to
items.os: The heart has stood for feeling since ancient times — Egyptians even pictured hearts weighed on scales after death; in English since the Middle Ages.
items.ex: With a heavy heart, Mia handed back the library book she loved.

items.p: a leopard never changes its spots
items.m: people cannot change their basic nature
items.os: From the Bible, where the prophet Jeremiah asks, 'Can the leopard change his spots?'
items.ex: Dad joked that our sock-stealing puppy proves a leopard never changes its spots.

items.p: at the end of your rope
items.m: out of patience, energy, or options
items.os: Likely from a tethered animal that can graze no farther than its rope allows; the British say 'end of your tether.'
items.ex: After three broken shoelaces in one week, Mom was at the end of her rope.

items.m: so worried or stuck you have no idea what to do next
items.os: From the Bible, Psalm 107, where storm-tossed sailors 'are at their wit's end.'
items.ex: After the tenth try at the math puzzle, Grandpa was at his wit's end.

items.m: reveal your most private thoughts and feelings
items.os: 'Bare' means to uncover — you pull the covers off your inner self; figurative in English since the 1600s.
items.ex: In her diary, Ana bares her soul about spelling-bee nerves.

items.m: very upset or offended, usually over something small
items.os: American, mid-1900s; pictures a person twisted like a warped piece of metal.
items.ex: Don't get bent out of shape over one wrong answer on the quiz.

items.m: overwhelmed by a strong emotion like worry, anger, or joy
items.os: In English since the 1400s: strong feeling was imagined pushing you right out of your body, leaving you standing beside yourself.
items.ex: Grandma was beside herself with joy when Priya reached the final round.

items.m: hold back words, laughter, or tears
items.os: From the real gesture — pressing your teeth into your lip to keep quiet; recorded in English since the 1500s.
items.ex: Sam bit his lip to keep from blurting out the answer.

items.m: suddenly become very angry
items.os: From electrical fuses, which burn out with a pop when too much current surges through; American, 1930s.
items.ex: Dad nearly blew a fuse when we left the freezer door open all night.

items.m: keep changing your mind or enthusiasm
items.os: From Aesop's fable of the satyr who distrusts a man blowing on his hands to warm them and on his soup to cool it.
items.ex: Lena blows hot and cold about joining the chess club.

items.m: explode with anger
items.os: American, early 1900s; probably pictures a volcano blasting its whole peak off.
items.ex: Coach blew his top when nobody had practiced their word lists.

items.m: keep feelings shut inside instead of letting them out
items.os: Feelings are pictured as fizzy liquid corked in a bottle, quietly building pressure; figurative since the 1800s.
items.ex: The counselor said not to bottle up worries about the test.

items.m: feel so proud you can hardly contain it
items.os: Feelings are pictured as pressure in a container — enough pride and you simply pop.
items.ex: Mom nearly burst with pride when Ravi spelled 'chrysanthemum' perfectly.

items.p: carry the weight of the world
items.m: feel burdened by enormous worries or responsibilities
items.os: From the Greek myth of Atlas, condemned to hold up the heavens — often pictured as the whole globe — on his shoulders.
items.ex: Ever since tryouts, Maya has been carrying the weight of the world on her shoulders.

items.m: fall apart emotionally, or stop working, under stress
items.os: From clothing whose stitched seams split open when strained too far.
items.ex: By the third missed bus, our field-trip plan was coming apart at the seams.

items.m: be kept waiting, usually longer than you'd like
items.os: English, 1600s: after a hot, dusty walk, a rest lets your burning feet cool down.
items.ex: We cooled our heels in the hallway while the judges tallied scores.

items.m: notice and be thankful for the good things you have
items.os: From the Christian habit of thankfully listing God's gifts; the 1897 hymn 'Count Your Blessings' spread the phrase.
items.ex: When Zoe moaned about second place, Grandpa told her to count her blessings.

items.m: looking sad and discouraged
items.os: From the way the corners of the mouth droop when someone is glum; English, 1600s.
items.ex: Leo was down in the mouth after fumbling his easiest word.

items.m: annoy or frustrate someone almost past bearing
items.os: Pictures someone so maddened they claw up the walls to escape; common since the mid-1900s.
items.ex: My little brother's pencil-tapping drives me up the wall during homework.

items.p: fed up to the back teeth
items.m: completely annoyed and out of patience
items.os: British; strengthens 'fed up' — you're stuffed with annoyance right up to your rearmost teeth.
items.ex: Mum is fed up to the back teeth with muddy shoes in the hallway.

items.m: feel sad or gloomy
items.os: Blue has meant 'sad' in English since the 1500s; the later sailors' tale about blue flags for a dead captain is doubtful.
items.ex: Rainy Saturdays make me feel blue until we bake cookies.

items.p: feel on top of the world
items.m: feel wonderfully happy and confident
items.os: American, early 1900s; success is pictured as standing on the planet's highest point with everything below you.
items.ex: After acing her recital, Nina felt on top of the world.

items.m: extremely angry or agitated
items.os: American, 1800s; pictures someone so wild with fury they'd need to be tied down.
items.ex: Dad was fit to be tied when the printer jammed on science-fair night.

items.m: suddenly become furiously angry
items.os: 'Fly' keeps its old sense of rushing violently; in English since the 1600s.
items.ex: The villain in our class play flies into a rage over a stolen crown.

items.m: become so excited you lose control or good judgment
items.os: Emotion is pictured as a current sweeping a swimmer off downstream.
items.ex: I got carried away decorating my book report and stayed up too late.

items.p: get it out of your system
items.m: do or say something so the urge finally stops nagging you
items.os: From the idea of the body flushing something upsetting out of its system; early 1900s.
items.ex: Coach let us run a lap to get the giggles out of our system.

items.m: steadily annoy someone
items.os: From the 1800s, when doctors talked constantly about nerves; irritation is pictured pressing right on them.
items.ex: Humming during silent reading gets on everyone's nerves.

items.p: get your knickers in a twist
items.m: get flustered or upset over something minor
items.os: British, 1960s; knickers are underpants, and twisted ones cause fuss out of all proportion.
items.ex: Don't get your knickers in a twist — we'll find your lucky pencil.

items.m: lose emotional control completely
items.os: Pictures a person shattering like a dropped plate; 1800s.
items.ex: Practice the hard words now so you don't go to pieces on stage.

items.m: smile as widely as possible with delight
items.os: A plain picture: a smile so wide it seems to stretch from one ear to the other; recorded by the 1700s.
items.ex: Tom grinned from ear to ear when his name made the finalist list.

items.m: be slightly crazy or act oddly
items.os: From machinery: one loose screw makes the whole contraption wobble; 1800s.
items.ex: Our robot vacuum bumps the same wall all day, like it has a screw loose.

items.m: become angry very quickly
items.os: From explosives: a short fuse burns down in seconds, leaving no time before the bang.
items.ex: My sister has a short fuse when she's hungry, so we bring snacks.

items.m: want something so much you can't stop hoping for it
items.os: To 'set' your heart is to fix it firmly in place on one wish; in English since the 1300s.
items.ex: Ella has her heart set on winning the district bee.

items.m: keep resenting someone long after they wronged you
items.os: 'Grudge' comes from Middle English grutchen, to grumble — old resentment kept muttering away inside.
items.ex: Ben doesn't hold a grudge; he congratulated the boy who beat him.

items.m: so angry you could jump up and down
items.os: English, 1600s; pictures rage so strong it literally makes you hop.
items.ex: Mom was hopping mad when the twins tracked paint across the rug.

items.m: stuck in a gloomy, low mood
items.os: Possibly from Flemish 'fonck,' meaning fright; it began as Oxford student slang for fear in the 1700s.
items.ex: Losing his library card put Theo in a funk all afternoon.

items.m: cheerful, lively, and energetic
items.os: Old medicine taught that invisible 'spirits' inside the body controlled mood — when they ran high, you sparkled.
items.ex: The class was in high spirits on the last day before break.

items.m: perfectly, blissfully happy
items.os: From Jewish and Islamic tradition, which pictured seven heavens — the seventh, highest one nearest to God.
items.ex: Ana was in seventh heaven when she got the top bunk at camp.

items.m: be so happy you leap in the air
items.os: Recorded in English since the 1500s; joy really can make people spring off the ground.
items.ex: Milo jumped for joy when the snow day was announced.

items.m: stay calm and think clearly under pressure
items.os: Anger has been pictured as heat in the head for centuries; a cool head stays clear.
items.ex: Spellers who keep a cool head remember to ask for the word's origin.

items.m: stay calm instead of getting upset
items.os: American, 1950s jazz slang, when 'cool' meant calm, stylish, and unruffled.
items.ex: Even when the microphone squealed, Priya kept her cool.

items.m: laugh long and extremely hard
items.os: One of the 1800s 'your head off' exaggerations, like shouting or working your head off.
items.ex: We laughed our heads off at Dad's upside-down pancake flip.

items.m: get angry or flustered
items.os: American, 1950s jazz slang: 'cool' was calm composure, and losing it meant cracking.
items.ex: The coach never loses his cool, even in overtime.

items.m: suddenly become angry
items.os: 'Temper' once meant your balanced blend of qualities, from Latin temperare, to mix — lose it and the balance tips.
items.ex: I almost lost my temper when my block tower got knocked over.

items.m: cause a loud, embarrassing fuss in public
items.os: From the theater: a dramatic 'scene' suddenly performed for everyone watching; 1700s.
items.ex: Please don't make a scene in the store over the cereal, buddy.

items.m: the ability to stay calm when things are frightening
items.os: Nerves pictured as steel cables that will not snap under strain; 1800s.
items.ex: It takes nerves of steel to spell the last word in a tiebreaker.

items.m: nervous, tense, and easily startled
items.os: Shortened from 'set the teeth on edge' — that unpleasant tingling in your teeth — a phrase found in the Bible and Shakespeare.
items.ex: Everyone was on edge waiting for the results to be posted.

items.m: in anxious suspense while you wait
items.os: Tenterhooks were the hooks that stretched new-woven cloth tight on a drying frame called a tenter; figurative by the 1700s.
items.ex: We sat on tenterhooks while the judges checked the spelling.

items.m: a little grumpy, unwell, or not yourself
items.os: English, 1600s; the story tying it to printers who ran out of 'sorts' — pieces of type — is unproven.
items.ex: Ben was out of sorts all morning until he finally ate breakfast.

items.m: calm down and regain control of your feelings
items.os: Pictures someone scattered by panic gathering their pieces back into one whole person; 1800s.
items.ex: Take a deep breath, pull yourself together, and walk back on stage.

items.m: shout and complain wildly and at length
items.os: Two old verbs for wild talk yoked together — 'rant' comes from Dutch randten, to talk nonsense; paired since the 1600s.
items.ex: Grandpa rants and raves at the TV referees every Saturday.

items.m: so frightened you can't move
items.os: From the body's real freeze response — sudden fear can literally stiffen your muscles.
items.ex: I was scared stiff during the thunderstorm until Mom lit candles.

items.p: take a load off your mind
items.m: remove a worry that has been weighing on you
items.os: Worry is pictured as a heavy load the mind carries; 'a load off my mind' appears by the 1700s.
items.ex: Finding the lost permission slip took a load off my mind.

items.m: relax; don't work or worry too hard
items.os: American, 1800s; doubles as a friendly goodbye.
items.ex: The doctor told Dad to take it easy for a week after his cold.

items.m: be wildly frustrated or worried
items.os: From the ancient mourning custom of literally tearing one's hair, described in Homer and the Bible.
items.ex: This maze puzzle has me tearing my hair out.

items.m: easily hurt or offended by criticism
items.os: A thin skin lets every little scratch through; figurative in English since the 1600s.
items.ex: Don't be thin-skinned about the coach's tips — they help.

items.m: extremely pleased and delighted
items.os: Tickling leaves you flushed pink with laughter; American, early 1900s.
items.ex: Grandma was tickled pink to get a hand-drawn birthday card.

items.m: unable to choose between two things you want equally
items.os: Pictures being pulled toward two choices at once, hard enough to tear you in two.
items.ex: Rosa was torn between art club and the spelling team.

items.m: let out your anger and complaints
items.os: Old medicine blamed the spleen for brewing anger and bad temper; 'venting' it released the fumes.
items.ex: Dad vented his spleen about the traffic, then apologized for grumbling.

items.m: feeling so happy you seem weightless
items.os: Joy pictured as weightlessness; popular in English since the late 1800s.
items.ex: Keisha was walking on air after spelling the winning word.

items.m: so worried you feel ill
items.os: Barely an exaggeration — severe worry really can upset your stomach and your sleep.
items.ex: Call home after practice so Mom isn't worried sick.

items.m: feeling and acting youthful whatever your age
items.os: The heart stands for your spirit, which needn't age with your body; a hit 1953 song made the phrase famous.
items.ex: Grandpa is young at heart — he still races us to the mailbox.

items.m: a joke built on a word's double meaning; a pun
items.os: 'Play' here is wordplay — juggling meanings for fun; the term dates from the 1700s.
items.ex: Her project title, 'Gone with the Wind Power,' is a play on words.

items.m: judge people by what they do, not what they promise
items.os: A blunt shortening of the proverb 'actions speak louder than words'; British suffragettes marched under 'Deeds, not words' in the early 1900s.
items.ex: Coach wants actions, not words — practice, don't just promise to.

items.m: be the one to tell someone important, often unhappy, information
items.os: 'Break' has meant to reveal something sealed since the 1500s, as if cracking open a letter.
items.ex: Who's going to break the news that the field trip is postponed?

items.m: strictly according to the rules
items.os: The book is whatever official volume holds the rules; Shakespeare's Juliet says Romeo kisses 'by the book.'
items.ex: Our umpire calls every play by the book.

items.m: scold someone loudly and harshly
items.os: American military slang from around World War II.
items.ex: The bus driver chewed us out for standing up before the stop.

items.m: talk honestly so tension or misunderstanding disappears
items.os: From the fresh, clean air after a thunderstorm breaks; figurative since the 1500s.
items.ex: The sisters cleared the air about the borrowed headphones.

items.m: suggest something indirectly, hoping someone catches on
items.os: Pictures letting a small clue fall casually where someone will notice it; 1700s.
items.ex: Ana keeps dropping hints that she wants a dictionary for her birthday.

items.m: a teasing reply to a confident claim that may backfire
items.os: From collections of dying people's memorable final sayings; turned into an ironic joke in early 1900s slang.
items.ex: 'This level is easy' — famous last words, said right before he lost.

items.m: manage to say anything while someone else talks nonstop
items.os: Pictures sliding a word in sideways, edge first, through a tiny gap in the chatter; 1800s.
items.ex: When the twins retell a movie, nobody gets a word in edgewise.

items.m: say the main thing immediately, without rambling
items.os: The 'point' is an argument's sharp tip — the part that actually pricks; in English since the Middle Ages.
items.ex: Our teacher gets straight to the point: 'Quiz Friday. Study.'

items.m: understand what someone is really telling you
items.os: From the plain idea of a delivered message finally reaching its reader; common since the mid-1900s.
items.ex: I yawned twice, and my chatty cousin finally got the message.

items.p: get the wrong end of the stick
items.m: completely misunderstand a situation
items.os: British, from the older 'worse end of the staff' of the 1500s; the popular story about Roman toilet sponge-sticks is a myth.
items.ex: Dad got the wrong end of the stick and arrived a day early for the recital.

items.p: give someone a piece of your mind
items.m: angrily tell someone exactly what you think of them
items.os: A 'piece' of your mind is a sample of your honest opinion, served blunt; in English since the 1500s.
items.ex: Mom gave the prank callers a piece of her mind.

items.m: learn news through gossip instead of official announcements
items.os: From 'grapevine telegraph,' American Civil War slang for tangled rumor networks — twisting like vines, unlike straight telegraph wires.
items.ex: I heard it through the grapevine that our teacher is getting married.

items.m: stay silent even though you want to speak
items.os: In English for a thousand years; the King James Bible of 1611 uses it too.
items.ex: I held my tongue about the surprise party all week.

items.m: in a certain way; sort of true
items.os: A polite softener from the 1800s, warning listeners that the words are approximate.
items.ex: Our garage is a laboratory, in a manner of speaking, during science-fair week.

items.m: written or printed, so it is clear and official
items.os: Black ink on white paper — once printed, words feel permanent; in English since the 1600s.
items.ex: The rules say it in black and white: no phones at the bee.

items.m: in simple, clear words anyone can understand
items.os: 'Plain' English was contrasted with lawyers' Latin and French in medieval England; the phrase dates from the 1500s.
items.ex: In plain English, 'photosynthesis' means plants making food from sunlight.

items.m: keep telling me the latest news
items.os: From ledgers: clerks 'posted' the newest figures into account books to keep them current; 1800s.
items.ex: Keep me posted on the bake sale — text me if you sell out.

items.m: say nothing; keep the secret
items.os: 'Mum' imitates the humming sound of lips pressed shut — mmm; in English since the 1300s.
items.ex: We're keeping mum about Dad's surprise gift.

items.m: meaning that vanishes when words move between languages
items.os: Often traced to poet Robert Frost's remark that poetry is what gets lost in translation; a 2003 film title made it everyday.
items.ex: Grandma's Hindi jokes get lost in translation, but we laugh anyway.

items.m: chat politely about unimportant things
items.os: 'Small talk' appears in Lord Chesterfield's famous letters of advice to his son, 1751.
items.ex: Dad made small talk with the other parents while we rehearsed.

items.m: soften your words instead of speaking bluntly
items.os: From mincing meat into tiny pieces — chopping harsh words fine so they're easier to swallow; 1500s.
items.ex: Our coach doesn't mince words: 'That spelling was sloppy.'

items.m: keep this a secret; don't tell anyone
items.os: 'Mum' is the hum of sealed lips; Shakespeare wrote 'seal up your lips and give no words but mum.'
