items.ex: Mum's the word about Mom's surprise party until Saturday.

items.m: said privately, not to be reported or repeated
items.os: American journalism slang of the 1930s; President Franklin Roosevelt's off-the-record press chats helped spread it.
items.ex: Off the record, the coach thinks we'll win districts.

items.m: stated publicly and officially, where it can be checked
items.os: From courts and registers, where statements are written into the official record; 1600s.
items.ex: The principal is on record promising a pizza party for perfect attendance.

items.m: say something nice about someone to help them
items.os: Slipping one helpful 'word' into a powerful person's ear; in English since the 1500s.
items.ex: Will you put in a good word for me with the librarian?

items.m: claim someone said things they never actually said
items.os: Ancient — the Bible's Second Book of Samuel already describes putting words in a messenger's mouth.
items.ex: Don't put words in my mouth — I said maybe, not yes.

items.m: notice the hidden meaning that isn't stated directly
items.os: From secret messages written in invisible ink between the visible lines of a letter.
items.ex: Reading between the lines of her note, I could tell she was nervous.

items.m: talk too much, often carelessly or boastfully
items.os: American slang, 1900s; the mouth pictured as a motor left running.
items.ex: He ran his mouth about winning, then went out in round one.

items.m: said when someone appears just as you mention them
items.os: Short for the 1600s superstition 'speak of the Devil and he shall appear' — a warning against naming him.
items.ex: Speak of the devil — we were just talking about you, Uncle Raj!

items.m: reveal a great deal without any words
items.os: A single look can say as much as whole volumes of books; 1700s.
items.ex: Her grin when the results went up spoke volumes.

items.m: explain something in the plainest, most detailed way
items.os: From spelling a word letter by letter for someone who can't catch it; figurative by the mid-1900s.
items.ex: Do I have to spell it out? Muddy cleats stay outside.

items.m: tell everyone the news
items.os: 'The Word' first meant the Gospel that preachers carried from town to town; now any news can travel the same way.
items.ex: Spread the word: the bake sale moved to Friday.

items.m: honest, direct speech with no tricks
items.os: American, 1800s; 'straight' meaning honest, with no bends or dodges in it.
items.ex: Time for some straight talk: homework comes before video games.

items.m: believe me without demanding proof
items.os: Your 'word' has been a pledge of honor since medieval times.
items.ex: Take my word for it — the cafeteria chili is spicy today.

items.m: talk extremely fast
items.os: American, 1800s: a mile a minute — sixty miles an hour — was then an astonishing, almost imaginary speed.
items.ex: After camp, Zoe talked a mile a minute about the canoe race.

items.m: talk on and on without ever reaching the point
items.os: The speech loops like a circle, ending exactly where it began — like the 'circular arguments' of logic class.
items.ex: Quit talking in circles and tell us who won.

items.m: discuss your work when you're not at work
items.os: British, 1800s; 'shop' meant your trade or workplace.
items.ex: At the picnic, the two teachers ended up talking shop about grading.

items.m: speak impressively about something, whether or not you can actually do it
items.os: From the American pairing 'talk the talk and walk the walk,' 1900s.
items.ex: He talks the talk about chess, but he's never beaten Grandma.

items.m: say something you know is false; lie boldly
items.os: A softer cousin of 'lie through your teeth,' an insult English speakers have hurled at bold liars since about 1300.
items.ex: He was talking through his teeth when he claimed his book report was done.

items.m: speak the plain truth, even when it's uncomfortable
items.os: American, 1960s; a catchphrase of plain speaking from the civil-rights era, later famous from sportscaster Howard Cosell.
items.ex: Grandma tells it like it is: 'Your room is a disaster.'

items.m: the final remark in an argument; also the newest, finest version of something
items.os: From quarrels where whoever speaks last seems to win; in English since the 1500s.
items.ex: My sister always needs the last word, even in whispers.

items.m: back up your words with matching actions
items.os: Squeezed from the American saying 'talk the talk and walk the walk,' 1900s.
items.ex: She says practice matters, and she walks the talk — twenty words every morning.

items.m: repeated or copied in exactly the same words
items.os: In English since the 1300s — Chaucer used it — matching the Latin 'verbatim.'
items.ex: Leo memorized the whole poem word for word.

items.m: I'm too amazed, moved, or shocked to speak
items.os: English, 1700s: language itself is pictured giving up on the job.
items.ex: Words fail me — you cleaned the whole kitchen without being asked!

items.m: stop talking right now
items.os: From zipping your lips shut; the zipper itself got its snappy name around 1923.
items.ex: The librarian's look said 'zip it' better than any words.

items.m: credit for trying hard, even though the attempt failed
items.os: From school grades, where A is the top mark; American, mid-1900s, usually said with a smile.
items.ex: The lopsided birthday cake earned Dad an A for effort.

items.m: a normal part of the job, even if hard or surprising
items.os: English, 1700s, from sailors and laborers — whatever the day's work happens to bring.
items.ex: Untangling three kites at once? All in a day's work for Grandpa.

items.m: returning to hard, repetitive work
items.os: From 'the daily grind' — grinding grain at a mill, slow and repetitive; 1800s.
items.ex: Vacation's over — back to the grind of word lists and math facts.

items.m: returning to hard, unpleasant work, said as a joke
items.os: Alludes to prisoners in tsarist Russia sentenced to labor in Siberian salt mines; Americans began joking with it in the early 1900s.
items.ex: Recess is over — back to the salt mines, spellers!

items.p: to have a stick in your ear
items.m: to have had too much to drink
items.os: Danish slang, 'at have en pind i øret', where a 'pind' is a little wooden stick; why a stick lodges in a tipsy ear, no Dane has ever explained.
items.ex: Uncle Lars danced so wildly at the wedding that Grandma joked he had a stick in his ear.
items.lit: at have en pind i øret

items.m: to avoid the real subject instead of speaking directly
items.os: Czechs say 'chodit kolem horké kaše' — circling a bowl of porridge too hot to touch; Germans picture a cat prowling around hot mash the same way.
items.ex: Stop walking around hot porridge and just tell Mom about the math test.

items.p: to feed the donkey sponge cake
items.m: to waste something fine on someone who won't appreciate it
items.os: Portuguese 'alimentar um burro a pão de ló': pão de ló is a feather-light festival sponge cake, utterly wasted on a donkey.
items.ex: Buying fancy gel pens for my little brother is feeding the donkey sponge cake — he just chews them.
items.lit: alimentar um burro a pão de ló

items.m: to feel sad and gloomy
items.os: French 'avoir le cafard'; the poet Baudelaire helped make 'cafard' (cockroach) the word for creeping gloom in his 1857 poems.
items.ex: Rainy Sundays with nobody to play with give me the cockroach.

items.p: a mouse's child will be a mouse
items.m: children usually turn out like their parents
items.os: A Persian saying about family likeness; its exact source is unrecorded, unlike its famous cousin about the wolf cub from the poet Saadi.
items.ex: Dad the old champion speller grinned 'a mouse's child will be a mouse' when I made the school bee final.
items.lit: بچه‌ی موش، موش می‌شود (bachche-ye mush, mush mishavad)

eq.p: the apple doesn't fall far from the tree

items.p: drop by drop a lake forms
items.m: small steady efforts add up to something big
items.os: Turkish 'Damlaya damlaya göl olur', the proverb parents quote as children drop coins one by one into a money box.
items.ex: Learn five spelling words a day — drop by drop a lake forms.

items.p: to have your butt between two chairs
items.m: to be awkwardly stuck between two choices or two worlds
items.os: French 'avoir le cul entre deux chaises' pictures a guest perched half on each of two chairs, comfortable on neither.
items.ex: With soccer and choir both meeting on Tuesdays, I've got my butt between two chairs.
items.lit: avoir le cul entre deux chaises

items.p: not to be out of the inn
items.m: to still face plenty of trouble before a problem is over
items.os: French 'ne pas être sorti de l'auberge'; in 1800s thieves' slang the 'auberge' (inn) meant prison — a place with meals and a bed you cannot leave.
items.ex: Two posters done and eight to go — our project group is not out of the inn yet.
items.lit: ne pas être sorti de l'auberge

items.p: to push grandma into the nettles
items.m: to push your luck or take something too far
items.os: From the cheeky French warning 'faut pas pousser mémé dans les orties' — don't shove granny into the stinging nettles; who first said it, nobody knows.
items.ex: Extra dessert AND a later bedtime? Don't push grandma into the nettles.
items.lit: faut pas pousser mémé dans les orties

items.m: to tease someone playfully or fool them
items.os: Spanish 'tomar el pelo'; why grabbing hair means teasing is lost — one old guess points to barbers, another to mocking tugs on a man's beard.
items.ex: You did NOT meet the national spelling champion at the mall — you're taking my hair!

items.p: the drop that made the barrel overflow
items.m: the small final problem that makes everything too much
items.os: German 'der Tropfen, der das Fass zum Überlaufen brachte' — one drop too many spills the whole barrel; Spanish speakers overflow a glass instead.
items.ex: The broken pencil was the drop that made the barrel overflow, and Mia burst into tears over her homework.
items.lit: der Tropfen, der das Fass zum Überlaufen brachte

eq.p: la gota que colmó el vaso
eq.lit: the drop that overfilled the glass

items.m: too late; the chance has already passed
items.os: Polish 'po ptakach' — the birds have flown, so there is nothing left to catch or do.
items.ex: We reached the bake sale after the birds — every last cookie was gone.

items.p: don't call the wolf from the forest
items.m: don't invite trouble by talking about it
items.os: Polish 'Nie wywołuj wilka z lasu': name the wolf aloud and it may pad out of the trees.
items.ex: Don't brag that you never lose your backpack — don't call the wolf from the forest.

items.p: to throw peas at a wall
items.m: to waste words on someone who won't listen
items.os: Polish 'rzucać grochem o ścianę' — dried peas bounce off a wall, and not one of them sticks.
items.ex: Telling my brother to clean his desk is throwing peas at a wall.

eq.p: like talking to a brick wall

items.m: to come back empty-handed and outsmarted
items.os: From a classic Arab tale written down in medieval proverb collections: the cobbler Hunayn avenged a rude customer by planting his slippers one by one along the road, tricking the man into abandoning his camel.
items.ex: I waited an hour in the book-fair line and returned with Hunayn's slippers — they had sold out.

items.m: to fall down hard
items.os: Persian 'zamin khordan', literally to eat the ground — the everyday Persian verb for taking a tumble.
items.ex: I ate the earth on the icy playground but got right back up.

eq.p: to fall flat on your face

items.m: to find sudden success or something very valuable
items.os: From the California gold rush of 1849, when one lucky swing of a pickaxe could make a miner rich.
items.ex: We struck gold when Grandpa turned out to be a walking dictionary.

items.m: to pause and carefully assess a situation
items.os: From shopkeepers counting every item on their shelves — 'taking stock' — before deciding what to buy next.
items.ex: After the practice test, we took stock of which word lists still needed work.

items.m: the final responsibility is mine and cannot be passed on
items.os: US President Harry Truman kept a desk sign reading 'The buck stops here' — the buck was a poker marker passed to the next dealer.
items.ex: Dad says the buck stops here when the carpool plan goes wrong.

items.m: to try to fix something by spending, without real thought
items.os: American business and political talk of the mid-1900s, when critics accused governments of spending instead of solving.
items.ex: Buying five spelling apps is just throwing money at the problem; you still have to practice.

items.m: to cut back on spending
items.os: Medieval purses were leather pouches pulled shut with drawstrings; tightening them kept coins from slipping out.
items.ex: After the car repair, Mom tightened the purse strings on weekend treats.

items.m: wasted time costs you as much as wasted money
items.os: Benjamin Franklin made it famous in his 1748 'Advice to a Young Tradesman,' though the idea is far older.
items.ex: Dad taped 'time is money' above my desk during exam week.

items.m: your opinion, offered humbly
items.os: American, 1800s; perhaps from poker's two-cent ante or Britain's older 'two pennies' worth' — no one is sure.
items.ex: Can I add my two cents' worth about the carpool schedule?

items.m: extremely valuable or useful
items.os: Ancient praise: the Roman playwright Plautus was already weighing things against gold around 200 BC.
items.ex: A quiet study corner is worth its weight in gold before a bee.

items.m: immediate payment, on the spot
items.os: American; frontier stores were said to use an upturned barrel as a counter, and buyers laid their money right on it.
items.ex: The yard-sale lady wanted cash on the barrelhead, so Dad counted out bills.

items.p: a fool and his money are soon parted
items.m: careless people quickly lose what they have
items.os: First recorded in Thomas Tusser's rhyming farm advice of 1573.
items.ex: Grandma quoted 'a fool and his money are soon parted' when I spent my whole allowance on stickers in one day.

items.p: in for a penny, in for a pound
items.m: once started, commit to it completely
items.os: English, 1600s: a debtor could be jailed for a penny the same as for a pound, so you might as well risk it all.
items.ex: We'd already baked one cake for the fair — in for a penny, in for a pound, so we made three.

items.m: a child's plea for coins before Bonfire Night
items.os: British children once wheeled a stuffed dummy of Guy Fawkes through the streets each November, calling 'penny for the guy!' to collect firework money.
items.ex: In her London letter, my pen pal explained asking a penny for the guy every November.

items.m: a debt collected cruelly, whatever the harm
items.os: In Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice (1596), the moneylender Shylock demands a pound of the merchant's flesh when a loan goes unpaid.
items.ex: Charging your sister interest on a borrowed pencil? Don't demand your pound of flesh.

items.m: money treated as the most important thing in life
items.os: Coined by Washington Irving in an 1836 story, echoing an older poet's 'almighty gold.'
items.ex: That shop cares only about the almighty dollar, Dad grumbled.

items.p: you get what you pay for
items.m: cheap things are usually poor quality
items.os: Old market wisdom, recorded in English since the 1800s and echoed in many languages.
items.ex: The bargain backpack ripped in a week — you get what you pay for.

items.p: a rising tide lifts all boats
items.m: when conditions improve, everyone benefits
items.os: A New England saying made famous by President John F. Kennedy in 1963 speeches about the economy.
items.ex: When the whole class studies together, a rising tide lifts all boats.

items.m: everyone must come and help
items.os: The bosun's cry ordering a ship's entire crew topside in an emergency or storm.
items.ex: Bake sale tomorrow — all hands on deck in the kitchen tonight!

items.m: we're off; the journey is starting
items.os: 'Aweigh' means the anchor has just lifted clear of the seabed — the moment a voyage begins; the US Naval Academy took it for its 1906 fight song.
items.ex: Anchors aweigh! Dad called as we pulled out for the state bee.

items.m: in trouble, accept whatever help is available
items.os: Sailors' saying from the 1700s: a ship caught in a gale shelters in whatever harbor it can reach, friendly or not.
items.ex: The library was closed, so we studied in the noisy cafeteria — any port in a storm.

items.m: prepare for coming trouble
items.os: Before a storm, sailors sealed the deck openings with canvas held down by wooden strips called battens.
items.ex: Exam week starts Monday — batten down the hatches.

items.m: a quiet period just before trouble begins
items.os: Sailors noticed the strange stillness that often settles just before a big storm breaks.
items.ex: The house is silent while the twins nap — the calm before the storm.

items.m: to pursue impossible dreams
items.os: From the old legend of a pot of gold at the rainbow's end — which you can never reach, since rainbows move with you.
items.ex: Hoping to win without studying is chasing rainbows.

items.m: to behave riskily, just short of breaking the rules
items.os: A ship steered too close to the wind's direction risks stalling with flapping sails.
items.ex: Whispering hints during review games sails close to the wind.

items.m: no matter what obstacles appear
items.os: American, late 1800s; often traced to cattle drives that pushed on through floods and badlands, though no one has proved it.
items.ex: Come hell or high water, we'll finish this project by Friday.

items.m: stopped completely, with no chance of progress
items.os: A sailing ship becalmed — no wind, no motion — was said to lie dead in the water.
items.ex: Without poster board, our science-fair plan was dead in the water.

items.m: a wish for good luck on a journey
items.os: A fair wind blows from behind and speeds a ship along; sailors' farewells grew into the toast 'fair winds and following seas.'
items.ex: Fair winds! Grandma wrote on the card before our big move.

items.m: fierce warnings about punishment
items.os: From the Bible, where burning sulfur — 'brimstone' — rains on the wicked cities of Sodom and Gomorrah.
items.ex: The coach's fire-and-brimstone speech about missed practices had us showing up early.

items.m: moving ahead at top speed and effort
items.os: A ship with every sail spread catches all the wind it can hold.
items.ex: With a week left before the deadline, our project team was at full sail.

items.m: to adjust to a new, unsteady situation
items.os: New sailors stumble for days until their bodies learn to balance on a rolling deck.
items.ex: Give the new student a week to get her sea legs.

items.m: to do far too much
items.os: From falling over a ship's rail into the sea; Americans began using it for wild excess in the early 1900s.
items.ex: One poster for the bee is fine; forty is going overboard.

items.m: stranded and left without help
items.os: A ship grounded on the beach when the tide slips out is left high and dry.
items.ex: Our ride forgot us after practice, leaving us high and dry.

items.m: in serious trouble
items.os: Deep water has meant danger since ancient times; the Bible's Psalms cry, 'I have come into deep waters.'
items.ex: He's in deep water for skipping two rehearsals.

items.m: gloomy, listless, and stuck
items.os: 1800s slang for low spirits, from 'dold,' meaning dull; sailors then gave the name to the windless belt near the equator where ships stalled for weeks.
items.ex: Rainy weekends put the whole family in the doldrums.

items.m: likely to happen soon
items.os: The offing is the stretch of sea visible from shore; a ship in the offing would reach the dock before long.
items.ex: With report cards in the offing, everyone suddenly loves homework.

items.m: to decline by resorting to ridiculous attention-grabbing stunts
items.os: In a 1977 Happy Days episode, Fonzie water-skis over a shark; TV fans later named it the moment a show runs out of ideas.
items.ex: Adding a third mascot? Our school newsletter has jumped the shark, Mom laughed.

items.m: to fall over suddenly
items.os: A capsizing ship rolls until its keel — its spine — points at the sky.
items.ex: He nearly keeled over after the double-lap relay.

items.m: to master the basics of a new job or activity
items.os: A green sailor's first task was memorizing which of a hundred ropes controlled which sail.
items.ex: The first week of scorekeeping is just learning the ropes.

items.p: like a ship without a rudder
items.m: aimless, with no one steering
items.os: The rudder is a ship's only steering blade; without it, wind and current decide everything.
items.ex: Without a team captain, our quiz club felt like a ship without a rudder.

items.m: to lose an opportunity by acting too late
items.os: Sailing ships could leave harbor only on a high tide; miss it and you waited a whole day.
items.ex: Sign up today — if we miss the tide, the workshop fills up.

items.p: nail your colors to the mast
items.m: to declare your position openly and refuse to back down
items.os: A ship lowered its flag — its 'colors' — to surrender; at the Battle of Camperdown in 1797, sailor Jack Crawford nailed the admiral's flag back onto the broken mast.
items.ex: She nailed her colors to the mast and defended the new library rules at assembly.

items.m: steady, calm, and balanced
items.os: A ship riding level on its keel neither tips nor wallows.
items.ex: Weekly checklists keep our homework on an even keel.

items.m: next in line and ready to go
items.os: American baseball, 1860s: the batter waiting to hit stands 'on deck,' a term borrowed straight from sailors.
items.ex: Finish your word, Maya — you're on deck for round two.

items.m: to spend generously on a celebration
items.os: British; helping push a neighbor's beached boat into the water was a classic act of generosity, later sailors' slang for treating everyone.
items.ex: For the bee victory, Mum really pushed the boat out — balloons, cake, the lot.

items.m: to spoil someone's happy plans
items.os: American; the 1964 Funny Girl showstopper 'Don't Rain on My Parade' fixed the image in everyone's ears.
items.ex: I hate to rain on your parade, but the field trip moved to March.

items.m: to endure trouble until it passes
items.os: A ship rides out a storm at anchor, bow to the waves, waiting for calm.
items.ex: We rode out the cafeteria chaos in a quiet corner of the library.

items.m: to manage something strictly and efficiently
items.os: On a well-run sailing ship every rope was taut and coiled; slack lines meant a sloppy crew.
items.ex: Ms. Alvarez runs a tight ship — pencils sharpened before the bell.

items.m: to succeed at something with ease
items.os: A ship gliding through calm water meets no resistance at all.
items.ex: She sailed through the qualifying round without one wrong letter.

items.m: a warning before serious action is taken
items.os: Warships fired a cannonball across a stranger's bow — hitting nothing — to order it to stop.
items.ex: Dad's 'quiet down back there' was just a shot across the bow.

items.m: succeed by your own effort or fail completely
items.os: From the medieval water ordeal, where the accused was thrown in to float or drown; Chaucer used 'fleteth or sinketh' in the 1300s.
items.ex: No practice rounds at this bee — it's sink or swim.

items.m: easy progress with no problems
items.os: The American cousin of Britain's older 'plain sailing,' probably from 'plane sailing,' a simplified navigation method that treats the sea as flat.
items.ex: After the tricky first paragraph, the essay was smooth sailing.

items.m: to carefully avoid
items.os: Helmsmen steer clear of rocks and other ships; George Washington's 1796 farewell address urged America to 'steer clear of permanent alliances.'
items.ex: Steer clear of the wet paint outside the gym.

items.p: take the wind out of your sails
items.m: to suddenly drain someone's confidence or momentum
items.os: A ship slipping to windward of a rival steals its breeze, leaving the enemy's sails hanging slack.
items.ex: The surprise tie-breaker word took the wind out of his sails.

items.m: to try something cautiously before committing
items.os: Like a bather dipping in a toe before diving.
items.ex: She tested the waters with one small practice bee before entering regionals.

items.m: the chance is gone for good
items.os: American, 1900s: once a ship leaves the dock, no ticket will get you aboard.
items.ex: Want to switch project topics now? That ship has sailed.

items.m: no one is watching; it is safe to act
items.os: In use since the 1500s; the favorite story credits smugglers signaling that no coast guards were in sight, though that is unproven.
items.ex: The coast is clear — hide Mom's birthday present now!

items.m: very drunk and unsteady
items.os: Sheets are the ropes that trim a ship's sails; with three flying loose, the vessel staggers about with no control.
items.ex: Grandpa joked that the wobbly party robot looked three sheets to the wind.

items.m: to help someone through a short difficulty
items.os: With no wind, a ship could still 'tide over' — riding a favorable tide forward until the breeze returned.
items.ex: A granola bar tided me over until dinner.

items.m: a completely unfamiliar situation
items.os: Old sea charts left unexplored regions blank — no depths marked, no warnings.
items.ex: Coaching her little brother put Maya in uncharted waters.

items.m: to be forced out and take the punishment
items.os: Storybook pirates make captives walk a plank into the sea — but real pirates almost never did; the scene spread through 1800s adventure fiction.
items.ex: Miss a deadline at that strict newspaper and you walk the plank, Dad joked.

items.m: past events that cannot be changed
items.os: America's inland answer to 'water under the bridge': once water spills over the dam, it never runs back.
items.ex: The missed field trip is water over the dam; let's plan the next one.

items.m: troubles tend to arrive all at once
items.os: From the 1726 English proverb 'it never rains but it pours'; the Morton Salt company stamped the cheerier American version on its cans in 1914.
items.ex: Lost homework, a flat bike tire, hiccups at the bee — when it rains, it pours.

items.m: to wait or wish for something that will not come
items.os: Becalmed sailors whistled softly to coax up a breeze — a superstition as old as sail; whistling too hard, they feared, would summon a gale.
items.ex: Expecting snow in July? You can whistle for the wind.

items.m: encouragement that speeds you along
items.os: A following wind fills the sails and drives the ship forward.
items.ex: The judges' applause put fresh wind in her sails.

items.m: trouble is building and will soon break out
items.os: Brewing is the slow bubbling of beer-making; sailors watched storms gather the same way, in dark, swelling clouds.
items.ex: Two captains and one ball — a storm is brewing at recess.

items.m: to pour out ideas together quickly
items.os: In the 1890s a 'brain-storm' meant a fit of madness; 1940s advertising man Alex Osborn re-invented it as a storm of ideas in group sessions.
items.ex: Let's brainstorm science-fair topics over dinner.

items.m: a small sign of coming trouble
items.os: Sailors scanned the horizon: one distant cloud could grow into tomorrow's gale.
items.ex: The only cloud on the horizon is Friday's dentist appointment.

items.m: someone who joins in only when things are easy
items.os: A sailor who puts to sea only in gentle weather; 'fair-weather' has branded unreliable companions since the 1700s.
items.ex: He's a fair-weather sailor — first to quit when practice gets hard.

items.m: the confusion that hides what is really happening
items.os: The Prussian general Carl von Clausewitz wrote in the 1830s that war wraps commanders in a fog of uncertainty; English writers later coined the exact phrase.
items.ex: With three group chats arguing about the schedule, the fog of war set in.

items.m: the same rare misfortune will not happen again
items.os: American proverb from the 1850s — and scientifically false: the Empire State Building is struck about twenty-five times a year.
items.ex: Misspell 'rhythm' twice? Relax — lightning never strikes twice.

items.m: a rare mix of events that makes a disaster far worse
items.os: Forecasters' term for storms that merge; Sebastian Junger's 1997 book The Perfect Storm, about a doomed fishing boat, made it everyday speech.
items.ex: Late bus, forgotten lunch, surprise quiz — a perfect storm of a Monday.

items.m: no chance at all
items.os: American, 1800s; the full phrase imagines a snowball lasting in the hottest place there is — it would melt in a blink.
items.ex: Our team has a snowball's chance of winning without practicing.

items.m: overwhelmed with too much work
items.os: American, 1800s; newspapers said losing candidates were 'snowed under' by avalanches of votes.
items.ex: I'm snowed under with book reports this week.

items.m: to politely postpone an offer until later
items.os: American baseball, 1880s: fans at a rained-out game got a 'rain check' ticket good for another day.
items.ex: Can I take a rain check on the sleepover? The bee is tomorrow.

items.m: to stop being careful and take a bold risk
items.os: The winds scatter whatever you toss to them — chaff, ashes, and, since the 1800s, caution itself.
items.ex: She threw caution to the winds and entered the older kids' division.

items.m: under suspicion or out of favor
items.os: The image of one gloomy cloud shadowing a single person goes back to the 1500s.
items.ex: After the missing-snacks mystery, the class hamster was under a cloud.

items.m: a hidden advantage saved for the right moment
items.os: Card cheats in frontier saloons hid winning aces inside their sleeves.
items.ex: Her ace up her sleeve was knowing every Greek root on the list.

items.m: completed at last
items.os: From footraces, where the tape at the finish line snaps as the winner bursts through.
items.ex: One more chapter and my reading log is across the finish line.

items.m: better prepared or positioned than expected
items.os: Gamblers' talk: a player ahead of the game has won more than they have staked.
items.ex: Doing Monday's homework on Saturday keeps me ahead of the game.

items.p: at this stage of the game
items.m: at this point in the process
items.os: From board and ball games, where each stage calls for different moves.
items.ex: At this stage of the game, changing topics would sink our project.

items.m: back at a familiar activity after a break
items.os: Cowboys thrown from a horse climb straight back on; Gene Autry's 1939 song 'Back in the Saddle Again' rode the phrase into every home.
items.ex: After spring break, it's back in the saddle with morning word drills.

items.m: a situation of total chaos
items.os: American, 1970: the Temptations' hit 'Ball of Confusion (That's What the World Is Today)' turned the title into slang for any hopeless muddle.
items.ex: Move-in day was a ball of confusion until Mom made a checklist.

items.m: to succeed every single time
items.os: Baseball: a batter who hits safely at every at-bat holds a perfect 1.000 average.
items.ex: She's batting a thousand on spelling quizzes this term.

items.m: away from the main action; failing to keep up
items.os: Hockey and football announcers' phrase for whatever happens far from the puck or ball — often where the referee isn't looking.
items.ex: Skim the class group chat daily or you'll be behind the play.

items.m: to hit or surprise someone from an unseen direction
items.os: A player's blind side is the side away from where they're looking; American football made the sudden unseen tackle a verb in the 1960s.
items.ex: The pop quiz blindsided everyone but Priya.

items.m: to surprise someone with a tricky, unexpected question or problem
items.os: Cricket: a googly spins the opposite way to what the batter expects, a delivery perfected around 1900 by bowler Bernard Bosanquet.
items.ex: The interviewer bowled me a googly: 'Spell your favorite word backward.'

items.m: to astonish someone completely
items.os: A perfect ball in cricket or skittles flattens everything it hits.
items.ex: Her flawless final round bowled the judges over.

items.m: to decide what the group does next
items.os: American football: the quarterback calls the play, telling every teammate where to run.
items.ex: For the bake sale, Mom calls the play and we follow.

items.m: to take the main responsibility for getting something done
items.os: In American football, one runner carries the ball while teammates block for him.
items.ex: Jaden carried the ball on our group's slideshow.

items.m: a final move that leaves an opponent no escape
items.os: From chess, via the Persian 'shah mat' — 'the king is helpless'; the word traveled through Arabic and Old French into English.
items.ex: Signing up early was checkmate — no one could claim her favorite topic.

items.m: an unexpected problem or tricky surprise
items.os: Baseball pitchers of the 1870s learned to spin the ball so it swerves away from the bat at the last instant.
items.ex: The essay question threw us a real curveball.

items.m: the situation is secretly rigged against you
items.os: Loaded dice are weighted to fall one way; archaeologists have found cheaters' dice in the ruins of Pompeii.
items.ex: With judges from their own school, our team felt the dice were loaded.

items.m: defeated or too exhausted to continue
items.os: A boxer who stays down through the referee's count of ten loses the match.
items.ex: After hosting the sleepover, Dad was down for the count by eight.

items.m: to abandon politeness and compete in earnest
items.os: Ice hockey players fling off their gloves before a fist-fight — bare knuckles mean business.
items.ex: The two debate teams dropped the gloves in the final round.

items.m: to get revenge or make things equal again
items.os: From games, where a tying goal 'evens' the scoreboard.
items.ex: She evened the score in the rematch with a perfect round.

items.m: honest, rule-following treatment of everyone
items.os: Shakespeare loved the phrase — his King John (1595) demands 'according to the fair play of the world.'
items.ex: The team returned the trophy — fair play matters more than winning.

items.m: the quickest to start
items.os: Racehorses burst from spring-loaded starting gates; the sharpest breaks first.
items.ex: Maya was first out of the gate with her science-fair form.

items.m: to clumsily ruin an opportunity
items.os: In American football, a runner who drops — fumbles — the ball may hand the game to the other team.
items.ex: I knew the word but fumbled the ball by rushing.

items.m: something that transforms a situation completely
items.os: American sports commentary for one play that flips a game; business meetings borrowed it in the 1990s.
items.ex: Flashcards on the bus were a game changer for my practice time.

items.m: a strategy worked out in advance
items.os: American football coaches of the 1940s drew up a 'game plan' of plays chosen for each opponent.
items.ex: Our study game plan: roots on Monday, review on Friday.

items.m: to begin before others and gain an advantage
items.os: From racing, where a favored runner once began a length ahead of the field.
items.ex: Waking up early gave me a head start on the word list.

items.p: get the show on the road
items.m: to finally start an activity or journey
items.os: American, early 1900s: traveling circuses and theater troupes packed their wagons and literally took the show on the road.
items.ex: Grab your backpacks — let's get this show on the road.

items.m: to try as hard as you possibly can
items.os: From marksmanship and archery, where a 'shot' has meant an attempt since the 1700s.
items.ex: Even if 'chiaroscuro' looks scary, give it your best shot.

items.m: to aim for the very top prize
items.os: From the Olympic gold medal; American broadcasters at the 1984 Los Angeles Games turned 'go for the gold' into a national cheer.
items.ex: This year she's going for gold at the national bee.

items.m: to defend or support someone actively
items.os: Baseball, early 1900s: a pinch hitter goes to bat in a struggling teammate's place.
items.ex: Mom went to bat for me when the schedule clashed with the bee.

items.m: at the proper time, after the usual wait
items.os: From 'due course,' the path something is owed to follow; English formal use since the 1500s.
items.ex: The principal promised the science-fair results would be announced in due course.

items.m: over a long time; eventually
items.os: English, 1600s, first as 'at the long run': prey that escapes a short sprint is still caught over a long chase.
items.ex: Reading every night feels slow, but in the long run it builds a huge vocabulary.

items.m: during the near future
items.os: From finance, where a 'term' is the fixed life of a loan or plan; everyday English by the 1900s.
items.ex: In the short term we'll rent skates, and buy a pair if Lena stays keen.

items.m: to pass empty time with idle amusements
items.os: English, 1700s, treating dull hours as an enemy you defeat with games and chatter.
items.ex: We killed time before the recital with twenty questions.

items.m: smoothly, regularly, and precisely on schedule
items.os: From the 1600s, when wind-up clockwork was the most precise machinery in the world.
items.ex: Every Saturday, like clockwork, Grandma calls at nine for our spelling game.

items.m: to hurry or do extra after a delay
items.os: English, 1600s, treating wasted hours as a debt you can repay by working faster.
items.ex: After a week of flu, Omar studied all weekend to make up for lost time.

items.m: the instant when something is finally put to the test
items.os: From Spanish bullfighting's 'el momento de la verdad,' the final sword thrust; Ernest Hemingway carried it into English in 1932.
items.ex: The judges opened the envelope — the moment of truth for our robotics team.

items.m: absolutely never
items.os: American, 1900s hyperbole: a number too vast to imagine stands in for 'never.'
items.ex: Never in a million years did I think I'd out-spell an eighth grader.

items.m: a sensation everyone talks about, then quickly forgets
items.os: From the proverb 'a wonder lasts but nine days,' already old when Chaucer echoed it in the 1300s.
items.ex: The cafeteria's robot server was a nine-day wonder; by October nobody looked up.

items.m: act immediately or lose the chance forever
items.os: An urgency formula in English since the 1300s; Elvis Presley's 1960 hit 'It's Now or Never' renewed it.
items.ex: Sign-ups close at noon, so it's now or never for the talent show.

items.m: living or lasting longer than expected, with the end near
items.os: American, late 1800s: extra days treated as a loan that must one day be repaid.
items.ex: Our wheezing old washing machine is on borrowed time, Dad says.

items.m: exactly on time
items.os: American, early 1900s, from the minute dots printed around a watch face.
items.ex: The bus leaves at 7:45 on the dot, with or without you.

items.p: on the spur of the moment
items.m: suddenly, without any planning
items.os: English, 1700s: the moment 'spurs' you into action the way a rider's spur jolts a horse.
items.ex: On the spur of the moment, Mom pulled over for roadside strawberries.

items.m: so rare it may happen only once in your life
items.os: English, 1800s, weighing one single chance against a whole lifespan.
items.ex: Watching the total eclipse from the schoolyard felt once in a lifetime.

items.m: in a rush, with barely enough time
items.os: From 'press' meaning to squeeze — a schedule squeezed too tight; English by the 1800s.
items.ex: Pressed for time, Ava ate breakfast while quizzing herself on prefixes.

items.m: a burst of fresh energy after feeling exhausted
items.os: From distance running: a gasping runner suddenly breathes easily again, an effect doctors described in the 1800s.
items.ex: Halfway through cleaning her room, Jo caught a second wind and finished the closet too.

items.m: to remain good, true, or popular for many years
items.os: English, 1700s, picturing time as the strictest examiner, which only lasting things pass.
items.ex: Grandma's chocolate-chip recipe has stood the test of time for forty years.

items.m: go as slowly and carefully as you need
items.os: English, 1700s: the time is yours, so you may spend it unhurried.
items.ex: 'Take your time,' the judge said, and Leo spelled each letter slowly.

items.m: a brief time of shining success and admiration
items.os: English, 1900s, pairing one fleeting moment with 'glory,' the old word for radiant fame.
items.ex: Holding the trophy overhead was Sam's moment of glory.

items.m: the third attempt often succeeds after two failures
items.os: American, 1800s, from old folk beliefs that three is a lucky, magical number; Britons say 'third time lucky.'
items.ex: Ella missed 'rhythm' twice in practice, but third time's the charm — she nailed it.

items.m: repeatedly; again and again
items.os: English, 1600s, doubling 'time' to mean endless repetition; Cyndi Lauper's 1983 ballad made it a pop classic.
items.ex: Time after time, Dad reminds us to charge the tablet before car trips.

items.m: to be secretly plotting together with someone
items.os: Persian pictures schemers whispering under one blanket — 'zir-e yek patu' — hidden from everyone else in the room.
items.ex: The twins were under one blanket all week, planning Dad's surprise party.
items.lit: زیر یک پتو بودن (zir-e yek patu budan)

items.p: the wolf's pup becomes a wolf
items.m: children grow up to have their parents' nature
items.os: From the Persian poet Saadi's Gulistan (1258), where a wolf cub raised lovingly by humans still grows into a wolf.
items.ex: Coach smiled 'the wolf's pup becomes a wolf' when the champion sprinter's daughter won her first race.
items.lit: گرگ‌زاده عاقبت گرگ شود (gorg-zâde âqebat gorg shavad)

items.m: to turn deep purple from embarrassment, cold, or a bruise
items.os: Turkish 'patlıcan gibi morarmak' compares a flushed or bruised face to the glossy purple of the eggplant, the star of Turkish kitchens.
items.ex: When the whole class sang happy birthday to her, Ayşe became an eggplant.

eq.p: to go red as a beet

items.m: skimping on quality brings disappointing results
items.os: Turkish 'Ucuz etin yahnisi yavan olur': a yahni is a slow-cooked stew, and one made from bargain meat has no flavor at all.
items.ex: The bargain glue let my whole diorama collapse — cheap meat's broth is tasteless, Dad sighed.

eq.p: you get what you pay for

items.m: to kick up a big fuss or commotion
items.os: Urdu 'gard uṛānā' pictures the choking cloud that a scuffle or a galloping horse throws up from a dusty lane.
items.ex: My sister raised dust in the kitchen when her last cookie went missing.

items.p: to walk with wooden shoes on thin ice
items.m: to charge clumsily into a delicate situation
items.os: Dutch 'zich met de klompen op het ijs wagen': klompen are heavy wooden clogs — the worst possible footwear for thin ice.
items.ex: Asking the teacher to cancel homework on test week was walking with wooden shoes on thin ice.
items.lit: zich met de klompen op het ijs wagen

eq.p: like a bull in a china shop

items.m: to miss out on both options by fitting neither
items.os: Dutch and French speakers — 'tussen twee stoelen vallen' — picture a guest hovering between two seats and landing on the floor.
items.ex: Signing up late, Leo fell between two chairs: both the chess club and the art club were already full.

items.m: to reluctantly accept something you strongly dislike
items.os: Norwegian 'å svelge en kamel', from the Bible verse about straining out a gnat but swallowing a camel (Matthew 23:24); Norwegian news writers made it everyday politics-speak.
items.ex: Sharing a room with my messy brother on vacation — I swallowed a camel.

items.p: time and tide wait for no man
items.m: time moves on whether you are ready, so act now
items.os: Among English's oldest proverbs, recorded around 1225; 'tide' then meant a stretch of time, not the sea.
items.ex: Grandpa tapped his watch before the museum trip: 'Time and tide wait for no man.'

items.m: sadness and hurt fade as time passes
items.os: Traced to the Greek playwright Menander, 300s BC — 'time is the healer of all necessary evils' — and echoed by Chaucer.
items.ex: Losing the finals stung, but time heals all wounds — by summer Lena was laughing about it.

items.m: spare time with nothing to do
items.os: English, 1600s–1700s, picturing idle hours as a weight left sitting in your hands.
items.ex: With homework done early, Marcus had time on his hands to build a card tower.

items.m: only the future will reveal the truth
items.os: English proverb since the 1500s, making time itself the final storyteller.
items.ex: Will the new study app help? Time will tell at report cards.

items.m: to return to an earlier time or its ways
items.os: From setting a clock's hands backward; English, 1900s, usually a wish to be young again.
items.ex: Grandma says school dances turn back the clock to her own gym-hall days.

items.p: two shakes of a lamb's tail
items.m: a very short time; almost instantly
items.os: Recorded by the 1840s: a lamb's tail wiggles so fast that two shakes take no time at all.
items.ex: 'Dinner's ready in two shakes of a lamb's tail,' Dad called from the kitchen.

items.m: later than the planned timetable
items.os: From the printed schedules of 1800s railroads, which fixed the exact minute each train was due.
items.ex: The bake sale started behind schedule because the cupcakes were still cooling.

items.m: in total confusion or disarray
items.os: From a medieval dice game where betting 'on six and seven' meant risking everything; Chaucer used it in the 1380s. The story about feuding London guilds came later.
items.ex: On the first day back, the classroom was at sixes and sevens — wrong desks, lost pencils, missing hamster.

items.m: a short nap
items.os: English, by 1821; a 'wink' was a moment of shut-eye, and forty was the old favorite number for 'a good many.'
items.ex: Grandpa grabs forty winks in his armchair before dinner.

items.m: slap my palm to celebrate or say hello
items.os: American slang from Black American culture, mid-1900s; the 'five' is your five fingers.
items.ex: 'Give me five!' cheered Dad when Zoe read her first chapter book alone.

items.m: a celebration slap of two raised palms
items.os: American; often credited to Dodgers Dusty Baker and Glenn Burke after a home run on October 2, 1977, though others claim it too.
items.ex: The whole team lined up for high fives after the quiz-bowl win.

items.m: almost always
items.os: English, 1700s–1800s, scoring near-certainty as nine successes in ten tries.
items.ex: Nine times out of ten, the missing remote is under Dad's cushion.

items.m: on hands and knees
items.os: English since the 1300s, first as 'on all four,' counting a crawler's limbs like an animal's four legs.
items.ex: We crawled on all fours hunting the hamster behind the couch.

items.m: extraordinarily rare and special
items.os: English, 1800s, from the days when a million of anything was almost beyond counting.
items.ex: Teachers like Ms. Rivera, who stays late to coach spellers, are one in a million.

items.m: a state of perfect happiness
items.os: From ancient Jewish and Islamic pictures of the sky as seven layers, the seventh being the holiest, nearest to God.
items.ex: Nadia was in seventh heaven when her library hold finally arrived.

items.m: dead and buried
items.os: From the traditional depth of graves: London's plague orders of 1665 required burials at least six feet deep.
items.ex: Grandpa jokes that his ancient flip phone should be six feet under by now.

items.p: six of one, half a dozen of the other
items.m: the two options are exactly the same
items.os: First recorded from novelist and sea captain Frederick Marryat in 1836 — six and half a dozen are, of course, the same number.
items.ex: Bus or subway to the museum? Six of one, half a dozen of the other.

items.m: a mysterious ability to know what the five senses cannot
items.os: The five senses were counted from Aristotle's time; English added a mysterious 'sixth' for intuition by the 1800s.
items.ex: Mom's sixth sense always knows when we're sneaking cookies.

items.m: to take a short break
items.os: American, early 1900s, from theater and band rehearsals pausing five minutes; jazz fans hear it in the 1959 tune 'Take Five.'
items.ex: 'Take five,' said the choir director, 'then we'll run the last verse.'

items.m: so common it is worth very little
items.os: British, 1800s, from street markets selling small goods ten for one penny; Americans say 'a dime a dozen.'
items.ex: Rubber-band bracelets are ten a penny at school this term.

items.m: a rule punishing every violation, however small
items.os: American, 1970s–80s, from drug-enforcement and school-discipline programs that allowed not a single exception.
items.ex: Our school has zero tolerance for phones during exams.

items.p: to have a spider on the ceiling
items.m: to be a little crazy or wonderfully odd
items.os: French 'avoir une araignée au plafond': the ceiling stands for the inside of your head, with a spider loose in the attic — Parisian slang from the 1800s.
items.ex: Our art teacher wears a different silly hat every day — she has a spider on the ceiling, in the best way.

eq.p: to have bats in the belfry

items.p: the early morning has gold in its mouth
items.m: starting early brings the best rewards
items.os: German 'Morgenstund hat Gold im Mund', a rhyme quoted since the 1500s; Italians agree that 'il mattino ha l'oro in bocca'.
items.ex: Grandpa taps my door at seven sharp: the early morning has gold in its mouth, and spelling practice awaits.

eq.p: the early bird catches the worm
il mattino ha l'oro in bocca
eq.lit: the morning has gold in its mouth

items.p: hunger drives the wolf out of the woods
items.m: need forces even the reluctant to act
items.os: French 'la faim fait sortir le loup du bois', from medieval winters when starving wolves crept out of the forest into villages.
items.ex: An empty snack shelf drove the wolf out of the woods — my brother finally learned to make toast.
items.lit: la faim fait sortir le loup du bois

eq.p: necessity is the mother of invention

items.m: check your work carefully before doing something you can't undo
items.os: A Russian tailors' rule — 'sem' raz otmer', odin raz otrezh'' — cloth measured seven times need only be cut once.
items.ex: Measure seven times, cut once: reread every answer before you hand in the test.
items.lit: семь раз отмерь, один раз отрежь (sem' raz otmer', odin raz otrezh')

items.p: the quieter you go, the further you get
items.m: patience and steadiness carry you farther than rushing
items.os: Russian coachman's wisdom — 'tishe edesh', dal'she budesh'' — drive your horses gently and they will carry you farther down the road.
items.ex: The quieter you go, the further you get: ten calm minutes of spelling a night beat one frantic hour.
items.lit: тише едешь — дальше будешь (tishe edesh' — dal'she budesh')

eq.p: slow and steady wins the race

items.p: a kind word opens iron gates
items.m: gentle words can win over even the hardest people
items.os: Told across Turkey and the Balkans; the Turkish line 'tatlı dil demir kapıyı açar' promises that a sweet tongue can swing open a gate of iron.
items.ex: A kind word opens iron gates — Maya's polite request got our class extra library time.

eq.p: you catch more flies with honey than with vinegar

items.p: the apple falls under the apple tree
items.m: children turn out like their parents
items.os: Hungarian and German version of a proverb recorded in German by the 1500s ('Der Apfel fällt nicht weit vom Stamm'); English borrowed it in the 1800s.
items.ex: Mom won her school bee, and now I'm in the final — the apple falls under the apple tree.
items.lit: az alma nem esik messze a fájától

eq.p: the apple doesn't fall far from the tree

items.m: to look sad or disappointed
items.os: English, 1700s: a drooping mouth and downcast eyes literally stretch the face longer — hence the joke 'why the long face?'
items.ex: Don't make a long face over one missed word — there's another bee in the spring.

items.m: carrying anger and looking for a fight over past unfairness
items.os: American, 1800s: a boy spoiling for a fight balanced a wood chip on his shoulder and dared anyone to knock it off — newspapers described the custom by 1830.
items.ex: Ever since he lost the kickball game, Sam has had a chip on his shoulder at recess.

items.m: a tiny amount compared to what is needed
items.os: From the Bible: Isaiah calls the nations 'as a drop of a bucket' (King James Bible, 1611).
items.ex: One canned good felt like a drop in the bucket, so our class set a goal of five hundred.

items.p: a leopard can't change its spots
items.m: people can't change their basic nature
items.os: From the Bible: the prophet Jeremiah asks whether the leopard can change his spots (Jeremiah 13:23).
items.ex: He promised to stop hiding my eraser, but a leopard can't change its spots.

items.m: a big fuss over something unimportant
items.os: British form of an idea as old as Cicero, who mocked politicians 'raising waves in a wine ladle' around 50 BC; Americans brew a tempest in a teapot instead.
items.ex: The mix-up over cupcake flavors became a storm in a teacup at the bake sale.

items.m: opposite to what feels natural or usual
items.os: From carpentry: planing wood against the direction of its fibers tears the surface; Shakespeare already used it figuratively in Coriolanus (1607).
items.ex: Skipping dessert goes against the grain for my sweet-toothed dad.

items.m: more advanced than most people or the current trend
items.os: American, 1900s, most likely from charts where a rising curve shows where a trend is heading; pilots' talk of the 'power curve' may also have helped.
items.ex: Practicing next year's word list put Riya ahead of the curve.

items.m: to discuss private family problems in public
items.os: From the French warning to 'wash your dirty linen at home', a line Napoleon famously repeated; English moved the linen out to the clothesline.
items.ex: Mom says arguments about chores stay home — no airing our dirty laundry at school.

items.m: sounding fierce but never acting on threats
items.os: From the old proverb 'barking dogs seldom bite', known in English since the 1500s.
items.ex: The gym teacher's growl is all bark and no bite — he hands out stickers after every class.

items.m: carrying every weapon or tool you could possibly need
items.os: 'To the teeth' has meant 'completely' since the 1300s; the tale that pirates gripped extra knives in their teeth is a later myth.
items.ex: Priya arrived at the bee armed to the teeth: dictionaries, flashcards, and three lucky pencils.

items.p: at the drop of a hat
items.m: instantly, without any hesitation
items.os: American, 1800s: dropping a hat was the signal to start a race or a frontier fight.
items.ex: My grandma will play checkers at the drop of a hat.

items.m: to rescue someone from trouble, or escape a failing situation
items.os: From bailing water out of a leaking boat with a bucket (old French 'baille'); later, pilots bailed out of planes by parachute.
items.ex: Dad bailed me out by driving my forgotten project to school.

items.m: to count on something completely
items.os: English, 1600s: banks were the safest place for money, so anything you could 'bank on' could be trusted.
items.ex: Rain or shine, Ms. Lee gives a Friday quiz — you can bank on it.

items.m: to produce good results after long effort
items.os: From orchards: a tree tended for years finally bears fruit; the figurative use is ancient and runs all through the Bible.
items.ex: Months of flashcards bore fruit when Ana aced the regional bee.

items.m: to keep arguing something already settled or hopeless
items.os: British politician John Bright was said to be 'flogging a dead horse' when he tried to rouse a sleepy Parliament in the 1860s.
items.ex: Asking for a dog again after Mom's tenth no is beating a dead horse.

items.m: stuck in a difficult position with no easy escape
items.os: American, 1920s, from the pool game kelly pool: touching the black eight ball first cost a penalty, so being trapped behind it spelled trouble.
items.ex: Losing my word list the night before the quiz put me behind the eight ball.

items.m: unfair or hurtful beyond acceptable limits
items.os: From boxing: the Queensberry rules of 1867 banned punches below the belt line.
items.ex: Teasing him about his stutter was below the belt.

items.m: to be absolutely certain about something
items.os: American, 1850s: in a gambler's stack of coins the bottom dollar is the very last — you stake it only on a sure thing.
items.ex: You can bet your bottom dollar Grandpa will be in the front row at the bee.

items.m: a view of everything from high above
items.os: English, 1600s: mapmakers drew towns as a soaring bird would see them, long before balloons or airplanes existed.
items.ex: From the ferris wheel we had a bird's-eye view of the whole school fair.

items.m: an unpleasant fact that must be accepted
items.os: From the days before sugar-coated medicine, when pills tasted foul and had to be gulped down anyway.
items.ex: Losing the final by one letter was a bitter pill to swallow.

items.m: family bonds come before all others
items.os: First written in a German beast-tale around 1180 and an English proverb by the 1600s; the internet claim that it originally meant the opposite ('blood of the covenant') is a modern myth.
items.ex: Cousins squabble all afternoon, but blood is thicker than water the moment someone else picks on one of them.

items.m: to brag about your own achievements
items.os: English, 1500s: important visitors had heralds to trumpet their arrival — anyone without one had to toot for himself.
items.ex: Not to blow my own trumpet, but I spelled every word right this week.

items.m: to do something never done before
items.os: From farming and building: the first cut of the plow or scoop of the shovel on untouched land.
items.ex: Our class broke new ground with the school's first student podcast.

items.m: to watch someone so closely it makes them uncomfortable
items.os: English, 1900s: pictures a pursuer running so close behind that you can feel their breath.
items.ex: I can't practice piano with my brother breathing down my neck.

items.m: to offer useful skills or ideas to a group
items.os: American business talk, 1900s: negotiators sit at a table, each side laying out what it can offer.
items.ex: Marcus brings calm nerves and a huge vocabulary to our quiz-bowl team.

items.m: small credits earned for pleasing someone
items.os: American, mid-1900s; some trace it to junior Girl Scouts called Brownies earning merit points, others to railroad demerits logged by a Superintendent Brown — nobody is sure.
items.ex: Wiping the whiteboard without being asked earned me brownie points with Ms. Cho.

items.p: burn a hole in your pocket
items.m: money you feel desperate to spend right away
items.os: English, 1500s: writers joked that coins felt red-hot, as if they would burn through the pocket unless spent at once.
items.ex: My birthday money burned a hole in my pocket until the book fair opened.

items.m: to keep loyally supporting a cause or quietly loving someone
items.os: American, 1920s: nightclub singers' sad love ballads were called torch songs, keeping a flame burning for someone gone; why a torch means devotion is still debated.
items.ex: Years after graduating, Dad still carries the torch for his old school's spelling team.

items.m: complete freedom to do whatever you choose
items.os: French for 'blank card': a signed blank sheet let the bearer fill in any terms, used for military surrenders in the 1700s.
items.ex: Mom gave me carte blanche to decorate my side of the room.

items.m: a business or product that reliably makes money
items.os: Business slang of the 1960s-70s, spread by a Boston consulting chart: a dairy cow needs little feed but keeps giving milk.
items.ex: The lemonade stand became the twins' cash cow every summer.

items.m: to try many options or ask many people
items.os: From fishing: a wide throw of the net gathers in more fish.
items.ex: Casting a wide net, Zoe invited every fourth grader to join the new club.

items.m: a game of chasing, escaping, and outwitting
items.os: English, 1600s, from the way a cat toys with a caught mouse, letting it dash off only to pounce again.
items.ex: Tag at recess turned into cat and mouse between Leo and the twins.

items.m: a short light sleep
items.os: American, 1800s: cats doze in brief snatches, ready to spring awake in an instant.
items.ex: Dad takes a cat nap before driving us to evening practice.

items.m: to be impatient to start
items.os: From racing: an eager horse chews and frets at the metal bit in its mouth before the off.
items.ex: The spellers were champing at the bit while the judges tested the microphone.

items.m: a reversal of your feelings or decision
items.os: English, 1800s, from the age-old idea of the heart as the home of feelings.
items.ex: Mia had a change of heart and shared her cupcake after all.

items.m: to choose only the best or most convenient bits
items.os: From fruit harvests, where pickers take the plumpest cherries and leave the rest; business slang by the mid-1900s.
items.ex: You can't cherry-pick only the easy words to practice.

items.m: to chat in a relaxed, unhurried way
items.os: British, late 1800s; the story that sailors gnawed salt-pork rinds while gossiping is popular but unproven.
items.ex: Grandpa and his friends chew the fat on the porch every Sunday.

items.m: one small weakness in an otherwise strong defense
items.os: English, 1600s: a 'chink' is a narrow gap — the one spot where a knight's armor could be pierced.
items.ex: Silent letters are the chink in my armor at spelling bees.

items.m: official confirmation that everything is fine
items.os: From the 1600s 'bill of health', a paper certifying that a ship's crew carried no plague before the port would let it in.
items.ex: The dentist sent me off with a clean bill of health and a new toothbrush.

items.m: to limit someone's freedom or power
items.os: From the ancient practice of trimming a bird's flight feathers; the Roman playwright Plautus was already using it as a metaphor.
items.ex: Losing tablet privileges clipped my brother's wings for the weekend.

items.m: to return to where things began
items.os: Shakespeare coined the phrasing in King Lear (1606) — 'the wheel is come full circle' — spinning on the old wheel of fortune.
items.ex: Mom came full circle, returning to teach at the very school she attended as a kid.

items.m: no matter what happens
items.os: English, 1600s, from farmers who had to work whatever the sky delivered.
items.ex: Come rain or shine, Grandma walks me to the bus stop.

items.m: to falsify financial records
items.os: English, 1600s: 'cooking' meant doctoring something up, and the account ledgers were the 'books'.
items.ex: Our class treasurer joked he would never cook the books over bake-sale money.

items.m: to push people to work harder
items.os: From 1800s wagon drivers who cracked a whip in the air above their ox teams to speed them up.
items.ex: Coach really cracked the whip the week before the tournament.

items.m: the very best of a group
items.os: English, 1600s: cream rises to the top of fresh milk; the French say the same with 'la crème de la crème'.
items.ex: The regional bee gathers the cream of the crop from every school.

items.m: the critical period when everything must get done
items.os: Winston Churchill popularized 'the crunch' for a decisive moment in the 1930s; American sportswriters later added 'crunch time'.
items.ex: The night before the science fair is crunch time in our kitchen.

items.m: already decided, with no room for change
items.os: English, 1600s: herb shops sold their stock cut and dried — ready-made, nothing fresh about it.
items.ex: The rules of the bee are cut and dried: misspell a word and you sit down.

items.m: very similar in character
items.os: From tailoring: the pieces of one suit are cut from a single bolt so the pattern and color match perfectly.
items.ex: My aunt and my mom are cut from the same cloth — both hum while they cook.

items.m: something that fizzles instead of impressing
items.os: British, 1800s: a squib is a small firework, useless once wet; people now often mishear the phrase as 'damp squid'.
items.ex: The much-hyped magic show was a damp squib — the rabbit never appeared.

items.m: something that helps and harms at the same time
items.os: An ancient image found in Arabic sayings and the Bible: a blade sharpened on both edges cuts both ways.
items.ex: Being the oldest is a double-edged sword: more privileges, more chores.

items.m: feeling sad and gloomy
items.os: English, 1500s: 'the dumps' meant a gloomy daze — Shakespeare wrote of 'doleful dumps' — possibly from a Dutch word for mental fog.
items.ex: Rosa was down in the dumps after fumbling her recital solo.

items.m: into a situation that grows stranger or more absorbing the deeper you go
items.os: From Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865), where Alice tumbles down a rabbit hole into a world of nonsense.
items.ex: One quick question about word origins sent us down the rabbit hole of Greek roots.

items.m: wearing your fanciest clothes
items.os: Scottish, 1700s: 'to the nine(s)' meant 'to perfection', origin unknown — the tale about nine yards of cloth for a suit is a myth.
items.ex: Everyone came dressed to the nines for the awards night.

items.m: false bravery borrowed from a drink
items.os: From the 1600s, when English soldiers fighting alongside the Dutch drank Dutch gin before battle; England's naval rivalry with Holland also spawned many mocking 'Dutch' phrases, so the true source is debated.
items.ex: Grandpa jokes that his hot cocoa is Dutch courage before family karaoke night.

items.m: to admit humiliatingly that you were wrong
items.os: American, 1800s: crow meat tastes foul, so eating it stood for swallowing humiliation; the yarn about a War of 1812 soldier forced to eat one is unproven.
items.ex: After bragging he'd win in one round, Jake ate crow when he missed his first word.

items.m: the calm center of chaos, or the very middle of trouble
items.os: From weather science: a hurricane spins around an eerily calm central 'eye'.
items.ex: During the assembly mix-up, the principal stood in the eye of the storm, calmly redirecting classes.

items.m: to lose respect, status, or favor
items.os: From the Bible: Paul's letter to the Galatians warns believers they could 'fall from grace' (Galatians 5:4).
items.ex: The star hall monitor fell from grace when he was caught running inside.

items.m: to be ignored completely
items.os: English, 1400s: a plea to someone who refuses to listen might as well reach ears that cannot hear.
items.ex: My hints about a puppy fall on deaf ears every birthday.

items.m: extremely careful, detailed searching
items.os: From the fine-toothed combs used for centuries to hunt lice and nits in hair, strand by strand.
items.ex: We went over my essay with a fine-tooth comb before I handed it in.

items.m: to hint so that others will praise you
items.os: English, 1700s: like an angler dangling bait, you dangle modest remarks and wait for a bite.
items.ex: Saying 'my project is probably terrible' was Ella's way of fishing for compliments.

items.m: to be exactly what is needed
items.os: American, 1800s theater: a performer good enough to 'fill the bill' — the printed playbill — could headline the whole show.
items.ex: We needed a fourth teammate who loved word puzzles, and Sam fit the bill.

items.m: a very short distance away
items.os: As far as a person can toss a stone; the Bible's Gospel of Luke describes Jesus praying 'about a stone's cast' from his friends.
items.ex: The library is a stone's throw away from our school, so we walk there for story time.

items.m: an extra skill or option to fall back on
items.os: From medieval archers, who carried a spare bowstring so a snapped string would not leave them defenseless; figurative in English by the 1500s.
items.ex: Learning piano gives you another string to your bow besides soccer.

items.m: failing to pay attention to an important responsibility
items.os: American, early 1900s, echoing the older railroad phrase 'asleep at the switch' about signalmen who dozed off and caused train wrecks.
items.ex: The hall monitor was asleep at the wheel and never noticed the paper airplanes.

items.m: stuck in a stubborn disagreement
items.os: English, 1600s; a loggerhead was a long-handled iron ball heated to melt tar aboard ships, and quarreling sailors may have swung them as weapons.
items.ex: My brother and I were at loggerheads over whose turn it was on the computer.

items.m: a whole collection of clever methods and skills
items.os: From the sly fox of European fables, who brags of a sack full of tricks while the cat knows only one; English use since the 1600s.
items.ex: For the science fair, Dad opened his bag of tricks and showed me three ways to build a volcano.

items.m: sounding much fiercer than one actually acts
items.os: An English proverb recorded since the 1600s, comparing loud, angry people to noisy dogs that rarely bite.
items.ex: Our coach yells a lot, but his bark is worse than his bite.

eq.p: chien qui aboie ne mord pas
eq.lit: a dog that barks does not bite

items.m: even if that is true; whatever the case
items.os: A fossil of older English grammar: speakers in Chaucer's day said 'be as be may,' using the old subjunctive 'be' for possibilities.
items.ex: Be that as it may, Mom said, homework still comes before video games.

items.m: an easy, comfortable situation
items.os: Poet Christopher Marlowe promised 'beds of roses' to his love in a famous 1590s poem, and the image came to mean a life of pure ease.
items.ex: Fifth grade is no bed of roses — there's a quiz almost every week.

items.m: to take on a dangerous task for the good of the group
items.os: From a medieval fable in which the mice agree a warning bell should hang on the cat's neck — but no mouse dares do it; told in Piers Plowman in the 1300s.
items.ex: Everyone wanted recess extended, but nobody would bell the cat and ask the principal.

items.m: using two safeguards in case one fails
items.os: British; from wearing both a belt and braces (suspenders) so your trousers can never fall down, common by the mid-1900s.
items.ex: Belt and braces, Dad emailed my project to the teacher and packed a printed copy too.

items.m: someone born into a noble or aristocratic family
items.os: A translation of Spanish 'sangre azul': pale-skinned Castilian nobles claimed their veins showed blue through their skin, unlike sun-browned laborers.
items.ex: The museum guide said the castle belonged to a family of blue blood.

items.m: sensible, realistic, and practical
items.os: English, common since the 1800s: a person standing firmly on solid earth instead of floating off in daydreams.
items.ex: Even after winning the spelling bee, she kept both feet on the ground and practiced daily.

items.m: to drive away very fast
items.os: American hot-rod slang from the mid-1900s: tires spun so hard they smoked and left streaks of melted rubber on the road.
items.ex: Dad joked we'd have to burn rubber to reach the recital on time.

items.m: extremely, almost comically busy
items.os: American, 1908: writer O. Henry described a man 'as busy as a one-armed man with the nettle-rash pasting on wall-paper.'
items.ex: Running the bake-sale table alone, Mom was busy as a one-armed paperhanger.

items.m: to bring something to a place that already has plenty of it
items.os: Newcastle was England's great coal port, so shipping coal there was pointless; the saying is recorded as early as 1538.
items.ex: Bringing cupcakes to a bakery party is like carrying coals to Newcastle.

items.m: grand dreams or plans that can never come true
items.os: Medieval French dreamers built 'castles in Spain' (châteaux en Espagne); by the 1500s English speakers had moved them into the air.
items.ex: Planning a treehouse with an elevator is fun, but it's castles in the air.

items.m: to capture rare, almost impossible success
items.os: American; often linked to Ben Franklin's 1752 kite experiment that drew electric charge into a jar, though baseball announcers made the phrase famous.
items.ex: Our tiny school choir caught lightning in a bottle and won the state contest.

items.m: to switch plans or leaders in the middle of a task
items.os: Abraham Lincoln, running for re-election during the Civil War in 1864, quoted an old farmer: it is 'not best to swap horses while crossing the river.'
items.ex: Halfway through my report I wanted a new topic, but Dad warned against changing horses midstream.

items.m: bad deeds eventually come back to hurt the person who did them
items.os: Poet Robert Southey printed it on an 1810 title page — 'Curses are like young chickens: they always come home to roost' — and Chaucer had a version 400 years earlier.
items.ex: He teased everyone all year, and when nobody picked him for a team, his chickens came home to roost.

items.m: to turn out wonderfully well
items.os: Popularized by the song 'Everything's Coming Up Roses' from the 1959 Broadway musical Gypsy.
items.ex: She worried about the tryout, but everything came up roses and she made the team.

items.m: the very first moment of morning light
items.os: English, 1800s; 'crack' meant a sudden break — the instant daylight splits the night sky, as in the older 'crack of day.'
items.ex: We woke at the crack of dawn to get a good spot at the science fair.

items.m: to argue or clash with someone
items.os: From sword duels, where blades literally crossed at the start of a fight; figurative in English since the 1600s.
items.ex: The two team captains crossed swords over which project idea was better.

items.m: to do whatever another person demands
items.os: From pipers and fiddlers who controlled the dancers with whatever tune they chose to play; figurative in English since the 1500s.
items.ex: At recess, everyone dances to Maya's tune because she owns the jump rope.

items.m: holding beliefs or loyalties so deep they can never change
items.os: Wool dyed before it is spun holds its color forever; English writers applied the image to people's fixed habits by the 1500s.
items.ex: Grandpa is a dyed-in-the-wool Cubs fan and never misses a game.

items.m: extremely sharp eyesight or attention to detail
items.os: Eagles can spot a rabbit from far over a mile away; English writers have praised 'eagle eyes' since the 1500s.
items.ex: Our teacher's eagle eye catches every misspelled word on the board.

items.m: completely honestly and by the rules
items.os: English, 1600s: 'square' meant honest and true, like a carpenter's perfectly squared corner, and the rhyme made the pair stick.
items.ex: She won the checkers tournament fair and square.

items.m: to make anger or trouble even worse
items.os: Fanning air onto a fire makes it blaze higher; English speakers have fanned figurative flames of anger for centuries.
items.ex: Repeating the rumor only fanned the flames of the argument at lunch.

items.m: to make yourself rich, often using a position meant to help others
items.os: Birds line their nests with soft feathers for comfort; English speakers applied it to people padding their own pockets by the 1500s.
items.ex: The class treasurer shouldn't feather his own nest with bake-sale money.

items.m: in excellent health
items.os: English, 1600s: 'fit' once meant well-made and suitable, and a fine fiddle was the model of good shape — the alliteration did the rest.
items.ex: After a week of rest, Grandma was fit as a fiddle and back in her garden.

items.m: to waste effort on something already hopeless
items.os: British, 1800s: sailors called wages already spent a 'dead horse,' and reformer John Bright reportedly said reviving Parliament's interest in reform was like flogging one.
items.ex: Asking for a later bedtime again is flogging a dead horse — Mom already said no twice.

items.m: a perfect chance that may never come again
items.os: English since the 1500s, when gold — the most precious metal — labeled anything supremely valuable, from golden ages to golden chances.
items.ex: The exchange program is a golden opportunity to learn French.

items.m: someone's chances are completely ruined
items.os: English, mid-1800s, origin unknown; the tale that it comes from reformer Jan Hus (whose name means 'goose') being burned in 1415 is a myth.
items.ex: If Mom finds the broken vase before I can explain, my goose is cooked.

items.p: have an ace up your sleeve
items.m: to keep a hidden advantage ready for the right moment
items.os: From card games: cheats hid a winning ace inside a sleeve, and stage magicians used the same trick for applause instead.
items.ex: Knowing the periodic-table song was the ace up my sleeve for the science quiz.

items.m: so silent you could hear the tiniest sound
items.os: English, 1700s; writers described rooms so hushed that even a falling pin would be heard.
items.ex: When the principal announced the winner, you could hear a pin drop in the gym.

items.m: a situation that explodes with anger when disturbed
items.os: Poking a real hornet's nest brings out a furious swarm; English speakers have 'stirred up hornets' nests' since the 1700s.
items.ex: Suggesting weekend homework stirred up a hornet's nest at the class meeting.

items.m: to fix the small remaining problems
items.os: From pressing clothes with a hot iron until every crease disappears; figurative in English since the 1800s.
items.ex: We ironed out the wrinkles in our skit the night before the school show.

items.m: a person everyone makes fun of
items.os: English, 1500s; 'stock' meant a solid block — the fixed target of jokes — and the popular story linking it to wooden punishment stocks is likely false.
items.ex: He feared tripping on stage would make him the laughing stock of the school, but everyone just cheered.

items.m: an idea or joke that fails completely
items.os: American, from a 1924 comic strip; the rock band Led Zeppelin took its name from a drummer's joke that they would 'go down like a lead balloon.'
items.ex: My idea of extra math practice over the holidays went over like a lead balloon with my classmates.

items.m: to rest and recover after a painful defeat
items.os: Animals instinctively lick their injuries to soothe them; English writers applied it to defeated people by the 1500s.
items.ex: After losing the quiz bowl, we licked our wounds with pizza and planned for next year.

items.p: like two peas in a pod
items.m: so alike you can hardly tell them apart
items.os: Peas from the same pod look identical; English writer John Lyly used the comparison in the 1580s.
items.ex: The twins are like two peas in a pod, right down to matching backpacks.

items.m: to say something plainly, with no hesitation or apology
items.os: From medieval English 'to find no bones' in a bowl of soup — nothing to choke on, so nothing to object to; recorded in the 1400s.
items.ex: Make no bones about it, the teacher said — the project is due Friday, no extensions.

items.m: a heavy burden you cannot escape
