items.os: From the Bible: Jesus said a wrongdoer would be better off dropped in the sea with a millstone — a huge grinding stone — tied to his neck.
items.ex: The overdue library book felt like a millstone around my neck all week.

items.m: helpless, forced to accept whatever someone demands
items.os: American, 1800s; possibly from draping a half-drowned swimmer over a barrel to drain water from the lungs — a story often told but never proven.
items.ex: With the project due tomorrow and the printer broken, we were over a barrel.

items.m: to suddenly take away someone's support or plans
items.os: American, early 1900s, from the image of yanking a rug from under a standing person.
items.ex: Canceling the field trip at the last minute pulled the rug out from under the whole class.

items.m: to make someone's hurt or embarrassment even worse
items.os: Salt stings fiercely in a cut; the tale that flogged sailors had salt rubbed in as extra cruelty is unproven — salt was actually used to prevent infection.
items.ex: Losing was bad enough; hearing the replay at lunch rubbed salt in the wound.

items.m: to be the boss of a household or group
items.os: The rooster lords over the henhouse; but the older English form from the 1500s was 'rule the roast,' perhaps meaning to preside over the meat at table.
items.ex: At our house the baby rules the roost, and everyone tiptoes at nap time.

items.m: to do something far better or faster than someone else
items.os: From racing in the 1800s: a runner or rider so fast they could loop around a rival and still win.
items.ex: In mental math, Priya runs circles around the rest of us.

items.m: to correct a false story with the true facts
items.os: From official records — court files and minutes that must be corrected when wrong; American, 1900s.
items.ex: She set the record straight: it was her sister, not her, who forgot the tickets.

items.m: the gift of smooth, persuasive speech
items.os: English, 1500s; silver's clear, musical ring made 'silver-tongued' the standard compliment for preachers and orators.
items.ex: With his silver tongue, my cousin talked the librarian into extending our study-room time.

items.m: to argue about tiny differences that don't matter
items.os: A hair is too fine to split; Shakespeare joked in Henry IV about a man who would quarrel over 'the ninth part of a hair.'
items.ex: Arguing whether the essay needs 500 or 501 words is just splitting hairs.

items.m: to hold back something that keeps growing stronger
items.os: Nautical: to 'stem' the tide is to point a ship's bow against the current and make headway; figurative in English since the 1600s.
items.ex: The librarian couldn't stem the tide of giggles once the class hamster escaped.

items.m: to stir up trouble or arguments on purpose
items.os: From cooking, where stirring brings whatever settled at the bottom swirling back up; American figurative use, 1900s.
items.ex: Don't stir the pot by asking who really won yesterday's kickball game.

items.m: a situation is becoming more tangled and interesting
items.os: Coined in the 1671 English comedy The Rehearsal, which mocked overstuffed plays: 'Ay, now the plot thickens very much upon us.'
items.ex: The plot thickens: the missing class hamster left tiny footprints by the art cabinet.

items.m: to issue a bold challenge
items.os: Medieval knights challenged a rival to a duel by throwing down a gauntlet — an armored glove; picking it up meant accepting the fight.
items.ex: Our rival school threw down the gauntlet with a challenge to a math relay.

items.m: a small gesture of respect or thanks
items.os: From the old custom of touching or lifting one's hat to greet or honor someone — everyday manners in the 1800s.
items.ex: The coach gave a tip of the hat to the players who cleaned up without being asked.

items.m: to raise the stakes or demands
items.os: From poker: the 'ante' is the chip every player must put in before the deal, and raising it makes the whole game costlier.
items.ex: The teacher upped the ante by offering extra recess for a perfect spelling week.

items.m: to balance carefully between two risky sides
items.os: From circus tightrope walkers, who cross a high wire where one wobble means a fall; figurative by the 1800s.
items.ex: Planning the surprise party, I walked a tightrope between keeping the secret and not lying to Grandma.

items.m: hidden, complicated workings behind a situation
items.os: From the prophet Ezekiel's vision in the Bible of gleaming wheels turning inside other wheels beside four-faced creatures.
items.ex: Choosing the school play turned out to be wheels within wheels, with committees behind committees.

items.p: fall seven times, stand up eight
items.m: keep getting back up no matter how many times you fail
items.os: Japanese saying tied to the daruma doll, a round-bottomed good-luck figure that pops upright every time it is knocked over.
items.ex: After stumbling in the first round, she whispered 'fall seven times, stand up eight' and kept spelling.
items.lit: 七転び八起き (nana korobi ya oki)

eq.p: if at first you don't succeed, try, try again

items.p: the child of a frog is a frog
items.m: children usually turn out like their parents
items.os: Japanese; the joke is that a tadpole looks nothing like a frog, yet a frog is exactly what it becomes.
items.ex: Dad fixes clocks just like Grandpa did — the child of a frog is a frog.
items.lit: 蛙の子は蛙 (kaeru no ko wa kaeru)

eq.p: the apple doesn't fall far from the tree

items.p: spilled water does not return to the tray
items.m: what is done can never be undone
items.os: From a Chinese tale retold in Japan: a scholar's wife left him when he was poor, and when she begged to return after he rose to fame, he spilled water and asked her to put it back in the tray.
items.ex: I can't unsend that grumpy text to my sister — spilled water does not return to the tray.
items.lit: 覆水盆に返らず (fukusui bon ni kaerazu)

items.p: if you chase two rabbits you will catch neither
items.m: trying for two goals at once often wins you neither
items.os: Known in Japan and Russia alike, and ancient Rome had it first: the Latin version warned that he who follows two hares catches neither.
items.ex: Pick the science fair or the play — chase two rabbits and you'll catch neither.
items.lit: 二兎を追う者は一兎をも得ず (nito o ou mono wa itto o mo ezu)

eq.p: за двумя зайцами погонишься — ни одного не поймаешь
eq.lit: chase two hares and you will catch neither

items.p: a wise hawk hides its talons
items.m: truly skilled people don't show off their talents
items.os: Japanese; the capable hawk keeps its sharp talons tucked away until the exact moment it strikes.
items.ex: Like a wise hawk hiding its talons, the new girl never mentioned she was a chess champion until the tournament.
items.lit: 能ある鷹は爪を隠す (nō aru taka wa tsume o kakusu)

items.m: sticking with something every day is itself a great strength
items.os: A Japanese motto beloved in schools and martial-arts dojos; its exact author is unknown.
items.ex: Ten minutes of piano every single day, Mom says — continuation is power.
items.lit: 継続は力なり (keizoku wa chikara nari)

eq.p: slow and steady wins the race

items.p: the bamboo that bends is stronger than the oak that resists
items.m: it is stronger to bend with trouble than to break resisting it
items.os: Quoted everywhere as a Japanese proverb, though this English wording is a loose Western retelling; Japan's classic version praises the willow that bends under snow and never breaks.
items.ex: When our field-trip plans changed, our teacher told us to be the bamboo that bends, not the oak that snaps.
items.lit: 柳に雪折れなし (yanagi ni yukiore nashi)

items.p: one kind word can warm three winter months
items.m: a little kindness comforts people for a long time
items.os: Usually credited to Japan, but it traces to a Chinese rhyming couplet: 'one kind word warms three winters; one cruel word chills even June.'
items.ex: The encouraging note in my lunchbox proved one kind word can warm three winter months.
items.lit: 良言一句三冬暖 (liáng yán yī jù sān dōng nuǎn)

items.m: people will write things they would be too ashamed to say aloud
items.os: Often listed as a Chinese proverb, but the oldest version is Roman: Cicero wrote around 50 BC that 'a letter does not blush.'
items.ex: Remember, paper and ink seldom blush — don't write in the yearbook what you wouldn't say to someone's face.

items.p: a book is like a garden carried in the pocket
items.m: a book brings beauty and delight anywhere you go
items.os: Quote collections credit it to both China and the Arab world, and no early source settles the question; the little pocket garden has traveled everywhere.
items.ex: With a paperback in her backpack, she carries a garden in her pocket on every bus ride.

items.p: teachers open the door, but you must enter by yourself
items.m: teachers can only guide you; the learning is your own job
items.os: From China's world of masters and apprentices: 'the master leads you in the door; the training is up to you.'
items.ex: My tutor showed me the shortcut, but teachers open the door — I had to practice the problems myself.
items.lit: 师傅领进门，修行在个人 (shīfu lǐng jìnmén, xiūxíng zài gèrén)

items.p: a single conversation with a wise man is worth a month's study of books
items.m: talking with a wise person can teach more than long study alone
items.os: Chinese; the original compliment is even bigger — one evening of your talk 'beats ten years of reading books.'
items.ex: Talking with Grandpa about the ocean taught me more than my whole library book on whales.
items.lit: 听君一席话，胜读十年书 (tīng jūn yī xí huà, shèng dú shí nián shū)

items.p: dig the well before you are thirsty
items.m: prepare for needs long before they arrive
items.os: China's ancient medical classic, the Huangdi Neijing, mocks those who wait until they are thirsty to dig a well — or until war breaks out to forge weapons.
items.ex: We started study cards in September — dig the well before you are thirsty.
items.lit: 临渴掘井 (lín kě jué jǐng)

eq.p: a stitch in time saves nine

items.p: pearls don't lie on the seashore
items.m: valuable things must be worked for; they are not just lying around
items.os: Quote books call it Chinese and add the second line, 'if you want one, you must dive for it,' but no classical source has been traced.
items.ex: Pearls don't lie on the seashore — if you want the trophy, you have to practice for it.

items.p: a gem is not polished without rubbing
items.m: people grow skillful and wise only through effort and hardship
items.os: From China's Book of Rites, over 2,000 years old: 'jade that is not carved cannot become a vessel' — and a person who does not learn cannot know the way.
items.ex: All those tricky word lists polished her like a gem before the spelling bee.
items.lit: 玉不琢，不成器 (yù bù zhuó, bù chéng qì)

items.p: better to light a candle than to curse the darkness
items.m: doing one small helpful thing beats complaining about the problem
items.os: Called an ancient Chinese proverb everywhere, but that label is a myth: the first known record is a 1907 sermon by English preacher William Watkinson, later beloved by Eleanor Roosevelt.
items.ex: Rather than grumble about litter at recess, our class lit a candle instead of cursing the darkness and started a cleanup club.

items.p: the best time to plant a tree was twenty years ago
items.m: if you missed the perfect moment to start, start now anyway
items.os: Everyone calls it a Chinese proverb, but no Chinese source exists; it surfaces in 20th-century English books, with the famous second line 'the second-best time is now.'
items.ex: I wished I'd started my project weeks ago, but Dad said the second-best time to plant a tree is now.

items.p: when the winds of change blow, some build walls and others build windmills
items.m: when things change, you can resist or find a way to benefit
items.os: Labeled a Chinese proverb in countless speeches, but it is unattested in Chinese and appears to be a modern invention.
items.ex: When the school switched to digital homework, some kids grumbled and built walls while others built windmills.

items.p: drop by drop is the water pot filled
items.m: small steady efforts add up to something great
items.os: From the Dhammapada, a Buddhist scripture over 2,000 years old: just as a water pot fills drop by drop, the wise fill themselves with good little by little.
items.ex: Learning five new words a night, drop by drop, filled her water pot by bee season.

items.m: all people on Earth belong to one family
items.os: From the Maha Upanishad, an ancient Sanskrit text; India made it the motto of the 2023 G20 summit.
items.ex: Our class welcomed pen pals from three countries, because the world is one family.

items.p: knowledge is wealth no thief can steal
items.m: education is a treasure that can never be taken from you
items.os: From the Tirukkural, the celebrated Tamil classic of about the 5th century: learning is the one imperishable wealth — all else is not true wealth.
items.ex: Grandma says my reading is knowledge — wealth no thief can steal.

items.m: even the greatest and most skilled make mistakes
items.os: Tamil; if even the mighty, sure-footed elephant can lose its footing, anyone can stumble.
items.ex: Don't feel bad about one wrong answer at the bee — even elephants slip.

items.m: respect the experience of older people by hearing them out
items.os: A teaching passed down orally across many African cultures, where elders are honored as keepers of a community's experience; no single people or text owns it.
items.ex: When Grandpa explains how to save my allowance, I remember: when an elder speaks, listen.

items.p: it takes a village to raise a child
items.m: raising a child well takes help from a whole community
items.os: World-famous as an African proverb, though scholars cannot trace one exact source; it echoes real sayings like the Igbo 'the community raises the child,' and a 1996 American book title made it a household phrase.
items.ex: Neighbors, coaches, and the librarian all helped me train for the bee — it takes a village to raise a child.

items.p: wisdom is like a baobab tree; no one person can embrace it
items.m: no one person can know everything; wisdom must be shared
items.os: From West Africa, recorded among the Akan and Ewe peoples of Ghana; a baobab's trunk is so enormous that no single pair of arms can reach around it.
items.ex: Our teacher put five of us on one research topic, since wisdom is a baobab tree no one person can embrace.

items.p: smooth seas do not make skillful sailors
items.m: hard times are what teach real skill
items.os: Widely shared as an African proverb, though its earliest source is untraced; versions of it are now quoted around the world.
items.ex: Losing those close games stung, but smooth seas do not make skillful sailors.

items.p: rain does not fall on one roof alone
items.m: troubles and luck come to everyone, not just you
items.os: Recorded among the peoples of Cameroon: a rainstorm soaks every roof in the village, just as hardship visits every family.
items.ex: When the whole grade got extra homework, Mom smiled: rain does not fall on one roof alone.

items.p: however long the night, the dawn will break
items.m: hard times always come to an end eventually
items.os: Widely quoted as an African proverb, often traced to the Hausa people of West Africa, though no single original wording is recorded.
items.ex: Studying for the bee felt endless, but however long the night, the dawn will break.

eq.p: the darkest hour is just before the dawn

items.p: when spiderwebs unite, they can tie up a lion
items.m: many small people working together can overcome something mighty
items.os: Amharic proverb from Ethiopia, famously quoted about unity across Africa: single web threads snap, but woven together they hold a lion.
items.ex: Our whole class packed the food-drive boxes in an hour — when spiderwebs unite, they can tie up a lion.
items.lit: ድር ቢያብር አንበሳ ያስር (dir biyabir anbesa yasir)

items.m: knowledge is meant to be passed along to others
items.os: Listed in collections of Ethiopian proverbs about the duty to share learning, though the original Amharic wording is not well recorded.
items.ex: After she mastered long division, she showed her little brother — he who learns, teaches.

items.p: a fool and water go the way they are diverted
items.m: people without their own judgment drift wherever others push them
items.os: Ethiopian proverb recorded in African proverb collections, comparing an easily led person to water steered by any ditch dug for it.
items.ex: Don't copy whatever the loudest kid does at recess — a fool and water go the way they are diverted.

items.p: words have no wings but can fly a thousand miles
items.m: gossip and news spread far and fast
items.os: Korean proverb, literally 'a word without feet travels a thousand li' — a li being about a third of a mile.
items.ex: She whispered the secret at morning recess, and by lunch the whole school knew — words have no wings but can fly a thousand miles.
items.lit: 발 없는 말이 천 리 간다 (bal eomneun mari cheon ri ganda)

items.p: even a sheet of paper is lighter when two lift it
items.m: every task, however small, is easier when people help each other
items.os: Korean proverb: even a single blank sheet of paper is better lifted by two people together.
items.ex: Dad and I carried the groceries in together — even a sheet of paper is lighter when two lift it.

items.p: the beginning is half the journey
items.m: just getting started carries you a long way toward finishing
items.os: Korean proverb — 'the start is the half' — said to nudge people past the fear of beginning.
items.ex: Just opening your book report file counts, because the beginning is half the journey.

eq.p: the beginning is half of the whole

items.m: check your work carefully before doing something you cannot undo
items.os: Russian tailors' and carpenters' proverb; Russians actually say 'measure seven times, cut once,' since cloth once cut is cut forever.
items.ex: Check every word before you ink your poster — measure ten times, cut once.
items.lit: семь раз отмерь, один раз отрежь (sem' raz otmer', odin raz otrezh')

items.p: a spoken word is not a sparrow; once it flies out you cannot catch it
items.m: you can never take back something you have said
items.os: Russian proverb: a word is not a sparrow — once it flies out, you will not catch it.
items.ex: I wished I hadn't blurted her surprise party plan, but a spoken word is not a sparrow; once it flies out you cannot catch it.
items.lit: слово не воробей, вылетит — не поймаешь (slovo ne vorobey, vyletit — ne poymayesh')

items.m: believe people, but still check the facts for yourself
items.os: Russian rhyming proverb 'doveryay, no proveryay'; President Reagan learned it in Russian to quote at 1980s nuclear arms talks.
items.ex: Mom believes my homework is done, but she still peeks at my planner — trust but verify.

items.m: work quickly but carefully, never in a reckless rush
items.os: Latin motto 'festina lente,' the favorite saying of Emperor Augustus, who felt a task done well was done fast enough; he borrowed it from Greek.
items.ex: In the spelling bee, hurry slowly: say each letter clearly instead of racing.

items.p: while there is life there is hope
items.m: as long as you keep going, things can still get better
items.os: From Cicero, who wrote to a friend in 49 BC that 'while there is life, there is hope' — aegroto dum anima est, spes esse dicitur.
items.ex: We were losing at halftime, but while there is life there is hope, so we kept playing hard.

items.m: understand your own strengths, weaknesses, and feelings
items.os: Ancient Greek maxim carved on the Temple of Apollo at Delphi and beloved by Socrates.
items.ex: Know thyself: I do my best homework right after a snack, so that's when I start.

items.p: the beginning is half of the whole
items.m: starting a task well means you are already halfway done
items.os: Ancient Greek proverb quoted by Aristotle and credited by some to Pythagoras.
items.ex: Once my science-fair poster had a title and a plan, the beginning was half of the whole.

items.p: don't count your chickens before they hatch
items.m: don't treat a hoped-for success as certain before it happens
items.os: From Aesop's fable of the milkmaid who daydreams her pail of milk into eggs, chicks, and riches — then spills it all.
items.ex: I started planning my trophy shelf before the bee, and Dad said not to count my chickens before they hatch.

items.p: slow and steady wins the race
items.m: patient, consistent effort beats careless speed
items.os: The moral of Aesop's tortoise-and-hare fable; the exact English line comes from Robert Lloyd's 1762 poem about the race.
items.ex: Ten spelling words a night, every night — slow and steady wins the race.

items.p: the squeaky wheel gets the grease
items.m: the person who complains loudest gets attention first
items.os: American, 1800s, from wagon wheels that got oiled only when they squeaked; often traced to Josh Billings' comic poem 'The Kicker,' though that attribution is unproven.
items.ex: Nobody fixed the wobbly desk until Maya asked three times — the squeaky wheel gets the grease.

items.p: a chain is only as strong as its weakest link
items.m: a team or plan fails at its most fragile part
items.os: English, 1700s; the philosopher Thomas Reid spelled out the chain-and-link image in a 1786 essay.
items.ex: Our relay team practiced handoffs together, because a chain is only as strong as its weakest link.

items.m: telling the truth works out best in the long run
items.os: English, late 1500s; the statesman Sir Edwin Sandys used the line in a 1599 survey of Europe's churches.
items.ex: I told Ms. Rivera I forgot my homework instead of inventing an excuse — honesty is the best policy.

items.m: behave the way you tell others to behave
items.os: Echoes the Bible's complaint about teachers who 'say, and do not' (Matthew 23); the snappy English rhyme settled in by the 1600s.
items.ex: If I tell my brother to make his bed, I'd better practice what I preach and make mine.

items.m: to stir a feeling of recognition or emotion in someone
items.os: From music: a struck chord can set nearby strings vibrating in sympathy; figurative in English since the 1800s.
items.ex: The story about a shy new student struck a chord with everyone in class.

items.m: someone may be secretly listening, so watch what you say
items.os: Old in many languages; the tale that Queen Catherine de' Medici hid listening tubes in palace walls is a myth — the saying is far older.
items.ex: Don't discuss Dad's surprise gift in the kitchen — the walls have ears.

items.m: interest grows once you begin; starting creates enthusiasm
items.os: From Rabelais' 1534 novel Gargantua: 'l'appétit vient en mangeant' — the appetite comes while eating.
items.ex: I dreaded my book report, but after one page I wanted to keep going — appetite comes with eating.

items.m: everyone is entitled to their own likes and dislikes
items.os: French saying 'chacun son goût,' echoing the old Latin rule that tastes are not to be argued about.
items.ex: My sister likes pineapple pizza and I don't — to each his own taste.

eq.p: there is no disputing about tastes

items.m: hard times are followed by better ones
items.os: French proverb 'après la pluie, le beau temps,' recorded in collections since the Middle Ages.
items.ex: The week of makeup tests ended with a class party — after the rain, fair weather.
items.lit: après la pluie, le beau temps

eq.p: every cloud has a silver lining

items.p: little by little the wolf eats the sheep
items.m: small, steady steps — good or bad — add up to something big
items.os: French country proverb about patience and creeping change; cousin of the gentler 'petit à petit, l'oiseau fait son nid' — little by little, the bird builds its nest.
items.ex: One skipped practice became five, and little by little the wolf eats the sheep.
items.lit: petit à petit le loup mange la brebis

items.p: who steals an egg steals an ox
items.m: small wrongs lead to big ones if nobody stops them
items.os: French rhyme 'qui vole un œuf vole un bœuf,' warning that little thefts train big thieves.
items.ex: Grandma says sneaking one cookie today becomes the whole jar tomorrow — who steals an egg steals an ox.
items.lit: qui vole un œuf vole un bœuf

items.m: different methods can reach the same goal
items.os: Medieval Latin; Alain de Lille wrote in the 1100s that 'a thousand roads lead men forever to Rome,' when Roman roads really did radiate from the capital.
items.ex: Flashcards, songs, or writing words out — all roads lead to Rome when you're studying spelling.
items.lit: mille viae ducunt homines per saecula Romam

items.m: an unhurried, steady pace carries you farthest
items.os: Italian rhyme 'chi va piano va sano e va lontano' — who goes gently goes safely and goes far.
items.ex: She learned one violin scale a week all year — who goes slowly goes far.
items.lit: chi va piano va sano e va lontano

eq.p: slow and steady wins the race

items.p: between saying and doing lies the sea
items.m: promising something is far easier than actually doing it
items.os: Italian proverb 'tra il dire e il fare c'è di mezzo il mare,' rhyming 'fare' (doing) with 'mare' (the sea).
items.ex: He promised to organize his desk all month, but between saying and doing lies the sea.
items.lit: tra il dire e il fare c'è di mezzo il mare

items.p: not all doughnuts come with a hole
items.m: things don't always turn out the way you planned
items.os: Italian kitchen proverb 'non tutte le ciambelle riescono col buco' — not every ring cake comes out of the oven with its hole.
items.ex: My volcano model fizzled instead of erupting, but not all doughnuts come with a hole.
items.lit: non tutte le ciambelle riescono col buco

items.p: he who sleeps does not catch fish
items.m: lazy or inattentive people miss their chances
items.os: Italian proverb 'chi dorme non piglia pesci,' from fishermen who must be on the water before dawn.
items.ex: Sign-ups for the robotics club filled by 8 a.m. — he who sleeps does not catch fish.

eq.p: the early bird catches the worm

items.m: settling money matters plainly keeps friendships healthy
items.os: Spanish 'cuentas claras, amistades largas' — clear accounts, long friendships; the French version says good accounts make good friends.
items.ex: We split the lemonade-stand money evenly right away, because clear accounts make good friends.

eq.lit: les bons comptes font les bons amis

items.p: shrimp that falls asleep is carried by the current
items.m: if you stop paying attention, you lose your chance
items.os: Latin American Spanish proverb 'camarón que se duerme se lo lleva la corriente' — the dozing shrimp drifts away downstream.
items.ex: I daydreamed during review and missed the study guide — the shrimp that falls asleep is carried by the current.
items.lit: camarón que se duerme se lo lleva la corriente

items.p: there is no evil that lasts a hundred years
items.m: no misfortune lasts forever
items.os: Spanish proverb 'no hay mal que dure cien años,' often finished '…ni cuerpo que lo resista' — nor a body that could endure it.
items.ex: Abuela reminded me my broken arm would heal by summer — there is no evil that lasts a hundred years.
items.lit: no hay mal que dure cien años

items.p: eyes that don't see, heart that doesn't feel
items.m: you don't grieve over what you don't know about
items.os: Spanish rhyme 'ojos que no ven, corazón que no siente,' recorded in proverb collections since the Middle Ages.
items.ex: Once the fair left town, my little sister stopped begging to go — eyes that don't see, heart that doesn't feel.
items.lit: ojos que no ven, corazón que no siente

eq.p: out of sight, out of mind

items.p: he who embraces too much, squeezes little
items.m: take on too many things and you'll do none of them well
items.os: Spanish proverb 'quien mucho abarca, poco aprieta,' already in use in Cervantes' day, picturing arms too full to grip anything.
items.ex: Signing up for five clubs at once, he learned that he who embraces too much, squeezes little.

eq.p: bite off more than you can chew

items.p: god helps those who rise early
items.m: early risers get the luck and the results
items.os: Spanish proverb 'a quien madruga, Dios le ayuda,' recorded since Spain's Golden Age in the 1500s.
items.ex: She reviewed her words before breakfast on bee day — god helps those who rise early.
items.lit: a quien madruga, Dios le ayuda

eq.p: the early bird catches the worm

items.p: he who has a mouth will get to Rome
items.m: if you're willing to ask questions, you can find your way anywhere
items.os: Portuguese 'quem tem boca vai a Roma,' beloved in Brazil; some insist the older form was 'vaia Roma' — boos even Rome — but the asking-directions sense won out.
items.ex: Lost in the huge new school, I just asked directions to the gym — he who has a mouth will get to Rome.
items.lit: quem tem boca vai a Roma

items.p: soft water on hard stone strikes until it bores through
items.m: gentle persistence eventually overcomes the hardest obstacle
items.os: Portuguese rhyme 'água mole em pedra dura, tanto bate até que fura,' descending from Ovid's Latin line that dripping water hollows the stone.
items.ex: Five minutes of piano every day, and by June she could play the whole song — soft water on hard stone strikes until it bores through.
items.lit: água mole em pedra dura, tanto bate até que fura

eq.p: constant dripping wears away the stone

items.p: haste is the enemy of perfection
items.m: rushing ruins careful work
items.os: Brazilian Portuguese saying 'a pressa é inimiga da perfeição,' recited by parents and teachers across Brazil.
items.ex: I rushed my map and misspelled two countries — haste is the enemy of perfection.
items.lit: a pressa é inimiga da perfeição

items.p: morning hour has gold in its mouth
items.m: early morning work is the most rewarding
items.os: German rhyme 'Morgenstund hat Gold im Mund,' recorded since the 1500s.
items.ex: I do my hardest math before school when my brain is fresh — morning hour has gold in its mouth.

eq.p: the early bird catches the worm

items.p: beginning is easy, persisting is art
items.m: starting something is simple; sticking with it is the real skill
items.os: German proverb 'Anfangen ist leicht, Beharren eine Kunst,' a classroom-wall favorite in Germany.
items.ex: Everyone joined the running club in September, but by March only a few of us were left — beginning is easy, persisting is art.
items.lit: Anfangen ist leicht, Beharren eine Kunst

items.m: trouble is sneaky and can pop up where you least expect it
items.os: German saying 'der Teufel ist ein Eichhörnchen'; old folk tales pictured the devil disguising himself as a quick, harmless-looking red squirrel.
items.ex: The quiz looked easy until the last question — the devil is a squirrel.

items.p: one must howl with the wolves one lives among
items.m: people tend to copy the behavior of those around them
items.os: German 'mit den Wölfen muss man heulen,' from a medieval Latin tag about learning to howl from the wolves you live with.
items.ex: At sleepaway camp everyone cheered the silly songs, so I joined in — one must howl with the wolves one lives among.
items.lit: mit den Wölfen muss man heulen

eq.p: when in Rome, do as the Romans do

items.p: he who digs a pit for others falls in himself
items.m: traps you set for others end up catching you
items.os: From the Bible's Book of Proverbs — 'whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein' — kept alive in Germany as the rhyme 'wer andern eine Grube gräbt, fällt selbst hinein.'
items.ex: He hid his sister's backpack as a prank, then missed the bus looking for his own — he who digs a pit for others falls in himself.
items.lit: Wer andern eine Grube gräbt, fällt selbst hinein

items.p: east or west, home is best
items.m: no place feels as good as your own home
items.os: Dutch rhyme 'oost west, thuis best,' printed in proverb books since the 1800s and adopted straight into English.
items.ex: The beach trip was fun, but sleeping in my own bed felt wonderful — east or west, home is best.

items.p: he who is outside the door has already made the hardest step
items.m: getting started is the hardest part of any undertaking
items.os: Quoted in English collections as a Dutch proverb about journeys, though the original Dutch wording is not well recorded.
items.ex: Once I finally sat down and opened my essay notebook, the rest flowed — he who is outside the door has already made the hardest step.

eq.p: the first step is the hardest

items.m: people who stand out attract criticism and trouble
items.os: Dutch proverb 'hoge bomen vangen veel wind,' a low, windswept country's image for prominent people drawing storms.
items.ex: After she won three bees in a row, everyone aimed to beat her — tall trees catch much wind.

eq.p: the nail that sticks out gets hammered down
eq.lit: 出る杭は打たれる (deru kui wa utareru)

items.p: patience is a bitter plant with sweet fruit
items.m: waiting is unpleasant, but the results are worth it
items.os: Turkish and Persian proverb; Turks say 'sabır acıdır, meyvesi tatlıdır' — patience is bitter, its fruit is sweet.
items.ex: Waiting all spring for the tomatoes we planted was hard, but patience is a bitter plant with sweet fruit.

eq.p: good things come to those who wait

items.p: one cup of coffee is remembered for forty years
items.m: a small kindness creates lasting friendship and loyalty
items.os: Turkish saying from Ottoman coffeehouse culture: 'bir fincan kahvenin kırk yıl hatırı vardır' — a cup of coffee carries forty years of goodwill.
items.ex: Years later, Grandpa still talks about the neighbor who shared lunch on his first day in town — one cup of coffee is remembered for forty years.
items.lit: bir fincan kahvenin kırk yıl hatırı vardır

items.p: a knife wound heals; a word wound festers
items.m: cruel words hurt far longer than physical injuries
items.os: Turkish proverb 'bıçak yarası geçer, dil yarası geçmez' — the knife's wound passes, the tongue's wound does not.
items.ex: My scraped knee healed in a week, but I still remember the mean nickname — a knife wound heals; a word wound festers.
items.lit: bıçak yarası geçer, dil yarası geçmez

items.p: the forest was shrinking but the trees kept voting for the axe
items.m: people can be tricked into supporting what harms them
items.os: Circulates online as a Turkish proverb — the axe fooled the trees because its handle was wood, one of their own — but no old Turkish source exists; it is likely modern.
items.ex: The class kept picking the recess monitor who canceled recess, and Dad sighed that the forest was shrinking but the trees kept voting for the axe.

items.p: doubt is the key to knowledge
items.m: questioning things is how real learning begins
items.os: Quoted in English collections as a Persian proverb prizing curiosity, though the original Persian wording is rarely given.
items.ex: She asked why the sky is blue instead of just nodding — doubt is the key to knowledge.

items.p: a good word is like a good tree
items.m: kind, truthful words take root and keep on giving
items.os: From the Quran (surah Ibrahim): a good word is like a good tree, its roots firm and its branches reaching the sky.
items.ex: The coach's one sentence of praise kept her practicing all year — a good word is like a good tree.
items.lit: كلمة طيبة كشجرة طيبة (kalima ṭayyiba ka-shajara ṭayyiba)

items.p: the hand you cannot bite, kiss
items.m: make peace with a power you cannot beat
items.os: Widespread Arab proverb, well known in its Egyptian form — the hand you can't bite, kiss it — and echoed in the Balkans too.
items.ex: You can't argue the umpire's call away, so shake hands and play on — the hand you cannot bite, kiss.
items.lit: الإيد اللي ما تقدرش تعضها بوسها (el-īd illi ma-ti'darsh te'oddaha, būs-ha)

items.p: seek knowledge even as far as China
items.m: no distance is too far to travel for learning
items.os: Famous Arabic saying attributed to the Prophet Muhammad — 'seek knowledge even in China' — though hadith scholars doubt he actually said it.
items.ex: She rode two buses across town every Saturday for chess lessons — seek knowledge even as far as China.
items.lit: اطلبوا العلم ولو في الصين (uṭlubū al-ʿilma wa-law fī aṣ-Ṣīn)

items.p: books are the food of youth
items.m: reading nourishes young minds the way food feeds bodies
items.os: From Cicero's speech Pro Archia (62 BC), praising study: haec studia adulescentiam alunt — these pursuits nourish youth.
items.ex: Our librarian hands out summer reading lists saying books are the food of youth.

items.p: a camel never sees its own hump
items.m: people notice others' faults but never their own
items.os: Arab proverb; an old version says the camel cannot see the crook of its own neck.
items.ex: He teased me for a messy desk while his own overflowed — a camel never sees its own hump.
items.lit: الجمل لا يرى عوجة رقبته (al-jamal lā yarā ʿawjat raqabatih)

eq.p: the pot calling the kettle black

items.p: the remedy against bad talk is distance
items.m: the best response to gossip or insults is to walk away
items.os: Cited in collections of Arabic and African proverbs about avoiding quarrels, though the original wording is not well recorded.
items.ex: When the lunch-table gossip started, she took her tray to another seat — the remedy against bad talk is distance.

items.p: every day of your life is a page of your history
items.m: everything you do each day becomes part of your story
items.os: Quoted in English collections as an Arab proverb about living thoughtfully; no single classical source is recorded.
items.ex: Grandpa writes in his journal each night because every day of your life is a page of your history.

items.p: haste comes from the devil, patience from the merciful
items.m: rushing leads to mistakes; patience is wise and good
items.os: Arabic saying rooted in a hadith: al-'ajala min ash-shaytan wa-t-ta'anni min ar-Rahman — haste is from Satan, deliberateness from the Most Merciful.
items.ex: I raced through the test and missed easy questions; my careful sister didn't — haste comes from the devil, patience from the merciful.
items.lit: العجلة من الشيطان والتأني من الرحمن (al-ʿajala min ash-shayṭān wa-t-taʾannī min ar-Raḥmān)

items.p: a leopard cannot change its spots
items.m: people cannot change their basic nature
items.os: From the Bible: the prophet Jeremiah asks, 'Can the leopard change his spots?'
items.ex: He promised to stop hogging the ball, but a leopard cannot change its spots.

items.p: birds of a feather flock together
items.m: similar people naturally group together
items.os: English, 1500s; the naturalist William Turner used a version in 1545, drawing on how birds of one kind fly in flocks.
items.ex: The puzzle fans always end up at the same lunch table — birds of a feather flock together.

items.p: half a loaf is better than none
items.m: getting part of what you want beats getting nothing
items.os: English proverb in John Heywood's 1546 collection: 'better is half a loaf than no bread.'
items.ex: We got twenty minutes of recess instead of forty, but half a loaf is better than none.

items.p: out of sight, out of mind
items.m: we forget things and people we no longer see
items.os: English by the 1200s as 'far from eye, far from heart'; printed in John Heywood's 1546 proverb collection.
items.ex: Mom keeps my video games in the closet on school nights — out of sight, out of mind.

eq.p: eyes that don't see, heart that doesn't feel
eq.lit: ojos que no ven, corazón que no siente

items.p: absence makes the heart grow fonder
items.m: being apart makes you miss and love someone more
items.os: The exact line closes Thomas Haynes Bayly's 1830s song 'Isle of Beauty,' though the idea opens an anonymous English poem from 1602.
items.ex: After a week at camp, I hugged even my annoying little brother — absence makes the heart grow fonder.

items.m: knowing something too well can make you stop respecting it
items.os: The moral of Aesop's fable of the fox who grows bold around the lion; Chaucer used the English form in the 1300s.
items.ex: By June the class treated the amazing robot lab like old furniture — familiarity breeds contempt.

items.p: an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure
items.m: stopping a problem early is far easier than fixing it later
items.os: Benjamin Franklin, 1735, urging Philadelphians to prevent house fires rather than fight them.
items.ex: Packing my backpack the night before beats hunting for homework at 7 a.m. — an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.

items.p: a penny saved is a penny earned
items.m: money you don't spend is as good as money you make
items.os: Usually credited to Benjamin Franklin, but he never wrote it; English versions like 'a penny saved is a penny got' date to the 1600s.
items.ex: I skipped the vending machine and dropped the dollar in my jar — a penny saved is a penny earned.

items.m: if you never waste anything, you will never lack it
items.os: English, first recorded in 1772; tightened from the older 'wilful waste makes woeful want.'
items.ex: Grandma turns leftover chicken into soup the next day — waste not, want not.

items.m: double-check before you act, because some actions can't be undone
items.os: Carpenters' and tailors' proverb, in English collections since the 1500s: wood and cloth, once cut, stay cut.
items.ex: Before gluing my diorama, I checked every piece — measure twice, cut once.

eq.lit: семь раз отмерь, один раз отрежь (sem' raz otmer', odin raz otrezh')

items.m: the end has come for someone or something
items.os: American theater slang, early 1900s: when the final curtain falls, the show is over.
items.ex: When Mom spotted the muddy footprints, I knew it was curtains for my afternoon plans.

items.m: an extremely angry expression
items.os: British image of a dark, glowering storm sky about to break, in use since the 1800s.
items.ex: The coach had a face like thunder when we skipped warm-ups.

items.m: to rush around busily without getting anywhere
items.os: From dogs spinning in circles after their own tails; common in American English by the 1900s.
items.ex: Without a checklist I spent all Saturday chasing my tail instead of finishing my project.

items.p: give a dog a bad name
items.m: once someone gets a bad reputation, it sticks unfairly
items.os: Short for the 1700s English proverb 'give a dog a bad name and hang him' — a bad label can doom even the innocent.
items.ex: After one messy locker check, everyone assumed Leo lost the class pencils too — give a dog a bad name.

items.p: a drowning man clutches at a straw of grass
items.m: someone in trouble grabs any tiny hope, however weak
items.os: Hindi 'डूबते को तिनके का सहारा' — even a floating straw feels like a boat to someone drowning.
items.ex: Down to her last lifeline in the quiz, she clutched at it like a straw of grass.
items.lit: डूबते को तिनके का सहारा (ḍūbte ko tinke kā sahārā)

items.p: the crocodile of your own pond
items.m: someone powerful only in their own small territory
items.os: Hindi 'अपने घर में तो कुत्ता भी शेर होता है' family of sayings — every creature is fierce at home.
items.ex: He bosses the playground at home but goes quiet at the district bee — a crocodile of his own pond.

eq.p: a big fish in a small pond
eq.lit: important only in a small place

items.m: two people united are far stronger than two alone
items.os: Hindi 'एक और एक ग्यारह' — write 1 beside 1 and you get 11, not 2. Unity multiplies strength.
items.ex: When Ahana and her study buddy team up, one and one make eleven.
items.lit: एक और एक ग्यारह (ek aur ek gyārah)

items.p: a diamond is judged by a jeweller
items.m: only an expert recognizes true worth
items.os: Hindi 'हीरे की परख जौहरी जाने' — an untrained eye sees a pebble where a jeweller sees a diamond.
items.ex: The new coach spotted her talent at once — a diamond is judged by a jeweller.
items.lit: हीरे की परख जौहरी जाने (hīre kī parakh jauharī jāne)

items.p: to apply turmeric before the wedding
items.m: to celebrate or prepare too early, before success is certain
items.os: From the haldi ceremony held just before Indian weddings — doing it early tempts fate.
items.ex: Planning the victory party before the results? That's applying turmeric before the wedding.

eq.p: don't count your chickens before they hatch

items.p: the sieve says to the needle, you have a hole in you
items.m: criticizing someone for a fault you have far worse yourself
items.os: Hindi 'छलनी क्या बोले सूप से जिसमें बहत्तर छेद' — a sieve with seventy-two holes mocking a needle's one eye.
items.ex: He teased her for one spelling slip after missing five — the sieve telling the needle it has a hole.
items.lit: छलनी बोले सूप से, जिसमें बहत्तर छेद

eq.p: the pot calling the kettle black
eq.lit: a fault-finder with the same fault

items.m: someone holding a valuable thing they don't know how to use
items.os: Indian saying 'बंदर के हाथ में नारियल' — the monkey can neither open the coconut nor let it go.
items.ex: Giving my little brother the dictionary was like handing a monkey a coconut.
items.lit: बंदर के हाथ में नारियल (bandar ke hāth meṉ nāriyal)

items.p: where there is a will, the mountain becomes a path
items.m: determination turns even huge obstacles into ways forward
items.os: Echoes the tale of Dashrath Manjhi, the 'Mountain Man' who carved a road through a hill with hand tools over 22 years.
items.ex: She learned 300 words in a month — where there is a will, the mountain becomes a path.
items.lit: जहाँ चाह वहाँ राह (jahān̐ chāh vahān̐ rāh)

eq.p: where there's a will there's a way

items.p: the crow that walked like a swan
items.m: copying others blindly can make you forget your own strengths
items.os: Hindi 'कौआ चला हंस की चाल, अपनी भी भूल गया' — the crow imitating a swan's glide forgot its own walk.
items.ex: Don't copy the champion's shortcuts blindly — remember the crow that walked like a swan.

items.p: to sharpen your knife on someone else's stone
items.m: to use another person's resources for your own gain
items.os: Punjabi-Hindi farming image: sneaking a free sharpen on the neighbour's grindstone.
items.ex: He kept borrowing my flashcards for his own prep — sharpening his knife on my stone.
items.lit: दूसरे के पत्थर पर छुरी तेज़ करना

items.p: a pinch of turmeric and he opened a grocery shop
items.m: boasting of a big enterprise with tiny means
items.os: Hindi 'चुटकी भर हल्दी लेकर पंसारी की दुकान' — one pinch of spice does not make a shopkeeper.
items.ex: He learned three roots and calls himself an etymology expert — a pinch of turmeric and he opened a shop.
items.lit: हल्दी की एक गाँठ लेकर पंसारी बनना

items.p: the mouth tastes of ghee only if the elders bless it
items.m: success comes easier with the blessings and help of elders
items.os: North Indian blessing culture: ghee — precious and rich — stands for good fortune granted by family.
items.ex: She touched Dadi's feet before the finals — the mouth tastes of ghee when elders bless it.
items.lit: बड़ों के आशीर्वाद से मुँह में घी

items.p: the peacock danced in the forest, but who saw it?
items.m: talent shown where nobody can see it goes to waste
items.os: Hindi 'जंगल में मोर नाचा किसने देखा' — even a peacock's dance needs an audience to matter.
items.ex: Practise your words aloud at the family dinner — a peacock dancing alone in the forest goes unseen.
items.lit: जंगल में मोर नाचा किसने देखा (jaṅgal meṉ mor nāchā kisne dekhā)

items.m: someone suddenly meek after being proud or bold
items.os: Hindi 'भीगी बिल्ली बनना' — a soaked cat loses all its swagger.
items.ex: He bragged all week, then went wet-cat quiet when his word came up.

items.m: to argue fiercely; to be at each other constantly
items.os: Kitchen image: garlic and ginger crushed together in every Indian masala, inseparable and clashing.
items.ex: The twins became garlic and ginger over who got the last flashcard.

items.p: the lamp's light does not fall at its own base
items.m: we often miss problems closest to us while helping others far away
items.os: Hindi 'चिराग़ तले अंधेरा' — the oil lamp lights the room but leaves darkness right beneath itself.
items.ex: The coach fixed everyone's spelling but missed his own son's — the lamp leaves darkness at its base.

items.p: to ask the fence to guard the field
items.m: trusting a protector who is the real danger
items.os: Hindi 'बाड़ ही खेत को खाए' — when the fence itself eats the crop, whom do you call?
items.ex: Letting the puppy guard the snacks table was asking the fence to guard the field.

items.m: grand claims backed by nothing
items.os: Hindi 'ऊँची दुकान फीके पकवान' — the fancy shop whose sweets turn out flavourless.
items.ex: The app promised 10,000 words but had 50 — big talk, empty pockets.
items.lit: ऊँची दुकान फीके पकवान (ūn̐cī dukān phīke pakvān)

items.p: only the wearer knows where the shoe pinches
items.m: only the person in a situation knows its real difficulty
items.os: Shared by Hindi 'जिसके पैर न फटी बिवाई, वो क्या जाने पीर पराई' and English tradition alike.
items.ex: It looks easy from the audience, but only the speller on stage knows where the shoe pinches.
items.lit: जिसके पैर न फटी बिवाई, वो क्या जाने पीर पराई

eq.p: walk a mile in someone's shoes

items.p: the mother asks for rain, the child asks for sweets
items.m: different people want different things from the same moment
items.os: Folk saying from farming homes: the same cloud means harvest to one and holiday treats to another.
items.ex: Mum wanted an early night; Veer wanted one more game — rain and sweets from the same cloud.
items.lit: माँ माँगे पानी, बच्चा माँगे मिठाई

items.m: doing your work sincerely is itself a sacred act
items.os: Popularised in India through Gandhi's teachings and the Bhagavad Gita's 'yoga of action' (karma yoga).
items.ex: Ahana skips no practice day — for her, work is worship.
items.lit: कर्म ही पूजा है (karma hī pūjā hai)

items.p: a single bamboo cannot make a raft
items.m: big things need many people working together
items.os: Told across India and Southeast Asia wherever bamboo rafts carry rivers — one pole just sinks.
items.ex: One speller can't win the team round — a single bamboo cannot make a raft.
items.lit: अकेला चना भाड़ नहीं फोड़ता (a lone chickpea can't burst the roaster)

items.m: basic needs must be met before higher pursuits
items.os: Hindi 'भूखे भजन न होय गोपाला' — the saint Kabir's line: no hymns are sung on an empty stomach.
items.ex: Breakfast before the morning drill — first food, then faith.
items.lit: भूखे भजन न होय गोपाला (bhūkhe bhajan na hoy gopālā)

items.p: the boat reaches the shore by the boatman's skill
items.m: success depends on the skill of the one guiding, not luck
items.os: River-crossing image from the Ganges plains; folk verses credit the majhi (boatman), not the current.
items.ex: The team made the finals — the boat reached shore by the coach-boatman's skill.
items.lit: नाव पार लगाना माझी का हुनर

items.m: very hardworking and active
items.os: Chaucer used it in the Canterbury Tales (1300s) — bees never seem to rest.
items.ex: She's as busy as a bee the week before finals.

items.m: having very poor eyesight
items.os: Bats fly at dusk and seem to blunder; in fact they see fine — the simile is older than the science.
items.ex: Without glasses I'm as blind as a bat.

items.m: very courageous
items.os: The lion has symbolized courage since ancient heraldry and Aesop.
items.ex: She was as brave as a lion on stage.

items.m: calm under pressure
items.os: Cucumbers stay cooler inside than the air around them — recorded in English verse by 1732.
items.ex: He stayed as cool as a cucumber in the spell-off.

items.m: extremely cold; unfeeling
items.os: Ancient comparison found across languages; ice is the universal benchmark of cold.
items.ex: Her reply was as cold as ice.

items.m: extremely lightweight
items.os: Feathers are the proverbial lightest thing one can hold; medieval in use.
items.ex: The new tablet is as light as a feather.

items.m: physically very strong
items.os: Oxen pulled plows and carts for millennia — the strength standard of farm life.
items.ex: The mover was as strong as an ox.

items.m: refusing to change one's mind
items.os: Mules famously refuse to move when they distrust a path — actually cautious, not dumb.
items.ex: He's as stubborn as a mule about his study method.

items.m: silent and unobtrusive
items.os: Mice move silently to avoid predators; proverbial since the Middle Ages.
items.ex: She slipped in as quiet as a mouse.

items.m: clever and cunning
items.os: The fox is the trickster of European folklore, from Aesop to Reynard.
items.ex: The negotiator was as sly as a fox.

items.m: vain about one's appearance
items.os: The peacock's tail display made it the emblem of vanity since ancient Greece.
items.ex: He strutted in as proud as a peacock.

items.m: mild and harmless
items.os: Lambs symbolize innocence in biblical and pastoral tradition.
items.ex: The huge dog is as gentle as a lamb.

items.m: very wise
items.os: The owl was the bird of Athena, Greek goddess of wisdom.
items.ex: Grandpa is as wise as an owl about people.

items.m: elegant in movement
items.os: Swans glide serenely on water — ballet's Swan Lake fixed the image forever.
items.ex: The skater was as graceful as a swan.

items.m: completely free
items.os: Birds embody freedom because they can simply fly away.
items.ex: School's out — I'm as free as a bird.

items.m: extremely hungry
items.os: Wolves gorge after long hunts; 'wolfing' food comes from the same image.
items.ex: After practice I'm as hungry as a wolf.

items.m: hard to catch or pin down; evasive
items.os: Eels coat themselves in slime — literally impossible to grip.
items.ex: The suspect was as slippery as an eel under questioning.

items.m: very happy and content
items.os: American; short for 'happy as a clam at high water,' when clams are safe from diggers.
items.ex: She's as happy as a clam with her new books.

items.m: completely extinct or obsolete
items.os: The dodo of Mauritius was wiped out by 1681, becoming extinction's mascot.
items.ex: Fax machines are as dead as a dodo.

items.p: as mad as a march hare
items.m: behaving wildly
items.os: Hares leap and box in March breeding season; Lewis Carroll immortalized the phrase.
items.ex: The puppy ran around as mad as a March hare.

items.m: very ill
items.os: Dogs eat anything and often regret it; recorded since the 1700s.
items.ex: He was as sick as a dog after the buffet.

items.m: completely bald
items.os: American; the bald eagle isn't bald — 'balde' meant white-headed in old English.
items.ex: The coach is as bald as an eagle.

items.m: pure white
items.os: Ancient and biblical; snow is the whiteness benchmark in every snowy culture.
items.ex: The new uniforms are as white as snow.

items.m: deep black
items.os: Coal was every hearth's black standard before electricity.
items.ex: The pony's coat was as black as coal.

items.m: flushed deep red (from embarrassment)
items.os: American version; the British say 'red as a beetroot.'
items.ex: He turned as red as a beet at the compliment.

items.m: inexperienced; naive
items.os: Green = unripe; grass doubles the greenness. Used of novices since the 1400s.
items.ex: The intern is as green as grass but eager.

items.m: very well-behaved; genuine
items.os: Gold was the standard of genuine value — 'good' originally meant authentic, not obedient.
items.ex: The toddler was as good as gold all flight.

items.m: extremely old
items.os: Hills are geology's elders; the phrase echoes the Book of Job.
items.ex: That joke is as old as the hills.

items.m: completely reliable and stable
items.os: Rock is the biblical and architectural symbol of firm foundation.
items.ex: Her support has been as solid as a rock.

items.m: perfectly transparent or understandable
items.os: Crystal (rock quartz) was the clearest substance known before optical glass.
items.ex: The instructions were as clear as crystal.

items.m: not clear at all (ironic)
items.os: 19th-century irony: mud is the opposite of clear.
items.ex: His explanation was as clear as mud.

items.m: extremely sharp; keenly intelligent
items.os: Razors are honed to the finest edge; applied to minds since the 1500s.
items.ex: Her wit is as sharp as a razor.

items.m: perfectly smooth
items.os: Silk was the smoothest fabric on the ancient trade routes.
items.ex: The landing was as smooth as silk.

items.m: in excellent health
items.os: Originally 'fit' meant suitable/fine — a well-kept violin was the pride of its owner.
items.ex: Grandma at ninety is as fit as a fiddle.

items.p: as snug as a bug in a rug
items.m: perfectly cozy and comfortable
items.os: Benjamin Franklin used it in 1772; rhyme made it stick.
items.ex: Wrapped in blankets, she was snug as a bug in a rug.

items.m: very easy
items.os: American: the ease is in eating pie, not baking it.
items.ex: For her, level ten was easy as pie.

items.m: completely flat
items.os: Pancakes have been the flatness benchmark since the 1500s.
items.ex: The tire was as flat as a pancake.

items.m: very sweet; charming
items.os: Honey was humanity's sweetener for millennia before sugar.
items.ex: Her thank-you note was as sweet as honey.

items.m: extremely eager and enthusiastic
items.os: British; Keen's was a famous mustard brand, and mustard bites sharply.
items.ex: The new recruit is as keen as mustard.

items.m: very tough or durable
items.os: Old leather boots harden with age; said of meat and people alike.
items.ex: Grandpa's as tough as old boots.

items.m: perfectly straight; honest
items.os: Arrows must fly true; crooked ones miss — hence honest people are straight arrows.
items.ex: The road ran as straight as an arrow.

items.m: extremely fast
items.os: Lightning is nature's speed limit in folk imagination.
items.ex: Her buzzer finger is as quick as lightning.

items.m: very fast
items.os: Wind outruns horses in every ancient epic.
items.ex: The sprinter ran as fast as the wind.

items.m: completely silent
items.os: Graveyards are proverbially the quietest places; Gothic literature loved it.
items.ex: The hall fell as silent as the grave before the winning word.

items.m: very pale from fear or illness
items.os: Ghosts are imagined white and bloodless across cultures.
items.ex: She went as pale as a ghost at the tiebreak.

items.m: tough and unsentimental
items.os: Iron nails bend for nothing; applied to characters since the 1800s.
items.ex: The drill sergeant is as hard as nails.

items.m: completely dry
items.os: Sun-bleached bones in fields were the countryside's driest objects.
items.ex: After the drought the riverbed was as dry as a bone.

items.m: unable to hear
items.os: Talking to a fence post gets the same response; 1500s humor.
items.ex: Without his hearing aid he's as deaf as a post.

items.m: very thin
items.os: Chaucer used it — a rake is all handle and teeth, no body.
items.ex: The marathoner is as thin as a rake.

items.m: very round or stout
items.os: Barrels were everyday round objects in every cellar.
items.ex: The pumpkin grew as round as a barrel.

items.m: clever and alert; shiny
items.os: Polished brass buttons gleamed on uniforms; brightness = intelligence.
items.ex: The kindergartner is as bright as a button.

items.m: very crafty
items.os: Fox cunning is universal folklore, from Aesop to the Panchatantra.
items.ex: The chess master is as cunning as a fox.

items.m: full of playful energy
items.os: Kittens pounce at everything; the image sells itself.
items.ex: The new puppy is as playful as a kitten.

items.m: perfectly punctual and predictable
items.os: Mechanical clocks were the first perfectly regular machines people knew.
items.ex: Her study schedule runs as regular as clockwork.

items.m: to sleep deeply without stirring
items.os: Logs lie heavy and motionless; recorded since the 1600s.
items.ex: After nationals she slept like a log.

items.m: to eat a great deal
items.os: Horses graze most of the day and consume enormous amounts.
items.ex: Growing teens eat like horses.

items.m: to eat very little
items.os: Birds peck tiny amounts — though relative to body weight they actually eat a lot.
items.ex: She eats like a bird before competitions.

items.m: to swim excellently
items.os: Fish are water's natives; the compliment is ancient.
items.ex: Their toddler already swims like a fish.

items.m: to sing beautifully
items.os: Angelic choirs are the Western ideal of perfect song.
items.ex: The soloist sings like an angel.

items.p: to fight like cats and dogs
items.m: to quarrel constantly
items.os: Proverbial natural enemies since the 1500s.
items.ex: The twins fight like cats and dogs but adore each other.

items.m: to work perfectly
items.os: A charm is a magic spell — success as if by magic.
items.ex: The mnemonic worked like a charm.

items.m: to fit perfectly
items.os: Gloves must match the hand exactly; recorded by the 1770s.
items.ex: The new role fits her like a glove.

items.m: to spread extremely fast
items.os: Wildfire leaps faster than anyone can run; used of rumors since the 1800s.
items.ex: News of her win spread like wildfire.

items.m: to run extremely fast
items.os: Wind as the racer no one beats — Homeric in age.
items.ex: When the bell rang, he ran like the wind.

items.p: to have a memory like a sieve
items.m: to forget everything
items.os: A sieve is designed to let things fall through — the anti-container.
items.ex: Without flashcards I have a memory like a sieve.

items.p: to have a memory like an elephant
items.m: to remember everything
items.os: Elephants recall waterholes and faces for decades — zoology agrees.
items.ex: She has a memory like an elephant for word origins.

items.m: to watch very closely
items.os: Hawks spot mice from hundreds of feet up.
items.ex: The proctor watched us like a hawk.

items.p: like water off a duck's back
items.m: criticism having no effect
items.os: Duck feathers are oiled; water simply rolls off.
items.ex: Insults roll off her like water off a duck's back.

items.p: like a fish out of water
items.m: completely out of place
items.os: Chaucer used it: a fish ashore is helpless in the wrong element.
items.ex: At the dance recital, the coder felt like a fish out of water.

items.p: like a bull in a china shop
items.m: clumsy in a delicate situation
items.os: The image of a bull among porcelain appeared in early 1800s London satire.
items.ex: He handled the negotiation like a bull in a china shop.

items.p: like a moth to a flame
items.m: irresistibly (and dangerously) attracted
items.os: Moths navigate by light and spiral fatally into flames; Shakespeare used the image.
items.ex: He's drawn to drama like a moth to a flame.

items.m: (getting along) extremely well and fast
items.os: Wooden houses burned fast; the friendship blazes up just as quickly.
items.ex: The lab partners got on like a house on fire.

items.p: like a rolling stone gathers no moss
items.m: a wanderer accumulates no responsibilities (proverbial simile)
items.os: Ancient proverb via Erasmus: stones that keep moving stay bare.
items.ex: He changes cities yearly — a rolling stone gathers no moss.

items.m: extremely sturdy
items.os: 20th-century; tanks are the armored benchmark of toughness.
items.ex: That old laptop is built like a tank.

items.m: very inexpensive
items.os: British; fried chips are the everyman's cheapest meal.
items.ex: The used books were as cheap as chips.

items.m: quick and nimble in every movement
items.os: Monkeys swing branch to branch with effortless ease; a staple of English simile lists.
items.ex: She's as agile as a monkey on the climbing frame at recess.

items.m: extremely bitter, in taste or in feeling
items.os: Gall is bile, the most bitter fluid the body makes; the comparison runs through the Bible and medieval medicine.
items.ex: Losing the final round on an easy word felt as bitter as gall.

items.m: confident to the point of cheekiness
items.os: Brass has meant shameless cheek since the 1500s; the tale that it honors London's Lord Mayor Brass Crosby is a myth.
items.ex: Bold as brass, he walked up and asked the principal for an extra recess.

items.m: very brightly lit
items.os: Used since the 1500s for night scenes lit up like noon.
items.ex: With the new floodlights, the soccer field at night is as bright as day.

items.m: easily snapped or shattered
items.os: Thin glass cracks at a tap; writers use it for fragile things and fragile feelings alike.
items.ex: The old book's pages were as brittle as glass, so we turned them slowly.

items.m: perfectly still and smooth, especially of water
items.os: A millpond is the quiet water dammed up to turn a mill wheel; sailors borrowed it for a flat sea in the 1700s.
items.ex: The lake was as calm as a millpond for our family canoe trip.

items.m: constantly changing moods or plans
items.os: Weather turns from sun to storm within an hour — the oldest emblem of fickleness.
items.ex: Her favorite subject is as changeable as the weather — art one week, science the next.

items.m: very happy and lively
items.os: Larks pour out song at first light, which is also why early risers are 'up with the lark.'
items.ex: Dad is as cheerful as a lark on pancake Saturdays.

items.m: completely clean, or entirely free of wrongdoing
items.os: English, 1700s; perhaps from a whistle's pure note or a whittled stick's smooth finish — no one is sure.
items.ex: After we scrubbed the desks, the classroom was as clean as a whistle.

items.m: extremely ordinary and found everywhere
items.os: Dirt is everywhere underfoot and worth nothing — American plain talk from the 1800s.
items.ex: Rubber-band bracelets are as common as dirt at our school this year.

items.m: thoroughly dishonest
items.os: American wordplay: 'crooked' means both bent and cheating, and nothing bends like a corkscrew.
items.ex: The villain in our class play is as crooked as a corkscrew.

items.m: charmingly small and adorable
items.os: American, 1800s; possibly from 'bright as a button,' since new buttons were small and shiny — the exact source is unsettled.
items.ex: Everyone said my baby brother looked as cute as a button in his tiny bow tie.

items.m: completely dark
items.os: Midnight is the deep middle of the night, long the measure of total blackness.
items.ex: The power went out and the hallway turned as dark as midnight.

items.m: very deep, or very profound
items.os: The ocean floor lies miles down — the natural yardstick for depth of water or of feeling.
items.ex: Grandma says her love for us is as deep as the ocean.

items.m: fragile and easily hurt
items.os: Petals bruise at a touch; poets have leaned on the image for centuries.
items.ex: Handle the science-fair model gently — it's as delicate as a flower.

items.p: as different as chalk and cheese
items.m: completely unlike each other despite looking similar
items.os: English since the 1390s, when the poet John Gower used it: a chalk lump and a cheese wheel look alike but could not be more different.
items.ex: The twins are as different as chalk and cheese — one loves math, the other drama.

items.m: extremely boring
items.os: Stagnant ditch water is murky and lifeless; English, 1700s — Americans later reshaped it into 'dull as dishwater.'
items.ex: He called the museum's rock room as dull as ditchwater — until he saw the geodes.

items.m: very keen and hardworking
items.os: Beavers gnaw and build dams non-stop; American WWII slang made 'eager beaver' the name for the keenest recruit.
items.ex: She's as eager as a beaver about the new coding club.

items.m: extremely aggressive and determined
items.os: The tiger has stood for ferocity in stories from India to England for centuries.
items.ex: Our quiet librarian turns as fierce as a tiger if anyone dog-ears a book.

items.m: steady and impossible to shake
items.os: Bedrock does not budge; the image reaches back to the Bible's house built on rock.
items.ex: Mom's bedtime rule is as firm as a rock on school nights.

items.m: full of energy and completely rested
items.os: 'Daisy' is Old English for 'day's eye' — the flower opens bright each morning, looking new-made.
items.ex: After a good night's sleep she arrived at the bee as fresh as a daisy.

items.m: very mild and peaceful
items.os: From the Bible, where Jesus tells his followers to be 'harmless as doves'; doves have signaled peace since Noah's ark.
items.ex: The new teacher is as gentle as a dove with nervous first-graders.

items.m: completely hard, or without pity
items.os: Ancient: the Book of Job describes a heart 'hard as a stone,' and the image never left English.
items.ex: The playground dirt bakes as hard as stone by August.

items.m: extremely heavy
items.os: Lead is the proverbial heavyweight of everyday metals; English writers have used the simile since the Middle Ages.
items.ex: My backpack is as heavy as lead on library day.

items.m: having a rough, croaky voice
items.os: A crow's caw is the harshest sound in the hedgerow; the simile appears in English writing from the 1500s.
items.ex: After cheering all game, Dad was as hoarse as a crow.

items.m: extremely hot
items.os: Fire is the oldest measure of heat there is; the simile appears in the earliest English texts.
items.ex: The metal slide was as hot as fire, so we waited for the shade.

items.m: completely innocent and blameless
items.os: Lambs stand for innocence throughout the Bible, and English kept the picture ever after.
items.ex: He looked as innocent as a lamb, but the frosting on his chin told the truth.

items.m: present in person, unmistakably real
items.os: From life-size portraits, 1700s; later joke-stretched to 'large as life and twice as natural,' a line Lewis Carroll borrowed.
items.ex: We turned around at the water park, and there was our principal, as large as life.

items.m: extremely lazy and slow-moving
items.os: Sloths hang motionless for hours and were literally named after the old word for laziness.
items.ex: On rainy Sundays our cat is as lazy as a sloth.

items.m: extremely loud
items.os: Thunder is the loudest sound in nature's kit; poets have reached for it since ancient times.
items.ex: The gym crowd's cheer was as loud as thunder when she spelled the winning word.

items.m: faithful no matter what
items.os: Dogs have followed and defended their people for thousands of years; loyalty is their proverbial trait.
items.ex: My little sister is as loyal as a dog — she comes to every one of my games.

items.m: very cheerful
items.os: Shakespeare used 'as merry as crickets' in Henry IV; a cricket's endless chirp by the hearth sounded like good cheer.
items.ex: Grandpa is as merry as a cricket the whole week before the county fair.

items.m: perfectly tidy
items.os: English, 1700s, first as 'neat as a new pin' — fresh pins gleamed dead straight before rust dulled them.
items.ex: Her cubby is as neat as a pin, every marker capped and sorted.

items.m: very jumpy and easily startled
items.os: Cats bolt at any sudden sound; Americans stretched it to 'nervous as a cat in a room full of rocking chairs.'
items.ex: I was as nervous as a cat waiting for my turn at the microphone.

items.m: very silly or eccentric
items.os: American, 1920s: a fruitcake is packed with nuts, and 'nuts' already meant crazy — a double joke.
items.ex: Our uncle's holiday costumes are as nutty as a fruitcake, and we love them.

items.m: drained of all color in the face
items.os: The pallor of the dead is an image as old as Greek epic; English took up the simile in the Middle Ages.
items.ex: He went as pale as death when he realized he'd left his project on the bus.

items.m: enduring trouble without complaint
items.os: In the Bible, Job loses everything yet keeps his faith; the New Testament itself praises 'the patience of Job.'
items.ex: Ms. Rivera is as patient as Job with the beginner recorder class.

items.m: completely clear and obvious
items.os: Daylight hides nothing; English speakers have measured obviousness by it since the 1500s.
items.ex: The answer was as plain as day once she reread the question.

items.m: delighted with yourself
items.os: Mr. Punch, the hook-nosed puppet of English seaside shows since the 1600s, crows with glee at his own tricks.
items.ex: She was as pleased as Punch when her poem made the school magazine.

items.p: as poor as a church mouse
items.m: having no money at all
items.os: A church keeps no kitchen or pantry, so a mouse living there finds nothing to nibble; English, 1600s.
items.ex: The knight in our story was as poor as a church mouse but rich in courage.

items.m: very pretty
items.os: From the 1800s, when a painted portrait was the standard of beauty worth keeping.
items.ex: The garden we planted for the science unit is as pretty as a picture.

items.p: as pure as the driven snow
items.m: morally spotless
items.os: 'Driven' snow is blown into untouched drifts; Shakespeare praised 'lawn as white as driven snow' in The Winter's Tale.
items.ex: In the play she's cast as a heroine as pure as the driven snow.

items.m: happening almost instantly
items.os: A flash of lightning is over before you can blink; the simile spread through English in the 1800s.
items.ex: Quick as a flash, she raised her hand with the answer.

items.m: fabulously wealthy
items.os: Croesus, king of Lydia in the 500s BC, minted some of the world's first gold coins; Greek writers made his name mean wealth itself.
items.ex: The story's dragon was as rich as Croesus, sleeping on a mountain of gold.

items.m: completely safe and dependable
items.os: Victorian Britain, mid-1800s: after risky railway shares crashed, bricks and mortar seemed the one sure investment — though that account is argued.
items.ex: Dad says the money in my school savings account is as safe as houses.

items.m: so rare it practically doesn't exist
items.os: Hens have no teeth at all; American frontier humor from the 1800s.
items.ex: Snow days in April are as scarce as hen's teeth.

items.m: very intelligent and alert
items.os: American, early 1900s, upgrading the older 'sharp as a needle' — a tack's fine point plus the slang 'sharp' for clever.
items.ex: Grandma is as sharp as a tack and beats us all at word games.

items.p: as shiny as a new pin
items.m: gleaming and spotless
items.os: Straight from the pin-maker, a pin shone bright before use dulled it — cousin to 'neat as a new pin.'
items.ex: He polished his bike until it was as shiny as a new pin.

items.m: bitterly disappointed
items.os: British football slang of the 1970s; why a parrot is anyone's guess — newspaper parrot-fever scares are one theory.
items.ex: He was as sick as a parrot when his team lost on the very last kick.

items.m: utterly quiet
items.os: A poets' image — the night sky blazes yet makes no sound; the carol 'O Little Town of Bethlehem' has 'the silent stars go by.'
items.ex: The library reading room was as silent as the stars during exams.

items.m: extremely slow
items.os: American: cold molasses barely pours, hence the full jibe 'slow as molasses in January.'
items.ex: The lunch line moves as slow as molasses on pizza day.

items.m: moving very slowly
items.os: The snail, gliding along on one foot at a few yards an hour, has meant slowness since ancient fables.
items.ex: Our old computer loads as slow as a snail.

items.m: perfectly smooth and even
items.os: Polished glass has no grain at all; sailors long used it for a windless sea.
items.ex: The frozen pond was as smooth as glass for skating.

items.m: very quiet or very gentle
items.os: A whisper is the softest the human voice goes; a storyteller's staple for faint sounds and light touches.
items.ex: Her footsteps were as soft as a whisper during the baby's nap.

items.m: extremely soft to the touch
items.os: Down is the fluffy under-feather of geese and ducks, prized for pillows for centuries.
items.ex: The new kitten's fur is as soft as down.

items.m: in perfect health or condition
items.os: A pun from the 1500s: 'sound' means healthy, and only an uncracked bell rings true.
items.ex: The vet said our dog's heart is as sound as a bell.

items.m: sharp-tasting, or sour-tempered
items.os: Vinegar is wine gone sharp; faces and moods have been measured against it since the Middle Ages.
items.ex: The lemonade came out as sour as vinegar, so we stirred in honey.

items.m: completely stable and reliable
items.os: Rock neither trembles nor drifts; the comparison is ancient and everywhere.
items.ex: Her hands were as steady as a rock during the egg-and-spoon race.

items.m: clinging to everything it touches
items.os: Glue's whole job is to grip; children's rhymes made the comparison stock, alongside 'stick to you like glue.'
items.ex: The melted marshmallow left my fingers as sticky as glue.

items.m: not moving at all
items.os: Statues hold one pose forever — the standard behind every freeze game.
items.ex: Stay as still as a statue while the nurse checks your eyes.

items.m: physically very strong
items.os: The bear is the strongest beast of northern forests, a strongman's badge since ancient times.
items.ex: Our moving-day helper is as strong as a bear.

items.m: strong and dependable
items.os: The oak, sacred to Zeus and Thor, is Europe's emblem tree of toughness.
items.ex: Grandpa is eighty and still as sturdy as an oak.

items.p: as sure as eggs is eggs
items.m: absolutely certain
items.os: English, 1600s; possibly a joke on the logician's 'as sure as x is x' — the bad grammar is part of the charm, and Dickens used it.
items.ex: As sure as eggs is eggs, Dad will cry at the graduation.

items.m: very tall
items.os: The giraffe is the tallest animal on Earth, browsing leaves eighteen feet up; a modern classroom favorite.
items.ex: By fifth grade he'd shot up as tall as a giraffe next to his cousins.

items.p: as tender as a mother's heart
items.m: deeply loving and gentle
items.os: A stock simile of Victorian storybooks, where a mother's heart was the softest thing imaginable.
items.ex: The school nurse treats every scraped knee with care as tender as a mother's heart.

items.m: extremely close friends who share everything
items.os: 'Thick' meant close-knit in the 1800s, and partners in crime must trust each other completely; English writers echoed an older French saying.
items.ex: My cousin and I are as thick as thieves every summer.

items.m: stretched or sealed completely tight
items.os: A drumhead must be stretched taut to make any sound at all.
items.ex: We rolled the sleeping bag and packed it as tight as a drum.

items.m: very shy and easily frightened
items.os: Rabbits bolt for the burrow at the first snapped twig.
items.ex: She was as timid as a rabbit in September but ran the class play by June.

items.m: very tough and hard-wearing
items.os: Tanned hide outlasts cloth many times over; boots and saddles made the comparison inevitable.
items.ex: Great-grandma is ninety-two and as tough as leather.

items.m: cozily warm
items.os: English since the 1400s ('warm as any toast') — bread hot from the fire warmed cold hands and cold mornings.
items.ex: Under two quilts I was as warm as toast during the storm.

items.m: having very little strength
items.os: Newborn kittens can barely lift their own heads.
items.ex: The flu left me as weak as a kitten for a week.

items.m: pale with fear or shock
items.os: Bedsheets were bleached and lye-washed to pure white; a frightened face drains to match.
items.ex: He turned as white as a sheet when the roller coaster crested the hill.

items.m: completely untamed and free
items.os: Wind answers to no fence or rein; balladeers have loved the comparison for centuries.
items.ex: The rescue pony at camp was as wild as the wind until the counselors earned its trust.

items.m: covered in wrinkles
