items.os: A prune is a plum dried until its skin puckers into folds — just like fingers after a long bath.
items.ex: After an hour in the pool my toes were as wrinkled as a prune.

items.m: to cry loudly and without holding back
items.os: Babies cry with their whole bodies; the jab at weeping grown-ups is as old as English itself.
items.ex: Dad cried like a baby at the end of the movie about the dog.

items.m: to fall ill or give up in large numbers
items.os: One cold snap fells whole swarms of flies at once; English, in common use by the 1900s.
items.ex: During flu week, kids were dropping like flies in every classroom.

items.m: to fight with great courage
items.os: The lion has been the courage-animal of epics and coats of arms since ancient times.
items.ex: She fought like a lion through the tiebreaker rounds.

items.p: float like a butterfly, sting like a bee
items.m: move lightly, then strike fast and hard
items.os: Boxer Muhammad Ali's motto, coined with his cornerman Drew Bundini Brown in the 1960s: dance out of reach, then hit in a flash.
items.ex: Our chess captain tells us to play like Ali: float like a butterfly, sting like a bee.

items.m: to move in a smooth, unbroken stream
items.os: Rivers run on without pause or seam; the image is as old as poetry itself.
items.ex: Once she relaxed, her speech flowed like a river.

items.m: to move with power and freedom
items.os: The eagle owns the high air; the Bible's Isaiah promises the faithful will 'mount up with wings as eagles.'
items.ex: Off the last ramp, her sled seemed to fly like an eagle.

items.m: to copy others without thinking for yourself
items.os: Sheep trail the flock wherever it drifts, no questions asked; shepherd cultures coined the jibe long ago.
items.ex: Don't follow like sheep — check the answer yourself before you copy it down.

items.m: to grow very fast
items.os: Weeds shoot up overnight with no care at all; fond talk for fast-sprouting kids.
items.ex: Aunt Pia gasped that I'd grown like a weed since spring.

items.m: to laugh loudly and wildly
items.os: The spotted hyena's whooping call sounds uncannily like shrieking laughter.
items.ex: The back row laughed like hyenas at the substitute's puns.

items.m: to live in great comfort and luxury
items.os: Kings ate first and best; envy of palace plenty is ancient.
items.ex: With leftover birthday cake for breakfast, I lived like a king.

items.m: to soften or give way instantly
items.os: Butter collapses the moment it touches a hot pan.
items.ex: His grumpy act melts like butter when the puppy trots in.

items.m: to move painfully slowly
items.os: Cold molasses barely pours — the American cousin of 'slow as molasses in January.'
items.ex: The class moves like molasses when it's time to line up for math.

items.m: to run smoothly and contentedly
items.os: A happy cat's purr is the sound of all being well; mechanics borrowed it for sweet-running engines.
items.ex: After Dad's tune-up, the old car purrs like a kitten.

items.m: to make a loud, fearsome sound
items.os: A lion's roar carries five miles across the savanna.
items.ex: The furnace roars like a lion when it first kicks on.

items.m: to tremble with fear or cold
items.os: Leaves quiver at the faintest breeze; Chaucer already had characters quaking 'like an aspen leaf.'
items.ex: I shook like a leaf before my first solo, then nailed it.

items.m: to sparkle brilliantly or perform outstandingly
items.os: A cut diamond throws light from every facet — the jeweler's benchmark for brilliance.
items.ex: Polish your speech until it shines like a diamond.

items.m: to drop straight down, or to fail completely
items.os: A stone goes down without a wobble — the swimmer's exact opposite.
items.ex: My popsicle-stick raft sank like a stone in the class regatta.

items.m: to rise high with grace and power
items.os: Eagles climb by riding warm air, barely beating a wing — the classic image of effortless triumph.
items.ex: Her practice-test scores soared like an eagle after a month of flashcards.

items.m: to glitter with lively brightness
items.os: Champagne's rising bubbles catch the light; writers lend that fizz to eyes and personalities.
items.ex: The frost on the field sparkled like champagne in the morning sun.

items.m: to stand completely motionless
items.os: Statues hold a single pose for centuries; drill fields and freeze tag both borrow it.
items.ex: For the class wax-museum project, I stood like a statue for ten whole minutes.

items.p: stick out like a sore thumb
items.m: to be painfully obvious and out of place
items.os: A bandaged, throbbing thumb sticks up stiffly and can't be hidden; American, early 1900s.
items.ex: In my neon costume I stuck out like a sore thumb at the dress rehearsal.

items.m: to repeat words without understanding them
items.os: Parrots mimic human speech perfectly while grasping none of it.
items.ex: Don't just talk like a parrot — explain the rule in your own words.

items.m: to disappear completely and quickly
items.os: Smoke thins into nothing before your eyes; the Psalms already used it for things that pass away.
items.ex: My free weekend vanished like smoke when the science fair got moved up.

items.m: to shriek loudly and eerily
items.os: In Irish legend the banshee's wail outside a house foretells a death in the family.
items.ex: The wind wailed like a banshee around our cabin all night.

items.m: to work extremely hard
items.os: Sheepdogs and sled dogs labor dawn to dusk for their keepers; the Beatles' 'A Hard Day's Night' (1964) sealed it in pop memory.
items.ex: Mom worked like a dog all weekend on the bake sale.

items.m: to shine with tiny points of wet light
items.os: Morning dew catches the first sun in a thousand beads — a poets' standby.
items.ex: Her sequined costume glistened like dew under the stage lights.

items.m: to be visible or noticeable from far away
items.os: Beacon fires and lighthouses exist for one purpose: to be seen at a distance.
items.ex: Her yellow raincoat stood out like a beacon in the crowded pickup line.

items.m: to rush forward with unstoppable force
items.os: A provoked bull lowers its head and runs straight through whatever stands in front of it.
items.ex: He charges like a bull for the door the second the bell rings.

items.m: to climb steep places with easy skill
items.os: Mountain goats trot up near-vertical cliffs on ledges the width of a coin.
items.ex: My little brother climbs like a mountain goat on the playground boulders.

items.m: to do things joyfully without fearing others' judgment
items.os: From the country song 'Come from the Heart' (1987) by Susanna Clark and Richard Leigh — often misattributed to Mark Twain.
items.ex: At the family reunion, Grandma danced like nobody's watching, and soon everyone joined her.

items.m: to give off a soft, steady, warm light
items.os: Embers are the coals that keep glowing long after the flames die down.
items.ex: Down the dark hallway, the night-light glowed like embers.

items.m: to boom and roll on and on
items.os: Thunder doesn't just clap — it rolls, bouncing off hills and clouds.
items.ex: The slammed locker echoed like thunder down the empty hallway.

items.m: to grow dimmer and less clear over time
items.os: Early photographs yellowed and paled in sunlight, so writers use them for dimming memories.
items.ex: Without practice, my summer vocabulary faded like an old photograph.

items.m: to collapse one after another in a chain
items.os: Stand dominoes in a row and one tap topples them all; the image even named Cold War 'domino theory' in 1954.
items.ex: Once one excuse failed, the rest fell like dominoes.

items.m: to shine with a warm golden light
items.os: Ships' fittings and doorknockers were rubbed daily until the brass gave back a mirror shine.
items.ex: After the rain, the autumn leaves gleamed like polished brass.

items.m: to hang in one spot in mid-air
items.os: Hummingbirds beat their wings about fifty times a second to stand still in the air.
items.ex: The drone hovered like a hummingbird over the soccer field.

items.m: to move in disciplined, orderly lines
items.os: Drilled troops step in time and in line — the picture behind every orderly column, down to ants on a sidewalk.
items.ex: The kindergartners marched like soldiers to the fire-drill line.

items.m: to fly apart in every direction
items.os: An autumn gust flings dry leaves everywhere; Homer was already comparing crowds to wind-blown leaves.
items.ex: When the sprinklers surprised us, the picnic scattered like leaves.

items.m: to flicker with small, bright points of light
items.os: Starlight bends in our moving air, so stars seem to wink — nursery-famous since 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star' (1806).
items.ex: The fairground lights twinkled like stars across the valley.

items.m: extremely hard or unyielding
items.os: Diamond is the hardest natural material on Earth — it scratches everything and nothing scratches it.
items.ex: The week-old bagel in my lunchbox was as hard as a diamond.

items.m: refusing to change your mind or budge
items.os: Goats plant their hooves and will not be dragged; speakers from Europe to South Asia reach for the same animal.
items.ex: My little sister is as stubborn as a goat about wearing her lucky socks.

items.m: calmly enduring long, slow work
items.os: Plow oxen pull steadily all day without complaint; in the Chinese zodiac the Ox stands for patient endurance.
items.ex: She's as patient as an ox, quizzing me on the same word list every night.

items.m: thoroughly typical of American life and values
items.os: American, early 1900s; apple pie was already the symbol of home cooking in the United States.
items.ex: Hot dogs at the school picnic are as American as apple pie.

items.m: completely bald
items.os: The coot, a water bird, has a bare white patch on its forehead; recorded since the 1400s.
items.ex: Grandpa jokes he's as bald as a coot in every family photo.

items.m: very large
items.os: Plain hyperbole — a house is the biggest thing on an ordinary street; common since the 1800s.
items.ex: The prize pumpkin at the county fair was as big as a house.

items.m: enormous
items.os: The elephant is the largest land animal, the classic classroom yardstick for hugeness.
items.ex: My backpack feels as big as an elephant on library day.

items.m: completely black; totally dark
items.os: Pitch is the tar sailors used to waterproof ships — so black it seems to swallow light; 'pitch-black' comes from it.
items.ex: When the power went out, the basement was as black as pitch.

items.m: glossy deep black, especially hair
items.os: From the Bible's Song of Solomon, where the beloved's hair is 'black as a raven'.
items.ex: The heroine in her book had hair as black as a raven.

items.m: seeing very poorly
items.os: Moles live underground and their tiny eyes see almost nothing; the simile is centuries old.
items.ex: Without his glasses, Dad is as blind as a mole.

items.m: bright, clear blue
items.os: The cloudless daytime sky is the oldest measure of blue there is.
items.ex: She colored the whale's pool as blue as the sky.

items.m: deeply tanned or brown all over
items.os: Chaucer used it in the Canterbury Tales (1300s), though no one is sure which brown berries he meant.
items.ex: After a summer of swim lessons she came home as brown as a berry.

items.p: as clean as a hound's tooth
items.m: perfectly clean; completely honest
items.os: American, 1800s — dogs' teeth gleam white; President Eisenhower demanded a campaign 'clean as a hound's tooth'.
items.ex: Mom wants the kitchen as clean as a hound's tooth before Grandma visits.

items.m: perfectly clear and easy to hear or understand
items.os: Before loudspeakers, a well-cast bell was the clearest sound a town ever heard.
items.ex: The announcer's voice came through the gym as clear as a bell.

items.m: very cold; without warmth or feeling
items.os: Shakespeare used it in Henry V, where Falstaff's feet are found 'cold as any stone'.
items.ex: By the end of the snowball fight my fingers were as cold as stone.

items.p: as comfortable as an old shoe
items.m: completely relaxed, familiar, and easy
items.os: American, 1800s; a shoe worn soft fits better than any new one ever will.
items.ex: Back at Grandma's kitchen table, everything felt as comfortable as an old shoe.

items.p: as constant as the northern star
items.m: absolutely steady and unchanging
items.os: In Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, Caesar boasts he is 'constant as the northern star' — the one star that never moves.
items.ex: Her Saturday spelling practice is as constant as the northern star.

items.m: wildly silly or foolish
items.os: The loon's wailing, laughing night call sounds unhinged — though 'loon' may also echo the old word 'lunatic', so the origin is tangled.
items.ex: My little brother acts as crazy as a loon after two cupcakes.

items.m: very grumpy or annoyed
items.os: A pun from the 1800s: two sticks laid over each other are literally 'crossed'.
items.ex: Dad was as cross as two sticks when we missed the bus.

items.m: very silly, in a harmless way
items.os: Northern English; why a brush should be daft is anyone's guess — the fun is in the nonsense.
items.ex: Our dog is as daft as a brush — he chases his own tail for fun.

items.m: refusing to hear anything at all
items.os: From Psalm 58, where the adder 'stoppeth her ear' against the snake-charmer's music.
items.ex: When cartoons are on, my brother is as deaf as an adder to chore reminders.

items.p: as different as night and day
items.m: completely unlike each other
items.os: Night and day are nature's oldest opposites; the pairing has been proverbial for centuries.
items.ex: The twins look alike but their hobbies are as different as night and day.

items.m: extremely dry; deadly boring
items.os: An old simile for anything powder-dry; Sir Walter Scott even invented a boring scholar named 'Dr Dryasdust'.
items.ex: She said the history chapter was as dry as dust until the pirate part.

items.m: extremely easy
items.os: The alphabet is the first thing schoolchildren master, so it stands for the simplest possible task.
items.ex: Once you learn the rule, spelling 'receive' is as easy as ABC.

items.p: as easy as falling off a log
items.m: requiring no skill or effort at all
items.os: American, 1800s; staying balanced on a floating log is hard — falling off takes no effort at all.
items.ex: For her, the practice round was as easy as falling off a log.

items.m: extremely fast
items.os: The cheetah, the fastest land animal, sprints near seventy miles an hour; a modern classroom favorite.
items.ex: He ran the relay leg as fast as a cheetah.

items.p: as fit as a butcher's dog
items.m: in excellent physical condition
items.os: Northern English; the butcher's dog lives beside the best scraps in town and thrives on them.
items.ex: After a season of soccer practice, Uncle Raj is as fit as a butcher's dog.

items.m: very swift-footed
items.os: Deer have stood for speed since ancient poetry; the old word 'fleet' survives almost nowhere else.
items.ex: The story's messenger was as fleet as a deer over the hills.

items.m: bright, clean, and full of energy
items.os: Victorian English; nothing looks newer than a just-painted front door.
items.ex: After her nap she was as fresh as paint and ready to study.

items.p: as fussy as a hen with one chick
items.m: overly worried about every small thing
items.os: A hen with a single chick guards it constantly; recorded in Brewer's Dictionary of Phrase and Fable.
items.ex: Mom gets as fussy as a hen with one chick before the spelling bee.

items.m: moving with light, elegant ease
items.os: The gazelle's leaping run made it the poets' image of grace, from the Song of Solomon onward.
items.ex: She crossed the stage to the microphone as graceful as a gazelle.

items.m: extremely happy
items.os: Possibly from Larry Foley, an 1800s Australian boxer who retired rich and cheerful — but no one is certain.
items.ex: He was as happy as Larry when school closed for the snow day.

items.p: as happy as a pig in mud
items.m: blissfully content
items.os: Pigs wallow in mud to cool off, and they genuinely seem to love it.
items.ex: Give my sister a library card and she's as happy as a pig in mud.

items.m: perfectly cheerful
items.os: Sandboys sold sand door to door in the early 1800s and were proverbially jolly; Dickens named an inn 'The Jolly Sandboys'.
items.ex: Grandpa was as happy as a sandboy pottering in his garden all Saturday.

items.p: as honest as the day is long
items.m: completely trustworthy
items.os: American, 1800s; a summer day feels endless, and honesty should stretch just as far.
items.ex: You can leave your lunch money with Priya — she's as honest as the day is long.

items.m: extremely hot
items.os: The furnace has measured fierce heat since the Bible's story of the fiery furnace.
items.ex: The car felt as hot as a furnace after sitting in the sun all day.

items.m: extremely hungry
items.os: A bear waking from winter hibernation eats everything in sight.
items.ex: After swim practice I'm always as hungry as a bear.

items.m: almost weightless; carefree
items.os: Shakespeare wrote in Othello that 'trifles light as air' can convince a jealous mind.
items.ex: With homework finished early, she felt as light as air all evening.

items.p: as limp as a rag doll
items.m: completely floppy and without strength
items.os: A rag doll is stuffed cloth with no bones — it flops however it is held.
items.ex: The toddler fell asleep as limp as a rag doll in Dad's arms.

items.m: very long, especially of a list
items.os: British; a list written out on paper really can run the length of an arm.
items.ex: Mom's back-to-school shopping list was as long as your arm.

items.m: absolutely furious
items.os: American; disturb a hornet and it attacks anything that moves.
items.ex: Coach was as mad as a hornet when we left the equipment in the rain.

items.m: extremely old
items.os: Methuselah lived 969 years in the Book of Genesis, the longest life in the Bible.
items.ex: The oak by the school gate looks as old as Methuselah.

items.m: existing longer than anyone can imagine
items.os: An old poetic superlative — nothing can be older than time itself.
items.ex: Arguing over the front seat is a sibling quarrel as old as time.

items.m: totally obvious
items.os: Originally 'plain as a packstaff' — the plain, worn pole a peddler carried; recorded since the 1500s.
items.ex: The answer was as plain as a pikestaff once she reread the question.

items.p: as plain as the nose on your face
items.m: impossible to miss
items.os: English, 1600s; nothing is more visible — except to its owner, which is the joke.
items.ex: The spelling mistake was as plain as the nose on your face.

items.m: pleasantly round and well-fed
items.os: Partridges fatten in autumn and were prized table birds; listed in Brewer's Dictionary of Phrase and Fable.
items.ex: By Thanksgiving the class hamster was as plump as a partridge.

items.m: arrogantly proud
items.os: Medieval preachers made Lucifer, the angel who fell through pride, the very measure of it.
items.ex: The story's villain was as proud as Lucifer and never said sorry.

items.m: almost instantaneous
items.os: A wink is one of the fastest things a body does; American, 1800s.
items.ex: She solved the anagram as quick as a wink.

items.m: bright red, especially from sunburn
items.os: Lobsters turn from dark blue-green to scarlet only when they are cooked.
items.ex: Dad forgot his sunscreen and came home as red as a lobster.

items.m: bright red, especially from blushing
items.os: The ripe tomato is the kitchen's reddest sight; a staple of classroom simile lists.
items.ex: He went as red as a tomato when the teacher read his poem aloud.

items.m: harsh and scratchy to the touch
items.os: Sandpaper is glued grit made for scraping wood smooth — the everyday opposite of smoothness.
items.ex: The cat's tongue felt as rough as sandpaper on my hand.

items.p: as safe as the Bank of England
items.m: absolutely secure
items.os: The Bank of England, founded in 1694, never failed — its vaults became a national byword for safety.
items.ex: Your secret is as safe as the Bank of England with me.

items.m: harmlessly foolish
items.os: Geese honk and flap at everything, so 'silly goose' has been an affectionate scold for centuries.
items.ex: You forgot your own backpack? You're as silly as a goose!

items.m: extremely slow
items.os: Aesop's tortoise raced the hare over 2,500 years ago and made slowness famous.
items.ex: The lunch line moved as slow as a tortoise today.

items.m: very quick-witted
items.os: American, 1800s — a whip cracks fast and sharp, like a quick mind.
items.ex: The new girl in class is as smart as a whip at word puzzles.

items.p: as smooth as a baby's bottom
items.m: perfectly smooth
items.os: New skin is the smoothest surface most people ever touch; a favorite of joking barbers.
items.ex: After sanding, the birdhouse roof was as smooth as a baby's bottom.

items.m: very serious and solemn
items.os: English, 1600s; judges must stay grave and clear-headed on the bench.
items.ex: She stayed as sober as a judge while everyone else giggled.

items.m: luxuriously soft
items.os: Velvet's dense pile made it the royal measure of softness since the Middle Ages.
items.ex: The kitten's ears are as soft as velvet.

items.m: very sour; sulky
items.os: The lemon is the kitchen's sourest fruit, so it also describes sour faces.
items.ex: He looked as sour as a lemon when his team lost the quiz.

items.m: completely rigid
items.os: A sawn plank is the everyday standard of stiffness.
items.ex: My legs were as stiff as a board after the long car ride.

items.m: perfectly straight; totally honest
items.os: Dice must be cut perfectly square to roll fair — a crooked die means a cheat.
items.ex: Draw the margin as straight as a die before you start.

items.m: rigidly upright in posture
items.os: The ramrod, the steel rod that packed a musket, stood for soldierly straightness.
items.ex: Grandpa still sits as straight as a ramrod at the dinner table.

items.m: very strong
items.os: Horses pulled the ploughs and wagons that built the world before engines.
items.ex: Dad carried all four grocery bags at once — he's as strong as a horse.

items.m: superhumanly strong
items.os: Hercules, the Greek hero, completed twelve impossible labors by sheer strength.
items.ex: You'd need to be as strong as Hercules to open that pickle jar.

items.m: mightily strong
items.os: In the Book of Judges, Samson's great strength lived in his uncut hair.
items.ex: The movers were as strong as Samson, hauling the piano upstairs.

items.p: as sure as night follows day
items.m: absolutely certain
items.os: The one sequence that has never failed; Shakespeare's Polonius says 'it must follow, as the night the day'.
items.ex: As sure as night follows day, Dad will ask about homework at dinner.

items.p: as sure as death and taxes
items.m: absolutely inevitable
items.os: Daniel Defoe wrote it in 1726; Benjamin Franklin's 1789 letter made it famous.
items.ex: As sure as death and taxes, there will be a quiz on Friday.

items.m: very sweet; charmingly nice
items.os: Sugar replaced honey as the everyday sweetener, and the simile followed it into the kitchen.
items.ex: The new babysitter is as sweet as sugar with the twins.

items.m: extremely fast and direct
items.os: Before bullets, the loosed arrow was the fastest thing most people ever saw.
items.ex: The paper airplane flew as swift as an arrow across the classroom.

items.m: so thick you cannot see through it, of fog
items.os: Victorian London's yellow-green smogs were nicknamed 'pea-soupers'.
items.ex: The morning fog was as thick as pea soup, so the bus crawled to school.

items.m: perfectly loyal and dependable
items.os: Chaucer used it in the 1300s; a good steel blade never fails its owner.
items.ex: Through every playground quarrel, Maya stayed as true as steel to her friend.

items.p: as useful as a chocolate teapot
items.m: completely useless
items.os: A British 1900s joke — hot tea would melt a chocolate teapot instantly.
items.ex: A broken umbrella is as useful as a chocolate teapot in this rain.

items.m: having no strength or willpower
items.os: From the Bible's Book of Ezekiel: 'all knees shall be weak as water'.
items.ex: After the flu, my arms felt as weak as water.

items.p: as welcome as flowers in May
items.m: warmly welcome and long awaited
items.os: An old English saying — after a hard winter, nothing is more wanted than May flowers.
items.ex: Grandma's surprise visit was as welcome as flowers in May.

items.m: exceptionally wise and fair
items.os: King Solomon in the Bible settled a dispute over a baby with one brilliant test.
items.ex: The principal was as wise as Solomon about the playground dispute.

items.m: shrewd and careful
items.os: From Jesus's advice in Matthew: 'be ye wise as serpents, and harmless as doves'.
items.ex: Be as wise as a serpent when a deal online sounds too good.

items.m: unyieldingly hard
items.os: Iron was the hardest thing in the pre-steel world; the carol 'In the Bleak Midwinter' has earth 'hard as iron'.
items.ex: The January playground dirt was as hard as iron under our cleats.

items.m: eyes opened huge with surprise or fear
items.os: From folktales — Andersen's 'The Tinderbox' has magic dogs with eyes as big as saucers.
items.ex: Her eyes went as big as saucers when the magician's dove appeared.

items.p: as crooked as a dog's hind leg
items.m: thoroughly dishonest
items.os: American; a dog's back leg zigzags in three directions at once.
items.ex: The story's sheriff turned out to be as crooked as a dog's hind leg.

items.m: sleekly agile
items.os: The big cats' rippling walk made 'panther' the poets' word for supple movement.
items.ex: The gymnast moved across the beam as lithe as a panther.

items.m: not subtle at all; comically obvious
items.os: A 20th-century ironic simile — sledgehammers do nothing quietly.
items.ex: His hint about wanting a bike for his birthday was as subtle as a sledgehammer.

items.p: as mad as a cut snake
items.m: furious; wildly crazy
items.os: Australian; a snake struck by a spade thrashes wildly in every direction.
items.ex: My cousin went as mad as a cut snake when the printer ate his project.

items.p: as broad as a barn door
items.m: very wide
items.os: Barn doors are built wide enough for loaded hay wagons; the simile is in Brewer's.
items.ex: The goalkeeper's shoulders looked as broad as a barn door.

items.m: comfortably warm
items.os: An old proverb — wool warms the sheep first and the shepherd after.
items.ex: Grandma's hand-knitted mittens keep me as warm as wool at the bus stop.

items.m: perfectly tidy
items.os: English, 1600s, perhaps from 'nine-pins' set in exact rows — the true origin is lost.
items.ex: She keeps her pencil case as neat as ninepence.

items.m: utterly poor
items.os: Coined by humorist T.C. Haliburton (1836): Job's turkey was so poor it had to lean against the fence to gobble.
items.ex: In the play, the miller starts out as poor as Job's turkey.

items.m: intensely bitter
items.os: Wormwood is a famously bitter herb; the Book of Proverbs uses it for bitterness itself.
items.ex: The medicine tasted as bitter as wormwood, so Mom brought juice.

items.m: very tall
items.os: For centuries the church steeple was the tallest thing on any skyline; listed in Brewer's.
items.ex: To a first grader, the sixth graders look as tall as a steeple.

items.m: to stay away from completely
items.os: Ancient advice — St Jerome joked in the 300s about avoiding certain company 'like the plague'.
items.ex: He avoids the squeaky cafeteria chair like the plague.

items.m: to talk quickly and endlessly
items.os: Magpies keep up a loud rattling chatter; the comparison is centuries old.
items.ex: The carpool chatters like a magpie all the way to school.

items.p: collapse like a house of cards
items.m: to fall apart suddenly and completely
items.os: A tower of playing cards falls at a single touch; writers have used the image since the 1600s.
items.ex: Without the star speller, the team's confidence collapsed like a house of cards.

items.m: to feel absolutely wonderful
items.os: American, 1920s, when a million dollars was the biggest sum anyone could imagine.
items.ex: In her new first-day outfit she felt like a million dollars.

items.p: go down like a lead balloon
items.m: to fail completely with an audience
items.os: A mid-1900s joke — a balloon made of lead could never rise; it even inspired the band name Led Zeppelin.
items.ex: Dad's broccoli joke went down like a lead balloon at dinner.

items.m: to smile hugely and mysteriously
items.os: Recorded in the 1780s, well before Alice in Wonderland — why Cheshire cats grin was never explained; Lewis Carroll just made it immortal.
items.ex: She grinned like a Cheshire cat when she saw her test score.

items.p: hit like a ton of bricks
items.m: to strike or shock with overwhelming force
items.os: American, early 1900s, from a builder's full load of bricks falling at once.
items.ex: The news that our teacher was moving hit the class like a ton of bricks.

items.p: know something like the back of your hand
items.m: to know completely and effortlessly
items.os: The back of your own hand is always in view — nothing is more familiar.
items.ex: She knows the walk to school like the back of her hand.

items.p: turn up like a bad penny
items.m: to keep reappearing where unwanted
items.os: From the proverb 'a bad penny always turns up' — counterfeit coins kept coming back in change.
items.ex: That lost sock turns up like a bad penny in every laundry basket but ours.

items.p: like a breath of fresh air
items.m: refreshingly new and welcome
items.os: From the relief of stepping outside after a stuffy room; standard praise since the 1800s.
items.ex: The substitute's game-based review was like a breath of fresh air.

items.p: sit like a bump on a log
items.m: to sit still and do nothing
items.os: American, 1800s — a bump on a log is the least useful part of a useless seat.
items.ex: Don't sit like a bump on a log — come help set the table!

items.p: like a dog with a bone
items.m: refusing to let a matter drop
items.os: A dog guards and gnaws its bone for hours; the image is proverbial.
items.ex: She was like a dog with a bone about finding the library's missing atlas.

items.p: like a dog with two tails
items.m: visibly delighted
items.os: British; if one wagging tail means joy, two must mean twice as much.
items.ex: He was like a dog with two tails when his project won the ribbon.

items.p: take to something like a duck to water
items.m: to learn something new easily and happily
items.os: Ducklings swim within hours of hatching — no lessons needed.
items.ex: My little sister took to chess like a duck to water.

items.p: like a kid in a candy store
items.m: overwhelmed with excited delight
items.os: American, early 1900s — endless sweets, impossible choices, pure joy.
items.ex: At the book fair she was like a kid in a candy store.

items.p: like a hot knife through butter
items.m: cutting through with no resistance at all
items.os: A heated blade melts its own path through cold butter.
items.ex: The new snowplow went through the drifts like a hot knife through butter.

items.p: like a lamb to the slaughter
items.m: going along unaware of coming trouble
items.os: From Isaiah in the Bible — a lamb goes quietly, not knowing what waits.
items.ex: He walked into the surprise quiz like a lamb to the slaughter.

items.m: helpless, forlorn, and following someone around
items.os: A puppy separated from its owner trails hopefully after anyone kind.
items.ex: The new student followed our class monitor around like a lost puppy.

items.p: rise like a phoenix from the ashes
items.m: to make a triumphant comeback after ruin
items.os: The phoenix of Egyptian and Greek legend burns to ash and is reborn from it.
items.ex: After losing round one, she rose like a phoenix from the ashes to win the bee.

items.m: someone who cheers everyone up
items.os: A sunbeam breaking into a dark room; a Victorian endearment ever since.
items.ex: The kindergarten teacher calls her helper a ray of sunshine.

items.p: like a red rag to a bull
items.m: certain to provoke instant fury
items.os: From bullfighting — but bulls are colorblind to red; the waving movement enrages them, so the famous reason is a myth.
items.ex: Mentioning the unfinished chores is like a red rag to a bull with Dad.

items.m: leaving instantly at top speed
items.os: From the speed of a fired bullet; recorded since the 1800s.
items.ex: When the recess bell rang, he was off like a shot.

items.p: like a thief in the night
items.m: arriving silently and without warning
items.os: From the New Testament — 'the day of the Lord so cometh as a thief in the night'.
items.ex: The first frost came like a thief in the night and took Mom's tomatoes.

items.m: to work perfectly without friction
items.os: Industrial-age praise — freshly oiled gears run silent and smooth.
items.ex: By June, our morning routine runs like a well-oiled machine.

items.p: like getting blood from a stone
items.m: almost impossible to obtain
items.os: From the old proverb 'you cannot get blood out of a stone', recorded since the 1600s.
items.ex: Getting my brother to share his fries is like getting blood from a stone.

items.m: crowded and busy with constant comings and goings
items.os: New York's Grand Central is one of the world's busiest rail terminals.
items.ex: Our kitchen is like Grand Central Station on school mornings.

items.m: nearly impossible to organize
items.os: American, late 1900s — cats go wherever they please; a Super Bowl ad about cat-herding cowboys sealed the phrase.
items.ex: Lining up first graders for the fire drill is like herding cats.

items.p: like looking for a needle in a haystack
items.m: a nearly hopeless search
items.os: Thomas More wrote of seeking 'a needle in a meadow' in the 1500s; the haystack version stuck.
items.ex: Finding one red crayon in the class art bin is like looking for a needle in a haystack.

items.m: unexpected help arriving exactly when needed
items.os: In Exodus, bread called manna fell each morning to feed the Israelites in the desert.
items.ex: The rain delay was like manna from heaven for our unfinished homework.

items.p: like nailing jelly to a wall
items.m: impossible to pin down
items.os: Theodore Roosevelt complained a treaty negotiation was like trying to nail currant jelly to a wall.
items.ex: Getting a straight answer about the field-trip date is like nailing jelly to a wall.

items.m: unbearably irritating, especially of sounds
items.os: The screech of fingernails on slate makes almost everyone shudder; a 20th-century classroom simile.
items.ex: My brother's recorder practice is like nails on a chalkboard.

items.m: completely unable to get along
items.os: Oil and water separate again no matter how hard you shake them.
items.ex: Those two teammates mix like oil and water, so Coach separates them.

items.m: silently, sorrowfully patient
items.os: From Twelfth Night — Viola describes hidden love sitting 'like Patience on a monument, smiling at grief'.
items.ex: She waited like Patience on a monument for her turn at the microphone.

items.m: extremely slow and difficult to get someone to do
items.os: From dentistry before anesthesia — nothing came out without a struggle.
items.ex: Getting my brother to practice piano is like pulling teeth.

items.m: easily persuaded to do anything
items.os: Putty is the glazier's soft paste that takes any shape it is pressed into.
items.ex: One puppy-dog look from the baby and Grandpa is like putty in her hands.

items.p: like rats deserting a sinking ship
items.m: abandoning a failing venture fast
items.os: Sailors' lore said rats fled a doomed ship first; Shakespeare mentions it in The Tempest.
items.ex: When cleanup time was announced, kids left the craft table like rats deserting a sinking ship.

items.m: a skill you never forget
items.os: A 20th-century saying — balance, once learned, stays for life: 'you never forget how'.
items.ex: After a year away, her multiplication tables came back like riding a bicycle.

items.p: like talking to a brick wall
items.m: getting no response at all
items.os: A wall hears everything and answers nothing; common since the early 1900s.
items.ex: Reminding him about his lunchbox is like talking to a brick wall.

items.p: like the cat that got the cream
items.m: smugly self-satisfied
items.os: British; cream was the richest treat a farm cat could ever steal.
items.ex: She looked like the cat that got the cream after acing the surprise quiz.

items.m: unbearably boring
items.os: Grass grows too slowly for any eye to see — the perfect image of nothing happening.
items.ex: My sister says golf on TV is like watching grass grow.

items.m: mind-numbingly dull
items.os: A 20th-century twin of 'watching grass grow' — the wall never entertains.
items.ex: He groaned that the awards preamble was like watching paint dry.

items.p: a mind like a steel trap
items.m: a mind that grasps and holds ideas instantly
items.os: American, 1800s — a steel trap snaps shut fast and never lets go.
items.ex: The champion has a mind like a steel trap for word origins.

items.p: read someone like an open book
items.m: to understand someone's thoughts easily
items.os: An open book hides nothing; the image goes back centuries in English writing.
items.ex: Mom reads me like an open book when I skip my chores.

items.m: to sleep deeply and peacefully
items.os: Ironic to new parents, but a baby's untroubled sleep is proverbial.
items.ex: After the championship game, he slept like a baby.

items.m: to spend wastefully and constantly
items.os: Water pours away and is gone — an image used since the 1700s.
items.ex: At the arcade, my cousin spends money like water.

items.m: to sweat heavily
items.os: Oddly, pigs barely sweat — one theory traces it to 'pig iron', which beads with moisture as it cools, but that is unproven.
items.ex: We were sweating like pigs after field day in the sun.

items.m: to work with tireless energy
items.os: In Homer's epics the Trojans fought and toiled without complaint; English adopted them as model workers in the 1800s.
items.ex: She worked like a Trojan on her volcano model all weekend.

items.m: an extremely loud, deep voice
items.os: Foghorns had to out-shout the sea to warn ships lost in fog.
items.ex: Our gym teacher has a voice like a foghorn — you hear it across two fields.

items.m: to sing beautifully
items.os: The nightingale's night song made it the poets' favorite singer for two thousand years.
items.ex: The soloist in the school choir sings like a nightingale.

items.m: to fight until both sides are destroyed
items.os: Irish legend tells of two cats who fought until only their tails were left — but the explaining story was almost certainly invented after the phrase.
items.ex: The two rival teams fought like Kilkenny cats over the tie-breaker.

items.m: to laugh loudly and gurglingly
items.os: British services slang from around World War II — the gurgle of an emptying drain.
items.ex: Grandad laughed like a drain at my knock-knock joke.

items.m: forgetting things almost instantly
items.os: From the belief that goldfish remember only three seconds — a myth; they can actually remember for months.
items.ex: I have a memory like a goldfish for where I left my water bottle.

items.m: moving away extremely fast
items.os: A cat splashed with hot water bolts blindly; recorded in Brewer's.
items.ex: He shot out of the wasp-filled shed like a scalded cat.

items.p: bicker like an old married couple
items.m: to squabble constantly but harmlessly
items.os: Long-married pairs are proverbial for affectionate, endless squabbling.
items.ex: My lab partner and I bicker like an old married couple over who holds the beaker.

items.m: to wait eagerly around someone's trouble or failure
items.os: Vultures wheel overhead when an animal weakens, waiting for their chance.
items.ex: The moment cookies came out, my brothers circled like vultures.

items.m: to cause sharp, sudden pain, of cold or words
items.os: Standard since the 1800s for bitter wind, cold, and cruel remarks.
items.ex: The January wind off the lake cut like a knife through our jackets.

items.m: soaked and bedraggled
items.os: One of English's oldest similes — recorded since the Middle Ages for anyone caught in the rain.
items.ex: She ran in from the storm looking like a drowned rat.

items.p: flat out like a lizard drinking
items.m: extremely busy
items.os: An Australian pun — a drinking lizard lies literally 'flat out', and so does a busy person.
items.ex: Mom's been flat out like a lizard drinking getting the bake sale ready.

items.p: enough is as good as a feast
items.m: having enough is as satisfying as having plenty
items.os: An English proverb recorded since the 1400s.
items.ex: One slice each, kids — enough is as good as a feast.

items.m: children often behave just like their parents
items.os: From the Latin proverb 'qualis pater, talis filius'.
items.ex: They both do the crossword at breakfast — like father, like son.

items.p: March comes in like a lion and goes out like a lamb
items.m: early March is stormy; late March is mild
items.os: An English weather proverb recorded since the 1600s.
items.ex: Our teacher tracks the forecast to test whether March comes in like a lion and goes out like a lamb.

items.p: a miss is as good as a mile
items.m: a narrow failure is still a failure
items.os: English, 1600s; originally 'an inch in a miss is as good as an ell'.
items.ex: She lost by one point, but a miss is as good as a mile.

items.p: more fun than a barrel of monkeys
items.m: extremely fun
items.os: American, 1800s — earlier versions had a cage or wagonload of monkeys.
items.ex: Grandpa says the science museum is more fun than a barrel of monkeys.

items.m: stopping trouble early beats fixing it later
items.os: Traced through Erasmus to medieval medicine.
items.ex: Pack your bag the night before — prevention is better than cure.

items.m: real events can be more surprising than made-up ones
items.os: Lord Byron coined the line in his poem Don Juan (1823).
items.ex: A fish that climbs waterfalls? Truth is stranger than fiction, said our teacher.

items.p: you catch more flies with honey than with vinegar
items.m: gentleness persuades better than harshness
items.os: An old proverb found in Italian and French centuries before English.
items.ex: Ask your sister nicely — you catch more flies with honey than with vinegar.

items.m: bursting with health and energy
items.os: British; fleas leap a hundred times their own height, the picture of lively health.
items.ex: After a week off school, she came back as fit as a flea.

items.m: completely dead or finished
items.os: British, 1700s; mutton is meat — a sheep past all possible recovery.
items.ex: By bedtime my phone battery was as dead as mutton.

items.p: as busy as a one-armed paperhanger
items.m: hopelessly overloaded with tasks
items.os: American, early 1900s; hanging wallpaper needs two hands, so one arm means comic chaos.
items.ex: Running the ticket table alone, Dad was as busy as a one-armed paperhanger.
